- [Garrett Birkhoff. Subdirect unions in universal algebra (1944).](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1944-08235-9)

### Free retracts lift through surjections

**Remember:** Lift the free generators, then restrict along the embedding.

*True by definition.* MSC 08B30 (Injectives, projectives). arXiv math.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An algebra P is a retract of F if homomorphisms i from P to F and r from F to P satisfy ri = id<sub>P</sub>. An algebra is free on S if every assignment of S into a member of the variety extends uniquely to a homomorphism.

**Problem.** In a variety of algebras, every retract of a free algebra lifts maps through surjective homomorphisms.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, precompose the given map with r to obtain a map from the free algebra. Choose a preimage of each generator’s image under the surjection and extend by freeness. Composing this lift with i lifts the original map because ri = id<sub>P</sub>.

**Paper or page:** [Generalization of terms via universal algebra](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18259). It says: “If a class of algebras K contains all its free algebras, an algebra P is projective in K if and only if it is a retract of a free algebra in K.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regular epimorphisms recover algebra surjections

**Remember:** A universal quotient cannot have a proper image.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 08C05 (Categories of algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A regular epimorphism is a homomorphism e with two properties for some parallel homomorphisms u,v. It satisfies eu = ev, and every homomorphism equalizing u,v factors uniquely through e.

**Problem.** In every variety of algebras, a homomorphism is surjective exactly when it is a regular epimorphism.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the map onto the image of e equalizes u,v and thus factors through e. Uniqueness makes the image inclusion composed with that factor the identity, so e is onto. Conversely, a surjection coequalizes the projections from its kernel relation universally because maps constant on its fibers descend uniquely. The ring epimorphism ℤ → ℚ fails this test because its image is proper.

**nLab:** [regular epimorphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/regular+epimorphism), [epimorphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/epimorphism). It says: “the inclusion ℤ → ℚ is an epimorphism of rings, and of commutative rings.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Relative congruences keep quotients torsion-free

**Remember:** Intersect the kernels as usual, but keep the new quotient in the class.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 08C15 (Quasivarieties). arXiv math.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A congruence is an equivalence relation compatible with all operations. A quasivariety is a class of algebras defined by implications from finite lists of equations to single equations. A congruence is relative to the class when its quotient lies in that class.

**Problem.** Relative congruences are closed under intersections. Their least upper bounds may differ from ordinary congruence joins.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the intersection quotient embeds in the product of the individual quotients, so it remains in the quasivariety. In ℤ², quotienting by either subgroup generated by (1,0) or (1,2) gives ℤ. Their sum gives a quotient of order two. Thus their ordinary join fails the relative congruence test for torsion-free abelian groups.

**Wikipedia:** [Quasivariety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasivariety). It says: “K contains a trivial algebra and is closed under isomorphisms, subalgebras, direct products, and ultraproducts.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Clone inclusions detect formula definability

**Remember:** Witnesses combine by the operation that combines the visible entries.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 08A40 (Operations and polynomials in algebraic structures, primal algebras). arXiv math.LO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A primitive positive formula uses atomic relations, equality, conjunction and existential quantifiers, with falsity allowed for the empty relation. An operation preserves a relation if applying it coordinatewise to any matching number of member tuples produces another member. A polymorphism preserves every basic relation.

**Problem.** Take two relational structures on the same finite set. The first defines every relation of the second by primitive positive formulas exactly when its polymorphisms preserve those relations.

**How the definition helps.** Collecting all preserving operations turns comparison of two formula languages into inclusion of two sets of operations (our own explanation). Equality and conjunction preserve compatibility with an operation. For an existential quantifier, apply the operation to the witnesses as well as the visible inputs (our own explanation). The finite preservation theorem supplies the converse.

**Paper or page:** [Mal'cev clones over a three-element set up to minor-equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06918v1). It says: “Then A pp-defines B if and only if Pol(A) ⊆ Pol(B).”

**Sources:**

- [David Geiger, Closed systems of functions and predicates](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1968.27.95)

### Alternating polymorphisms characterize affine integer programming

**Remember:** Permute within each parity and cancel an equal final pair.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 08A70 (Applications of universal algebra in computer science), 08A40, 68Q25. arXiv cs.CC, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An L-input polymorphism from H to H̃ is a homomorphism from Hᴸ to H̃. For odd L ≥ 3 it is alternating if it satisfies two laws on all inputs. It permits all permutations within each parity of positions, and replacing equal final inputs by any other equal pair leaves its value unchanged.

**Problem.** Fix a finite promise template (H,H̃). The affine integer programming relaxation solves PCSP(H,H̃) exactly when alternating polymorphisms exist for every odd arity L ≥ 3.

**How the definition helps.** Alternation captures the symmetries and cancellation of an alternating sum of integer weights (our own explanation). The affine integer programming characterization of Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal turns correctness into existence of these operations at every odd arity.

**Paper or page:** [Approximate Graph Colouring and Crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.08293). It says: “AIP solves PCSP(H, H̃) if and only if there exist L-ary alternating polymorphisms from H to H̃ for any odd L ≥ 3.”

**Sources:**

- [Lorenzo Ciardo, Stanislav Živný, Approximate Graph Colouring and Crystals, arXiv:2210.08293 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.08293)
- [Libor Barto, Jakub Bulín, Andrei Krokhin, Jakub Opršal, Algebraic Approach to Promise Constraint Satisfaction, Journal of the ACM (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3457606)

### Cyclic polymorphisms decide the CSP dichotomy

**Remember:** Rotate every argument one place without changing the answer.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 08A70 (Applications of universal algebra in computer science), 08A40, 68Q25. arXiv cs.CC, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A polymorphism of a structure A is a map from Aⁿ to A that preserves every relation of A, coordinate by coordinate. Pol(A) is the set of all polymorphisms. A polymorphism f is cyclic when f(x₁, x₂, …, xₙ) = f(x₂, …, xₙ, x₁) for all inputs.

**Problem.** Let A be a finite relational structure. Then CSP(A) is solvable in polynomial time if Pol(A) contains a cyclic polymorphism of arity at least 2, and NP-hard otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** Cyclicity expresses the tractability criterion with one symmetry of one relation-preserving operation (our own explanation). The finite CSP dichotomy theorem of Bulatov and Zhuk, in its cyclic polymorphism formulation, supplies the complexity conclusion.

**Paper or page:** [Solving promise equations over monoids and groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08434), [Solving promise equations over monoids and groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08434). It says: “Let A be a finite relational structure. Then CSP(A) is tractable if Pol(A) contains a cyclic polymorphism of arity at least 2. Otherwise CSP(A) is NP-hard.”

**Sources:**

- [Alberto Larrauri, Stanislav Živný, Solving promise equations over monoids and groups, ACM Transactions on Computational Logic 26(1) (2024), arXiv:2402.08434](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08434)
- [Dmitriy Zhuk, A Proof of the CSP Dichotomy Conjecture, Journal of the ACM (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3402029)
- [Mikael Goldmann, Alexander Russell, The Complexity of Solving Equations over Finite Groups, Information and Computation (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1006/inco.2002.3173)

### Minion homomorphisms are exactly gadget reductions

**Remember:** Preserve arities and commute with every substitution of variables.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 08A70 (Applications of universal algebra in computer science), 08A40, 68Q25. arXiv cs.CC, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A minor of an n-input operation f substitutes one of m variables for each input, allowing repetitions and unused variables. A minion is a collection of operations closed under all such substitutions. A minion homomorphism preserves arity and sends every minor of f to the same substitution in the image of f.

**Problem.** For finite promise templates, PCSP(A,A′) gadget-reduces to PCSP(B,B′) exactly when a minion homomorphism sends Pol(B,B′) into Pol(A,A′).

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, substituting variables in constraints corresponds to taking minors of polymorphisms. The gadget reduction characterization of Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal expresses the reduction by preservation of these substitutions in the reverse direction.

**Paper or page:** [An invitation to the promise constraint satisfaction problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.13538). It says: “the following two statements are equivalent: PCSP(A, A′) is reducible to PCSP(B, B′) by a gadget reduction (and hence in log-space), there is a minion homomorphism Pol(B, B′) → Pol(A, A′).”

**Sources:**

- [Andrei Krokhin, Jakub Opršal, An invitation to the promise constraint satisfaction problem, ACM SIGLOG News (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3559736.3559740)
- [Libor Barto, Jakub Bulín, Andrei Krokhin, Jakub Opršal, Algebraic Approach to Promise Constraint Satisfaction, Journal of the ACM (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3457606)

### Named constants force idempotent polymorphisms

**Remember:** Preserving each singleton forces every constant tuple to return its entry.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 08A70 (Applications of universal algebra in computer science). arXiv math.LO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** To name the constants of a finite core C, add a unary relation {a} for each a in C. A polymorphism preserves each basic relation by sending every list of its tuples to another member tuple under coordinatewise application.

**Problem.** Naming all elements of a finite core forces each polymorphism f to satisfy f(a,…,a) = a. For a fixed finite relational signature, this preserves the constraint problem up to polynomial-time reductions in both directions.

**How the definition helps.** Preserving the singleton {a} forces f(a,…,a) to belong to {a} (our own explanation). For example, swapping two elements preserves equality but fails to preserve either singleton (our own example). The constraint problem asks whether an input structure admits a homomorphism to the fixed structure. The cited core theorem supplies the reductions.

**Paper or page:** [Mal'cev clones over a three-element set up to minor-equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06918v1). It says: “For a finite relational structure A, let A′ denote its core, extended by all constants. Then A pp-constructs A′ and vice-versa.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Constant terms select unique idempotents

**Remember:** A constant expression that fixes each idempotent leaves room for just one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 08B05 (Equational logic, Mal'tsev conditions). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Consider a variety of nonempty algebras whose basic operations have positive arity. An element is idempotent if every basic operation returns it on inputs all equal to it. The variety is polarized if one unary term has constant, idempotent value in each member.

**Problem.** A variety of this kind is polarized exactly when every member has exactly one idempotent.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, every unary term fixes every idempotent by induction on the term. A constant idempotent term therefore gives exactly one idempotent. Conversely, represent the unique idempotent of the free algebra on one generator by a term. Every assignment of the generator preserves idempotence, so the term always gives the unique idempotent in each member.

**Paper or page:** [Mal'tsev products of varieties, I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08841v1). It says: “Each algebra in V has precisely one idempotent if and only if the variety V is polarized.”

**Sources:**

- [Tomasz Penza, Anna B. Romanowska. Mal'tsev products of varieties, I, Corollary 1.3.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08841v1)

### Filters in residuated lattices are ideals of subtractive varieties

**Remember:** Ideal terms return one when all their designated inputs are one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 08B05 (Equational logic, Mal'tsev conditions), 08A30, 06F05. arXiv math.LO, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** With a designated constant 1, an ideal term t(x,y) satisfies t(x,1) = 1 identically, where x and y denote tuples. A 1-ideal contains 1 and contains t(a,b) for every ideal term, every algebra tuple a and every ideal tuple b.

**Problem.** In a commutative integral residuated lattice with normal operators, the 1-ideals are exactly the filters that are closed under the operators. So these filters form a modular lattice, the image of the congruence lattice under θ ↦ 1/θ.

**How the definition helps.** The cited filter characterization identifies 1-ideals with filters closed under the normal operators. In our own deduction, s(x,y) = y → x satisfies s(x,x) = 1 and s(x,1) = x. The ideal theorem for subtractive varieties therefore makes θ ↦ 1/θ a complete lattice homomorphism onto the modular ideal lattice.

**Paper or page:** [Why most papers on filters are really trivial (including this one)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15022), [Why most papers on filters are really trivial (including this one)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15022). It says: “If A is a commutative integral residuated lattice with normal operators, then the 1-ideals (which we may call the filters) of A are exactly the filters of the commutative residuated lattice reduct that are closed under fλ”

**Sources:**

- [Paolo Aglianò, Why most papers on filters are really trivial (including this one), arXiv:2309.15022 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15022)

### Loop identities force relation loops

**Remember:** Apply the same expression to both ends of the edges.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 08B05 (Equational logic, Mal'tsev conditions). arXiv math.LO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A loop condition asks for one expression that takes equal values on two specified lists of variables under every assignment. Its directed graph has an edge between corresponding variables, pointing from left to right. A graph on an algebra is compatible if applying any operation to edges coordinate by coordinate gives another edge.

**Problem.** A loop condition holds throughout a variety, a class defined by equations, exactly when the following graph test always succeeds. Map its pattern into any compatible graph on a member, sending edges to edges. Whenever such a map exists, the graph must contain an edge from a vertex to itself.

**How the definition helps.** In our own forward proof, apply the term coordinatewise to the mapped pattern edges. Compatibility gives an edge, and the identity makes its endpoints equal. Conversely, generate a compatible graph from the pattern edges in the free algebra on the variables. A loop there comes from a single term applied to those edges, and equality in the free algebra gives its identity.

**Paper or page:** [Loop conditions with strongly connected graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03177v1). It says: “For any algebra A ∈ V and any digraph G compatible with A, if there is a digraph homomorphism G꜀ → G, then G has a loop.”

**Sources:**

- [Miroslav Olšák. Loop conditions with strongly connected graphs, Proposition 2.2.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03177v1)

### Malcev theories are exactly those whose simplicial algebras are Kan

**Remember:** A Malcev term cancels a repeated pair at either end.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 08B05 (Equational logic, Mal'tsev conditions), 18N50. arXiv math.AT, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A theory is Malcev if some ternary term p satisfies both cancellation laws for every x,y. These laws are p(x,x,y) = y and p(x,y,y) = x. A simplicial set is Kan if every horn in every positive dimension extends to a simplex.

**Problem.** An algebraic theory is Malcev exactly when all its simplicial algebras are Kan complexes. For groups this is Moore's theorem that simplicial groups are Kan.

**How the definition helps.** The Malcev–Kan characterization translates the existence of one cancellation term into the existence of fillers for all horns. In our own explanation, the two term identities let the filler construction correct a face while preserving earlier matches. The converse in the cited characterization recovers such a term from horn filling.

**Paper or page:** [Examples and cofibrant generation of effective Kan fibrations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10568). It says: “Let 𝒯 be an algebraic theory. The following are equivalent: (i) 𝒯 is a Malcev theory. … (iii) All simplicial algebras of 𝒯 are Kan complexes.”

**Sources:**

- [Benno van den Berg, Freek Geerligs, Examples and cofibrant generation of effective Kan fibrations, arXiv:2402.10568 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10568)

### Size bounds give rewriting tables

**Remember:** Bound the generated algebras and put their common term operations in a table.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 08B05 (Equational logic, Mal'tsev conditions). arXiv math.LO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A pseudovariety is a class of finite algebras with the same operations, closed under quotients, subalgebras and finite products. Uniform local finiteness bounds the size of every subalgebra generated by k elements by a number depending only on k.

**Problem.** Fix a positive number of variables and a uniformly locally finite pseudovariety with finitely many basic operations of finite arity. A finite table decides whether two expressions agree throughout the class.

**How the definition helps.** The size bound leaves only finitely many generated algebras with a marked generating tuple, up to isomorphism (our own). Evaluate each expression on all these tuples and choose one representative expression for each resulting list of values (our own). Tabulate the result of each basic operation on the representatives (our own). Reading expressions from the variables upwards now gives identical representatives exactly when the identity holds (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Finite model theory for pseudovarieties and universal algebra: preservation, definability and complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.02653). It says: “for every term t(x⃗) there is a unique i ≤ ℓ such that K ⊨ t(x⃗) ≈ uᵢ(x⃗)”

**Sources:**

- [Finite model theory for pseudovarieties and universal algebra: preservation, definability and complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.02653)

### Absorbing polynomials make commutators symmetric

**Remember:** Reorder the variables and the same pairs still generate the commutator.

*True by definition.* MSC 08B10 (Congruence modularity, congruence distributivity). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A polynomial operation uses the algebra operations, variables and fixed parameters. A k-input polynomial f absorbs a tuple a if f(x) = f(a) for every tuple x agreeing with a in at least one coordinate.

**Problem.** In an algebra with a Malcev term, permuting a list of congruences leaves its higher commutator unchanged.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, Theorem 7 generates the higher commutator from pairs (f(a),f(b)) for polynomials f absorbing a. Each coordinate pair (aᵢ,bᵢ) must belong to its listed congruence. Reindexing the tuples and polynomial arguments together preserves absorption and gives exactly the same generating pairs for the permuted list.

**Paper or page:** [CSAT and CEQV for nilpotent Maltsev algebras of Fitting length &gt; 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.00689v2). It says: “Then \[α₁,…,αₖ\] is generated as a congruence by the set”

**Sources:**

- [Michael Kompatscher, CSAT and CEQV for nilpotent Maltsev algebras of Fitting length &gt; 2, Theorem 7](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.00689v2)

### Distributivity bounds irreducible factor sizes

**Remember:** Distributivity keeps irreducible factors within the size of the finite generators.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 08B26 (Subdirect products and subdirect irreducibility). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A variety is congruence-distributive if each member’s lattice of congruences satisfies the distributive law. A nontrivial algebra is subdirectly irreducible if every embedding into a product with surjective coordinate maps has an injective coordinate map.

**Problem.** Suppose finitely many finite algebras generate a congruence-distributive variety. Each subdirectly irreducible member has at most as many elements as the largest generator.

**How the definition helps.** Jónsson’s lemma places each subdirectly irreducible member in a homomorphic image of a subalgebra of an ultraproduct of generators, up to isomorphism. For a finite list of finite generators, each such ultraproduct is isomorphic to one generator. Taking subalgebras and quotients cannot increase its size (our own deduction).

**Wikipedia:** [Subdirectly irreducible algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdirectly_irreducible_algebra). It says: “By Jónsson's Lemma, subdirectly irreducible algebras of a congruence-distributive variety generated by a finite set of finite algebras are no larger than the generating algebras”

**Paper or page:** [Structural completeness in quasivarieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02754v1). It says: “Suppose that K is a class of algebras such that V(K) = V is congruence distributive”

**Sources:**

- [Bjarni Jónsson, Algebras whose congruence lattices are distributive](https://doi.org/10.7146/math.scand.a-10850)

### Equational Noetherianity yields separating maps

**Remember:** Reduce the whole diagram to finite equations while keeping the pair distinct.

*True by definition.* MSC 08C15 (Quasivarieties), 08A45. arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Consider systems of equations in finitely many variables. A class K is equationally Noetherian if every such system has a finite subsystem with identical solutions in each member of K.

**Problem.** Let K be an equationally Noetherian class in one fixed signature. Every finitely generated member of its quasivariety embeds into a product of members of K.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, finite equations capture all relations of a chosen finite generating tuple on solutions in K. If all such solutions equated two distinct term values, that conditional equation would hold throughout the quasivariety, contradicting their distinctness. A separating solution therefore induces a homomorphism to a member of K. The product of these maps is injective.

**Paper or page:** [Coherent Conditions: Algebraic Geometry for Arbitrary Classes of Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23647v1). It says: “A is separated by K”

**Sources:**

- [K. R. van Nispen, Coherent Conditions: Algebraic Geometry for Arbitrary Classes of Algebras, Theorem 4.6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23647v1)

### Free algebras give structural cores

**Remember:** Generate from the free algebra and keep the same free algebra.

*True by definition.* MSC 08C15 (Quasivarieties). arXiv math.LO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A quasivariety is a class of algebras defined by implications between finite lists of equations and single equations. In its free algebra, every assignment of the generators into a member extends uniquely to a map preserving the operations. The quasivariety is structurally complete if it is the smallest quasivariety containing its free algebra on countably infinitely many generators.

**Problem.** The quasivariety generated by the countably generated free algebra of any quasivariety is structurally complete.

**How the definition helps.** Our own proof uses the same free algebra twice. It belongs to the smaller quasivariety it generates, and assignments into that class still extend uniquely. Thus it remains free there and generates the whole smaller class. The characterization theorem identifies this generation test with minimality among quasivarieties having the same equations.

**Paper or page:** [Structural completeness in quasivarieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02754v1). It says: “is structurally complete and it is the structural core of Q.”

**Sources:**

- [Paolo Aglianó, Alex Citkin. Structural completeness in quasivarieties, Corollary 3.2.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02754v1)

## 11 Number theory

### A bounded remainder gives unique division

**Remember:** Keep the remainder between zero and one less than the divisor.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For integers a and b with b &gt; 0, call (q,r) a quotient-remainder pair when its integer entries satisfy two conditions. They give a = bq + r and 0 ≤ r &lt; b.

**Problem.** Every integer a has exactly one quotient-remainder pair for each positive integer divisor b.

**How the definition helps.** The bound makes the difference of any two allowed remainders too small to be a nonzero multiple of b (our own). Without it, 7 equals both 2·3 + 1 and 3·3 − 2 (our own). Existence still uses the fact that there is a greatest integer at most a/b (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Division Theorem/Positive Divisor/Uniqueness](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Division_Theorem/Positive_Divisor/Uniqueness). It says: “the integers q, r such that a = q b + r and 0 ≤ r &lt; b are unique:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A Bézout equation makes coprime factors cancel

**Remember:** Multiply the equation for one by the factor you want to keep.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Call integers a and b coprime when some integers x and y satisfy ax + by = 1. The usual definition asks that their greatest common divisor be 1.

**Problem.** If a divides bc and a is coprime to b, then a divides c.

**How the definition helps.** Both terms in c = acx + bcy are multiples of a, by our own use of the defining equation. Bézout’s identity does the work of showing that the equation for 1 exists whenever the greatest common divisor is 1.

**Paper or page:** [Euclid's Lemma](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Euclid's_Lemma). It says: “Then a ∣ c.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Common divisors explain Euclid’s algorithm

**Remember:** Taking the remainder preserves all common divisors.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For two nonnegative integers, at least one positive, the greatest common divisor is the largest positive integer dividing both. For two positive integers, prime factorization gives another definition using the smaller exponent of each prime.

**Problem.** Let a and b be nonnegative integers with b &gt; 0. The greatest common divisor of a and b equals that of b and the remainder after dividing a by b.

**How the definition helps.** The common-divisor definition makes each division step preserve exactly the same divisors (our own). If a = qb + r, a divisor of b divides a exactly when it divides r (our own). Each nonzero remainder is smaller than the preceding divisor, so the process stops (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Euclidean Algorithm](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Euclidean_Algorithm). It says: “Thus the GCD of a and b is the value of the variable a after the termination of the algorithm.”

**Sources:**

- [Euclid, Elements, Book VII, Proposition 2, translated by Thomas L. Heath.](https://mathcs.clarku.edu/~djoyce/java/elements/bookVII/propVII2.html)

### Defining the least common multiple by divisibility includes zero

**Remember:** Least by divisibility still works when the only multiple is zero.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the least common multiple as the nonnegative common multiple that divides every common multiple. Do not require it to be the smallest positive common multiple.

**Problem.** For all nonnegative a and b, the common multiples are exactly the multiples of their least common multiple. If either input is zero, this least common multiple is zero.

**How the definition helps.** The divisibility definition says at once that every common multiple is a multiple of the chosen number. In our own example, 0 and 6 have no positive common multiple, but 0 works under this definition. For positive inputs, the division algorithm shows that the smallest positive common multiple divides every common multiple.

**nLab:** [least common multiple](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/least+common+multiple). It says: “if a\|c and b\|c, then d\|c.”

### Nonnegative integers make divisibility an order

**Remember:** Keep one sign so mutual divisibility means equality.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Put the divisibility relation on the nonnegative integers, including zero. Say a divides b if b = ak for some nonnegative integer k.

**Problem.** Divisibility is a partial order on the nonnegative integers.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, multiplier 1 gives reflexivity, and multiplying witnesses gives transitivity. If positive a and b divide each other, their two multipliers have product 1, so both equal 1. Zero divides only zero, giving antisymmetry there too. On all integers, 2 and −2 violate antisymmetry.

**nLab:** [greatest common divisor](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/greatest+common+divisor). It says: “The natural numbers 0, 1, 2, … are partially ordered by the divisibility relation”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ordering by divisibility makes gcd(0,0) equal 0

**Remember:** Everything divides 0, so 0 sits at the top of the divisibility order.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors), 06B23. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For integers a,b, their gcd is the nonnegative common divisor divisible by every common divisor. On nonnegative integers, divisibility orders x below y exactly when x divides y.

**Problem.** With this definition, Bézout's identity holds for all pairs: gcd(a, b) generates the same ideal as a and b. The natural numbers form a complete distributive lattice under gcd and lcm.

**How the definition helps.** Every integer divides zero, so gcd(0,0) = 0 gives the generator of (0,0) required by Bézout’s identity. The usual Bézout theorem covers the other pairs. In our own lattice check, every nonempty family containing a positive integer has a gcd among that integer’s finitely many divisors. The empty meet is zero, completeness supplies all joins, and finite distributivity follows from prime exponents with zero greatest.

**Wikipedia:** [Greatest common divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_common_divisor). It says: “However, zero is its own greatest divisor if greatest is understood in the context of the divisibility relation, so gcd(0, 0) is commonly defined as 0. This preserves the usual identities for GCD, and in particular Bézout's identity”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prime exponents give the divisor product

**Remember:** For each prime, the smaller and larger exponents add to the original total.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For positive integers a,b, define gcd(a,b) and lcm(a,b) by their prime exponents. At every prime take respectively the minimum and maximum of its exponents in a and b, counting absence as exponent zero.

**Problem.** For positive integers a and b, their greatest common divisor times their least common multiple equals ab.

**How the definition helps.** The exponent definitions reduce the identity to adding the smaller and larger exponents of each prime (our own). Their sum equals the sum of the two original exponents (our own). Unique prime factorization makes the descriptions agree with the usual definitions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Greatest common divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_common_divisor). It says: “a × b is the product of their least common multiple and their greatest common divisor”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced fractions constrain rational roots

**Remember:** Cancel common factors before testing a rational root.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors), 12D05. arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Write a rational number as p/q with positive q and no common divisor greater than 1. An unrestricted fraction allows common factors in the numerator and denominator.

**Problem.** Let p/q be a nonzero rational root of an integer polynomial, written in lowest terms. Then q divides the leading coefficient and p divides the constant coefficient.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, clearing denominators gives q dividing the leading coefficient times a power of p. Similarly, p divides the constant coefficient times a power of q. Coprimality cancels the powers in both divisibilities. Without reduction, 2/2 solves x − 1 = 0, yet 2 divides neither coefficient.

**Paper or page:** [Rational Root Theorem](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Rational_Root_Theorem). It says: “the constant term a₀ of P(x) is divisible by p.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Divisible differences make congruence respect sums and products

**Remember:** The differences of the sums and products are still multiples of m.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For integers a and b and a positive integer m, a ≡ b modulo m means that m divides a − b. Equivalently, a and b have the same remainder on division by m.

**Problem.** If a ≡ b and c ≡ d modulo m, then a + c ≡ b + d and ac ≡ bd modulo m.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, each new difference is an integer combination of the original differences. For sums, (a + c) − (b + d) = (a − b) + (c − d). For products, ac − bd = a(c − d) + d(a − b). Both are therefore multiples of m.

**Wikipedia:** [Modular arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic). It says: “Congruence modulo m is a congruence relation, meaning that it is an equivalence relation compatible with addition, subtraction, and multiplication.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Modular units make cancellation safe

**Remember:** Cancel only when you can multiply by an inverse.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A residue class modulo n groups integers with the same remainder on division by n. For n &gt; 1, a unit is a class you can multiply by another class to get 1.

**Problem.** If a is a unit modulo n and ax ≡ ay modulo n, then x ≡ y modulo n.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying both sides by the inverse cancels a. In our own example modulo 6, doubling either 1 or 4 gives the class of 2. Cancellation fails because 2 has no inverse modulo 6.

**Paper or page:** [Integer Coprime to Modulus iff Linear Congruence to 1 exists](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Integer_Coprime_to_Modulus_iff_Linear_Congruence_to_1_exists). It says: “The linear congruence: ax ≡ 1 (mod m) has a solution x”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Modular units permute complete residue systems

**Remember:** Multiplying by the inverse undoes every change of residue.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A complete residue system modulo n &gt; 1 lists one integer from each class of integers with the same remainder. Define a unit as a class with an inverse for multiplication modulo n.

**Problem.** Multiplying each member of a complete residue system by a unit gives another complete residue system.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying by the inverse sends every residue class back to its starting point. Our own argument therefore gives a permutation without checking individual remainders. Bézout’s identity shows that having an inverse is equivalent to sharing no prime factor with n.

**nLab:** [multiplicative group of integers modulo n](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/multiplicative+group+of+integers+modulo+n). It says: “This consists of all those elements k ∈ ℤ/n which are represented by coprime integers to n.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Only coprime residues return to one

**Remember:** Only residues you can undo can return to one.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a modulus m greater than 1, a unit is a residue with a multiplicative inverse. Equivalently, its representatives are coprime to m. Define the order of a unit as the least positive exponent that raises it to 1 modulo m.

**Problem.** A residue has a positive power equal to 1 modulo m exactly when it is a unit.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, finiteness gives two equal powers of a unit, and cancellation gives a positive power equal to one. Conversely, if xᵏ = 1 with k positive, then xᵏ⁻¹ is an inverse. The nonunit 2 modulo 4 illustrates the obstruction because its positive powers are 2 and then 0.

**Paper or page:** [Integer has Multiplicative Order Modulo n iff Coprime to n](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Integer_has_Multiplicative_Order_Modulo_n_iff_Coprime_to_n). It says: “Let the multiplicative order of a modulo n exist. Then: a ⟂ n that is, a and n are coprime.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Shared remainders make congruences compatible

**Remember:** Check the modulus both congruences share.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For positive moduli m,n, residues a modulo m and b modulo n are compatible if gcd(m,n) divides b − a.

**Problem.** Two congruences with positive moduli have one solution class modulo their least common multiple exactly when their residues are compatible.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, a common solution forces gcd(m,n) to divide b − a, excluding 0 modulo 4 paired with 1 modulo 6. Conversely, Bézout’s identity writes a compatible difference as b − a = mu + nv. Then a + mu solves both congruences. All solutions differ from this one by exactly the multiples of lcm(m,n).

**Wikipedia:** [Chinese remainder theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_remainder_theorem). It says: “has a solution if and only if gcd(nᵢ,nⱼ) divides aᵢ − aⱼ whenever i ≠ j.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A primitive root makes Euler’s criterion a parity test

**Remember:** Even powers of a primitive root are exactly the squares.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A primitive root g modulo an odd prime p is a residue whose powers list every nonzero residue. This gives a way to describe the nonzero squares as even powers of one fixed residue.

**Problem.** A nonzero residue a modulo an odd prime p is a square exactly when aᵐ ≡ 1 modulo p, with m = (p − 1)/2.

**How the definition helps.** Writing residues as powers of a primitive root turns the square test into an exponent test (our own argument). The squares are exactly the even powers. The power gᵐ squares to 1 but differs from 1, so it equals −1 modulo p. The proof uses the theorem that every prime modulus has a primitive root.

**nLab:** [quadratic reciprocity law](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quadratic+reciprocity+law). It says: “whose kernel is the set of squares in the multiplicative group (ℤ/p)∗”

**Paper or page:** [Euler's Criterion/Quadratic Residue](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Euler's_Criterion/Quadratic_Residue). It says: “a is a quadratic residue of p”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Centered remainders locate the primes where two is a square

**Remember:** For two, count the even multiples in the upper half.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p, the centered remainder is the representative between −p/2 and p/2. Unlike the least nonnegative remainder, it uses a negative sign for representatives in the upper half.

**Problem.** For an odd prime p, 2 is a square modulo p exactly when p has remainder 1 or 7 upon division by 8.

**How the definition helps.** Centering makes precisely the even numbers above p/2 negative in the list 2, 4, …, p − 1 (our own argument). Their count is (p − 1)/2 minus p/4 rounded down. Checking the four odd remainders modulo 8 gives an even count only for 1 and 7. Gauss’s lemma says an even count means 2 is a square.

**Paper or page:** [Second Supplement to Law of Quadratic Reciprocity](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Second_Supplement_to_Law_of_Quadratic_Reciprocity). It says: “p ≡ ±1 (mod 8)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Centered remainders turn Gauss’s lemma into a product

**Remember:** Use centered remainders, then multiply their signs.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p, the centered remainder of an integer is its unique representative strictly between −p/2 and p/2. For integers outside the multiples of p, the Legendre symbol is 1 for squares modulo p and −1 otherwise.

**Problem.** For an odd prime p and an integer a coprime to p, put m = (p − 1)/2. The Legendre symbol equals the product of the signs of the centered remainders of a, 2a, …, ma.

**How the definition helps.** Centered remainders expose the signs that ordinary positive remainders hide (our own argument). Their absolute values run from 1 to m because distinct indices in this range are neither equal nor opposite modulo p. Multiplying and cancelling 1⋯m gives aᵐ modulo p. Euler’s criterion identifies this power with the Legendre symbol.

**Paper or page:** [Gauss's Lemma (Number Theory)](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Gauss's_Lemma_(Number_Theory)). It says: “Let n denote the number of elements of S whose least positive residue modulo p is greater than p/2.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prime moduli limit square roots

**Remember:** Over a prime modulus, two square roots agree up to sign.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** An integer p &gt; 1 is prime if, for all integers a,b, divisibility of ab by p implies divisibility of a or b by p.

**Problem.** For any prime p, a residue has at most two square roots modulo p.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, two roots x,y of the same residue give p dividing (x − y)(x + y). The product test forces y ≡ x or y ≡ −x modulo p. Modulo 8, the four classes 1,3,5,7 all square to 1. Euclid’s lemma supplies the product test for primes in the usual divisor sense.

**Wikipedia:** [Vieta's formulas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vieta%27s_formulas). It says: “the quadratic polynomial P(x) = x²−1 has four roots (1, 3, 5, and 7)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prime moduli make a positive symbol a square test

**Remember:** One sign detects a square, but two minus signs can hide nonsquares.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p, the Legendre symbol gives 0 to multiples of p, +1 to nonzero squares modulo p, and −1 otherwise. The Jacobi symbol for an odd positive integer multiplies these signs over its prime factors, counting repetitions.

**Problem.** For an odd prime p, a Jacobi symbol of +1 guarantees a square modulo p. This implication can fail for an odd composite modulus.

**How the definition helps.** Restricting to primes leaves one sign, so two minus signs cannot cancel (our own argument). For example, 2 is a nonsquare modulo both 3 and 5, so its symbol modulo 15 is +1 (our own argument). A square modulo 15 would stay square modulo 3 (our own argument).

**Wikipedia:** [Jacobi symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_symbol). It says: “However, the Jacobi symbol equals +1 if, for example, a is a non-residue modulo exactly two of the prime factors of n.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Jacobi symbol gives quadratic reciprocity without factoring

**Remember:** Jacobi multiplies the Legendre symbols over the prime factors of the bottom number.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let a be an integer and n an odd positive integer. The Jacobi symbol (a/n) multiplies the Legendre symbols for all prime factors of n, counting repetitions and taking an empty product as one. For an odd prime p, (a/p) is zero on multiples of p, one on nonzero squares modulo p, and minus one otherwise.

**Problem.** For coprime odd positive m,n, the product (m/n)(n/m) equals −1 exactly when both are 3 modulo 4, and equals 1 otherwise. Repeated flipping and reduction compute (a/p).

**How the definition helps.** The product definition permits a composite denominator after flipping. Multiplying prime reciprocity laws gives one minus sign for each pair of prime factors both congruent to 3 modulo 4. Each integer has an odd number of such factors exactly when it is 3 modulo 4, counting multiplicities (our own explanation). Reduction modulo the denominator and the supplementary laws for −1 and 2 allow iteration.

**Wikipedia:** [Jacobi symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_symbol). It says: “The following facts, even the reciprocity laws, are straightforward deductions from the definition of the Jacobi symbol and the corresponding properties of the Legendre symbol.”

**Sources:**

- [F. Lemmermeyer, Reciprocity Laws: From Euler to Eisenstein, Springer (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-12893-0)

### The Legendre symbol turns quadratic reciprocity into one formula

**Remember:** (a/p) is a sign that says whether a is a square mod p.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let p be an odd prime. The Legendre symbol (a/p) is 1 if a is a nonzero square modulo p. It is −1 if a is not a square modulo p, and 0 if p divides a.

**Problem.** For distinct odd primes p,q, quadratic reciprocity gives (p/q)(q/p) = −1 if both primes are 3 modulo 4, and +1 otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** Each symbol is a sign for distinct odd primes, so their product records whether the two square tests agree (our own explanation). The quadratic reciprocity theorem determines this product from the two primes modulo 4.

**Wikipedia:** [Legendre symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_symbol). It says: “Thus Legendre's contribution lay in introducing a convenient notation that recorded whether a is a residue or a non-residue modulo p.”

**Sources:**

- [A.-M. Legendre, Essai sur la théorie des nombres, Paris (1798), p. 186](https://archive.org/details/essaisurlathor00lege)

### The power definition tests whether minus one is a square

**Remember:** Minus one passes the power test exactly when the exponent is even.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let p be an odd prime and set m = (p − 1)/2. Define the Legendre symbol of a as the value in {−1, 0, 1} congruent to aᵐ modulo p. The other definition gives 1 for nonzero squares, −1 for nonsquares, and 0 for multiples of p.

**Problem.** For an odd prime p, −1 is a square modulo p exactly when p has remainder 1 upon division by 4.

**How the definition helps.** Put a = −1 in the power definition and check whether m is even (our own argument). Euler’s criterion carries the work of showing that the sign 1 still means a nonzero square (our own argument).

**Paper or page:** [First Supplement to Law of Quadratic Reciprocity](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/First_Supplement_to_Law_of_Quadratic_Reciprocity). It says: “p ≡ 1 (mod 4)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Treating 0 separately gives equal numbers of quadratic residues and nonresidues

**Remember:** Leave zero out, and residues are exactly half of the nonzero classes.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p, a quadratic residue is a nonzero class equal to x² modulo p for some nonzero class x. A nonresidue is any other nonzero class.

**Problem.** Modulo an odd prime p, there are (p − 1)/2 residues and (p − 1)/2 nonresidues. The product of two nonresidues is a residue, and a residue times a nonresidue is a nonresidue.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the squares form the even powers of a generator of the nonzero classes. The two exponent parities have equal size, and adding exponents gives the product rules. Counting zero as a residue adds one extra residue. It also breaks the mixed product rule because zero times a nonresidue is zero.

**Wikipedia:** [Quadratic residue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_residue). It says: “In this case, it is customary to consider 0 as a special case and work within the multiplicative group of nonzero elements of the field”

**Sources:**

- [K. Ireland and M. Rosen, A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory, 2nd ed., Springer, 1990](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-2103-4)

### Counting factor pairs below a hyperbola shortens the divisor sum

**Remember:** Count both strips and subtract their shared square.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the divisor count of n as the number of ordered positive integer pairs with ab = n. Each positive divisor a gives exactly one pair (a,n/a). The notation ⌊x⌋ means x rounded down.

**Problem.** For a positive integer N, let m be √N rounded down. The total divisor count through N equals twice the sum of ⌊N/a⌋ for a = 1, …, m, minus m².

**How the definition helps.** In our own count, each pair with ab ≤ N has a ≤ m or b ≤ m. Each strip contains the sum of ⌊N/a⌋ over 1 ≤ a ≤ m, by symmetry. The strips share the full m by m square, so subtract m² once.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet hyperbola method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_hyperbola_method). It says: “the inner sum runs over all ordered pairs (x,y) of positive integers such that xy = k.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ordered factorizations make Dirichlet convolution associative

**Remember:** Both groupings count each ordered triple of factors once.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** An arithmetic function assigns a number to each positive integer. The Dirichlet convolution at n sums f(a)g(b) over ordered positive integer pairs with ab = n. The usual divisor formula writes b as n/a.

**Problem.** For arithmetic functions f, g and h, both ways to group their Dirichlet convolutions give the same function.

**How the definition helps.** The ordered pair definition makes either grouping sum over the same triples with abc = n (our own argument). The only work is matching an outer factor pair and an inner factor pair to one ordered triple (our own argument).

**Paper or page:** [Dirichlet Convolution is Associative](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Dirichlet_Convolution_is_Associative). It says: “(f ∗ g) ∗ h = f ∗ (g ∗ h)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prime-power values make the Möbius function multiplicative

**Remember:** On coprime inputs, join the lists of prime factors.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the Möbius function by multiplying values for the prime powers in its input. Give exponent 1 the value −1 and each larger exponent the value 0. The empty product gives μ(1) = 1.

**Problem.** If positive integers m and n share no prime factor, then μ(mn) = μ(m)μ(n).

**How the definition helps.** Inputs with no shared prime contribute separate factors to the defining product (our own argument). Unique factorization gives the familiar rule. Repeated primes give zero, and otherwise each distinct prime changes the sign.

**Paper or page:** [Möbius Function is Multiplicative](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Möbius_Function_is_Multiplicative). It says: “The Möbius function μ is a multiplicative function”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Requiring f(1) = 1 makes multiplicative functions a group

**Remember:** Asking f(1) = 1 throws out only the zero function, which has no inverse.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A complex-valued arithmetic function f is multiplicative if f(1) = 1 and f(mn) = f(m)f(n) for every coprime pair of positive integers. Dirichlet convolution sums f(d)g(n/d) over all positive divisors d of n.

**Problem.** Under Dirichlet convolution, the multiplicative functions form an abelian group. Its identity is ε, with ε(1) = 1 and ε(n) = 0 for n &gt; 1. For example, the Möbius function μ is the inverse of the constant function 1.

**How the definition helps.** In our own check, the coprime product rule gives f(n) = f(1)f(n), so only the zero function fails normalization. Convolution is commutative and associative with identity ε, and splitting divisors of coprime products preserves multiplicativity. The cited inverse theorem supplies a multiplicative inverse for every normalized function. For the constant function 1, the Möbius divisor-sum identity gives that inverse.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_convolution), [Multiplicative function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_function). It says: “every not constantly zero multiplicative function has a Dirichlet inverse which is also multiplicative. In other words, multiplicative functions form a subgroup of the group of invertible elements of the Dirichlet ring.”

**Sources:**

- [T. M. Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory, Springer, 1976](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5579-4)

### Defining primes by invertibility gives the converse of Wilson’s theorem

**Remember:** Each factor of an invertible product is invertible.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A41 (Primes). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Call an integer n &gt; 1 prime if every nonzero remainder modulo n has a multiplicative inverse. An inverse is a number whose product with the original number leaves remainder 1.

**Problem.** If n &gt; 1 and the product of 1 through n − 1 is congruent to −1 modulo n, then n is prime.

**How the definition helps.** The product has an inverse, so every factor has one. In our own proof, an inverse for a factor is the product of the other factors times the inverse of the whole product. Bézout’s identity connects this test with the usual definition of a prime as having exactly two positive divisors.

**Wikipedia:** [Modular arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic). It says: “every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse, if and only if m is prime.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Leaving 1 out of the primes makes factorization unique

**Remember:** 1 is the empty product, with no factors to equal, so it is not prime.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A41 (Primes), 11A05. arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A positive integer p is prime if every expression of p as a finite product of positive integers has a factor equal to p. Finite products include the empty product, whose value is 1.

**Problem.** Every positive integer has exactly one prime factorization up to reordering, with the empty product allowed.

**How the definition helps.** In our own example, counting 1 as prime gives endlessly many factorizations of 6 by inserting extra factors of 1. The empty product excludes 1 because it has no factor equal to 1. The usual proof then gives existence by induction and uniqueness by Euclid’s lemma.

**nLab:** [prime number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/prime+number), [too simple to be simple](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/too+simple+to+be+simple), [biased definition](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/biased+definition), [fundamental theorem of arithmetic](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fundamental+theorem+of+arithmetic), [unique factorization monoid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/unique+factorization+monoid). It says: “hence might look like it deserves to be counted as a prime number, too, this would break the uniqueness of this prime factorization.”

**Sources:**

- [Chris K. Caldwell, Angela Reddick, Yeng Xiong, Wilfrid Keller, The History of the Primality of One: A Selection of Sources, Journal of Integer Sequences 15 (2012), Article 12.9.8](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL15/Caldwell2/cald6.html)

### The product recurrence for Fermat numbers gives infinitely many primes

**Remember:** Each new odd term leaves remainder two on division by every earlier term.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A41 (Primes). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the first Fermat number as 3. Define each later one as 2 plus the product of all earlier ones. This replaces the usual power formula.

**Problem.** There are infinitely many primes, since the Fermat numbers have pairwise disjoint sets of prime divisors.

**How the definition helps.** By the recurrence, any common divisor of two terms divides 2, and all terms are odd. Each term therefore supplies a prime divisor that did not divide any earlier term. In our own comparison, the difference of squares gives the usual formula by induction. Term n is 1 plus 2 raised to 2ⁿ, starting at n = 0.

**Wikipedia:** [Fermat number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_number). It says: “no two Fermat numbers share a common integer factor greater than 1.”

### Allowing the empty product lets prime factorization include the number 1

**Remember:** The number 1 is the product of no primes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A51 (Factorization; primality), 11A05. arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** The product of an empty list of numbers is defined to be 1. The product of a list with one number is that number. A prime factorization of n is then any finite list of primes, possibly empty, whose product is n.

**Problem.** Every positive integer is a product of primes, and the list of primes is unique up to order.

**How the definition helps.** The empty product lets one statement cover every positive integer, with no exceptions. The number 1 is the product of the empty list, and a prime p is the product of the list (p). Without these conventions, the theorem and its proof need separate cases for 1 and for the primes, as the page says. The real work still lies in uniqueness, through Euclid's lemma (our own remark).

**Wikipedia:** [Empty product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empty_product). It says: “As another example, the fundamental theorem of arithmetic says that every positive integer can be written uniquely as a product of primes. However, if we do not allow products with only 0 or 1 factors, then the theorem (and its proof) become longer.”

### Prime exponents make coprime factors of powers into powers

**Remember:** If the factors share no primes, each exponent belongs to just one factor.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A51 (Factorization; primality), 11A05. arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** The prime exponent of a positive integer at p counts the factors p in its prime factorization. For an integer k ≥ 2, define a perfect kth power by requiring every prime exponent to be divisible by k.

**Problem.** If two positive integers share no prime factor and their product is a perfect kth power, each is a perfect kth power.

**How the definition helps.** In our own generalization from squares, coprimality means each prime’s exponent in the product comes entirely from one factor. Divisibility by k therefore holds for every exponent of either factor. Unique factorization identifies this condition with being a kth power.

**Paper or page:** [Coprime Divisors of Square Number are Square](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Coprime_Divisors_of_Square_Number_are_Square). It says: “Then both s and t are square.”

### Euclidean remainders stop continued fractions exactly at rationals

**Remember:** A rational input runs the Euclidean algorithm on its denominator.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For the regular continued fraction, take the greatest integer no larger than the current number as the next digit. Subtract that digit and stop if the remainder is zero. Otherwise repeat with the reciprocal of the remainder.

**Problem.** The regular continued fraction of a real number terminates exactly when the number is rational.

**How the definition helps.** The digit rule makes each new denominator smaller for a rational input (our own argument). Write the input as p/q with q positive and divide p by q with remainder r. A zero remainder ends the expansion, and otherwise the next input is q/r with 0 &lt; r &lt; q. Conversely, a finite sequence of integer additions and reciprocals gives a rational value.

**nLab:** [continued fraction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/continued+fraction). It says: “The expression is an infinite continued fraction if and only if the real number is irrational”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Requiring the last partial quotient above 1 makes continued fractions unique

**Remember:** After the integer digit, forbid a final one.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A simple continued fraction \[a₀; a₁, …, aₙ\] is a₀ + 1/(a₁ + 1/(… + 1/aₙ)). Here a₀ is an integer and the other terms are positive integers. The canonical form also requires aₙ &gt; 1 when n ≥ 1.

**Problem.** Every rational number has exactly one canonical simple continued fraction. Its terms are the quotients of the Euclidean algorithm.

**How the definition helps.** In our own example, 3/2 = \[1; 2\] = \[1; 1, 1\], and the final-one rule rejects the second expansion. In canonical form each complete quotient after the first exceeds one, so its reciprocal has integer part zero. Floors and reciprocals therefore recover every digit uniquely. Euclidean division produces these digits and terminates at an integer, greater than one after the first step.

**Wikipedia:** [Simple continued fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_continued_fraction). It says: “These two representations agree except in their final terms. In the longer representation the final term in the continued fraction is 1; the shorter representation drops the final 1, but increases the new final term by 1.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Banning trailing nines makes decimals unique

**Remember:** Use trailing zeros, never an endless tail of nines.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A63 (Radix representation; digital problems). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A canonical decimal for x ≥ 0 uses its integer part without redundant leading zeros and digits dₙ in {0,…,9} for n ≥ 1. Their place-value series must sum to x minus its integer part, and the digits must not eventually all equal nine.

**Problem.** Every nonnegative real number has exactly one decimal representation under this rule.

**How the definition helps.** Without a tail of nines, later digits cannot cancel the difference at the first differing place (our own). For example, 0.4999… and 0.5000… represent the same number without the rule (our own). The work in existence lies in choosing digits by successive rounding down and showing the partial values converge (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Decimal representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_representation). It says: “decimal representations with a trailing infinite sequence of 9 are sometimes excluded.”

### Floor differences construct real digits in any integer base

**Remember:** Round at each scale and subtract to read the next digit.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A63 (Radix representation; digital problems), 26A03. arXiv math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Choose an integer base b ≥ 2 and a real number x with 0 ≤ x &lt; 1. Start with x, multiply repeatedly by b, and record each value rounded down to an integer, including the initial zero. Each digit equals the next recorded integer minus b times the preceding one.

**Problem.** Every real number from 0 up to but not including 1 has a base-b expansion for every integer b ≥ 2.

**How the definition helps.** The weighted digit sum cancels every intermediate rounded value. Our own proof uses these rounded values directly instead of carrying a fractional remainder from step to step. Rounding bounds give digits from 0 through b − 1 and an error smaller than the last place value. Those place values tend to zero.

**Paper or page:** [Existence of Base-N Representation](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Existence_of_Base-N_Representation). It says: “Given a number x ∈ \[0, 1), there exists a representation of that number in a base-p positional system.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### No consecutive powers makes base-φ numerals unique

**Remember:** In base φ, forbid 11 and each integer has one numeral.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A63 (Radix representation; digital problems), 11B39. arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let φ = (1 + √5)/2. A finite standard base-φ numeral is a finite set of integer exponents with no two consecutive, representing the sum of the corresponding powers of φ.

**Problem.** Every non-negative integer has exactly one finite base-φ numeral in standard form.

**How the definition helps.** In our own check, φⁿ + φⁿ⁻¹ = φⁿ⁺¹ makes adjacent powers ambiguous, and the rule excludes that pair. Two distinct allowed sums differ at a largest exponent k. Smaller nonconsecutive powers on the other side total strictly less than the infinite sum φᵏ⁻¹ + φᵏ⁻³ + ⋯ = φᵏ. Bergman’s representation theorem supplies existence for nonnegative integers.

**Wikipedia:** [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden<sub>ratio</sub><sub>base</sub>](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/https%3A//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio_base). It says: “Despite using an irrational number base, when using standard form, all non-negative integers have a unique representation as a terminating (finite) base-φ expansion.”

**Paper or page:** [On the representation of the natural numbers by powers of the golden mean](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.07544). It says: “Well known is the standard representation, introduced by George Bergman in 1957, where a unique representation is obtained by requiring that no consecutive powers φⁿ and φⁿ⁺¹ do occur in the representation.”

### Place values give digit divisibility tests

**Remember:** Replace the base by 1 or −1 before adding the digits.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11A63 (Radix representation; digital problems). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For an integer base b ≥ 2, read the digits of a nonnegative integer as polynomial coefficients. Start with the constant coefficient at the rightmost digit. Evaluating the polynomial at b gives the integer.

**Problem.** A base-b integer is divisible by b − 1 exactly when its digit sum is. It is divisible by b + 1 exactly when its alternating digit sum is.

**How the definition helps.** Place value turns a divisibility test on the whole digit string into a substitution in its polynomial. Our own generalization uses b ≡ 1 modulo b − 1 and b ≡ −1 modulo b + 1. Polynomial evaluation respects congruence, so those substitutions give the digit sum and the alternating digit sum. This replaces separate decimal tests with one calculation.

**Paper or page:** [Divisibility by 11](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Divisibility_by_11), [Divisibility by 9](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Divisibility_by_9). It says: “a divisibility test for 11 is achieved by alternately adding and subtracting the digits and taking the result modulo 11.”

### Reading decimals as series makes 0.999… equal 1

**Remember:** The series for 0.999… is geometric, and it sums to exactly 1.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A63 (Radix representation; digital problems), 40A05. arXiv math.HO, math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A decimal b₀.b₁b₂b₃… denotes the sum b₀ + b₁/10 + b₂/100 + ⋯, where b₁, b₂, b₃, … are its digits. The sum is the limit of the sums of successively longer initial parts.

**Problem.** 0.999… = 1.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, the decimal series has first term 9/10 and ratio 1/10. The geometric sum formula gives (9/10)/(1 − 1/10) = 1.

**Wikipedia:** [0.999...](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/0.999...). It says: “A common development of decimal expansions is to define them as infinite series.”

### Remainder order gives decimal periods

**Remember:** A remainder that returns starts the same digits again.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A63 (Radix representation; digital problems). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** In long division, use the current remainder to determine the next digit and remainder. Measure a repeating block by the first return to a remainder that is on the repeating part. The multiplicative order of 10 modulo m is the least positive exponent that makes its power congruent to 1.

**Problem.** Take a reduced fraction a/q between 0 and 1. Remove all factors of 2 and 5 from q, and suppose the result m is greater than 1. The decimal period is the multiplicative order of 10 modulo m.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplicative order measures exactly the first return of a remainder after the initial decimal digits. In our own proof, write q = dm, where d holds the factors 2 and 5, and choose j with d dividing 10ʲ. After j digits, the remainder returns k digits later exactly when q divides a × 10ʲ × (10ᵏ − 1). Since a and 10 are coprime to m, this means that m divides 10ᵏ − 1.

**Wikipedia:** [Repeating decimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeating_decimal). It says: “the period equals r, where r is the multiplicative order of 10 mod n”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The series definition makes repeating decimals rational

**Remember:** The repeated digits give a geometric series with a rational sum.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A63 (Radix representation; digital problems), 97F40. arXiv math.NT, math.HO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define a decimal as the sum of its digits times their place values 1, 1/10, 1/100, and so on. A repeating decimal has a block of digits that repeats forever after a finite start.

**Problem.** Every repeating decimal names a rational number.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, a repeated block of k digits contributes a geometric series with rational first term a and ratio r = 10⁻ᵏ. Its sum a/(1 − r) is rational. Adding the finite initial part preserves rationality.

**Wikipedia:** [Repeating decimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeating_decimal). It says: “A repeating decimal can also be expressed as an infinite series. That is, a repeating decimal can be regarded as the sum of an infinite number of rational numbers.”

### No consecutive Fibonacci numbers makes Zeckendorf sums unique

**Remember:** No two neighbours allowed, so each number has one Fibonacci decomposition.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B39 (Fibonacci and Lucas numbers and polynomials and generalizations), 11A67. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Use the shifted Fibonacci numbers F₁ = 1, F₂ = 2 and Fₙ₊₁ = Fₙ + Fₙ₋₁. A Zeckendorf decomposition of N writes N as a sum of distinct terms Fₙ. No two of the terms may be next to each other in the sequence.

**Problem.** Every positive integer has exactly one Zeckendorf decomposition.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, banning neighbours excludes 3 = F₁ + F₂ and leaves 3 = F₃. By induction, the largest allowed sum below index k is Fₖ − 1, obtained by taking alternate terms. Thus for Fₖ ≤ N &lt; Fₖ₊₁ the term Fₖ is forced. The remainder is less than Fₖ₋₁, so induction represents it uniquely without using the forbidden neighbour, starting with 0 and 1.

**Wikipedia:** [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeckendorf's<sub>theorem</sub>](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/https%3A//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeckendorf%27s_theorem). It says: “every positive integer can be represented uniquely as the sum of one or more distinct Fibonacci numbers in such a way that the sum does not include any two consecutive Fibonacci numbers”

**Paper or page:** [Generalizing Zeckendorf's Theorem to Homogeneous Linear Recurrences, I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08455). It says: “Zeckendorf's theorem states that every positive integer can be written uniquely as the sum of non-consecutive shifted Fibonacci numbers {Fₙ}, where we take F₁=1 and F₂=2.”

**Sources:**

- [Thomas C. Martinez, Steven J. Miller, Clayton Mizgerd, Chenyang Sun, Generalizing Zeckendorf's Theorem to Homogeneous Linear Recurrences, I, arXiv:2001.08455 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08455)

### The Fibonacci matrix turns index addition into matrix multiplication

**Remember:** Powers of Q add exponents, so Fibonacci indices add too.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B39 (Fibonacci and Lucas numbers and polynomials and generalizations), 11B37. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let Q be the 2 × 2 matrix with rows (1, 1) and (1, 0). For n ≥ 0, define Fₙ as the entry in row 2, column 1 of Qⁿ. The usual definition starts with F₀ = 0 and F₁ = 1 and adds the previous two terms to get the next.

**Problem.** For all m, n ≥ 1, Fₘ₊ₙ = FₘFₙ₊₁ + Fₘ₋₁Fₙ.

**How the definition helps.** The matrix law gives Qᵐ⁺ⁿ = QᵐQⁿ. Multiplication by Q shows inductively that Qᵏ has rows (Fₖ₊₁,Fₖ) and (Fₖ,Fₖ₋₁) for k ≥ 1. In our own calculation, the lower left entry of the product is FₘFₙ₊₁ + Fₘ₋₁Fₙ.

**Wikipedia:** [Fibonacci sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_sequence). It says: “Moreover, since AⁿAᵐ = Aⁿ⁺ᵐ for any square matrix A, the following identities can be derived”

### Tile counts give Fibonacci binomial sums

**Remember:** Fix the number of long tiles and choose their places.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B39 (Fibonacci and Lucas numbers and polynomials and generalizations), 05A15. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For n ≥ 1, define Fₙ as the number of tilings of a strip of length n − 1. Use tiles of length one or two, and count the empty tiling once. The usual definition starts with F₁ = F₂ = 1 and adds two successive terms.

**Problem.** Let C(a,b) count the b-element subsets of an a-element set. For n ≥ 1, Fₙ is the sum of C(n−k−1,k) for k from 0 to ⌊(n−1)/2⌋.

**How the definition helps.** The tiling definition lets us count by the number of long tiles (our own). With k long tiles, there are n−1−k tiles altogether (our own). Choose k of those positions for the long tiles (our own). Splitting tilings by their last tile gives the usual recurrence with the same starting values (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Fibonacci Number as Sum of Binomial Coefficients](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Fibonacci_Number_as_Sum_of_Binomial_Coefficients). It says: “Fₙ = (n − 1 choose 0) + (n − 2 choose 1) + (n − 3 choose 2) + ⋯ + (n − j choose j − 1) + (n − j − 1 choose j)”
