### With the Fibonacci matrix, Cassini's identity is a determinant

**Remember:** The determinant of Q is −1, so its n-th power has determinant (−1)ⁿ.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B39 (Fibonacci and Lucas numbers and polynomials and generalizations), 15A15. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let Q be the 2 × 2 matrix with rows (1, 1) and (1, 0). For n ≥ 0, define Fₙ as the entry in row 2, column 1 of Qⁿ. The usual definition starts with F₀ = 0 and F₁ = 1 and adds the previous two terms to get the next.

**Problem.** For every n ≥ 1, Fₙ₊₁Fₙ₋₁ − Fₙ² = (−1)ⁿ.

**How the definition helps.** Using a matrix entry as the definition is our own framing. Multiplying by Q gives the rows (Fₙ₊₁,Fₙ) and (Fₙ,Fₙ₋₁) of Qⁿ by induction for n ≥ 1. Its determinant is therefore Fₙ₊₁Fₙ₋₁ − Fₙ². Multiplicativity also gives det(Qⁿ) = det(Q)ⁿ = (−1)ⁿ.

**Wikipedia:** [Fibonacci sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_sequence). It says: “Taking the determinant of both sides of this equation yields Cassini's identity,”

**Paper or page:** [Cassini's Identity](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Cassini's_Identity). It says: “Let Fₖ be the kth Fibonacci number. Then: Fₙ₊₁ Fₙ₋₁ − Fₙ² = (−1)ⁿ”

### Prime powers count factorial factors

**Remember:** Count multiples of p once more at every power of p.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B65 (Binomial coefficients; factorials; \\(q\\)-identities), 11A51. arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p and a positive integer a, count the positive powers of p that divide a. This count equals the largest integer e for which pᵉ divides a.

**Problem.** For a positive integer n, the exponent of p in n! is the sum of ⌊n/pⁱ⌋ over i ≥ 1. The brackets mean to round down.

**How the definition helps.** The count definition lets us add the contributions of all factors of n! one power of p at a time (our own). The number of factors divisible by pⁱ is ⌊n/pⁱ⌋ (our own). Unique factorization ensures the exponent of a product is the sum of the individual exponents (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Legendre's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_formula). It says: “Each multiple of p² contributes an additional factor of p, each multiple of p³ contributes yet another factor of p, etc.”

### Rotating subsets proves prime divisibility

**Remember:** A nontrivial subset on a prime-sized circle has a full set of rotations.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B65 (Binomial coefficients; factorials; \\(q\\)-identities), 05A19. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define C(p,k) as the number of k-element subsets of p labeled positions on a circle. Its usual formula is p!/(k!(p−k)!).

**Problem.** If p is prime and 0 &lt; k &lt; p, then p divides C(p,k).

**How the definition helps.** Counting subsets lets us group them into sets of p rotated copies (our own). Any nonzero shift visits all positions since p is prime (our own). A subset fixed by such a shift must therefore be empty or full (our own). The factorial formula follows by counting ordered selections and dividing by the number of orders of each subset (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Binomial Coefficient of Prime](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Binomial_Coefficient_of_Prime). It says: “∀ k ∈ ℤ: 0 &lt; k &lt; p: (p choose k) ≡ 0 (mod p)”

### Block counts split Bell numbers into Stirling numbers

**Remember:** Sort the partitions by their numbers of blocks.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B73 (Bell and Stirling numbers), 05A18, 05A15. arXiv math.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A set partition divides a set into nonempty groups, with each element in exactly one group. The Bell number B(n) counts all partitions of n elements. The Stirling number S(n,k) counts those with k groups.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 0, B(n) is the sum of S(n,k) over 0 ≤ k ≤ n.

**How the definition helps.** Every partition has exactly one group count, so adding the counts gives B(n). The empty set contributes once, with zero groups. In our own comparison, defining the numbers by recurrences requires proving that those recurrences count these partitions.

### Coprime coordinates rule out primes with remainder three

**Remember:** A forbidden prime would have to divide both coordinates.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11D09 (Quadratic and bilinear Diophantine equations), 11A15, 11E25. arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Call a sum a² + b² primitive if a and b have greatest common divisor 1. Unlike an unrestricted sum, it does not allow a prime to divide both coordinates.

**Problem.** No prime with remainder 3 modulo 4 divides a primitive sum of two squares.

**How the definition helps.** Coprimality prevents a prime dividing the sum from dividing both coordinates (our own argument). If p also divided b, it would divide a, so b has an inverse modulo p. Dividing by b² would make −1 a square modulo p, impossible for a prime with remainder 3 modulo 4. Without coprimality, 7 divides 7² + 49².

**Wikipedia:** [Sum of two squares theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sum_of_two_squares_theorem). It says: “2450 = 7² + 49².”

### Primitive Pythagorean triples correspond to coprime pairs of opposite parity

**Remember:** Coprime m and n, one of them even, give each primitive triple once.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11D09 (Quadratic and bilinear Diophantine equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Pythagorean triple is three positive integers a, b, c with a² + b² = c². It is primitive when a, b and c have no common divisor larger than 1.

**Problem.** Take a primitive triple with b even. Exactly one coprime pair of integers m &gt; n &gt; 0 has opposite parity and gives all three coordinates below. They are a = m² − n², b = 2mn and c = m² + n².

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, (c+a)/2 and (c−a)/2 are coprime positive integers because a,c are odd and coprime. Their product (b/2)² forces both to be squares, uniquely determining m and n and giving all three formulas. Their sum c is odd, so m,n have opposite parity. The pair (3,1) violates parity and gives the nonprimitive triple (8,6,10).

**Wikipedia:** [Pythagorean triple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_triple). It says: “Every primitive triple arises (after the exchange of a and b, if a is even) from a unique pair of coprime numbers m, n, one of which is even.”

### Complex norms show that sums of two squares multiply

**Remember:** Multiply each complex number by its conjugate to read off two squares.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms). arXiv math.NT. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Use the complex norm N(z) = z z̄, where z̄ is the complex conjugate. For z = a + bi, this norm is a² + b².

**How the definition helps.** The norm turns the four-variable identity into the rule N(zw) = N(z)N(w). Unlike direct polynomial expansion, this proof uses the fact that conjugation preserves products (our own). The two squares come from the real and imaginary parts of zw.

**Wikipedia:** [Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahmagupta%E2%80%93Fibonacci_identity). It says: “the Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity is equivalent to the multiplicative property for absolute values of complex numbers”

**Remember:** Sum reciprocal factorials and multiplying by a denominator factorial clears the first terms.

*True by definition.* MSC 11J72 (Irrationality; linear independence over a field), 26A09. arXiv math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

Subtracting the terms through 1/q! from e and multiplying by q! then gives an integer. Its jth tail term is at most (q + 1)⁻ʲ, so this positive integer is at most 1/q.

### An infinite prime valuation makes the product law include zero

**Remember:** An infinite exponent keeps the same rule when a factor is zero.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p and nonzero integer n, the p-adic valuation of n is the exponent of p in the prime factorization of \|n\|. Set the valuation of 0 to ∞, since every power of p divides 0.

**Problem.** For any integers a and b, the p-adic valuation of ab is the sum of their p-adic valuations. Here adding any valuation to ∞ gives ∞.

**How the definition helps.** If either factor is zero, the valuation of the product and the sum of the valuations both equal ∞. For nonzero factors, unique prime factorization shows that the exponents add. Our own comparison explains why the convention at zero gives one rule for all integers.

**Wikipedia:** [p-adic valuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/p-adic_valuation). It says: “Zero has an infinite valuation.”

**Paper or page:** [Characterization of P-adic Valuation on Integers](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Characterization_of_P-adic_Valuation_on_Integers). It says: “∃ k ∈ ℤ: n = pʳ k : p ∤ k”

### Defining the gcd as a generator gives Bézout’s identity

**Remember:** The gcd lives in aℤ + bℤ, so it is some ax + by.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors), 13F07. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For integers a and b, not both zero, let S be the set of all ax + by with integer x and y. Define gcd(a, b) as the positive d for which S consists of all integer multiples of d. The usual definition takes the largest positive integer that divides both a and b.

**Problem.** For integers a and b, not both zero, there are integers x and y with ax + by = gcd(a, b).

**How the definition helps.** Since d belongs to dℤ, it belongs to S and equals ax + by for some integers x and y. Bézout’s identity identifies this positive generator with the usual greatest common divisor (our own comparison).

**nLab:** [greatest common divisor](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/greatest+common+divisor). It says: “From the point of view of principal ideals in a pid or Bézout domain R, the gcd corresponds to taking their join: (gcd(a, b)) = (a) + (b).”

**Wikipedia:** [Bézout's identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zout%27s_identity). It says: “The reason is that the ideal Ra + Rb is principal and equal to Rd.”

**Paper or page:** [Bézout's Identity](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Bézout's_Identity). It says: “Furthermore, gcd{a, b} is the smallest positive integer combination of a and b.”

### Generating multiples makes the greatest common divisor scale

**Remember:** Scale the whole set of combinations and its generator scales too.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For integers a and b, form every sum ax + by with integers x and y. Define their greatest common divisor as the nonnegative integer d whose multiples are exactly these sums.

**Problem.** For integers a, b and c, the greatest common divisor of ca and cb is \|c\| times that of a and b.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying every sum by c gives exactly the sums formed from ca and cb. In our own argument, these are precisely the multiples of \|c\|d, including when c is zero. For inputs other than the pair (0, 0), Bézout’s identity connects this definition to the largest positive common divisor.

**nLab:** [greatest common divisor](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/greatest+common+divisor). It says: “(gcd(a, b)) = (a) + (b).”

### Matrix form carries Bézout coefficients through Euclidean division

**Remember:** The first row records how to make the last nonzero remainder.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For each Euclidean division a = qb + r with 0 ≤ r &lt; b, use the matrix with rows (0, 1) and (1, −q). Starting with the identity, multiply each successive matrix on the left through the first division with remainder zero.

**Problem.** For positive inputs, the top row of the final matrix gives Bézout coefficients. These are integer weights that combine the inputs to give their greatest common divisor.

**How the definition helps.** The first row tracks one integer combination of the inputs through every division. Our own matrix formulation replaces substitution backwards through the divisions. The Euclidean algorithm shows that the final column contains the greatest common divisor followed by zero.

**Paper or page:** [Extended Euclidean Algorithm](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Extended_Euclidean_Algorithm). It says: “computing two integers a and b such that a m + b n = d.”

### The divisibility definition makes the gcd associative

**Remember:** Greatest lower bounds of three elements do not care about brackets.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11A05 (Multiplicative structure; Euclidean algorithm; greatest common divisors), 06B99. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Order the nonnegative integers by divisibility, so a comes below b if b = ak for some nonnegative integer k. Define gcd(a, b) as their greatest lower bound, meaning the common divisor that every common divisor divides. The usual definition takes the largest common divisor by size and needs a separate convention for gcd(0, 0).

**Problem.** For all nonnegative integers a, b, and c, gcd(a, gcd(b, c)) = gcd(gcd(a, b), c).

**How the definition helps.** Both groupings have exactly the common divisors of a, b and c as their divisors (our own argument). Each grouping therefore divides the other, so they agree. Bézout’s identity gives the pairwise greatest lower bounds, with 0 serving for the pair (0, 0).

**nLab:** [greatest common divisor](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/greatest+common+divisor). It says: “The greatest common divisor of a, b is their meet in this lattice.”

### A sign and a power of five describe every odd class

**Remember:** The sign handles the remainder modulo four, and powers of five handle the rest.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For k ≥ 3, assign each odd class x modulo 2ᵏ a sign s. Take s = 1 when x ≡ 1 modulo 4 and s = −1 otherwise. Its signed class sx is always 1 modulo 4.

**Problem.** Every odd class modulo 2ᵏ has a unique expression as its sign times 5ᵗ with 0 ≤ t &lt; 2ᵏ⁻².

**How the definition helps.** The sign reduces our own count to the 2ᵏ⁻² classes that are 1 modulo 4. Every power of 5 lies among them. The order theorem gives exactly 2ᵏ⁻² distinct powers, so they exhaust these classes.

**Paper or page:** [Order of 5 in Units of Ring of Integers Modulo 2<sup>n</sup>](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Order_of_5_in_Units_of_Ring_of_Integers_Modulo_2^n). It says: “The order of 5 in U is 2ⁿ⁻².”

### Chinese remainder coordinates multiply root counts

**Remember:** Count the roots in each coordinate and multiply those counts.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For coprime moduli m and n, represent a residue class modulo mn by its two classes modulo m and n. Add and multiply the two coordinates separately.

**Problem.** For an integer polynomial f, let R(m) count its roots among the residue classes modulo m. For coprime positive integers m,n, R(mn) = R(m)R(n).

**How the definition helps.** With our own application of these coordinates, a root is exactly a pair of roots, one in each coordinate. The Chinese remainder theorem does the work of showing that every pair comes from exactly one class modulo mn.

**Wikipedia:** [Chinese remainder theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_remainder_theorem). It says: “one may do the same computation independently in each ℤ/nᵢℤ”

### Discrete logarithms make power congruences linear

**Remember:** Taking exponents turns a power into multiplication.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Choose a primitive root g modulo a prime p, so its powers give all nonzero classes. The discrete logarithm of a nonzero class is its exponent on g, taken modulo p − 1.

**Problem.** Let k ≥ 1 be an integer and let d be the greatest common divisor of k and p − 1. For nonzero a modulo p, xᵏ ≡ a modulo p has d solutions if d divides its discrete logarithm, and none otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** Let b and t label a and x. In our own notation, the power equation becomes kt ≡ b modulo p − 1. The primitive root theorem supplies the labels. The usual count for a linear congruence gives the result.

**Wikipedia:** [Discrete logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_logarithm). It says: “the discrete logarithm amounts to a group isomorphism”

### Return periods reduce the primitive root test to prime divisors

**Remember:** Return exponents are multiples of the order, so prime quotients detect shorter orders.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For n &gt; 1, a unit is a class with a multiplicative inverse modulo n. Define its order as the positive integer whose multiples are exactly the exponents that return it to 1. Let d count all units modulo n.

**Problem.** A unit generates every unit modulo n exactly when its power with exponent d/q differs from 1 for every prime divisor q of d.

**How the definition helps.** In our own use of the divisibility definition, the exponent d/q gives 1 precisely when the order divides d/q. Every proper divisor of d divides one of those exponents, so the test rules out all shorter orders at once. The division algorithm proves the return times are all multiples of the first one. Lagrange’s theorem shows that the order divides d.

**Wikipedia:** [Multiplicative order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_order). It says: “the order of a (mod n) always divides φ(n).”

### Simple roots have unique lifts modulo prime powers

**Remember:** A nonzero derivative makes the next correction unique.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Call a root a modulo a prime p simple if the polynomial derivative at a is nonzero modulo p. A lift is a root modulo a higher power of p that reduces to a.

**Problem.** For a polynomial with integer coefficients, each simple root modulo p has a unique lift modulo every higher power of p.

**How the definition helps.** The derivative at a simple root has an inverse modulo p, so the next correction is unique. Adding tpᵏ to a root modulo pᵏ changes the polynomial value by tpᵏ times its derivative modulo pᵏ⁺¹. For our own counterexample, the root 1 of x² − 1 modulo 2 lifts to both 1 and 3 modulo 4.

**Wikipedia:** [Hensel's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hensel%27s_lemma). It says: “then this root can be lifted to a unique root modulo any higher power of p.”

### The Frobenius map makes Fermat’s theorem include zero

**Remember:** Raise every residue to the pth power in characteristic p.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p, the Frobenius map sends each class modulo p to its pth power.

**Problem.** For every prime p and every integer a, the pth power of a is congruent to a modulo p.

**How the definition helps.** The Frobenius map fixes 1 and preserves addition, so it fixes every sum of copies of 1. These sums represent all classes modulo p, including zero. Our own comparison uses this map in place of multiplication in the group of nonzero classes. The binomial theorem proves additivity because p divides each intermediate binomial coefficient.

**nLab:** [Fermat's little theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Fermat%27s+little+theorem). It says: “the preservation of addition follows easily from the binomial theorem”

**Paper or page:** [Fermat's Little Theorem/Corollary 1](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Fermat's_Little_Theorem/Corollary_1). It says: “If p is a prime number, then nᵖ ≡ n (mod p).”

### The group of modular units gives Euler’s theorem

**Remember:** Count the invertible residues to get φ(n), the size of their group.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A07 (Congruences; primitive roots; residue systems). arXiv math.NT, math.GR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let n ≥ 2 and define φ(n) as the size of the group of units modulo n. These are the residues with multiplicative inverses. The usual definition counts integers from 1 to n that are coprime to n.

**Problem.** If a is coprime to n, then a raised to the power φ(n) is 1 modulo n. When n is prime, this gives Fermat’s little theorem.

**How the definition helps.** The group definition lets Lagrange’s theorem show that the number of powers of a divides φ(n). Those powers form a subgroup of size k, where aᵏ is 1 modulo n. Since φ(n) is a multiple of k, raising a to φ(n) gives 1. The work moves into Lagrange’s theorem and into using Bézout’s identity to identify the invertible residues (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Euler's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_theorem). It says: “Lagrange's theorem states that the order of any subgroup of a finite group divides the order of the entire group”

### A product of differences gives Zolotarev’s sign

**Remember:** Each difference contributes one copy of the multiplier.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a list of distinct numbers, multiply the later entry minus the earlier entry for every pair of positions. Define the sign of a permutation as the new product divided by the original product. This gives the same sign as counting reversals.

**Problem.** Multiplication by a permutes the residues modulo an odd prime p whenever p does not divide a. Its sign is the Legendre symbol, which equals 1 for squares modulo p and −1 otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying each entry by a multiplies each difference by a modulo p (our own argument). There are p(p − 1)/2 differences, all nonzero modulo p. Fermat’s little theorem reduces the exponent to (p − 1)/2, and Euler’s criterion identifies the result. The difference product gives the usual permutation sign because exchanging two entries reverses its sign.

**nLab:** [quadratic reciprocity law](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quadratic+reciprocity+law). It says: “is the sign or signature of a permutation on ℤ/p given by multiplying by a.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Euler’s power formula makes the Legendre symbol multiplicative

**Remember:** Raise a nonzero residue to half the group order to read its sign.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let p be an odd prime and let p not divide a. Define the Legendre symbol (a/p) as the sign congruent to a raised to (p − 1)/2 modulo p. The usual definition assigns +1 to nonzero squares modulo p and −1 to other nonzero residues.

**Problem.** If p does not divide a or b, then (ab/p) = (a/p)(b/p). In particular, the product of two nonsquares modulo p is a square.

**How the definition helps.** The power definition makes the symbol multiplicative because powers of products are products of powers. The work moves into Euler’s criterion, which shows that the power gives +1 exactly on nonzero squares. Fermat’s little theorem first shows that the power is ±1. The nonzero squares give all the roots of the degree (p − 1)/2 polynomial that tests for +1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Legendre symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_symbol), [Euler's criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_criterion). It says: “By Euler's criterion, which had been discovered earlier and was known to Legendre, these two definitions are equivalent.”

### Permutation signs make the Jacobi symbol multiplicative in its numerator

**Remember:** Multiply residues by a and take the sign of the resulting permutation.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 20B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For odd positive n and an integer a coprime to n, multiplication by a permutes the residues modulo n. Define the Jacobi symbol (a\|n) as the sign of this permutation.

**Problem.** For odd n &gt; 0 and a and b coprime to n, (ab\|n) = (a\|n)(b\|n).

**How the definition helps.** Multiplication by ab composes the permutations for a and b, so their signs multiply (our own argument). The generalized Zolotarev lemma identifies this sign with the usual Jacobi symbol.

**Wikipedia:** [Zolotarev's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zolotarev%27s_lemma). It says: “a generalization of Zolotarev's lemma is that the Jacobi symbol above is the sign of this permutation.”

### The Kronecker symbol matches primitive real characters with quadratic fields

**Remember:** Let the bottom of the symbol be any integer, and characters become symbols.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 11R11, 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For integers D and n ≠ 0, multiply the Legendre symbols at odd prime factors of \|n\|, counting multiplicity. For each factor 2, include 0 for even D, +1 for D ≡ ±1 modulo 8, and −1 otherwise. Negate for D and n both negative. At n = 0 use 1 if \|D\| = 1 and 0 otherwise (our own details).

**Problem.** For every nonzero D ≡ 0 or 1 modulo 4, n ↦ (D/n) is a real Dirichlet character modulo \|D\|. It is primitive exactly for fundamental discriminants, including 1 by convention, and the nontrivial primitive characters correspond bijectively to quadratic fields. For such a field of discriminant D, (D/p) equals 1, −1 or 0 according as p splits, stays prime or ramifies.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing every integer denominator defines the character values even at negative or even arguments (our own). Quadratic reciprocity gives periodicity, the classification of quadratic characters gives primitivity, and the quadratic splitting law gives the prime behavior (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kronecker symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker_symbol). It says: “In particular, primitive real Dirichlet characters χ are in a 1–1 correspondence with quadratic fields F=ℚ(√m), where m is a nonzero square-free integer”

### Counting cyclic generators gives the totient divisor sum

**Remember:** Each element generates exactly one subgroup, so each is counted once.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define φ(d) as the number of generators of a cyclic group of size d. A generator is an element whose powers fill the group. The usual definition counts the integers from 1 to d that are coprime to d.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, the sum of φ(d) over the positive divisors d of n is n.

**How the definition helps.** Counting generators counts each element of a cyclic group exactly once, in the subgroup it generates (our own argument). A cyclic group of order n has exactly one subgroup of each order d dividing n. That subgroup contributes φ(d) elements.

**Wikipedia:** [Euler's totient function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_totient_function). It says: “φ(d) is also equal to the number of possible generators of the cyclic group”

### Counting divisible integers makes the totient a Möbius sum

**Remember:** Weight common divisors by Möbius values to test coprimality.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Euler’s totient φ(n) counts integers from 1 to n with greatest common divisor 1 with n. The Möbius function μ has divisor sum 1 at 1 and 0 elsewhere. Use the sum of μ(d) over common divisors d to test whether two numbers have greatest common divisor 1.

**Problem.** For each positive integer n, φ(n) is the sum of μ(d)·(n/d) over positive divisors d of n.

**How the definition helps.** The common-divisor sum replaces the greatest-common-divisor test with weights that can be summed in either order (our own argument). The divisors common to k and n are exactly those dividing their greatest common divisor. Möbius cancellation therefore gives weight 1 exactly when that greatest common divisor is 1. Each divisor d of n contributes μ(d) once for each of its n/d multiples.

**Paper or page:** [Euler Phi Function in terms of Möbius Function](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Euler_Phi_Function_in_terms_of_Möbius_Function). It says: “∑ (d \| n) μ(d) n/d = φ(n)”

### Counting modular units makes Euler’s totient multiplicative

**Remember:** Count invertible residues, and a pair counts exactly when both entries are invertible.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11A07. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define φ(n) as the number of units in ℤ/nℤ, the ring of residues modulo n. A unit is a residue with a multiplicative inverse. The usual definition counts integers from 1 to n that are coprime to n.

**Problem.** For coprime positive integers m and n, φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n).

**How the definition helps.** Counting units makes the product formula follow from the fact that a pair is invertible exactly when both entries are. The Chinese remainder theorem identifies residues modulo mn with pairs of residues modulo m and n, preserving addition and multiplication. The work moves into that theorem and into Bézout’s identity, which makes a residue invertible exactly when it is coprime to n (our own).

### Dirichlet convolution makes divisor power sums multiplicative

**Remember:** Convolve the constant one with kth powers by summing over divisor pairs.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The Dirichlet convolution f ∗ g has value at n given by summing f(d)g(n/d) over all positive divisors d of n. Set σₖ = 𝟙 ∗ gₖ, where 𝟙 is the constant function 1 and gₖ(n) = nᵏ. Equivalently, σₖ(n) is the sum of the kth powers of the positive divisors of n.

**Problem.** If m and n are coprime positive integers, then σₖ(mn) = σₖ(m)σₖ(n). This includes the divisor count when k = 0.

**How the definition helps.** The convolution definition gives multiplicativity because both 𝟙 and gₖ multiply across coprime inputs. Instead of proving this separately for each divisor sum, prove that convolution preserves this property. The work moves into splitting each divisor of mn uniquely as a divisor of m times a divisor of n.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_convolution), [Divisor function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisor_function). It says: “The Dirichlet convolution of two multiplicative functions is again multiplicative”

### Prime-power series turn convolution into ordinary multiplication

**Remember:** Split each exponent independently and multiply the resulting series.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A multiplicative function f has value 1 at 1 and satisfies f(ab) = f(a)f(b) when a and b share no prime. Encode its values at each prime p by a power series whose coefficient of degree k is f(pᵏ). The convolution of f and g at n sums f(a)g(b) over ordered positive factors with ab = n.

**Problem.** The Dirichlet convolution of two multiplicative functions is multiplicative. Its series at each prime is the product of the input series at that prime.

**How the definition helps.** Convolution splits each prime exponent between the two factors, just as series multiplication splits a degree (our own argument). Unique prime factorization ensures those choices are independent, so the full sum is the product of the coefficient sums (our own argument).

**Paper or page:** [Dirichlet Convolution Preserves Multiplicativity](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Dirichlet_Convolution_Preserves_Multiplicativity). It says: “Then their Dirichlet convolution f ∗ g is again multiplicative.”

### Prime-power sums multiply to give the Euler product

**Remember:** An Euler product chooses one exponent for each prime.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11M41. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A complex function f on positive integers is multiplicative if f(1) = 1 and f(ab) = f(a)f(b) for every coprime pair a,b. For each prime p, its local factor is the series ∑ₖ≥₀ f(pᵏ).

**Problem.** Suppose f is multiplicative and the sum of \|f(n)\| over positive integers converges. The sum of f(n) then equals the product of its local factors over all primes.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding a finite product chooses one exponent per prime, so unique factorization gives each allowed integer once (our own argument). Absolute convergence lets the finite-prime sums tend to the full sum as more primes are included (our own argument).

**Wikipedia:** [Euler product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_product). It says: “the existence of such a formal Euler product expansion is a necessary and sufficient condition that a(n) be multiplicative”

**Definition.** Define μ(n) as the sum of the primitive nth roots of unity. These are the roots for which n is the least positive power that gives 1. The usual formula gives (−1)ᵏ for a product of k distinct primes, and zero if a prime square divides n.

**Problem.** The sum of μ(d) over all positive divisors d of n is 1 if n = 1 and 0 otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** The primitive-root definition groups the nth roots of unity by their exact orders d dividing n. For n = 1 their sum is 1. For n &gt; 1 the geometric series over powers of a primitive nth root sums to zero (our own). Möbius inversion identifies μ uniquely from these divisor sums (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Möbius function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_function). It says: “each nth root of unity is a primitive dth root of unity for exactly one divisor d of n.”

### Square divisors give a count of squarefree integers

**Remember:** Use Möbius weights on square divisors to count numbers without them.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11N25. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A positive integer is squarefree when no prime square divides it. Its indicator, equal to 1 for squarefree integers and 0 otherwise, sums μ(d) over positive d whose square divides the integer. The Möbius function μ has divisor sum 1 at 1 and 0 at every larger integer.

**Problem.** The fraction of squarefree integers among the first N positive integers tends to 6/π² as N grows.

**How the definition helps.** Summing the indicator counts each square divisor d² once for each of its multiples (our own argument). Dividing by N gives a sum over d ≤ √N with terms μ(d)⌊N/d²⌋/N. Removing the floors costs at most 1/√N in total. Absolute convergence gives the limit ∑ μ(d)/d² = 1/ζ(2), which equals 6/π² by the Euler product and Basel sum.

### The unit group exponent gives Carmichael’s least universal power

**Remember:** The group exponent is the least power that sends every element to one.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11A07. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For n ≥ 2, define λ(n) as the exponent of the group of units modulo n. This is the least positive power that sends every invertible residue to 1. A formula instead computes λ on prime powers and takes their least common multiple.

**Problem.** Every residue a coprime to n raised to λ(n) is 1 modulo n. No smaller positive power works for all such a, and λ(n) divides φ(n). Here φ(n) counts the invertible residues modulo n.

**How the definition helps.** The universal power and its minimality follow from the definition. This power is the least common multiple of the element orders, each of which divides φ(n) by Lagrange’s theorem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Carmichael function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_function). It says: “if λ(n) is considered as defined by the recurrence of the previous section, then it satisfies the property stated in the introduction”

**Sources:**

- [R. D. Carmichael, Note on a new number theory function, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 16 (1910), 232–238](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1910-01892-9)

### The product definition of primes makes factorization unique

**Remember:** A prime that divides a product divides a factor, which you can cancel.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A51 (Factorization; primality), 13F15. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Call an integer p prime if \|p\| &gt; 1 and p divides at least one factor whenever it divides a product. The usual divisor definition requires that p has no divisors except ±1 and ±p. An integer that meets the divisor definition and has \|p\| &gt; 1 is called irreducible.

**Problem.** If a nonzero integer factors into primes, the factorization is unique up to order and signs.

**How the definition helps.** The product definition lets the first prime on one side divide some prime on the other side (our own). Two primes with this divisibility relation differ at most by a sign. Cancel that pair and repeat (our own). The work moves into Euclid’s lemma, which proves the product rule from the usual divisor definition, using Bézout’s identity.

**Wikipedia:** [Euclid's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid%27s_lemma). It says: “It is used to define prime elements, a generalization of prime numbers to arbitrary commutative rings.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A repeating block fixes a quadratic irrational

**Remember:** A repeating tail is a fixed point of its block map.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Read each continued fraction digit a as the map t ↦ a + 1/t. Define the map of a block by composing its digit maps, instead of viewing the block only as a list.

**Problem.** An irrational real number with an eventually periodic regular continued fraction satisfies a quadratic equation with integer coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** The repeating tail t returns to itself under its block map (our own argument). Composing digit maps gives a fraction (At + B)/(Ct + D) with integer coefficients. Positive digits give C &gt; 0, so clearing the denominator gives a quadratic equation. Applying the initial digit maps keeps the irrational result in the same quadratic field.

**Wikipedia:** [Periodic continued fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_continued_fraction). It says: “if x is a regular periodic continued fraction, then x is a quadratic irrational number.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Matrix products give the determinant formula for continued fraction convergents

**Remember:** Multiply digit matrices in order to put consecutive convergents side by side.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a simple continued fraction with integer a₀ and positive integer later digits, let Mᵢ have rows (aᵢ, 1) and (1, 0). Define the rows of M₀⋯Mₙ as (hₙ, hₙ₋₁) and (kₙ, kₙ₋₁), respectively. The fraction hₙ/kₙ is the nth convergent.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, kₙhₙ₋₁ − kₙ₋₁hₙ = (−1)ⁿ. Thus hₙ and kₙ have no common divisor greater than one. Consecutive convergents differ by ±1/(kₙkₙ₋₁).

**How the definition helps.** The matrix product makes the left side the negative of its determinant. Each of the n + 1 factors has determinant −1. The work moves into showing that the matrices give the numerators and denominators of the usual nested fractions. Each matrix represents the map t ↦ aᵢ + 1/t, so composition builds the fraction (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Simple continued fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_continued_fraction). It says: “has determinant (−1)ⁿ⁺¹, and thus belongs to the group of 2 × 2 unimodular matrices GL(2, ℤ).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced quadratic surds are exactly those with purely periodic continued fractions

**Remember:** Above one, with conjugate between minus one and zero, means it repeats immediately.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions), 11R11. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A quadratic surd is ζ = (P + √D)/Q with integers P, Q and D. Here D &gt; 0 is not a square, and Q divides P² − D. The surd is reduced, with conjugate η = (P − √D)/Q, when ζ &gt; 1 and −1 &lt; η &lt; 0.

**Problem.** The continued fraction of a quadratic surd repeats from its first term exactly when the surd is reduced. Then the expansion of −1/η repeats the same block in reverse order.

**How the definition helps.** The inequalities select exactly the surds on which Galois’s pure periodicity theorem applies. On reduced surds, taking the negative reciprocal of the conjugate reverses the continued fraction step and hence the repeating block (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Periodic continued fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_continued_fraction). It says: “Galois proved that the regular continued fraction which represents a quadratic surd ζ is purely periodic if and only if ζ is a reduced surd.”

**Sources:**

- [É. Galois, Démonstration d'un théorème sur les fractions continues périodiques, Annales de Mathématiques pures et appliquées 19 (1828–1829) 294–301](https://www.numdam.org/item/AMPA_1828-1829__19__294_0/)

### The coefficient definition of binomial coefficients gives Lucas’s theorem

**Remember:** Read binomial coefficients as polynomial coefficients, then factor by base-p digits.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B65 (Binomial coefficients; factorials; \\(q\\)-identities), 11A07. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define C(m, n) as the coefficient of Xⁿ in (1 + X)ᵐ for nonnegative integers m and n. The coefficient is zero for n &gt; m. The other definitions count n-element subsets or use the formula m!/(n!(m − n)!) when n ≤ m.

**Problem.** Let p be prime and let mᵢ and nᵢ be the base-p digits of m and n. Then C(m, n) is congruent modulo p to the product of C(mᵢ, nᵢ) over the digit positions.

**How the definition helps.** The coefficient of Xⁿ in (1 + X)ᵐ separates by digit positions (our own explanation). In characteristic p, raising 1 + X to pⁱ gives 1 + X<sup>(pⁱ)</sup>. Thus digit mᵢ contributes the factor (1 + X<sup>(pⁱ)</sup>)<sup>mᵢ</sup>. Unique base-p expansion forces choice nᵢ from that factor, contributing C(mᵢ,nᵢ), including zero when nᵢ &gt; mᵢ.

**Wikipedia:** [Lucas's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%27s_theorem). It says: “Comparing the coefficients of Xⁿ in the very first and last sum, we obtain Lucas's theorem.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Generating functions make Bernoulli polynomial differences telescope to power sums

**Remember:** Shifting x changes the series so its difference has no denominator.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B68 (Bernoulli and Euler numbers and polynomials). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define Bₙ(x) as n! times the coefficient of tⁿ in the power series t exp(xt)/(exp(t) − 1). Another definition requires the integral of Bₙ from x to x + 1 to equal xⁿ.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, Bₙ(x + 1) − Bₙ(x) = nxⁿ⁻¹. For positive integers p and m, the sum of kᵖ from k = 0 to m − 1 equals (Bₚ₊₁(m) − Bₚ₊₁(0))/(p + 1).

**How the definition helps.** The series definition turns the difference at x + 1 and x into multiplication by exp(t) − 1, which cancels the denominator (our own). Comparing coefficients in t exp(xt) proves the difference formula. Summing it cancels all intermediate values and leaves only the two endpoints. To reconcile the definitions, integrate the series from x to x + 1 and compare the result with exp(xt) (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Bernoulli polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_polynomials). It says: “Using either the above integral representation of xⁿ or the identity Bₙ(x + 1) − Bₙ(x) = nxⁿ⁻¹, we have”

### Taking B₁ = +1/2 removes a sign exception from two formulas

**Remember:** Plus one half is what ζ(0) = −1/2 asks for.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B68 (Bernoulli and Euler numbers and polynomials), 11B57. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For n ≥ 0, define Bₙ as n! times the coefficient of tⁿ in t/(1 − exp(−t)). In particular B₁ = +1/2 (our own formulation).

**Problem.** For integers n ≥ 1 and m ≥ 0, define Tₖ = C(m+1,k) Bₖ nᵐ⁺¹⁻ᵏ. Then 1ᵐ + ⋯ + nᵐ equals the sum of Tₖ for 0 ≤ k ≤ m divided by m+1. Also Bₙ = −nζ(1 − n) for every integer n ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** The positive linear coefficient gives the required sign in Faulhaber’s formula for the sum ending at n. The zeta special-value formula uses the same convention because ζ(0) = −1/2 (our own explanation).

**Wikipedia:** [Bernoulli number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_number). It says: “In the above Knuth meant B₁⁻; instead using B₁⁺ the formula avoids subtraction”

- [D. E. Knuth, Johann Faulhaber and sums of powers, Mathematics of Computation (1993)](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1993-1197512-7)

### The generating function makes Bernoulli polynomial reflection one substitution

**Remember:** Reflect x in the Bernoulli generating function and its series variable changes sign.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B68 (Bernoulli and Euler numbers and polynomials). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the Bernoulli polynomial Bₙ(x) as n! times the coefficient of tⁿ in t·exp(tx)/(exp(t) − 1). Another definition sets B₀ = 1 and fixes each later Bₙ by two rules. Its derivative is n·Bₙ₋₁, and its integral over \[0, 1\] is zero.

**Problem.** For every n ≥ 0, Bₙ(1 − x) = (−1)ⁿBₙ(x).

**How the definition helps.** Replacing x by 1 − x gives the same generating function as replacing t by −t (our own argument). Comparing coefficients of tⁿ gives the factor (−1)ⁿ.

**Paper or page:** [Generating Function for Bernoulli Polynomials](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Generating_Function_for_Bernoulli_Polynomials). It says: “Then the generating function for Bₙ is:”

### Change of polynomial basis makes the Stirling matrices inverse

**Remember:** Changing basis back undoes the first change.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B73 (Bell and Stirling numbers), 05A10. arXiv math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The nth falling factorial is x(x − 1)⋯(x − n + 1), with the zeroth equal to 1. Define signed first-kind Stirling numbers by expanding falling factorials in powers of x. Define second-kind Stirling numbers by expanding powers of x in falling factorials.

**Problem.** For any degree bound, the two square tables of Stirling coefficients, from degree zero to that bound, are inverse matrices.

**How the definition helps.** Each table undoes the change of basis made by the other. In our own proof, uniqueness of polynomial coefficients makes their product the identity matrix. Starting from counting definitions requires identifying the coefficients with signed counts of permutations by cycles and with counts of set partitions.

**Paper or page:** [Inverse of Stirling's Triangle expressed as Matrix](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Inverse_of_Stirling's_Triangle_expressed_as_Matrix). It says: “Then: A = B⁻¹ that is: B = A⁻¹”

### Missing labels give the explicit second Stirling formula

**Remember:** Subtract functions that miss labels, then forget the label names.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B73 (Bell and Stirling numbers), 05A10, 05A18. arXiv math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** An onto function uses every target at least once. Define S(n,k) as the number of onto functions from n inputs to k labeled targets divided by k!.

**Problem.** For positive integers n and k, k! S(n,k) equals the sum of (−1)ᵏ⁻ʲ (k choose j) jⁿ over j from 0 through k.

**How the definition helps.** Counting onto functions lets inclusion–exclusion remove functions that miss a target. In our own count, a fixed set of j permitted targets allows jⁿ functions. Forgetting target names turns each onto function into a partition of the inputs, and every partition has k! labelings.

**Wikipedia:** [Stirling numbers of the second kind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling_numbers_of_the_second_kind). It says: “This can be derived by using inclusion-exclusion to count the surjections from n to k”

**Paper or page:** [Sum over k of m choose k by -1<sup>m-k</sup> by k to the n](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Sum_over_k_of_m_choose_k_by_-1^m-k_by_k_to_the_n). It says: “∑ₖ (m choose k) (−1)ᵐ⁻ᵏ kⁿ = m! {n brace m}”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### An integer basis describes all solutions of a linear equation

**Remember:** One basis vector sets the answer and the other leaves it unchanged.

*True by definition.* MSC 11D04 (Linear Diophantine equations), 11A05. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For integers a and b, not both zero, let d be their greatest common divisor. Choose u = (r, s) with ar + bs = d, and put v = (b/d, −a/d). Use integer coordinates h and t to write each pair as hu + tv.

**Problem.** The equation ax + by = c has integer solutions exactly when d divides c. If so, all solution pairs are (c/d)u + tv with t any integer.

**How the definition helps.** In our own coordinates, ax + by becomes hd, so the equation fixes h and leaves t free. Bézout’s identity supplies u. The matrix with columns u and v has determinant −1, so its inverse gives unique integer coordinates for every integer pair.

**Paper or page:** [Solution of Linear Diophantine Equation](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Solution_of_Linear_Diophantine_Equation). It says: “x = x₀ + (b/d)k, y = y₀ − (a/d)k”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Excluding square n gives Pell's equation infinitely many solutions

**Remember:** Exclude square parameters and choose the positive solution with least x.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11D09 (Quadratic and bilinear Diophantine equations), 11A55. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Pell's equation is x² − ny² = 1, with n a given positive integer that is not a perfect square. Its fundamental solution is the solution in positive integers with the smallest x.

**Problem.** For every nonsquare positive n, Pell's equation has a fundamental solution (x₁, y₁). All solutions in positive integers come from xₖ + yₖ√n = (x₁ + y₁√n)ᵏ.

**How the definition helps.** Excluding squares removes the factorization (x − my)(x + my) = 1 for n = m², which forces y = 0 (our own). Lagrange’s theorem on Pell’s equation gives a positive solution for every nonsquare n. Divide any positive solution unit repeatedly by the least one until its value lies between 1 inclusive and that least unit exclusive. Only 1 can remain, since every norm-one unit greater than 1 has positive coefficients (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Pell's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell%27s_equation). It says: “Joseph Louis Lagrange proved that, as long as n is not a perfect square, Pell's equation has infinitely many distinct integer solutions.”

**Sources:**

- [H. W. Lenstra Jr., Solving the Pell equation, Notices of the AMS 49 (2002) 182–192](https://www.ams.org/notices/200202/fea-lenstra.pdf) (link not checked)

### Pell solutions form a group as units of norm one

**Remember:** Norm-one elements multiply, and their conjugates give inverses.

*True by definition.* MSC 11D09 (Quadratic and bilinear Diophantine equations), 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a positive nonsquare integer n, identify each integer pair (x,y) with x + y√n in ℤ\[√n\]. A Pell solution has norm one, meaning that multiplication by its conjugate x − y√n gives x² − ny² = 1.

**Problem.** The Pell solutions form a group under (x, y)(u, v) = (xu + nyv, xv + yu). The identity is (1, 0), and (x, −y) is the inverse of (x, y).

**How the definition helps.** The norm-one definition gives a group because norms multiply and conjugation gives inverses (our own). Instead of checking the group laws on pairs, use multiplication in ℤ\[√n\] (our own). The work moves into checking that conjugation preserves products, which follows from replacing √n by −√n (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Pell's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell%27s_equation). It says: “a pair of integers (x, y) solves Pell's equation if and only if x + y√n is a unit with norm 1 in ℤ\[√n\].”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The determinant of one period gives the Pell sign

**Remember:** Each digit flips the determinant, and the determinant is the Pell norm.

*True by definition.* MSC 11D09 (Quadratic and bilinear Diophantine equations), 11A55. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a nonsquare integer D &gt; 1, let a be √D rounded down. Encode the repeating digit block of t = √D + a by multiplying the matrices \[\[b, 1\], \[1, 0\]\] in digit order. Each matrix represents the digit map u ↦ b + 1/u.

**Problem.** Let x/y be the convergent formed from the first k digits of √D, where k is its shortest period length. Then x² − Dy² equals −1 for odd k and 1 for even k.

**How the definition helps.** Each digit contributes determinant −1, so the period matrix has determinant (−1)ᵏ (our own argument). Its first column is (x + ay, y), since adding a changes only the initial digit. The matrix fixes t, whose quadratic equation is t² − 2at + a² − D = 0. Comparing coefficients gives second column ((D − a²)y, x − ay), so the determinant is x² − Dy².

**Paper or page:** [Solution to Pell's Equation](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Solution_to_Pell's_Equation). It says: “and all solutions of: x² − ny² = ±1 are given in this way.”

**Sources:**

- [H. W. Lenstra Jr., Solving the Pell equation, Algorithmic Number Theory (2008), pp. 1–24](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781139049801.002)

### The quadratic norm makes Pell solutions close approximations

**Remember:** The conjugate of a Pell solution is small because the norm has magnitude one.

*True by definition.* MSC 11D09 (Quadratic and bilinear Diophantine equations), 11A55. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For integers x and y and a positive nonsquare integer D, define the norm of x + y√D as (x + y√D)(x − y√D). It equals x² − Dy².

**Problem.** For positive integer solutions of x² − Dy² = ±1, x/y is a convergent of √D. A convergent is a fraction obtained by stopping its regular continued fraction.

**How the definition helps.** The product definition makes \|x − y√D\| the reciprocal of x + y√D for either sign (our own argument). The approximation error is therefore 1/\[y²(x/y + √D)\]. Since x ≥ y and D ≥ 2, this is less than 1/(2y²). Legendre’s approximation theorem gives the conclusion, since any common divisor of x and y has square dividing 1.

**Paper or page:** [Solution of Pell's Equation is a Convergent](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Solution_of_Pell's_Equation_is_a_Convergent). It says: “Then a/b is a convergent of √n.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Counting Gaussian factors gives the two-square divisor formula

**Remember:** Count Gaussian integers of norm n, one for each ordered pair of coordinates.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11A25, 11D09. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For n &gt; 0, count ordered integer pairs (a,b) satisfying a² + b² = n, including zero and negative coordinates. Equivalently, count Gaussian integers a + bi with norm n, where the norm is a² + b².

**Problem.** Let d₁ and d₃ count positive divisors of n with remainders 1 and 3 modulo 4. For n &gt; 0, the number of pairs is 4(d₁ − d₃).

**How the definition helps.** Counting Gaussian integers turns each representation into independent factor choices and one of four unit choices (our own argument). A prime with remainder 1 modulo 4 splits into conjugate factors, giving e + 1 choices for exponent e. A prime with remainder 3 gives one choice for even e and none otherwise, while 2 always gives one. The divisor difference has these same factors because odd divisor signs multiply and even divisors contribute zero.

**Wikipedia:** [Sum of squares function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sum_of_squares_function). It says: “r₂(n) = 4(d₁(n) − d₃(n))”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Counting representations with order and signs gives Jacobi's four-square formula

**Remember:** Count every sign and every order, and the count is a divisor sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The number r₄(n) counts integer 4-tuples (x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄) with x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₄² = n. Order and signs both count, so r₄(1) = 8.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, r₄(n) is 8 times the sum of the divisors of n that are not divisible by 4. In particular, r₄(p) = 8(p + 1) for a prime p.

**How the definition helps.** Counting every ordered signed tuple gives the coefficient of qⁿ in θ(q)⁴, where θ(q) sums q<sup>(m²)</sup> over all integers m (our own). Jacobi’s four-square identity evaluates this coefficient as eight times the stated divisor sum. For prime p, both divisors 1 and p contribute (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Jacobi's four-square theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi%27s_four-square_theorem). It says: “Two representations are considered different if their terms are in different order or if the integer being squared (not just the square) is different”

**Sources:**

- [M. D. Hirschhorn, A simple proof of Jacobi's four-square theorem, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 101 (1987) 436–438](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9939-1987-0908644-9)

### Gaussian divisors give the two-square theorem for primes

**Remember:** A proper nonunit Gaussian divisor of p has norm p.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11D09. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Gaussian integer is a complex number a + bi with integer coordinates. Its norm, the product with a − bi, is a² + b². Representing p by two squares now means finding a Gaussian integer of norm p.

**Problem.** A prime is a sum of two integer squares exactly when it is 2 or has remainder 1 upon division by 4.

**How the definition helps.** The norm definition turns a two-square representation into a factorization problem (our own argument). For p congruent to 1 modulo 4, the first supplement gives u with u² congruent to −1 modulo p. Then p divides (u + i)(u − i) but neither factor, so Gaussian unique factorization splits p into nonunits, necessarily of norm p. Finally, 2 = 1² + 1², and squares modulo 4 exclude primes with remainder 3.

**Paper or page:** [Fermat's Two Squares Theorem](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Fermat's_Two_Squares_Theorem). It says: “Then p can be expressed as the sum of two squares either: p = 2 or: p ≡ 1 (mod 4)”

**Sources:**

- [L. Euler, Demonstratio theorematis Fermatiani omnem numerum primum formae 4n+1 esse summam duorum quadratorum (1760), E241](https://scholarlycommons.pacific.edu/euler-works/241/)

### Gaussian factorization gives uniqueness for prime two-square sums

**Remember:** Switching Gaussian factors or rotating them does not change the squares.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11D09. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Gaussian integer a + bi has integer coordinates and norm a² + b². Represent p = a² + b² by the factor pair a + bi and a − bi. Gaussian factors agree up to a unit when one is the other multiplied by 1, −1, i, or −i.

**Problem.** If a prime is the sum of two positive squares, the two squares are unique up to order.

**How the definition helps.** Gaussian unique factorization makes the two factors unique up to order and multiplication by units (our own argument). Each factor has prime norm p, so multiplicativity of the norm prevents a split into two nonunits. Multiplication by units and conjugation only change signs or exchange the coordinates.

**Paper or page:** [Fermat's Two Squares Theorem/Uniqueness Lemma](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Fermat's_Two_Squares_Theorem/Uniqueness_Lemma). It says: “Then that expression would be unique except for the order of the two summands.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Gaussian norms force even exponents at primes that stay prime

**Remember:** A Gaussian prime equal to its conjugate appears twice in a norm.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11D09. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** View a² + b² as the norm of the Gaussian integer a + bi, the product of that number with its conjugate. The norm of a product is the product of the norms.

**Problem.** A positive integer is a sum of two integer squares exactly when every prime with remainder 3 modulo 4 has an even exponent.

**How the definition helps.** Writing a sum of squares as a product with its conjugate forces certain prime factors to occur in pairs (our own argument). A prime with remainder 3 modulo 4 stays prime among Gaussian integers and appears equally often in conjugate factors. Conversely, each such even power is a square and hence a norm. Gaussian prime classification supplies norm p for every other prime, and multiplication combines the norms.

**Wikipedia:** [Sum of two squares theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sum_of_two_squares_theorem). It says: “its prime decomposition contains no factor pᵏ, where prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and k is odd.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Quaternion norms show that sums of four squares multiply

**Remember:** Quaternion norms multiply, so sums of four squares multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11R52. arXiv math.NT, math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A quaternion has the form α = a + bi + cj + dk, with real coefficients. Its conjugate ᾱ reverses the signs of i, j and k. Define the squared norm N(α) = αᾱ, which equals a² + b² + c² + d².

**Problem.** A product of two sums of four real squares is again a sum of four squares. If both inputs use integers, the resulting squares also use integers.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying quaternions multiplies their squared norms. Conjugation reverses products, and ββ̄ is real, so αββ̄ᾱ = N(β)N(α) (our own). The four coefficients of αβ give the required squares and are integers when the input coefficients are integers (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Euler's four-square identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_four-square_identity). It says: “the absolute value of the product of two quaternions is equal to the product of their absolute values”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A half-open lattice cell turns Blichfeldt’s theorem into overlap

**Remember:** Fold the set into one cell and count overlaps.

*True by definition.* MSC 11H16 (Nonconvex bodies). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A full lattice in Euclidean space consists of all integer combinations of a basis. Its half-open cell consists of combinations of that basis with coefficients in \[0, 1). Each point belongs to exactly one lattice translate of the cell.

**Problem.** For a full lattice, every bounded measurable set of volume greater than the cell volume contains two distinct points differing by a lattice vector.

**How the definition helps.** The half-open cell gives each point exactly one translated copy inside a common region of known volume. Cut the set along cell boundaries and translate each piece back into the cell. Translation preserves volume, so the pieces must overlap if their volumes add to more than the cell volume. Points from different pieces that land together differ by a nonzero lattice vector (our own formulation).

**Wikipedia:** [Blichfeldt's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blichfeldt%27s_theorem). It says: “translate each of those pieces by an integer vector so that they all move into the same unit square.”

**Sources:**

- [H. F. Blichfeldt, A new principle in the geometry of numbers, with some applications, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 15, 227–235 (1914).](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1914-1500976-6)

### Scaled errors make convergents optimal below the next denominator

**Remember:** Multiply the approximation error by the denominator to get the absolute linear error.

*True by definition.* MSC 11J70 (Continued fractions and generalizations), 11A55. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A convergent is a fraction obtained by stopping a regular continued fraction. For a rational approximation a/b to an irrational number x, define its scaled error as \|bx − a\|.

**Problem.** Let p/q and P/Q be successive convergents with q &lt; Q. Among integer pairs (a,b) with 0 &lt; b &lt; Q, the pair (p,q) minimizes the scaled error.

**How the definition helps.** Scaling makes bx − a linear in the integer pair, so its values combine under addition (our own argument). The determinant ±1 makes (p,q) and (P,Q) an integer basis, and their signed errors have opposite signs. When 0 &lt; b &lt; Q, two nonzero coefficients must have opposite signs, so their error contributions add in magnitude. With just one coefficient, the pair is a positive multiple of (p,q).

**Paper or page:** [Convergents are Best Approximations](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Convergents_are_Best_Approximations). It says: “\|qₙ x − pₙ\| ≤ \|b x − a\|”

### The next complete quotient gives the exact convergent error

**Remember:** Keep the whole tail, and subtraction leaves the determinant.

*True by definition.* MSC 11J70 (Continued fractions and generalizations), 11A55. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A convergent is the fraction obtained by stopping a regular continued fraction after finitely many digits. The next complete quotient t is the full remaining tail, starting with the next digit. For successive convergents r/s and p/q, retaining that tail gives x = (pt + r)/(qt + s).

**Problem.** For irrational x, the error \|x − p/q\| equals 1/\[q(qt + s)\]. It is smaller than 1/(qQ), where Q is the next denominator.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping the tail makes the numerator collapse when we subtract p/q (our own argument). The convergent recurrences give the tail formula and \|qr − ps\| = 1. The next denominator is q times the integer part of t, plus s. Since t is irrational, this denominator is smaller than qt + s.

**Paper or page:** [Bound for Difference of Irrational Number with Convergent](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Bound_for_Difference_of_Irrational_Number_with_Convergent). It says: “\|x − Cₙ\| &lt; 1/(qₙ qₙ₊₁)”

### Continuous averages reduce equidistribution to individual Fourier waves

**Remember:** Test each wave, then approximate every continuous test by sums of waves.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K06 (General theory of distribution modulo \\(1\\)), 42A10. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A real sequence is equidistributed modulo one if its sample averages for every continuous 1-periodic function tend to that function’s integral over \[0,1\]. Each sample average uses the first N sequence terms, with N tending to infinity.

**Problem.** A real sequence is equidistributed modulo one exactly when its sample averages of exp(2πikx) tend to zero for every nonzero integer k.

**How the definition helps.** With continuous test functions, it suffices to check a dense family of finite wave sums (our own). Fejér’s theorem gives uniform approximation, and continuous upper and lower approximations to interval indicators recover the counting definition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Theorem 1.2 (Weyl's criterion)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06909v1). It says: “Then (xₙ) is uniformly distributed mod 1 if and only if for every non-zero v ∈ ℤᵏ, lim as N → ∞ of (1/N) ∑ₙ₌₁ᴺ e(v·xₙ) = 0,”

### Primitive characters make every Gauss sum have absolute value √N

**Remember:** A primitive character on units factors through no smaller divisor modulus.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a Dirichlet character χ modulo N, define G(χ) = ∑ χ(a)exp(2πia/N), summing over all residues a modulo N. Call χ primitive if each proper positive divisor d of N admits two units congruent modulo d with different χ-values.

**Problem.** For every primitive Dirichlet character χ modulo N, \|G(χ)\| = √N. So G(χ) is never zero, and formulas may divide by it.

**How the definition helps.** Primitivity gives the Gauss sum identity G<sub>b</sub> = χ̄(b)G(χ) for every Fourier coefficient G<sub>b</sub>, including nonunit frequencies (our own). Finite Parseval gives ∑\|G<sub>b</sub>\|² = Nφ(N), while the identity gives φ(N)\|G(χ)\|². The principal character modulo 4 factors through modulus 1 and has Gauss sum i − i = 0 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sum), [Dirichlet character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_character). It says: “If χ is also primitive, then \|G(χ)\|=√N, in particular, it is nonzero.”

### The character form makes conjugation of the Gauss sum a sign

**Remember:** Conjugate the exponential and the Legendre symbol supplies the sign.

*True by definition.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations), 11A15. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p, set ζ = exp(2πi/p). Give each residue a weight χ(a), equal to 0 at zero, 1 at nonzero squares, and −1 elsewhere. Define the quadratic Gauss sum G as the sum of χ(a)ζᵃ over all residues modulo p.

**Problem.** The quadratic Gauss sum satisfies G² = χ(−1)p.

**How the definition helps.** In the weighted sum, conjugation replaces a by −a and multiplies G by χ(−1) (our own argument). Counting square roots and using the zero sum of all powers ζ⁰ through ζᵖ⁻¹ gives the usual sum of ζ raised to a². The magnitude theorem gives G times its conjugate as p, which yields the stated square.

**nLab:** [quadratic reciprocity law](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quadratic+reciprocity+law). It says: “S² = (−1/p) p.”

### Euler’s product shows zeta has no zeros where Re s &gt; 1

**Remember:** A product of nonzero factors with summable logarithms is not zero.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Problem.** The Riemann zeta function has no zero in the half-plane Re s &gt; 1.

**How the definition helps.** The Euler product is the exponential of an absolutely convergent sum, so it cannot vanish (our own). For σ = Re(s) &gt; 1, the logarithms from the power series for −log(1 − p⁻ˢ) are bounded in magnitude by 2p⁻σ. Summability follows by comparison with ∑ₙ≥₂ n⁻σ (our own). Euler’s product formula identifies this product with the usual zeta series.

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function). It says: “Both sides of the Euler product formula converge for Re(s) &gt; 1.”

**How the definition helps.** The coefficient definition makes the series for σₖ the product of the series for 1 and nᵏ. Grouping terms whose indices multiply to n recovers the usual divisor-sum definition of convolution. The work moves into justifying that order of summation for actual complex s, where both series converge absolutely (our own).

### Setting p(0) = 1 makes partition formulas work without special cases

**Remember:** Zero has exactly one partition: the empty one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P81 (Elementary theory of partitions), 05A17. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For any integer n, p(n) counts finite multisets of positive integers with sum n. The empty multiset gives p(0) = 1, and no multiset has negative sum.

**Wikipedia:** [Partition function (number theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28number_theory%29). It says: “As base cases, p(0) is taken to equal 1, and p(k) is taken to be zero for negative k.”

**Problem.** An odd prime number p stays prime in the Gaussian integers exactly when it leaves remainder 3 on division by 4.

**How the definition helps.** Presenting the ring by x² + 1 reduces primality of p to whether that quadratic is irreducible modulo p (our own). Indeed, the quotient by p has no zero divisors exactly when the quadratic has no root modulo p (our own). The remaining number theory says that −1 is a square modulo an odd prime exactly when the prime leaves remainder 1 modulo 4 (our own).

### Primitive roots give the cyclotomic factorization of xⁿ − 1

**Remember:** Group the roots by the first positive power that gives one.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R18 (Cyclotomic extensions), 11C08. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Problem.** For every n ≥ 1, xⁿ − 1 is the product of Φₐ over all positive divisors a of n. The degree of Φₙ is φ(n), the number of integers from 1 to n coprime to n.

**How the definition helps.** The primitive-root definition groups the linear factors of xⁿ − 1 by the least positive power that gives 1. That power divides n, and each root occurs once. Counting the roots exp(2πik/n) with k coprime to n gives the degree. The work moves into proving that Φₙ is irreducible over ℚ, so the two definitions agree.

### With p-adic integers as residue sequences, compatible residue roots give roots

**Remember:** A polynomial vanishes when it vanishes in every coordinate.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S05 (Polynomials), 12J25. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Fix a prime p. A p-adic integer is a sequence of residues aₙ modulo pⁿ satisfying aₙ₊₁ ≡ aₙ modulo pⁿ for every n ≥ 1. Add and multiply sequences coordinate by coordinate.

**Problem.** Let f be a polynomial with p-adic integer coefficients. Then f has a p-adic root exactly when there are roots rₙ of f modulo pⁿ with rₙ₊₁ ≡ rₙ modulo pⁿ for every n.

**How the definition helps.** With the residue-sequence definition, a compatible sequence of roots is itself a root (our own). The ring operations act on each residue separately, so f of the sequence is the sequence of the values f(rₙ), which are zero (our own). Reducing a p-adic root gives the converse (our own). The work moves to proving that this ring agrees with the metric completion (our own).

### Frobenius restriction gives quadratic reciprocity for Legendre symbols

**Remember:** Restrict Frobenius from the field of roots of unity to its quadratic subfield.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 11R32, 11R18. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For distinct odd primes p,q, take L = ℚ(ζₚ) with ζₚ a primitive pth root of unity. Put K = ℚ(√p\*), where p\* is the sign choice of p congruent to 1 modulo 4. At a prime ideal of L above q, Frobenius is the unique automorphism inducing the qth-power map on its residue field.

**Problem.** For distinct odd primes p and q, (q/p) = (p\*/q). Here the usual Legendre symbol distinguishes nonzero squares from nonsquares modulo its denominator.

**How the definition helps.** Frobenius on L restricts to Frobenius on its quadratic subfield K. The cyclotomic action raises ζₚ to q, and the squares modulo p fix K, giving sign (q/p) (our own explanation). The quadratic action on √p\* gives sign (p\*/q). The quadratic subfield theorem identifies K, for example by a quadratic Gauss sum (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Proofs of quadratic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proofs_of_quadratic_reciprocity). It says: “The key fact about φ that we need is that for any subfield K of L, φ fixes K ⟺ q splits completely in K.”

**Paper or page:** [An Infinitely Large Napkin: Alg Nt: Frobenius](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “For distinct odd primes p, q we have (p/q) = (q\*/p).”

### Group transfer turns Gauss’s lemma into a power formula

**Remember:** Gauss’s sign is the transfer, and the transfer is a power.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 20K01. arXiv math.NT, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For odd prime p and a nonzero residue a, choose one representative from each pair {x,−x} of nonzero residues. For each representative r, write ar = εᵣs modulo p, where s represents its image pair and εᵣ is ±1. The transfer of a is the product of these signs.

**Problem.** Let p be an odd prime and let p not divide a. Gauss’s lemma says (a/p) = (−1)ᵐ, where m counts the least positive residues of a, 2a, …, ((p − 1)/2)a above p/2. Here (a/p) is +1 for a square modulo p and −1 otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying the equations ar = εᵣs cancels the representatives, since multiplication by a permutes their pairs (our own). The sign product therefore equals a raised to (p − 1)/2 modulo p. Using representatives 1 through (p − 1)/2 gives one negative sign for each residue above p/2. Euler’s criterion identifies the product with (a/p).

**Wikipedia:** [Gauss's lemma (number theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_lemma_%28number_theory%29). It says: “Gauss's lemma may then be viewed as a computation that explicitly identifies this homomorphism as being the quadratic residue character.”
