### Primary Eisenstein integers make cubic reciprocity plain symmetry

**Remember:** Choose the associate that is ±2 mod 3, then cubic symbols swap.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 11R18. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An Eisenstein integer is a + bω for integers a,b and a primitive cube root of unity ω. An Eisenstein integer coprime to 3 is primary if it is congruent to 2 or −2 modulo 3.

**Problem.** If α and β are primary and coprime, then the cubic residue symbols satisfy (α/β)₃ = (β/α)₃. Among λ, ωλ and ω²λ, one is primary whenever the norm of λ is coprime to 3.

**How the definition helps.** A primary numerator removes the possible cube-root-of-unity correction in Eisenstein’s cubic reciprocity law (our own explanation). The six units have distinct residues modulo 3, so exactly one rotation by 1, ω or ω² has residue ±2. The remaining sign has no effect because −1 is a cube (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cubic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_reciprocity). It says: “A number is primary if it is coprime to 3 and congruent to an ordinary integer modulo (1−ω)², which is the same as saying it is congruent to ±2 modulo 3.”

**How the definition helps.** The four units represent the four invertible residues modulo (1 + i)³, so exactly one unit multiple is congruent to 1 (our own). This fixes both numerators when quartic reciprocity interchanges the primes. Gauss’s quartic reciprocity law then supplies the sign for those primary representatives (our own explanation).

Partial summation and the lower-order contribution of higher prime powers give the equivalence with the prime number theorem (our own).

The count stays positive, and intersecting the large characters’ kernels costs at most one dimension per character.

### The stabilizer of a sumset extends Cauchy–Davenport to all abelian groups

**Remember:** Measure sumsets against their stabilizer, and subgroups stop being counterexamples.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B13 (Additive bases, including sumsets), 11P70. arXiv math.CO, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For finite nonempty sets A,B in an abelian group, define A + B = {a + b ∣ a∈A, b∈B}. Its stabilizer K consists of all group elements g such that (A + B) + g = A + B.

**Problem.** Kneser's theorem bounds \|A + B\| from below for finite nonempty sets A and B in any abelian group. With K the stabilizer, it says \|A + B\| ≥ \|A + K\| + \|B + K\| − \|K\|.

**How the definition helps.** The stabilizer records the whole period subgroup, so Kneser’s theorem uses one bound for both periodic and aperiodic sumsets. For A = B = H a finite subgroup, K = H and the bound gives equality (our own example).

### Balanced indicators expose missing progressions

**Remember:** Subtract the density before looking for missing patterns.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a cyclic group of prime order N, let A have density α = \|A\|/N. Define its balanced indicator at x as 1 − α for x in A and −α otherwise.

**Problem.** Fix k≥3, with N≥k and Nαᵏ⁻¹≥2. If A contains no k-term progression with nonzero difference, its balanced indicator has Gowers norm of order k−1 at least αᵏ/(2k).

**How the definition helps.** Centering turns a missing progression into a discrepancy from the count for the constant function α (our own argument). With only zero differences, the normalized count equals α/N, at most αᵏ/2. Replacing each indicator in turn by α expresses the discrepancy as k terms. The generalized von Neumann inequality bounds each term by the balanced indicator’s norm.

**Paper or page:** [An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014). It says: “Let k ≥ 3, let G be a finite additive group with (N,(k−1)!) = 1”

**Sources:**

- [Ben Green and Terence Tao, An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm, arXiv:math/0503014v4](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014)

### Centered Fourier uniformity counts three-term progressions

**Remember:** Remove the constant term so Fourier coefficients measure the counting error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A have density δ in a finite abelian group G of size n. For each homomorphism χ from G to the complex unit circle, average (1ₐ−δ) times the conjugate of χ. Here 1ₐ is the indicator of A. Call A Fourier ε-uniform if every such average has modulus at most ε.

**Problem.** Suppose n is odd and A is Fourier ε-uniform. The number of pairs (x,r) with x, x+r and x+2r in A differs from δ³n² by at most εn².

**How the definition helps.** Centering removes the constant Fourier coefficient, leaving only terms that measure the counting error (our own explanation). In the Fourier expansion, each nonconstant term uses frequencies χ, χ and χ⁻². Odd order makes χ⁻² nonconstant whenever χ is nonconstant. Uniformity bounds that factor by ε, and Parseval’s identity bounds the sum of the other squared moduli by one.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “Let G be an additive group of odd order and suppose A ⊆ G is Fourier ε-uniform.”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)

### Coset averages absorb large Fourier coefficients

**Remember:** A character survives coset averaging exactly when it is trivial on the subspace.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a subspace H of the vector space 𝔽ₚⁿ over the field of prime order p, define g(x) as the mean of f on x+H. This coset average preserves the range \[0,1\]. A normalized Fourier coefficient averages a function times the conjugate of a character, a homomorphism to the unit circle.

**Problem.** For every f from 𝔽ₚⁿ to \[0,1\] and ε&gt;0, there is a subspace H of codimension at most ε⁻². Every normalized Fourier coefficient of f minus its coset model has modulus at most ε.

**How the definition helps.** Coset averaging preserves selected frequencies while keeping the model bounded, which truncating a Fourier series need not do (our own explanation). Intersect the kernels of the characters whose coefficients exceed ε in modulus. Parseval bounds their number by ε⁻², so at most that many independent linear conditions define H. Character orthogonality shows that averaging preserves these coefficients and either preserves or kills every other coefficient.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “being a linear combination of at most 1/ε² characters with coefficients bounded in magnitude by 1”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)
- [Fox and Zhao, Removal lemmas and approximate homomorphisms, Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 31 (2022), Lemma 5.2](https://doi.org/10.1017/s0963548321000572)

### Cube products yield the triangle inequality

**Remember:** Expand the cube of a sum, then bound each mixed cube.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Choose x and d steps independently and uniformly in a finite abelian group. Multiply the complex function values at x plus each subset sum of the steps, conjugating values for odd-sized subsets. The Gowers Uᵈ norm is the 2ᵈ-th root of the mean product.

**Problem.** For d ≥ 2, the Gowers Uᵈ norm of f+g is at most the sum of their Gowers Uᵈ norms.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding the cube product for f+g gives a term for every assignment of f or g to its vertices (our own). The Gowers–Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bounds each averaged term by the product of its vertex norms. Summing gives (‖f‖ᵤᵈ + ‖g‖ᵤᵈ) raised to 2ᵈ, and taking the root proves the inequality.

**Paper or page:** [Parseval-type identities for Gowers uniformity norms in finite abelian groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08968). It says: “Then we have ‖f₀+f₁‖(Uᴬ˒ˡ) ≤ ‖f₀‖(Uᴬ˒ˡ)+‖f₁‖(Uᴬ˒ˡ).”

**Sources:**

- [Martin Niepel, Parseval-type identities for Gowers uniformity norms in finite abelian groups, arXiv:2508.08968v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08968)

### Fourier moments expose large coefficients

**Remember:** A large fourth moment needs a large coefficient when the second moment is bounded.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be real on a finite abelian group. A character χ is a homomorphism to the complex unit circle. Its Fourier coefficient f̂(χ) is the mean of f times the conjugate of χ. Define the U² norm as the fourth root of the sum of \|f̂(χ)\|⁴ over all characters.

**Problem.** If δ ≥ 0, \|f\| ≤ 1 and the U² norm of f is at least δ, some character χ satisfies \|f̂(χ)\| ≥ δ².

**How the definition helps.** The fourth moment directly bounds the largest coefficient when the second moment is bounded (our own argument). Indeed, the fourth moment is at most the largest squared modulus times the second moment. Parseval’s identity makes the second moment equal to the mean of \|f\|². The usual definition averages products over parallelograms, and character orthogonality proves the two formulas agree.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “‖f‖(U²(G)) = ‖f̂‖(ℓ⁴(Ĝ)).”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)

### Independence keeps entropic distance nonnegative

**Remember:** An independent difference cannot have less entropy than either summand.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite distribution with positive probabilities p, its entropy H is the sum of −p log p over its outcomes. Draw independent samples X′ and Y′ from two given distributions on an abelian group. Their entropic Ruzsa distance is H(X′ − Y′) − (H(X′) + H(Y′))/2.

**Problem.** Entropic Ruzsa distance is nonnegative for any two finitely supported distributions on an abelian group.

**How the definition helps.** Independent sampling rules out cancellation from using the same fair bit twice, which would give distance −log 2 (our own example). Conditioning on one draw leaves the entropy of the other unchanged in the difference. Conditioning cannot increase entropy, so the difference has entropy at least the larger individual entropy and hence at least their mean.

**Paper or page:** [Marton's Conjecture in abelian groups with bounded torsion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02244v2). It says: “if X,Y are independent, then H\[X\], H\[Y\] are both at most H\[X ± Y\].”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Multiplicative differences expose Fourier structure

**Remember:** A large cube average forces many differences with large Fourier coefficients.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a complex function f on a finite abelian group, its multiplicative difference Δₕf(x) is f(x+h) times the conjugate of f(x). Define ‖f‖ᵤ₃⁸ as the mean over h of ‖Δₕf‖ᵤ₂⁴. For any g, ‖g‖ᵤ₂⁴ sums the fourth powers of its normalized Fourier coefficient moduli.

**Problem.** Let \|f\|≤1 and ‖f‖ᵤ₃≥η&gt;0. For at least a fraction η⁸/2 of the shifts h, some normalized Fourier coefficient of Δₕf has modulus at least η⁴/√2.

**How the definition helps.** The recursive definition exposes an average of Fourier moments directly (our own argument). Each moment is at most one, so a fraction at least η⁸/2 of the shifts must reach η⁸/2. Parseval bounds the sum of squared coefficient moduli by one. The fourth moment therefore forces one coefficient to reach η⁴/√2.

**Paper or page:** [An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014). It says: “Let G be an arbitrary finite additive group, and let f : G → 𝒟 be a bounded function”

**Sources:**

- [Ben Green and Terence Tao, An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm, arXiv:math/0503014v4](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014)

### Quadratic phases preserve cube norms

**Remember:** A quadratic phase cancels across the eight cube vertices.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An additive difference replaces P(x) by P(x + h) − P(x) for a chosen step h. Call exp(2πiP) a quadratic phase if P takes values modulo 1 and every third additive difference vanishes. The eighth power of the Gowers U³ norm averages products over x and three independent uniform steps. Include all eight subset sums of the steps added to x, conjugating the function values from odd-sized subsets.

**Problem.** On a finite abelian group, multiplying a function by a quadratic phase does not change its Gowers U³ norm.

**How the definition helps.** Defining quadratic phases by differences makes their eight factors cancel inside the norm. In our own calculation their product is the exponential of a signed third difference, hence equals 1. This avoids choosing coefficients for a quadratic formula. The cited representation theorem identifies these difference-defined phases with explicit quadratic formulas on groups of odd order.

**Paper or page:** [An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014v4). It says: “Conversely, all such functions x ↦ Mx · x + ξ · x + c are globally quadratic phase functions.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regular Bohr sets absorb small shifts

**Remember:** Small changes in radius control small shifts.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a finite abelian group, a character sends sums to products on the unit circle. A Bohr set B contains the elements that d chosen characters all send within distance r of 1. Call B regular if scaling r by 1 + t changes its size by at most 100d\|t\| times its original size. Require this for d ≥ 1 and \|t\| ≤ 1/(100d).

**Problem.** Take 0 &lt; ρ &lt; 1 and a shift x from the Bohr set with radius ρr. The uniform probabilities on B and B + x differ by at most 200ρd when we sum their absolute differences.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity bounds the size gained when the radius expands to (1 + ρ)r (our own proof). The enlarged set contains both B and B + x, so their symmetric difference has size at most twice the gain. For 100ρd ≤ 1, dividing by \|B\| gives the required bound. Otherwise 200ρd &gt; 2, and the sum of absolute probability differences is at most 2.

**Paper or page:** [Sparse graph counting and Kelley-Meka bounds for binary systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12248v5). It says: “If B is a regular Bohr set of rank d”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Zero extension removes the ambient modulus

**Remember:** Divide by the interval’s cube norm to cancel the ambient group.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For positive integers N,d,M with d ≥ 2 and M &gt; 2ᵈN, extend f on {1,…,N} by zero to ℤ/Mℤ. Multiply its values at x plus each subset sum of d steps, conjugating values for odd-sized subsets. Average over independent uniform x and steps, take the 2ᵈ-th root, and divide by the corresponding root for the interval indicator.

**Problem.** For d ≥ 2, this normalized interval norm is independent of the choice of M &gt; 2ᵈN.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by the indicator’s norm cancels the proportion of cubes inside the interval (our own explanation). Without that division, the average includes zeros from cubes outside the interval. Each surviving step lifts to the integer difference between its endpoint and the base point. The bound on M ensures that every lifted vertex agrees with its interval representative.

**Wikipedia:** [Gowers norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gowers_norm). It says: “This definition does not depend on Ñ, as long as Ñ &gt; 2ᵈN.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Discrete logarithms build Sidon sets

**Remember:** Equal exponent sums give equal products of monic linear factors at θ.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B75 (Other combinatorial number theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let q be a prime power and h ≥ 2. Choose a generator θ of the multiplicative group of the field with qʰ elements. For each λ in its subfield with q elements, record the exponent a modulo qʰ − 1 such that θᵃ = θ − λ.

**Problem.** The q exponents form a Sidon set of order h in the cyclic group of order q raised to h minus 1. This means an h-term sum, with repeats allowed, determines its summands up to order.

**How the definition helps.** Equal exponent sums give equal products of h monic linear factors at θ (our own proof). Their difference has degree below h, while θ has degree h over the smaller field. The difference must vanish identically, and unique factorization recovers every factor with its multiplicity.

**Paper or page:** [The Bose-Chowla argument for Sidon sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12711v3). It says: “is a classical Sidon set of order h modulo qʰ − 1 and cardinality q.”

**Sources:**

- [Melvyn B. Nathanson, The Bose–Chowla argument for Sidon sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12711v3)

### Positive genus makes Siegel's theorem on integral points exclude Pell equations

**Remember:** Genus at least one, or three points at infinity, means finitely many integer points.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11D45 (Counting solutions of Diophantine equations), 14G05, 14H25. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a smooth geometrically integral affine curve C over a number field, take its smooth projective completion. Its genus is the dimension of the space of regular differentials on that completion. Its points at infinity are the geometric points of the completion outside C (our own formulation).

**Problem.** Fix an affine embedding of C and call its points integral when all coordinates lie in the number field’s ring of integers. C has finitely many integral points if its genus is positive or it has genus zero and at least three points at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** The two cases combine into 2g − 2 + s &gt; 0 for genus g and s geometric points at infinity (our own). Siegel’s theorem gives finiteness under that condition. The affine line and the Pell curve x² − 2y² = 1 have genus zero and respectively one and two missing points (our own). Both have infinitely many integer points.

**Wikipedia:** [Siegel's theorem on integral points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel%27s_theorem_on_integral_points). It says: “The condition is sharp. A curve of genus zero with one or two points at infinity can have infinitely many integral points”

**Sources:**

- [C. L. Siegel, On some applications of Diophantine approximations, trans. C. Fuchs, ed. U. Zannier, Quaderni/Monographs 2, Edizioni della Normale, 2014 (German original 1929)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-88-7642-520-2)

### Degree at least 3 and irreducibility make Thue equations finite

**Remember:** Equate an irreducible homogeneous binary form of degree at least three to a nonzero rational.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11D57 (Multiplicative and norm form equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Thue equation is f(x,y) = r for a nonzero rational r and a homogeneous binary polynomial f over ℚ. The polynomial must be irreducible over ℚ and have degree at least three.

**Problem.** Thue proved in 1909 that a Thue equation has only finitely many integer solutions. Later work gives explicit bounds for the solutions.

**How the definition helps.** The degree condition excludes Pell’s equation x² − 2y² = 1, which has infinitely many integer solutions (our own). Irreducibility excludes (x − y)³ = 1, whose solutions include every pair (y + 1,y) (our own). Thue’s approximation theorem gives finiteness by bounding exceptionally close rational approximations to roots of f(t,1). Baker’s effective bounds for linear forms in logarithms give explicit solution bounds (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Thue equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thue_equation). It says: “where f is an irreducible bivariate homogeneous polynomial of degree at least 3 over the rational numbers, and r is a nonzero rational number.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Thue, Über Annäherungswerte algebraischer Zahlen, J. reine angew. Math. 135 (1909) 284–305](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1909.135.284)
- [E. Bombieri and W. M. Schmidt, On Thue's equation, Invent. Math. 88 (1987) 69–81](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01405092)

### Hilbert symbols complete local classification

**Remember:** Multiply one Hilbert sign for each pair of diagonal coefficient positions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11E08 (Quadratic forms over local rings and fields), 11E95. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over the p-adic numbers ℚₚ, write a nonsingular quadratic form as a sum of squares with nonzero coefficients. The Hilbert symbol (a,b) equals 1 if z² = ax² + by² has a nonzero solution over ℚₚ, and −1 otherwise. The Hasse invariant multiplies these signs over all unordered pairs of distinct coefficient positions.

**Problem.** Two nondegenerate quadratic forms over ℚₚ are isometric exactly when their dimensions, determinant square classes, and Hasse invariants agree.

**How the definition helps.** The extra sign retains the interactions between coefficients that the determinant loses (our own). Over ℚ₃, the diagonal triples (1, 1, 1) and (1, 3, 3) have equal determinant square classes (our own). Their Hasse invariants differ because the symbol of (3, 3) is −1 over ℚ₃ (our own). The local classification theorem does the work of proving that no further invariant is needed (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The density of integral quadratic forms having a k-dimensional totally isotropic subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10495v1), [The density of integral quadratic forms having a k-dimensional totally isotropic subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10495v1). It says: “This is independent of the choice of diagonal form.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Hilbert symbol turns quadratic reciprocity into one product formula

**Remember:** At each place, the Hilbert symbol asks whether a conic has a point.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E08 (Quadratic forms over local rings and fields), 11S31, 11A15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A place v of ℚ is either a prime p or the real place ∞. The completion ℚᵥ is then the p-adic numbers ℚₚ or the real numbers ℝ. For nonzero a and b, the Hilbert symbol (a,b)ᵥ is 1 if ax² + by² = z² has a nonzero solution in ℚᵥ. Otherwise it is −1.

**Problem.** For nonzero rationals a,b, the symbol (a,b)ᵥ equals 1 at all but finitely many places v. Its product over all places is 1. This formula contains quadratic reciprocity and its two supplementary laws.

**How the definition helps.** The symbol is defined at every place, including the real place and the prime 2, so the whole law fits into one symmetric formula. In words, the conic ax² + by² = z² fails to have a point at an even number of places. The supplementary laws come from the factors at 2 and at the real place. The definition makes the law easy to state, not easy to prove: over ℚ the usual proof of the product formula uses quadratic reciprocity itself.

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_symbol). It says: “Therefore, the following product formula ∏ᵥ (a,b)ᵥ = 1 makes sense. It is equivalent to the law of quadratic reciprocity.”

**Sources:**

- [J. Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, Springer (1999), p. 334](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-03983-0)

### Hyperbolic planes localize Witt indices

**Remember:** Count the largest number of hyperbolic planes that split off together.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E12 (Quadratic forms over global rings and fields), 11E81. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A hyperbolic plane over a field is the binary quadratic form xy. The Witt index of Q is the largest number of hyperbolic planes occurring together in an orthogonal decomposition of Q over that field.

**Problem.** For a nonsingular quadratic form over a number field, its Witt index equals the smallest of its Witt indices over all completions of the field.

**How the definition helps.** Counting planes lets us repeat the local test for a single nonzero zero (our own). If every completion has one, the Hasse–Minkowski theorem gives one over the number field (our own). It supplies a hyperbolic plane, which splits off over the number field and every completion (our own). Witt cancellation lowers all the indices by one, so induction gives the minimum formula (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The density of integral quadratic forms having a k-dimensional totally isotropic subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10495v1), [The density of integral quadratic forms having a k-dimensional totally isotropic subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10495v1). It says: “If (V₁,Q) and (V₂,Q) are regular and isometric, then (V₁⊥,Q) and (V₂⊥,Q) are also isometric.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Spinor genera classify indefinite forms

**Remember:** A spinor genus remembers which local rotations lift.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E12 (Quadratic forms over global rings and fields), 11E41. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix integral lattices in one nonsingular rational quadratic space. A rotation is a linear map preserving the form with determinant one. Two lattices share a proper spinor genus if a rational rotation followed by local rotations matches them over every ring of p-adic integers. Each local rotation must lift to the spin group, the algebraic double cover of the rotation group.

**Problem.** A proper spinor genus of a nondegenerate indefinite integral form of rank at least three has exactly one proper integral isometry class.

**How the definition helps.** The spinor genus restricts local rotations to ones that strong approximation can match on the lattices (our own). Indefiniteness makes the real spin group noncompact (our own). Strong approximation supplies one rational spin rotation with all the required local lattice images (our own). The resulting rational rotation identifies the integral lattices because their local images agree at every prime (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Spinor genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinor_genus). It says: “An important result is that for indefinite forms of dimension at least three, each spinor genus contains exactly one proper equivalence class.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Genus equivalence becomes a square test

**Remember:** Compare forms over the reals and every p-adic integer ring to test genus.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms), 11E41. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a negative fundamental discriminant D and take primitive positive definite integral binary forms of discriminant D. Proper classes use determinant-one integral changes of variables and multiply by Gauss composition. Two classes share a genus if their forms are properly equivalent over ℝ and over ℤₚ for every prime p.

**Problem.** Two classes are in the same genus exactly when the first composed with the inverse of the second is a square in the class group.

**How the definition helps.** Gauss’s genus characters multiply under composition and distinguish genera by their joint values (our own). Two classes have equal values precisely when their quotient lies in the principal genus. Gauss’s principal genus theorem identifies this subgroup with the squares.

**Wikipedia:** [Genus of a quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus_of_a_quadratic_form). It says: “The principal genus, the genus containing the principal form, is precisely the subgroup C²”

### Letting the middle coefficient be odd matches form discriminants with fields

**Remember:** Allow odd middle coefficients, and every quadratic field has its forms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Gauss studied forms ax² + 2bxy + cy² with an even middle coefficient. Eisenstein's convention allows every integer form ax² + bxy + cy², with discriminant b² − 4ac. A fundamental discriminant is a square-free D ≡ 1 mod 4, or 4m with m square-free and ≡ 2 or 3 mod 4.

**Problem.** For each fundamental discriminant D ≠ 1 there is exactly one quadratic field of discriminant D. Its narrow class group is isomorphic to the class group of primitive forms of discriminant D. For D &lt; 0 one uses only positive definite forms.

**How the definition helps.** With odd middle coefficients allowed, the norm forms of all quadratic fields are integer forms of the field's own discriminant (our own). For example, the ring of integers of ℚ(√−3) has norm form x² + xy + y², which Gauss's even convention does not allow (our own). Under that convention no discriminant D ≡ 1 mod 4 has any forms at all (our own). The hard part is the correspondence between forms and ideals, where composition of forms becomes multiplication of ideals.

**Wikipedia:** [Binary quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_quadratic_form), [Discriminant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant). It says: “(Gauss and many subsequent authors wrote 2b in place of b; the modern convention allowing the coefficient of xy to be odd is due to Eisenstein).”

### Proper equivalence makes Gauss's classes of quadratic forms a group

**Remember:** Gauss counted only orientation-preserving changes of variable, and got a group.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Two binary quadratic forms are properly equivalent if one turns into the other by an integer change of variables with determinant 1. Lagrange also allowed determinant −1.

**Problem.** For a nonsquare quadratic discriminant Δ, proper classes of primitive integral forms form a finite abelian group under composition. For Δ &lt; 0 take positive definite forms. For fundamental Δ this group is isomorphic to the narrow class group of ℚ(√Δ).

**How the definition helps.** Determinant-one substitutions preserve orientation, keeping a class distinct from its inverse whenever its order exceeds two (our own). Allowing determinant −1 identifies (a,b,c) with (a,−b,c), which represents its inverse (our own). Gauss composition gives the group law, and the form–ideal correspondence identifies it with the narrow class group for fundamental Δ.

**Wikipedia:** [Binary quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_quadratic_form). It says: “Lagrange used a different notion of equivalence, in which the second condition is replaced by αδ − βγ = ±1. Since Gauss it has been recognized that this definition is inferior to that given above.”

### Even self-dual lattices give modular symmetry

**Remember:** Evenness gives translation and self-duality gives inversion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E45 (Analytic theory (Epstein zeta functions; relations with automorphic forms and functions)), 11H06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a positive definite lattice, its theta series sums exp(πiz‖v‖²) over all lattice vectors v, where z has positive imaginary part. An even lattice has even integer squared lengths. A self-dual lattice equals the set of vectors whose dot products with all lattice vectors are integers.

**Problem.** The theta series of an even self-dual positive definite lattice of rank n is a modular form of weight n/2 for the full modular group. This means it satisfies the translation and inversion laws and is holomorphic on the upper half-plane and at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** The two lattice conditions match the two generators of the modular group (our own). Evenness fixes every exponential under z replaced by z + 1 (our own). Poisson summation turns inversion into the theta series of the dual, so self-duality closes the formula (our own). The analytic work goes into Poisson summation and the Fourier transform of a Gaussian (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Leech lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leech_lattice). It says: “the theta function of an even unimodular lattice of rank n is actually a modular form of weight n/2 for the full modular group”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dimension parity survives Witt equivalence

**Remember:** A hyperbolic plane changes dimension by two.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E81 (Algebraic theory of quadratic forms; Witt groups and rings). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Start with nonsingular quadratic forms over a field of characteristic different from two. Two forms represent the same Witt class if adding copies of the plane xy to each makes them equal after a change of variables. The Witt ring adds classes by summing forms in separate variables and multiplies classes by taking tensor products.

**Problem.** Dimension modulo two is a surjective ring map from the Witt ring to the field with two elements. Its kernel, the fundamental ideal, is maximal.

**How the definition helps.** Adding a hyperbolic plane preserves dimension parity, so parity is well defined on Witt classes. Orthogonal sums add dimensions and tensor products multiply them (our own). A one-dimensional form maps to 1, giving surjectivity. The quotient by the kernel is a field, so the kernel is maximal (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Witt group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_group). It says: “Although classes may contain spaces of different dimension, the parity of the dimension is constant across a class”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Isotropic Pfister forms split completely

**Remember:** Build a Pfister form by tensoring binary forms x² − ay².

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11E81 (Algebraic theory of quadratic forms; Witt groups and rings). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a field of characteristic other than two, a Pfister form is a tensor product of binary forms x² − ay² with each a nonzero. In contrast, an arbitrary quadratic form of the same dimension need not have this tensor structure.

**Problem.** A Pfister form that vanishes at a nonzero vector is hyperbolic. That is, it is an orthogonal sum of planes with form xy.

**How the definition helps.** Tensor structure excludes the isotropic real form of signature (3,1), since a four-dimensional real Pfister form has signature (4,0) or (2,2) (our own). Write the form as φ ⊥ (−aφ) with φ a shorter Pfister form. If φ is isotropic, induction makes both summands hyperbolic. Otherwise isotropy makes a a ratio of represented values, so roundness gives aφ ≅ φ and opposite diagonal terms form planes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Pfister form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pfister_form). It says: “every isotropic Pfister form is in fact hyperbolic”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Nondegeneracy lets an isotropic vector split off a plane

**Remember:** Pair an isotropic vector with a second vector to split off a plane.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11E81 (Algebraic theory of quadratic forms; Witt groups and rings). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Q be a quadratic form on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic different from two. Two vectors u and v pair by B(u,v) = Q(u + v) − Q(u) − Q(v). Nondegeneracy means every nonzero vector pairs nontrivially with some vector. An isotropic vector is a nonzero vector where Q vanishes.

**Problem.** A nondegenerate quadratic form has an isotropic vector exactly when it splits as xy plus a form in separate variables.

**How the definition helps.** Nondegeneracy gives an isotropic vector u a partner v, which we scale so B(u,v) = 1 (our own). Replacing v by v − Q(v)u makes its value zero and preserves the pairing (our own). On their span the form is xy, so the span splits off by orthogonality (our own). The degenerate form Q(x,y) = x² vanishes at (0,1) but contains no such plane (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The density of integral quadratic forms having a k-dimensional totally isotropic subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10495v1). It says: “A regular quadratic space (V,Q) is isotropic if and only if V has a subspace V₀ such that the quadratic space (V₀,Q) is a hyperbolic plane.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining j on elliptic curves makes modular transformations preserve it

**Remember:** Changing the lattice basis does not change the elliptic curve or its j-invariant.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F03 (Modular and automorphic functions), 14H52. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define j on isomorphism classes of complex elliptic curves, identifying curves when their lattices differ by a nonzero complex scale. A lattice is the integer span of two real-linearly independent complex numbers. In lattice coordinates use j = 1728g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²). Here g₂ and g₃ are 60 times the sum of λ⁻⁴ and 140 times the sum of λ⁻⁶ over nonzero lattice points, respectively.

**Problem.** Let j(τ) be the j-invariant of ℂ/(ℤ + ℤτ), where Im τ &gt; 0. Then j((aτ + b)/(cτ + d)) = j(τ) for integers a, b, c and d with ad − bc = 1.

**How the definition helps.** Changing basis preserves the lattice, and scaling it preserves j. For τ′ = (aτ + b)/(cτ + d), the scaled generators cτ + d and aτ + b form another basis since ad−bc = 1. Thus multiplying ℤ + ℤτ′ by cτ + d gives the original lattice. Under scaling by α, numerator and denominator of j both scale by α⁻¹² (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form). It says: “For example, the j-invariant j(z) of an elliptic curve, regarded as a function on the set of all elliptic curves, is a modular function.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Bounding modular forms at the cusp makes each space finite-dimensional

**Remember:** No poles at the cusp, so only finitely many forms fit.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let G have finite index in SL₂(ℤ), and let k be an integer. For γ with rows (a,b),(c,d), set (f\|ₖγ)(z) = (cz+d)⁻ᵏf((az+b)/(cz+d)). A weight k modular form is holomorphic on the upper half-plane, satisfies f\|ₖγ = f for all γ∈G, and has bounded transforms at every cusp. This means f\|ₖγ stays bounded as Im(z) → ∞ for every γ∈SL₂(ℤ).

**Problem.** For finite-index G in SL₂(ℤ), the space Mₖ(G) of weight k modular forms is finite-dimensional. For the full modular group and even k → ∞, its explicit dimension formula has leading term k/12.

**How the definition helps.** Cusp holomorphy makes modular forms holomorphic sections on the compactified modular curve, so Riemann–Roch gives finite dimension (our own). Without that condition, the full group admits the linearly independent weight-four functions E₄jⁿ for all n ≥ 0 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form). It says: “For example, the spaces Mₖ(G) and Sₖ(G) are finite-dimensional, and their dimensions can be computed thanks to the Riemann–Roch theorem in terms of the geometry of the G-action on H”

**Sources:**

- [J.-P. Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 7, Springer, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4684-9884-4)

### Lattice homogeneity gives Eisenstein series their modular transformation law

**Remember:** Scaling the lattice scales every term, while choosing another basis changes nothing.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In the lattice definition, a modular form of weight k is a function F on lattices with F(αΛ) = α⁻ᵏF(Λ) for every α ≠ 0. A lattice is the integer span of two real-linearly independent complex numbers. The function f(τ) = F(ℤ + ℤτ) must be holomorphic for Im τ &gt; 0 and bounded as Im τ tends to infinity.

**Problem.** For even k &gt; 2, let Gₖ(τ) sum (m + nτ)⁻ᵏ over all integer pairs except (0, 0), with Im τ &gt; 0. It satisfies Gₖ(−1/τ) = τᵏGₖ(τ) and Gₖ(τ + 1) = Gₖ(τ).

**How the definition helps.** The lattice definition makes the transformation law a direct consequence of scaling each summand. The sum is over nonzero lattice points, so choosing another basis leaves it unchanged. Replacing τ by τ + 1 keeps the lattice, and replacing τ by −1/τ scales it by 1/τ (our own checks). The work is to justify absolute convergence, check holomorphy at infinity, and prove the lattice and matrix definitions agree.

**Wikipedia:** [Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form). It says: “The key idea in proving the equivalence of the two definitions is that such a function F is determined, because of the second condition, by its values on lattices of the form ℤ + ℤτ, where τ ∈ H.”

### Newforms give a Hecke eigenbasis including primes that divide the level

**Remember:** Throw out forms inherited from lower levels, and all Hecke operators diagonalize.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight), 11F25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a weight k and positive level N for Γ₀(N) with trivial character. The old subspace is spanned by g(dz) for weight-k cusp forms g of levels M properly dividing N and positive d dividing N/M. The new subspace is its orthogonal complement for the Petersson inner product.

**Problem.** On this new subspace the usual Hecke operators Tₙ commute and are self-adjoint, including Tₚ for primes dividing N. Thus the space has a basis of simultaneous eigenforms for the full Hecke algebra.

**How the definition helps.** Atkin–Lehner newform theory makes each bad-prime operator scalar on each new eigenline, with real eigenvalue for trivial character (our own). Old copies of a lower-level eigenform g, including g(z) and g(pz), can share all good-prime eigenvalues. On such old subspaces a bad-prime operator can fail to be self-adjoint (our own). The orthogonal newform basis and its real Hecke eigenvalues give self-adjointness on the new subspace.

**Wikipedia:** [Atkin–Lehner theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atkin%E2%80%93Lehner_theory). It says: “the algebra of operators on newforms they generate is a finite-dimensional C\*-algebra that is commutative; and by the spectral theory of such operators, there exists a basis for the space of newforms consisting of eigenforms for the full Hecke algebra.”

**Sources:**

- [A. O. L. Atkin and J. Lehner, Hecke operators on Γ₀(m), Math. Ann. 185 (1970) 134–160](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01359701)

### Vanishing at the cusps makes the Petersson inner product finite

**Remember:** Forms that die at the cusp have finite length.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight), 11F25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A modular form of weight k is a holomorphic function f on the upper half-plane with f((az+b)/(cz+d)) = (cz+d)ᵏ f(z) for the modular group. It must stay bounded as Im z grows. It has a Fourier expansion Σ aₙ qⁿ with q = e to the power 2πiz. A cusp form is one with a₀ = 0, so it vanishes at the cusp.

**Problem.** The Petersson integral of f ḡ yᵏ dx dy / y² over a fundamental domain converges when f or g is a cusp form. The Hecke operators, natural averaging operators Tₙ on modular forms, are self-adjoint for it. So the cusp forms have a basis of common Hecke eigenforms with real Fourier coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** A zero constant coefficient gives exponential decay at the cusp, ensuring convergence when either form is cuspidal (our own). The Hecke adjointness theorem gives commuting self-adjoint operators on the cusp space of the full modular group. The spectral theorem supplies a simultaneous eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. Normalizing each first Fourier coefficient to one makes its nth coefficient the Tₙ eigenvalue (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cusp form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusp_form), [Petersson inner product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersson_inner_product). It says: “Cuspidality is what is required to make this integral finite.”

- [E. Hecke, Über Modulfunktionen und die Dirichletschen Reihen mit Eulerscher Produktentwicklung. I, Math. Ann. 114 (1937)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01594160)

### Cusp constants become residues

**Remember:** Constant terms become residues when the cusp is filled in.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F23 (Relations with algebraic geometry and topology), 11F11. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use a torsion-free subgroup of finite index in the determinant-one integer matrices. Assume that, after moving each cusp to infinity by an integral modular substitution, its stabilizer consists of translations. The cusp is a boundary point, and its width h is the least positive translation in this stabilizer. A weight two form f gives the invariant differential f(τ)dτ.

**Problem.** At each cusp, expand the transformed form in exp(2πiτ/h). The sum of its constant coefficients, each multiplied by its own cusp width, is zero.

**How the definition helps.** Each weighted constant coefficient equals 2πi times the residue of the differential at that cusp (our own). Writing q = exp(2πiτ/h) gives dτ = h dq/(2πiq) (our own). Holomorphy of the form leaves at most a simple pole there (our own). The residue theorem on the compact curve gives the result (our own).

**nLab:** [modular form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/modular+form). It says: “Using the Kodaira-Spencer isomorphism one can show that the space of cusp forms of weight 2 are the differentials on the corresponding modular curve.”

### Sections add modular weights

**Remember:** Multiplying sections adds the exponents of their tensor powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F23 (Relations with algebraic geometry and topology), 11F11. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the compactified complex moduli stack of elliptic curves with the chosen level structure, let ω be the extended Hodge line bundle. Its fiber at an elliptic curve is the line of translation-invariant differentials. A modular form of weight k is a global holomorphic section of ω⊗ᵏ.

**Problem.** The product of forms of weights k and ℓ at the same level has weight k + ℓ. If one factor vanishes at every cusp, the product does too.

**How the definition helps.** Tensoring the two sections adds their tensor powers and preserves vanishing at the cusps (our own). The work is identifying sections on the compactification with analytic forms that are holomorphic at the cusps (our own).

**nLab:** [modular form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/modular+form). It says: “A modular form of weight k is a section of ω⊗ᵏ.”

### Weight two cusp forms give differentials

**Remember:** A cusp zero cancels the simple pole in the differential.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F23 (Relations with algebraic geometry and topology), 11F11. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix full level N ≥ 3 over ℂ, which records a basis of the points killed by N. The Hodge line assigns each elliptic curve its line of translation-invariant differentials and extends over the compact curve. A weight two form is a section of its tensor square. A cusp form vanishes at every cusp, a point added to compactify the curve.

**Problem.** Weight two cusp forms on the compact complex modular curve are its holomorphic one-forms.

**How the definition helps.** Vanishing at a cusp cancels the possible simple pole there (our own). The Kodaira–Spencer isomorphism identifies the squared Hodge line with differentials allowing simple poles at cusps. The usual analytic proof instead checks that f(τ)dτ extends in a local coordinate at each cusp (our own).

**nLab:** [modular form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/modular+form). It says: “Using the Kodaira-Spencer isomorphism one can show that the space of cusp forms of weight 2 are the differentials on the corresponding modular curve.”

### Hecke operators at distinct primes commute

**Remember:** Translations in separate prime factors commute.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F70. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p outside the level, put K = GL₂(ℤₚ) and choose one representative g from each coset gK in K diag(p,1) K. On right K-invariant adelic forms, the local Hecke operator sums right translations by these representatives in the p-component (our own).

**Problem.** Hecke operators at distinct primes outside the level commute on classical modular forms.

**How the definition helps.** The moves at one prime leave the other prime factor alone (our own). Their sums therefore commute term by term (our own). The work is the adelic description of classical forms and the comparison of local translations with classical Hecke operators (our own).

**nLab:** [automorphic form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/automorphic+form). It says: “These are the adelic automorphic forms. They may be thought of as subsuming ordinary modular forms for all level structures.”

### Normalizing eigenforms by a(1) = 1 makes coefficients equal Hecke eigenvalues

**Remember:** Set the first coefficient to one, and the coefficients become eigenvalues.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F30. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A normalized Hecke eigenform of weight k for SL₂(ℤ) is a cusp form with first Fourier coefficient one and an eigenvalue for every Tₘ.

**Problem.** For a normalized Hecke eigenform, Tₘ f = a(m) f for all m. The coefficients satisfy a(m)a(n) = Σ dᵏ⁻¹ a(mn/d²), summed over d dividing gcd(m,n). So the coefficients are multiplicative, and the L-function of f has an Euler product.

**How the definition helps.** The first Fourier coefficient of Tₘf equals a(m), so the eigenvalue equals a(m). The level-one Hecke multiplication law gives the divisor sum, hence multiplicativity and the Euler product (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hecke operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_operator). It says: “Thus for normalized cuspidal Hecke eigenforms of integer weight, their Fourier coefficients coincide with their Hecke eigenvalues.”

### Quasimodularity preserves derivatives

**Remember:** Allow the extra chain-rule term instead of losing derivatives.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F37. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A weight k quasimodular form on SL₂(ℤ) admits a polynomial Pτ(X) whose coefficient functions are holomorphic on the upper half-plane and at infinity. Its constant term is f(τ). Every γ in SL₂(ℤ) with bottom row (c,d) satisfies (cτ+d)⁻ᵏf(γτ) = Pτ(c/(cτ+d)) (our own).

**Problem.** Differentiation maps a weight k quasimodular form to a weight k + 2 quasimodular form. The ordinary modular forms are not closed under differentiation, as the derivative of E₄ shows.

**How the definition helps.** The polynomial allows exactly the extra factors that the chain rule introduces (our own). Differentiation raises the weight by two and the polynomial degree by at most one. The ordinary weight-four Eisenstein series E₄ has a nonzero extra term, so its derivative fails the ordinary modular law (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Almost holomorphic modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_holomorphic_modular_form). It says: “Ramanujan observed that the derivative of any quasimodular form is another quasimodular form.”

**Paper or page:** [Quasimodular forms and modular differential equations which are not apparent at cusps: I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.04890v1). It says: “of quasimodular forms on Γ is closed under differentiation.”

**Sources:**

- [Don Zagier, Elliptic Modular Forms and Their Applications](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-74119-0_1)

### Refinements select Hecke eigenlines

**Remember:** A root chooses a direction in the two old copies.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F85. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be a normalized cusp eigenform of weight k, level N and trivial character, and let p be a prime outside N. A refinement at p chooses a root of X² − aₚX + pᵏ⁻¹, where aₚ is the pth Fourier coefficient.

**Problem.** At level Np, Uₚ replaces each nth Fourier coefficient by the coefficient at pn. If the roots differ, the span of f(τ) and f(pτ) has two Uₚ eigenlines. Each refinement labels the line with the chosen eigenvalue.

**How the definition helps.** The chosen root specifies one eigenvalue and hence one line (our own). If β is the other root, the line with eigenvalue α is generated by f(τ) − β f(pτ) (our own). The work is computing Uₚ on this span and showing that its characteristic polynomial is the original pth Hecke polynomial (our own).

### Even self-dual lattices give modular theta series

**Remember:** Even norms give translation and self-duality gives inversion.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F27 (Theta series; Weil representation; theta correspondences), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A positive definite integral lattice L is even if every squared length is even. It is self-dual if L equals the set of vectors in its real span pairing integrally with every lattice vector. Its theta series sums exp(πiτ⟨v,v⟩) over v in L for τ in the upper half-plane.

**Problem.** An even self-dual positive definite lattice of rank 8m, for positive integral m, has a scalar theta series of weight 4m for SL₂(ℤ). The odd self-dual lattice ℤ⁸ fails the translation rule.

**How the definition helps.** Evenness fixes every summand under τ ↦ τ + 1, while self-duality returns the same lattice under inversion (our own). For ℤ⁸, translation changes the sign of the terms from vectors of squared length one (our own). Gaussian Poisson summation proves the inversion formula at −1/τ with weight 4m (our own). Translation and inversion generate the modular group, and positive definiteness gives holomorphy at infinity (our own).

### Distinct indices become orthogonal

**Remember:** As level grows, the nonzero moduli in the formula grow too.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F30 (Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms), 11F72. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix even k ≥ 4 and positive integers q,m,n. Choose a Petersson-orthonormal basis B of weight k cusp forms for Γ₀(q) with trivial character and the unscaled Petersson integral. The normalized sum is Γ(k−1)(4π√(mn))¹⁻ᵏ times ∑ over f ∈ B of the conjugate mth coefficient times the nth coefficient.

**Problem.** As the positive integer q grows, this sum tends to one for equal indices and zero otherwise. The error is O(q to the power 1−k), with k,m,n fixed.

**How the definition helps.** The Petersson formula gives the stated diagonal and restricts every other modulus c to positive multiples of q. The trivial Kloosterman bound cancels the denominator c (our own). The Bessel factor is O(c¹⁻ᵏ), so summing gives O(q¹⁻ᵏ) (our own).

### Harmonic weights normalize Petersson diagonals

**Remember:** Weight each form by the reciprocal of its squared norm.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F30 (Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms), 11F72. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix even k ≥ 4 and positive integer q, and choose an orthogonal basis of weight k cusp forms for Γ₀(q) with trivial character. The harmonic weight of each basis vector f is Γ(k−1)(4π)¹⁻ᵏ divided by its squared Petersson norm, using unscaled hyperbolic area.

**Problem.** Divide the nth Fourier coefficient by n to the power (k−1)/2 and call the result a(n). For positive m and n, the Petersson formula writes the weighted sum of conjugate a(m) times a(n) as a diagonal term plus other terms. The diagonal term equals one for m = n and zero otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** The reciprocal squared norm cancels any rescaling of a basis vector, and the common factor sets the diagonal coefficient to one. The Petersson norm integrates \|f(z)\|² times y to the power k against hyperbolic area on the quotient. In our own derivation, expanding a sum of translates of one Fourier mode in the orthogonal basis supplies the reciprocal norm. Computing its other Fourier coefficients gives the remaining terms in the formula.

**Wikipedia:** [Petersson trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersson_trace_formula). It says: “a kind of orthogonality relation between coefficients of a holomorphic modular form.”

**Paper or page:** [Trace formula and functional equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16921v2). It says: “δ(m=n) + 2π i⁻ᵏ ∑₍c&gt;0, c≡0 (D)₎ Sχ(m,n;c)/c J₍k−1₎(4π√(mn)/c).”

### Poincaré series extract coefficients

**Remember:** Average one mode to recover one coefficient.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F30 (Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For even k &gt; 2 and integer n ≥ 1, the nth Poincaré series sums the weight k transforms of exp(2πinτ). Take one transform per left coset of the stabilizer of infinity in SL₂(ℤ).

**Problem.** Pair a cusp form with this series using the Petersson integral, linear in the cusp form, without dividing by the domain’s area. The result is its nth Fourier coefficient times Γ(k − 1) divided by (4πn) to the power k − 1. These series span the space of cusp forms.

**How the definition helps.** Averaging one Fourier mode turns the integral over a modular domain into a strip integral against that mode (our own). This replaces integrating a general product by Fourier orthogonality, which selects one coefficient (our own). A cusp form orthogonal to every series then has all coefficients zero (our own). Absolute convergence justifies unfolding the sum for k &gt; 2 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Poincaré series (modular form)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_series_%28modular_form%29). It says: “In general, the Poincaré series is, for n ≥ 1, a cusp form.”
