### Dual isogenies make Fricke involutive

**Remember:** Dualize the isogeny twice to recover it.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F32 (Modular correspondences, etc.), 14G35. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over ℂ, a point of Y₀(N) represents an elliptic curve and a quotient map φ with cyclic kernel of order N. Its dual is the reverse map whose composite with φ multiplies points by N. Define the Fricke map by sending φ to its dual.

**Problem.** The Fricke map on Y₀(N) is an involution. It extends to an involution of its smooth compactification X₀(N).

**How the definition helps.** Dualizing twice recovers φ, so the Fricke map squares to the identity (our own). The dual isogeny theorem gives this identity and preserves cyclic kernels (our own). The cited proposition identifies dualization with the classical map τ ↦ −1/(Nτ). An automorphism of a smooth curve extends to its smooth projective compactification (our own).

**nLab:** [Hecke correspondence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hecke+correspondence). It says: “sending (E,E′) to E and E′ respectively”

**Paper or page:** [Coleman Integration on Modular Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.14513v1). It says: “where φ̂ is the dual isogeny of φ.”

**Sources:**

- [A. O. L. Atkin and J. Lehner, Hecke operators on Γ₀(m) (1970)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01359701)

### Factorial powers isolate ordinary forms

**Remember:** Factorial powers keep units and kill the rest.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F33 (Congruences for modular and \\(p\\)-adic modular forms), 11F85. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let U be a Hecke operator preserving a finite free module over the p-adic integers. Its ordinary part is the largest direct summand on which U acts invertibly and whose complementary summand has powers tending to zero. Define the ordinary projector by taking the limit of the powers with exponents n!.

**Problem.** The limit exists and is idempotent. Its image is the ordinary part, and it commutes with every operator that commutes with U.

**How the definition helps.** Factorial exponents eventually select the identity on the invertible part and zero on the nilpotent part modulo each power of p (our own). This constructs the projector without factoring a characteristic polynomial (our own). The finite-module decomposition supplies those two parts, and reduction preserves the resulting projectors (our own). Every operator commuting with U commutes with the powers and their limit (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Twisted Triple Product p-adic L-function for Finite Slope Families of Hilbert Modular Forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13230v2). It says: “is the ordinary projector $e<sub>n.o</sub> = \\lim <sub>n\\to \\infty </sub> U<sup>n!</sup>$.”

**Sources:**

- [Haruzo Hida, Galois representations into GL₂(ℤₚ\[\[X\]\]) attached to ordinary cusp forms (1986)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01390329)

### Completions preserve quasimodular products

**Remember:** Multiply the completions, then take the constant coefficient.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F37 (Forms of half-integer weight; nonholomorphic modular forms), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A level-one almost holomorphic modular form of weight k transforms with weight k and is polynomial in 1/Im(τ). Its coefficients are holomorphic on the upper half-plane and at the cusp. Its constant coefficient is a quasimodular form, whose depth is the degree of this completion.

**Problem.** The product of level-one quasimodular forms of weights k and ℓ is quasimodular of weight k + ℓ. Its depth, the degree of the completion, is at most the sum of the depths.

**How the definition helps.** The constant coefficient of a product is the product of the constant coefficients (our own). The product of the two completions is modular and has degree at most the sum (our own). The work is the completion theorem, which identifies this definition with the polynomial transformation law (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Almost holomorphic modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_holomorphic_modular_form). It says: “An almost holomorphic modular form is determined by its holomorphic part”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Half-integral weights compose

**Remember:** Keep the square root in the group element.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F37 (Forms of half-integer weight; nonholomorphic modular forms), 11F27. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The metaplectic cover consists of pairs (γ,φ) with γ ∈ SL₂(ℝ) and φ holomorphic on the upper half-plane. For bottom row (c,d) of γ, require φ(τ)² = cτ+d everywhere. The product with (δ,ψ) is (γδ, τ ↦ φ(δτ)ψ(τ)).

**Problem.** For each integer k, transform f by evaluating it at γτ and dividing by φ(τ) to the power 2k + 1. These transformations give a right group action of weight k + ½.

**How the definition helps.** The group law already multiplies the chosen roots in the order that a slash action needs (our own). Raising that factor to the odd power 2k + 1 preserves the law (our own). The work is identifying the group of pairs with the metaplectic cover (our own).

**nLab:** [metaplectic group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/metaplectic+group). It says: “double cover of the symplectic group”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Quadratic indices rule out negative terms

**Remember:** A negative direction produces arbitrarily negative traces in its orbit.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F46 (Siegel modular groups; Siegel and Hilbert-Siegel modular and automorphic forms). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A degree g Siegel Fourier index is a symmetric g-by-g matrix T with integer diagonal and half-integer off-diagonal entries. Its Fourier mode at the symmetric period matrix Z is exp(2πi tr(TZ)).

**Problem.** Take a level-one holomorphic function that obeys the Siegel modular law in degree at least two. Its Fourier terms indexed by matrices with a negative direction vanish. In degree one, the modular function j has a pole at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Integral basis changes preserve coefficient magnitudes for scalar forms (our own). A negative direction gives a primitive integer vector of negative value by rational approximation (our own). Extend it to a basis and add large multiples to another vector, forcing the transformed traces toward minus infinity (our own). Boundedness on the period cell at imaginary part I then forces the common coefficient magnitude to vanish (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Siegel modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_modular_form). It says: “Corollary to this theorem is the fact that Siegel modular forms of degree g &gt; 1 have Fourier expansions and are thus holomorphic at infinity.”

**Sources:**

- [Max Koecher, Zur Theorie der Modulformen n-ten Grades. I](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01180269)

### Fourier slices become Jacobi forms

**Remember:** The Fourier index is the index in the translation rule.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F50 (Jacobi forms), 11F46. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write e(t)=exp(2πit). A holomorphic Jacobi form φ on ℍ×ℂ satisfies φ(γτ,z/(cτ+d))=(cτ+d)ᵏe(mcz²/(cτ+d))φ(τ,z) for every γ∈SL₂(ℤ) with bottom row (c,d). It satisfies φ(τ,z+λτ+μ)=e(−m(λ²τ+2λz))φ(τ,z) for all integers λ,μ and has Fourier support 4mn≥r² (our own).

**Problem.** A degree-two Siegel modular form depends on a symmetric two-by-two complex matrix with positive definite imaginary part. For a level-one form of weight k, expand in the last diagonal entry ω. For each integer m &gt; 0, the coefficient of exp(2πimω) is a Jacobi form of weight k and index m.

**How the definition helps.** The Jacobi definition packages exactly how one Fourier slice transforms under the subgroup preserving the expansion direction (our own). A translation contributes the exponential for that slice's index (our own). The work is restricting the Siegel transformation law to this subgroup and checking the resulting Fourier support (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Jacobi form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_form). It says: “Examples in two variables include Jacobi theta functions, the Weierstrass ℘ function, and Fourier–Jacobi coefficients of Siegel modular forms of genus 2.”

**Sources:**

- [Martin Eichler and Don Zagier, The Theory of Jacobi Forms (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4684-9162-3)

### Residue classes separate theta components

**Remember:** Each residue class gets one coefficient function.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F50 (Jacobi forms), 11F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write q=exp(2πiτ) and ζ=exp(2πiz). For each residue μ modulo 2m, define θμ by summing q raised to r²/(4m) times ζʳ over integers r≡μ modulo 2m. The theta decomposition expresses a Jacobi form as ∑μ hμ(τ)θμ(τ,z) (our own).

**Problem.** For a classical level-one Jacobi form of weight k and positive integer index m, the 2m coefficient functions are unique. Together they transform with weight k − ½ by the inverse transpose of the matrices transforming the theta series.

**How the definition helps.** Separate frequencies into disjoint residue classes, so their coefficient functions cannot cancel between classes (our own). Translation by τ forces coefficients with equal 4mn − r² and equal r modulo 2m to agree (our own). The work is proving the theta transformation law and deducing the modular law for the coefficient vector (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Hermitian Jacobi Forms Having Modules as their Index and Vector-Valued Jacobi Forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.16508v1). It says: “are equivalent to the existence of a smooth function $F:\\mathcal{H}\\to \\mathbb {C}\[D\]$, which is then determined by $\\Phi $”

**Sources:**

- [Martin Eichler and Don Zagier, The Theory of Jacobi Forms (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4684-9162-3)

### Analytic conductor unifies convexity

**Remember:** One conductor tracks level, gamma shifts, and height.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a unitary cuspidal L-function on GL(d) over ℚ, d ≥ 2, let N denote its arithmetic conductor, which measures ramification at finite primes. Its gamma factors have the form Γℝ(s+κ), where Γℝ(z) = Γ(z/2) exp(−z log(π)/2). Define C(t) as N times the product of 3 + \|it+κ\| over these shifts.

**Problem.** For every ε &gt; 0 and ½ ≤ σ ≤ 1, \|L(σ+it)\| is at most a constant times C(t) raised to (1−σ)/2+ε. The constant depends only on d and ε.

**How the definition helps.** The analytic conductor combines the finite conductor and all archimedean factors in the standard convexity bound (our own). The convexity theorem for cuspidal GL(d) L-functions gives the stated exponent by interpolation across the critical strip (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Oscillations and first-ever negative Fourier coefficients of symmetric square L-functions over sparse set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18994v1), [A new zero-free region for Rankin-Selberg L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16889v6). It says: “The hybrid convexity bound of the symmetric square L-function and the twisted symmetric square L-function is given by:”

**Sources:**

- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 5](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/053)

### Eisenstein symmetry gives functional equations

**Remember:** The completed kernel carries its symmetry into the integral.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations), 11F67. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For normalized level-one cusp eigenforms f,g of weight k, define their Rankin–Selberg integral using the completed level-one Eisenstein series E\*(τ,s). Integrate yᵏf(τ) times the conjugate of g(τ) times E\*(τ,s) over SL₂(ℤ)∖ℍ with hyperbolic area, where y=Im(τ) (our own).

**Problem.** The completed Rankin–Selberg L-function of two level-one cusp eigenforms of the same weight satisfies the symmetry s ↔︎ 1 − s in unitary normalization.

**How the definition helps.** Only the Eisenstein series depends on s, so its symmetry passes directly to the integral. Unfolding integrates the defining sum over one strip and identifies the result with the completed coefficient series up to a constant. Continuing the Eisenstein series gives the meromorphic continuation needed to compare both sides.

**Wikipedia:** [Rankin–Selberg method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankin%E2%80%93Selberg_method). It says: “The analytic continuation and functional equation then boil down to those of the Eisenstein series.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Even weights give two reflected sums

**Remember:** An even weight survives the reflection of the contour.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an entire cusp-form completion satisfying Λ(s)=εΛ̃(1−s), an auxiliary weight is an even entire function G with G(0)=1. Require rapid decay as the imaginary part tends to either infinity, uniformly on each bounded vertical strip (our own).

**Problem.** Write I(Λ) for the upward integral of Λ(½+u)G(u)/u on Re u = 2, divided by 2πi. For completions of polynomial growth on vertical strips, Λ(½) = I(Λ) + εI(Λ̃). Each integral gives a weighted coefficient sum when its Dirichlet series converges absolutely there and its gamma factor decays exponentially.

**How the definition helps.** Evenness preserves G when the functional equation reflects the integral (our own). Moving the contour to Re u = −2 crosses only the kernel pole, with residue Λ(½) (our own). Reflection turns the remaining integral into −εI(Λ̃) (our own). Absolute convergence allows termwise integration on the original line (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Subconvexity of Shintani's zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.13558v3). It says: “Let G(u) be any function which is holomorphic and bounded in \|Re(u)\| &lt; 4, even, with G(0) = 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 5](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/053)

### Mellin completion turns inversion into reflection

**Remember:** Inversion in y reflects the Mellin variable.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be a holomorphic cusp form of weight k for SL₂(ℤ), so f has modular symmetry and vanishes at infinity. Its Fourier coefficients a(n) define L(s) = ∑ a(n)/nˢ. Define Λ(s) by integrating f(iy)yˢ dy/y over y &gt; 0.

**Problem.** The integral gives an entire continuation of (2π)⁻ˢΓ(s)L(s). It satisfies Λ(s) = iᵏΛ(k−s).

**How the definition helps.** In our own derivation, the integral turns modular inversion into the substitution y ↦ 1/y. The identity f(i/y) = (iy)ᵏf(iy) then gives the reflection. Decay at infinity and modular inversion give convergence at both ends for every s. Integrating the Fourier series term by term identifies the integral with the completed series for large Re s.

**nLab:** [L-function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/L-function). It says: “may also be obtained as the Mellin transform of f.”

**Sources:**

- [Hecke, Über die Bestimmung Dirichletscher Reihen durch ihre Funktionalgleichung (1936)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01565437)

### Removing zeta isolates the adjoint

**Remember:** Removing scalar matrices removes the zeta factor.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a level-one holomorphic cusp eigenform, let Aₚ have the two unitary-normalized local parameters on its diagonal. On complex two-by-two matrices set Cₚ(B)=AₚBAₚ⁻¹. The adjoint Euler factor is 1/det(I−p⁻ˢCₚ) on trace-zero matrices (our own).

**Problem.** The resulting L-functions satisfy L(s,f×f̃) = ζ(s)L(s,Ad f), where f̃ denotes the dual. The adjoint function has a finite, nonzero value at 1.

**How the definition helps.** Conjugation splits into its trace-zero action and the identity on scalar matrices (our own). The full Rankin–Selberg factor therefore includes the extra factor 1/(1−p⁻ˢ) at every prime (our own). Their product is ζ(s) (our own). The Rankin–Selberg pole theorem and the simple pole of ζ give a finite nonzero quotient at one (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2). It says: “a\_{\\mathrm{Sym}<sup>j</sup>(\\pi )\\times \\mathrm{Sym}<sup>j</sup>(\\widetilde{\\pi })}(v<sup>\\ell </sup>)&amp; =1+\\sum <sub>r=1</sub><sup>j</sup> a\_{\\mathrm{Sym}<sup>2r</sup>(\\pi )\\otimes \\omega <sub>\\pi </sub><sup>-r</sup>}(v<sup>\\ell </sup>)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Root numbers fix vanishing parity

**Remember:** A negative sign allows only odd central Taylor powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an automorphic L-function, completion multiplies the series by the exponential and gamma factors in its functional equation. In the self-dual case, the same completed function Λ occurs on both sides. Its root number is the sign ε in Λ(s) = εΛ(1−s).

**Problem.** Suppose Λ is holomorphic at ½ and does not vanish identically. Its vanishing order there is even for ε = 1 and odd for ε = −1. The original series has the same order if its completing factor is holomorphic and nonzero there.

**How the definition helps.** In our own argument, completion makes reflection multiply each central Taylor term by a sign. A term of degree j acquires the factor (−1)ʲ. The first nonzero term must therefore have the parity prescribed by ε. Proving the functional equation supplies the symmetry this argument needs.

**Wikipedia:** [Functional equation (L-function)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_equation_%28L-function%29). It says: “Λ the L-function multiplied by a gamma-factor, and ε a complex number of absolute value 1”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Unfolding reads the Petersson pairing

**Remember:** The constant residue of E leaves precisely the inner product.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For weight k cusp forms f,g on SL₂(ℤ), set h(z)=yᵏf(z) overline(g(z)), where y=Im(z). For Re s&gt;1, the Eisenstein series E(z,s) sums (Im γz)ˢ over left cosets of the stabilizer of infinity. Define I(s) by integrating h(z)E(z,s) over the modular surface with hyperbolic area (our own).

**Problem.** Write a(n) and b(n) for the Fourier coefficients of f and g. For Re s &gt; 1, I(s) equals Γ(s+k−1)(4π)<sup>(−(s+k−1))</sup> times the sum of a(n)b̄(n)/nˢ⁺ᵏ⁻¹. Its residue at s = 1 is 3/π times the Petersson inner product of f and g.

**How the definition helps.** The Eisenstein series puts a known constant residue inside the integral defining the pairing. Unfolding integrates each summand over a translated domain and joins these domains into a strip. Integration across the strip keeps exactly the matching Fourier indices. In our own normalization, the remaining gamma integral gives the stated factor, and the residue of E is 3/π.

**Wikipedia:** [Rankin–Selberg method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankin%E2%80%93Selberg_method). It says: “The integral was identified with the convolution L-function by a technique called "unfolding”

**Sources:**

- [Rankin, Contributions to the theory of Ramanujan’s function τ(n) and similar arithmetical functions (1939)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100021095)

### Cusp divisors add periods

**Remember:** Shared endpoints cancel as terms of a divisor.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F67 (Special values of automorphic \\(L\\)-series, periods of automorphic forms, cohomology, modular symbols), 11F75. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A degree-zero divisor of rational cusps is a formal integer sum of points in ℚ ∪ {∞} whose coefficients sum to zero. A weight two modular symbol is an additive map from these divisors to complex numbers, invariant when the modular group under consideration moves the cusps. It assigns the pair (α,β) the value on β − α.

**Problem.** For a weight two cusp form, write its period from α to β as P(α,β). Then P(α,β) + P(β,γ) = P(α,γ). These periods define a linear symbol invariant under the congruence subgroup.

**How the definition helps.** Addition of endpoint divisors cancels the middle cusp, giving the path addition formula immediately (our own). The usual analytic description integrates the differential of a cusp form along paths between cusps (our own). Vanishing at the cusps gives convergence, and simple connectivity of the upper half-plane gives path independence (our own). Invariance of the differential gives invariance of the resulting symbol (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Modular symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_symbol). It says: “Informally, {α,β} represents a homotopy class of paths from α to β in the upper half-plane.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Satake makes convolution commutative

**Remember:** Turn convolution into multiplication of symmetric Laurent polynomials.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F70 (Representation-theoretic methods; automorphic representations over local and global fields), 11F25. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a p-adic field F with integer ring O, set K=GLₙ(O). The spherical Hecke algebra consists of compactly supported complex functions on GLₙ(F) invariant under left and right multiplication by K. Its product is convolution with Haar measure giving K volume one (our own).

**Problem.** The spherical Hecke algebra of GLₙ(F) is commutative.

**How the definition helps.** The transform replaces convolution of functions by ordinary multiplication of symmetric Laurent polynomials, which allows negative exponents (our own). Directly comparing the two convolution integrals is unnecessary (our own). The Satake isomorphism proves that the transform preserves products and detects equality.

**Paper or page:** [On the geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.16571v1). It says: “The map S induces an isomorphism”

**Sources:**

- [Ichirō Satake, Theory of spherical functions on reductive algebraic groups over p-adic fields (1963)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02684781)

### Bessel weights transfer modulus sums

**Remember:** Transform the modulus weight before summing over the spectrum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11F30. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Choose a smooth weight H supported in a compact subinterval of (0,∞). At real t, define its transformed weight by integrating 4 cosh(πt) K(2it,4πx) H(x) against dx/x. Here K denotes the decaying modified Bessel function, with order first and argument second.

**Problem.** For positive integers m,n, weight the modulus c by H(√(mn)/c)/c in the sum of opposite-sign Kloosterman sums S(m,−n;c). The level one summation formula gives a spectral sum and integral, both using the transformed weight.

**How the definition helps.** One integral converts the chosen modulus weight into a weight for every spectral parameter t. The spectral sum uses Fourier coefficients of cusp eigenfunctions, and the integral uses the Eisenstein series. In our own specialization, compact support gives the required derivative bounds and leaves only finitely many moduli. The equality itself is the Kloosterman summation theorem.

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3). It says: “(𝓛±H)(t) ≔ ∫₀∞ 𝒥±₍t₎(x) H(x) dx/x”

**Sources:**

- [N. V. Kuznetsov, Petersson’s conjecture for cusp forms of weight zero and Linnik’s conjecture (1981).](https://doi.org/10.1070/SM1981v039n03ABEH001518)
- [Henryk Iwaniec and Emmanuel Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory (2004), Theorem 16.5.](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/053)
- [Peter Humphries and Rizwanur Khan, Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3)

### Centralizers combine conjugate terms

**Remember:** One orbit of conjugate elements needs one quotient integral.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Γ act freely and discretely by orientation-preserving isometries on ℍ with compact quotient X. For γ∈Γ, let C be its centralizer in Γ. Its orbital integral integrates k(d(z,γz)) over C∖ℍ with hyperbolic area, for a smooth compactly supported distance weight k.

**Problem.** The orbital integral equals the integral over X of the sum of diagonal kernel terms indexed by the conjugacy class of γ.

**How the definition helps.** Left cosets Cg label the conjugates g⁻¹γg exactly once (our own). Translating a fundamental region of Γ by those representatives gives a fundamental region of C up to null sets (our own). Changing variables gives the orbital integral (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “with the first term corresponding to the identity element and the remaining terms forming a sum over the other conjugacy classes”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Completed factors make scattering unitary

**Remember:** On the critical line the scattering quotient divides conjugates.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11M36. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, normalize the Eisenstein eigenfunction so its horizontal average is yˢ + φ(s)y¹⁻ˢ at height y. The coefficient φ(s) measures scattering at the narrowing end. Complete the Riemann zeta function by setting Λ(w) = Γ(w/2)ζ(w) divided by π to the power w/2.

**Problem.** The scattering coefficient equals Λ(2s−1)/Λ(2s). It has absolute value one on Re(s) = ½, including its limiting value −1 at s = ½.

**How the definition helps.** The Eisenstein constant-term formula gives the displayed quotient. On the critical line, reflection and conjugation make its numerator the conjugate of its denominator (our own). Away from the midpoint, the zeta zero-free line ensures a nonzero denominator (our own). At the midpoint the poles at zero and one have opposite residues, giving the limit −1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_zeta_function). It says: “In this case the determinant of the scattering matrix is given by: φ(s) = π¹ᐟ² Γ(s−1/2) ζ(2s−1) / (Γ(s) ζ(2s)).”

**Sources:**

- [Henryk Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, second edition (2002).](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/053)

### Congruence gives Selberg’s spectral gap

**Remember:** Finite area alone cannot prevent a small positive eigenvalue.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Call a subgroup of SL(2,ℤ) a congruence subgroup if it contains every matrix congruent to the identity modulo some positive integer. Each such subgroup acts on the upper half-plane by fractional linear transformations.

**Problem.** For congruence subgroups, every positive discrete Laplace eigenvalue on the quotient is at least 3/16. General finite-index subgroups can have arbitrarily small positive eigenvalues.

**How the definition helps.** Containing a principal congruence subgroup is exactly the hypothesis of Selberg’s 3/16 theorem. Cyclic covers obtained by cutting the punctured modular torus along a nonseparating curve show why finite index alone fails (our own). Smoothed cosine values on n successive sheets give mean-zero test functions with Rayleigh quotient O(1/n²) (our own). Below ¼ the variational principle gives a discrete eigenvalue (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg's 1/4 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg%27s_1/4_conjecture). It says: “Selberg showed that the eigenvalues are at least 3/16.”

**Sources:**

- [Atle Selberg, On the estimation of Fourier coefficients of modular forms (1965).](https://doi.org/10.1090/pspum/008/0182610)

### Cusp truncation gives finite norms

**Remember:** Cut the two power terms, not the whole cusp.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, the horizontal average of the Eisenstein series E(z,s) at height y is yˢ+φ(s)y¹⁻ˢ. For Y&gt;1, truncate E by subtracting this average in the standard cusp above Y and keeping E elsewhere.

**Problem.** For fixed real t ≠ 0 and s = ½+it, the truncated series is square integrable for hyperbolic area. Its squared norm equals 2 log Y + O(1) as Y grows, with the error bound depending on t.

**How the definition helps.** The two constant-mode waves cause divergence, while all remaining modes decay exponentially (our own). Below Y each wave contributes log Y since \|φ(s)\|=1 (our own). Their cross term stays bounded for fixed t≠0 (our own). The Maass–Selberg relation gives the full norm formula (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Maass–Selberg relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maass%E2%80%93Selberg_relations). It says: “However the integral defining the inner product does not converge, so the Eisenstein series first have to be truncated.”

**Sources:**

- [Henryk Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, second edition (2002).](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/053)

### Free compact quotients simplify traces

**Remember:** No fixed points or cusps means only closed geodesics remain.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Γ be a discrete group of orientation-preserving isometries of the hyperbolic plane. Require Γ to have no nonidentity element of finite order and to have compact quotient.

**Problem.** In Selberg’s trace formula, the geometric sum contains only the identity and terms indexed by oriented closed geodesics.

**How the definition helps.** The two conditions exclude rotations about interior points and transformations that produce cusp ends. In our own examples, the modular group contains both the rotation z ↦ −1/z and the translation z ↦ z + 1. Every remaining nonidentity element translates along a geodesic, which closes on the quotient. The trace formula supplies the contribution of each class.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “the group Γ has no parabolic or elliptic elements (other than the identity).”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Kuznetsov signs select odd forms

**Remember:** Subtracting the two signs cancels every even contribution.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11F30. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use the level one Kuznetsov formula, which relates Fourier coefficients on the modular surface to finite exponential sums. For positive integers m,n, take half the difference of its identities for (m,n) and (m,−n). Use the same even analytic test function with the decay required by the formula in both identities.

**Problem.** Only odd cusp forms contribute on the spectral side. These are Laplace eigenfunctions that change sign under x ↦ −x and have zero horizontal average. Each product of normalized coefficients carries the test weight divided by L(1,ad f), the adjoint L-function of the form evaluated at one.

**How the definition helps.** The difference assigns weight (1−ε)/2 to a form whose reflection sign is ε. This gives weight one to odd forms and zero to even forms. The continuous integrals in the two identities agree and cancel. Our own subtraction uses the signed coefficient formulas proved by Kuznetsov summation.

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3). It says: “ε₍f₎⁽¹ ∓ ¹⁾⁄² λ₍f₎(m) λ₍f₎(n)/L(1, ad f)”

**Sources:**

- [N. V. Kuznetsov, Petersson’s conjecture for cusp forms of weight zero and Linnik’s conjecture (1981).](https://doi.org/10.1070/SM1981v039n03ABEH001518)
- [Peter Humphries and Rizwanur Khan, Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3)

### Length weights recover primitive counts

**Remember:** Subtract the shorter repeats before counting the new geodesics.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, call an oriented closed geodesic primitive if it traverses its path only once. For each primitive length ℓ, counting multiplicity, place mass ℓ/(2 sinh(mℓ/2)) at mℓ for each positive integer m. Add masses at equal lengths.

**Problem.** The Laplace eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, determine how many primitive oriented geodesics have each length.

**How the definition helps.** Selberg’s trace formula recovers the length masses from the spectrum once Weyl’s law gives the area (our own). At length ℓ, subtract the contributions from repeats of shorter primitive geodesics (our own). Divide the remainder by ℓ/(2 sinh(ℓ/2)) to obtain the primitive count (our own). Finiteness below each length bound makes this recursion possible (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “so the lengths of primitive closed geodesics are spectral invariants.”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Mean zero gives heat decay

**Remember:** Remove constants before asking the heat flow to decay.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Γ be a subgroup of SL(2,ℤ) containing every matrix congruent to the identity modulo some positive integer. On its upper half-plane quotient, take square integrable functions whose integral against hyperbolic area is zero.

**Problem.** At time t ≥ 0, heat flow on this space has operator norm at most exp(−3t/16).

**How the definition helps.** The zero integral removes the constant functions, which heat flow leaves unchanged. Selberg proved that every positive discrete Laplace eigenvalue here is at least 3/16. The continuous spectrum begins at ¼. In our own deduction, heat flow multiplies a spectral component at λ by exp(−tλ), giving the bound.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg's 1/4 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg%27s_1/4_conjecture). It says: “Selberg showed that the eigenvalues are at least 3/16.”

**Sources:**

- [Atle Selberg, On the estimation of Fourier coefficients of modular forms (1965).](https://doi.org/10.1090/pspum/008/0182610)

### Odd reflection removes Eisenstein spectrum

**Remember:** Reflection makes the average at the only cusp vanish.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, determinant-one integer matrices identify points z = x+iy of the upper half-plane by fractional linear transformations. Call a square integrable function odd if f(−x+iy) = −f(x+iy) almost everywhere.

**Problem.** On the odd subspace the Laplacian has an orthonormal eigenbasis with finite multiplicities and no finite accumulation of eigenvalues.

**How the definition helps.** Oddness makes the horizontal average vanish at every height where the integral exists. In our own proof, integrate over the period from −½ to ½ and pair x with −x. The surface has just one narrowing end, or cusp, so this average tests the entire cuspidal condition. The Laplacian commutes with reflection, and its spectrum on the cuspidal subspace is discrete.

**Wikipedia:** [Maass wave form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maass_wave_form). It says: “A Maass form f is called even, if i(f)=f and odd if i(f)=−f.”

**Sources:**

- [Henryk Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, second edition (2002).](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/053)

### Opposite signs remove Kuznetsov diagonals

**Remember:** Opposite nonzero frequencies cannot match on the diagonal.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11F30. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, pair Fourier modes of frequencies m and −n for positive integers m,n. Use an even test function h analytic in the strip \|Im(t)\| ≤ ½+δ for some δ &gt; 0. Require h to decay there at least as fast as (1+\|t\|) to the power −2−δ.

**Problem.** In the Kuznetsov formula relating Fourier coefficient averages to exponential sums, these pairs have zero diagonal contribution, even when m = n.

**How the definition helps.** Opposite signs forbid equality of the actual frequencies. In our own derivation, the identity transformation contributes the integral of exp(2πi(m+n)x) over one period. That integral vanishes, whereas equal signed frequencies give an integral of one. The Kuznetsov formula evaluates the remaining contributions.

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3). It says: “δ(m,±n) 𝒩±h±”

**Sources:**

- [N. V. Kuznetsov, Petersson’s conjecture for cusp forms of weight zero and Linnik’s conjecture (1981).](https://doi.org/10.1070/SM1981v039n03ABEH001518)
- [Peter Humphries and Rizwanur Khan, Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3)

### Resolvent differences have finite traces

**Remember:** Subtract before tracing to cancel the slow spectral tail.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11M36. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, let Δ be the nonnegative Laplacian. For real a &gt; ½ define its shifted inverse R(a) = (Δ − ¼ + a²)⁻¹. For distinct a,b &gt; ½ take D = R(a) − R(b).

**Problem.** The singular values of D have finite sum, so D has a trace. Neither shifted inverse alone has this property. After subtracting the identity contribution in Selberg’s trace formula, the trace equals F(a) − F(b), where F(a) = Z′(½+a)/(2a Z(½+a)).

**How the definition helps.** Subtraction cancels the leading inverse eigenvalue term (our own). By Weyl’s law the individual terms have order 1/n, while their differences have order 1/n² (our own). The Fourier weight for R(a) is exp(−a\|u\|)/(2a) (our own). Selberg’s trace formula identifies the remaining geodesic sum with the stated difference of logarithmic derivatives of Selberg zeta (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “The trace formula is also central to the analytic theory of the Selberg zeta function.”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Short Fourier support removes orbit terms

**Remember:** If the weight cannot reach a length, that orbit cannot contribute.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let X be a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, and let L be its shortest closed geodesic length. Choose a smooth even function g supported in a compact subset of (−L,L). Define h(r) = ∫ℝ g(u) exp(iru) du.

**Problem.** Write each Laplace eigenvalue as ¼ + r², counting multiplicity. Then ∑ h(r) = area(X)/(4π) times ∫ℝ r h(r) tanh(πr) dr.

**How the definition helps.** The support condition kills every closed geodesic term because each length is at least L. In our own application of Selberg’s trace formula, only the identity contributes. An even weight positive at L would retain the shortest geodesics.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “∑ₙ₌₀∞ h(rₙ) = μ(X)/(4π) ∫₋∞∞ r h(r) tanh(πr) dr + ∑₍{T}₎ log N(T₀)/(N(T)¹ᐟ² − N(T)⁻¹ᐟ²) g(log N(T)).”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Weighted counts control unweighted errors

**Remember:** Count repeats with their primitive length, then remove them.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11M36. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, call a closed geodesic primitive if it makes one circuit. For each oriented primitive geodesic P of length ℓ, set N(P) = exp(ℓ). Count each positive integer m with mℓ ≤ log X using weight ℓ, and sum over P to obtain Ψ(X).

**Problem.** Fix ½ &lt; θ &lt; 1 and suppose Ψ(X) = X + O(X raised to θ). Then the number of primitive P with N(P) ≤ X differs from ∫₂ˣ du/log u by O((X raised to θ)/log X).

**How the definition helps.** Each repeat retains its primitive length weight, so repeats can be subtracted before partial summation (our own). Double circuits contribute O(√X) by the assumed bound on Ψ (our own). Higher repeats contribute O(X¹ᐟ³ log X) because the shortest length allows only O(log X) exponents (our own). Partial summation removes log N(P) and gives the stated error (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Prime geodesic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_geodesic). It says: “weighted counting functions analogous to the Chebyshev function”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Zero cusp averages give discrete spectra

**Remember:** Remove the constant Fourier term to remove the continuous part.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The modular surface identifies points z = x+iy of the upper half-plane under determinant-one integer matrices acting by fractional linear transformations. A square integrable function belongs to the cuspidal subspace when its periodic lift satisfies ∫₀¹ f(x+iy) dx = 0 for almost every y &gt; 0.

**Problem.** On this subspace the nonnegative Laplacian has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Each eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, and only finitely many lie below any fixed bound.

**How the definition helps.** The zero average removes the horizontally constant mode that can extend far into the narrowing end, called the cusp. In our own proof, the circle Poincaré inequality bounds a zero-average function by its horizontal derivative. With bounded energy, this makes the squared integral above height Y uniformly small as Y grows. Compactness on the remaining bounded region gives discrete spectrum.

**Wikipedia:** [Maass wave form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maass_wave_form). It says: “Then Δₖ operates on C(Γ∖ℋ,k) and has a discrete spectrum.”

**Sources:**

- [Henryk Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, second edition (2002).](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/053)

### Cyclotomic determinants detect abelian quotients

**Remember:** Over ℚ, the full determinant sees every abelian quotient of the image.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Combine an elliptic curve’s Galois actions on all points of finite order into one representation, called its adelic representation. Its matrices have entries in the profinite integers, which record compatible residues modulo every positive integer. The closed commutator subgroup is the smallest closed normal subgroup with abelian quotient.

**Problem.** For an elliptic curve over ℚ, the kernel of the determinant on its adelic image equals the closed commutator subgroup of that image.

**How the definition helps.** Taking all torsion orders together makes the determinant record the action on every root of unity (our own). At each order the Weil pairing identifies the determinant with the exponent of the action on roots of unity (our own). Kronecker–Weber identifies the field generated by all these roots with the maximal abelian extension of ℚ (our own). Its fixing subgroup is therefore the closed commutator subgroup, and its image remains the closed commutator subgroup in the adelic image (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Degrees of points with rational j-invariant on X₀(n) and X₁(n)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13199v1). It says: “Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over $\\Q$. Then, we have $\\cG<sub>E</sub> \\cap \\SL(\\Zhat) = \[\\cG<sub>E</sub>, \\cG<sub>E</sub>\]$.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Monodromy isolates infinite inertia

**Remember:** Finite inertia is exactly the part left when monodromy vanishes.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11F85. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a continuous ℓ-adic representation ρ of a p-adic local Galois group, assume ℓ≠p and fix a tame ℓ-adic parameter t on inertia. Its monodromy operator is the nilpotent N satisfying ρ(g)=exp(t(g)N) on some open inertia subgroup (our own).

**Problem.** The original representation has finite inertia image exactly when N is zero.

**How the definition helps.** On that subgroup, zero monodromy gives trivial action and hence finite full inertia image (our own). Otherwise the logarithms t(g)N take infinitely many values, since t has open image in ℤℓ (our own). Grothendieck’s monodromy theorem supplies the description (our own).

**nLab:** [Weil-Deligne representation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Weil-Deligne+representation). It says: “N is a nilpotent monodromy operator”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Residual semisimplification removes lattice dependence

**Remember:** Every stable lattice gives the same simple factors after reduction.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A stable lattice is a free module over the coefficient field’s valuation ring that spans the representation and is preserved by Galois. Reduce its matrices modulo the maximal ideal. Semisimplification replaces that reduction by the direct sum of its irreducible factors.

**Problem.** For a continuous representation over a finite extension of ℚₚ, all stable lattices have isomorphic semisimplified reductions. Their reductions can differ before this step.

**How the definition helps.** Brauer–Nesbitt identifies the semisimplifications because every group element has the same reduced characteristic polynomial on both lattices (our own). Let the unramified ℤₚ quotient fix e and send f to f+te for t∈ℤₚ (our own). Reduction on the lattice spanned by e,f gives a nontrivial extension (our own). On the lattice spanned by e/p,f the reduction is trivial (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer–Nesbitt theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer%E2%80%93Nesbitt_theorem). It says: “the characteristic polynomials of ρ₁(g) and ρ₂(g) coincide for all g ∈ G, then ρ₁ and ρ₂ are isomorphic representations.”

**Paper or page:** [Stable free lattices in residually reducible Galois deformations and control theorem of Selmer groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03608v2). It says: “the semi-simplification (T/ϖT)ˢˢ of the residual representation is decomposed into two distinct characters”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Semisimplification makes Frobenius traces decisive

**Remember:** Traces remember the simple pieces and forget how they fit together.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite-dimensional group representation V, choose a chain of invariant subspaces from 0 to V with irreducible successive quotients. Its semisimplification is the direct sum of those quotients.

**Problem.** Consider two continuous representations of a number field’s Galois group over the same finite extension of ℚℓ. Suppose inertia, the group acting trivially on the residue field, acts trivially outside finitely many primes. Equal Frobenius traces outside finitely many primes imply isomorphic semisimplifications.

**How the definition helps.** Traces see the diagonal blocks of an extension, so a nonsplit extension and its split sum have identical traces (our own). Chebotarev density and continuity extend Frobenius trace equality to the whole Galois group (our own). In characteristic zero, Brauer–Nesbitt then identifies the semisimplifications (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer–Nesbitt theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer%E2%80%93Nesbitt_theorem). It says: “Then the representation is uniquely determined by the values of the traces of ρ(Frobₚ)”

**Paper or page:** [Eisenstein degeneration of Euler systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02078v2). It says: “there are exactly three isomorphism classes of continuous Galois representations”

**Sources:**

- [Eisenstein degeneration of Euler systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02078v2)

### The Weil pairing gives the determinant

**Remember:** On the determinant line, Galois acts on roots of unity.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an elliptic curve over a number field, let E\[n\] be its geometric n-torsion for n≥1. The determinant character on E\[n\] is the Galois action on its exterior square, a free rank-one ℤ/nℤ-module (our own).

**Problem.** For an elliptic curve over a number field, the determinant of each Galois element acting on E\[n\] gives its exponent on nth roots of unity.

**How the definition helps.** The alternating Weil pairing induces a map from the exterior square to the nth roots of unity. Perfection makes it an isomorphism, and Galois equivariance identifies the two actions (our own). On a basis wedge the action multiplies by the determinant, so on roots it raises to that exponent (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weil pairing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_pairing). It says: “With this definition it can be shown that w is alternating and bilinear,”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining L-factors by ℓ-adic cohomology makes isogenous elliptic curves share them

**Remember:** An isogeny preserves the whole rational representation, including its inertia-fixed part.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 14G10. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At a finite prime v of a number field K, take V=H¹ét(E over K̄,ℚℓ) with ℓ different from the residue characteristic. Let I be inertia and F geometric Frobenius, inverse to the residue-field power map. The local factor is 1/det(1−N(v)⁻ˢF acting on Vᴵ) (our own).

**Problem.** Elliptic curves that are isogenous over a number field have the same L-factor at every prime, good or bad.

**How the definition helps.** The factor depends only on the rational Galois representation (our own). An isogeny induces an isomorphism because composition with its dual acts as multiplication by its degree on cohomology (our own). The isomorphism preserves inertia invariants and Frobenius determinants (our own). Comparison with the classical local factors supplies the geometric input (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse–Weil zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Weil_zeta_function). It says: “A more refined definition became possible with the development of étale cohomology”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre and John Tate, Good reduction of abelian varieties (1968)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970722)

### Local-condition Selmer groups sit between rational points and Tate–Shafarevich torsion

**Remember:** The local test leaves exactly the everywhere locally trivial torsors.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11R34. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an elliptic curve E over a number field K and integer n≥2, let E\[n\] denote its geometric n-torsion. The n-Selmer group consists of classes in H¹(K,E\[n\]) mapping to zero in H¹(Kᵥ,E) at every place v (our own).

**Problem.** There is an exact sequence 0 → E(K)/nE(K) → n-Selmer group → Ш\[n\] → 0. Here Ш, the Tate–Shafarevich group, classifies torsors that have a point over every completion. A torsor is a curve on which E acts freely and transitively over an algebraic closure.

**How the definition helps.** The global Kummer sequence maps H¹(K,E\[n\]) onto H¹(K,E)\[n\] with kernel E(K)/nE(K) (our own). The Selmer condition selects precisely the inverse image of the everywhere locally trivial classes, namely Ш\[n\] (our own). Restricting the surjection therefore gives the stated exact sequence (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selmer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selmer_group). It says: “More generally one can define the Selmer group of a Galois module”

**Sources:**

- [Joseph H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Chapter X, §4 (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-09494-6)

### Quadratic twists split odd torsion

**Remember:** The twist supplies the minus part of the torsion.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L/K be a quadratic extension of number fields and let σ be its nonidentity automorphism. The quadratic twist of an elliptic curve becomes isomorphic to the original curve over L. Under this identification σ acts on L-rational points by applying the original action and then negating the result.

**Problem.** For any odd positive integer n, the points killed by n over L split as a direct sum. The two groups are the K-rational points killed by n on the original curve and on its quadratic twist.

**How the definition helps.** The twist supplies the subgroup with σP=−P, while the original curve supplies the subgroup with σP=P (our own). For odd n, dividing P+σP and P−σP by two gives unique components (our own). For n=2 the signs coincide (our own). On y²=x³−x all four two-torsion points are rational, so the two subgroups overlap (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The Effect of Quadratic Base Change on Torsion of Elliptic Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03709v2). It says: “If n is an odd positive integer we have E(K(√d))\[n\] ≃ E(K)\[n\] ⊕ Eᵈ(K)\[n\].”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Requiring y ≠ 0 makes congruent numbers the curves of positive rank

**Remember:** A rational affine point with nonzero y gives a triangle.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11D25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A positive rational A is congruent if it is the area of a right triangle with rational sides. Equivalently, y²=x³−A²x must have a rational affine point with y≠0.

**Problem.** A rational point with y ≠ 0 on the curve has infinite order: no multiple of it in the group law is zero. So A is congruent exactly when the curve has positive rank, which means infinitely many rational points.

**How the definition helps.** The condition y≠0 excludes the three affine points of order two, which exist for every A (our own). The quoted torsion theorem makes every remaining affine rational point a point of infinite order. Such a point exists exactly when the curve has positive rank (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruent<sub>number</sub>](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/https%3A//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruent_number). It says: “the only torsion points on this elliptic curve are those with y equal to 0, hence the existence of a rational point with y nonzero is equivalent to saying the elliptic curve has positive rank.”

**Paper or page:** [A Theorem of Fermat on Congruent Number Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09604). It says: “Equivalently, A is a congruent number if and only if the congruent number curve y²=x³−A²x has a rational point (x,y)∈ℚ² with y≠0.”

**Sources:**

- [Lorenz Halbeisen, Norbert Hungerbühler, A Theorem of Fermat on Congruent Number Curves, arXiv:1803.09604 (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09604)

### Scheme kernels retain inseparable degrees

**Remember:** Kernel rank counts geometric points with their multiplicities.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 14K02. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An isogeny is a surjective homomorphism of elliptic curves with finite kernel. Its kernel as a group scheme is the entire fiber over zero, including multiplicities. Its rank counts that fiber by the dimension of its coordinate algebra over the base field.

**Problem.** Over a global function field, the kernel rank equals the isogeny degree. This includes inseparable isogenies, where some fiber multiplicities exceed one.

**How the definition helps.** Counting the full fiber retains the multiplicities that counting geometric points loses (our own). Relative Frobenius, the map given locally by taking pth powers in characteristic p, has degree p and only one geometric kernel point (our own). An isogeny is finite and flat, so every fiber has the same total multiplicity as the generic fiber (our own). The cited factorization uses the full subgroup scheme when constructing the quotient.

### Tate's limit definition makes the canonical height quadruple under doubling

**Remember:** Doubling P shifts the limit by one step and frees a factor of four.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G50 (Heights), 11G05. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On an elliptic curve over a number field, let h(P) be the logarithmic height of its x-coordinate, with h(O)=0. In the normalization for this x-coordinate height, define ĥ(P) as the limit of h(2ⁿP)/4ⁿ.

**Problem.** The canonical height of 2P is four times the canonical height of P.

**How the definition helps.** Replacing P by 2P shifts the index by one, giving ĥ(2P)=4ĥ(P) (our own). The duplication formula bounds h(2P)−4h(P) uniformly, so the normalized sequence converges by a geometric-series estimate (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Néron–Tate height](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%A9ron%E2%80%93Tate_height). It says: “Although the global Néron–Tate height is quadratic, the constituent local heights are not quite quadratic.”

**Sources:**

- [André Néron, Quasi-fonctions et hauteurs sur les variétés abéliennes (1965)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970644)
- [Joseph H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Chapter VIII (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-09494-6)

### Ordered integrals split at junctions

**Remember:** A path junction cuts the sequence of integration times once.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Along a piecewise smooth path, write each integration form as fᵢ(t) dt in the path parameter. For polylogarithms the forms are dz/(z − a), where a is a puncture. Integrate f₁(t₁) ⋯ fₙ(tₙ) over 0 &lt; t₁ &lt; ⋯ &lt; tₙ &lt; 1, using ordinary volume in these parameters.

**Problem.** Let paths γ and δ meet end to end and avoid the poles of the forms. The joined integral equals ∑ₖ Iγ(ω₁,…,ωₖ) Iδ(ωₖ₊₁,…,ωₙ), summing from k=0 to n. Empty integrals equal one.

**How the definition helps.** The ordered integration times cross the path junction only once (our own). Fixing the number k before the junction splits the simplex into a product of two ordered regions (our own). Summing their integrals gives the formula (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Duality on symmetric multiple polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08711). It says: “(Path composition formula) $\\displaystyle I<sub>\\gamma \\cdot \\gamma '</sub>(e\_{a<sub>1</sub>}\\cdots e\_{a<sub>k</sub>})=\\sum <sub>i=0</sub><sup>k</sup>I<sub>\\gamma </sub>(e\_{a<sub>1</sub>}\\cdots e\_{a<sub>i</sub>})I<sub>\\gamma '</sub>(e\_{a<sub>i+1</sub>}\\cdots e\_{a<sub>k</sub>})$.”

**Sources:**

- [Duality on symmetric multiple polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08711)

### Discriminant forms classify even overlattices

**Remember:** Even extensions correspond to subgroups on which the discriminant form vanishes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H06 (Lattices and convex bodies (number-theoretic aspects)), 11E81. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonsingular even integral lattice L, let L\* consist of rational vectors pairing integrally with L. Its discriminant form on L\*/L takes x+L to ⟨x,x⟩/2 modulo ℤ. A subgroup is isotropic if this value vanishes on every element.

**Problem.** Even lattices containing L with finite index in the same rational space correspond to isotropic subgroups of L\*/L. Up to isometries preserving L, they correspond to orbits of those subgroups under isometries of L.

**How the definition helps.** The finite quadratic form makes evenness a test on cosets of L (our own). Every integral extension already lies in the dual, since its vectors pair integrally with L (our own). The correspondence theorem for subgroups of a quotient now supplies all candidates (our own). Polarization shows that zero values on a subgroup also give integral pairings (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Derived equivalence of elliptic K3 surfaces and Jacobians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16638v3). It says: “the set of O(T)-orbits of isotropic subgroups of Aₜ”

**Sources:**

- [Viacheslav V. Nikulin, Integral symmetric bilinear forms and some of their applications](https://doi.org/10.1070/im1980v014n01abeh001060)

### Even positive definite unimodular lattices need dimension divisible by 8

**Remember:** Evenness gives translation symmetry, and unimodularity gives inversion symmetry.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11H06 (Lattices and convex bodies (number-theoretic aspects)), 11E12. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A lattice in ℝⁿ is unimodular when its Gram matrix, the matrix of dot products of a basis, has integer entries and determinant ±1. It is even when every vector x has even norm x·x, and odd otherwise.

**Problem.** A positive definite even unimodular lattice exists only when the dimension n is divisible by 8. Odd unimodular lattices exist in every dimension, for example ℤⁿ. The E₈ and Leech lattices are even, of dimensions 8 and 24.

**How the definition helps.** Evenness gives the theta series period one, and Poisson summation gives the inversion factor (z/i) raised to n/2 (our own). The threefold composite of z ↦ −1/(z+1) fixes z and gives total factor exp(−πin/4) (our own). The nonzero series forces this factor to equal one, hence 8 divides n (our own). The odd lattice ℤⁿ lacks the translation symmetry (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Unimodular lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimodular_lattice). It says: “If the lattice is even, the form has level 1, and if the lattice is odd the form has Γ₀(4) structure (i.e., it is a modular form of level 4).”

**Sources:**

- [J.-P. Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 7, Springer, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4684-9884-4)
- [J. Milnor and D. Husemoller, Symmetric Bilinear Forms, Springer, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-88330-9)

### Unit covolume gives a Hermite maximum

**Remember:** Fix cell volume before maximizing the shortest length.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H55 (Quadratic forms (reduction theory, extreme forms, etc.)), 11H31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Normalize a Euclidean lattice by scaling until a fundamental cell has volume one. The Hermite invariant is the squared length of its shortest nonzero vector after this scaling. Without normalization, scaling alone makes shortest length unbounded.

**Problem.** In each dimension, some lattice attains the maximum Hermite invariant. Equivalently, some lattice attains the best lattice sphere-packing density in that dimension.

**How the definition helps.** Fixing cell volume puts the shortest-length function on a space where Mahler’s compactness theorem applies (our own). The cubic lattice has shortest length one, so it suffices to consider lattices with shortest length at least one (our own). Mahler’s theorem makes that set compact, and shortest length varies continuously there (our own). Packing balls of radius half the shortest length gives the corresponding density maximum (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Mahler's compactness theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_compactness_theorem). It says: “The assertion of Mahler's theorem is equivalent to the compactness of the space of unit-covolume lattices in ℝⁿ whose systole is larger or equal than any fixed ε&gt;0.”

**Sources:**

- [Kurt Mahler, On lattice points in n-dimensional star bodies I. Existence theorems](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1946.0072)

### Primitive counting explains the zeta factor

**Remember:** Every nonzero lattice vector has one primitive starting point.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H60 (Mean value and transfer theorems). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a bounded measurable compactly supported function on ℝⁿ, its primitive Siegel transform sums its values on the primitive vectors of a lattice. A nonzero lattice vector is primitive if no integer k≥2 divides it in the lattice.

**Problem.** For n≥2, average the primitive transform over unit-covolume lattices using the SLₙ(ℝ)-invariant probability measure. The mean equals the integral of the function divided by ζ(n), the sum of reciprocal nth powers.

**How the definition helps.** The primitive sum separates the first point on each lattice ray from its multiples (our own). Each positive integer dilation by k has an integral factor of 1 divided by the n-th power of k (our own). Invariance under determinant-one linear maps makes the averaged primitive counting measure a constant times Lebesgue measure (our own). Siegel’s mean value theorem for all nonzero lattice points fixes that constant (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Inversion formulae for Siegel transforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11689v3), [Some measure-theoretical and dynamical properties of successive minima on the space of unimodular lattices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.14373v1). It says: “Then ∫ₓ f̂ dμₓ = (1/ζ(n)) ∫ℝⁿ f dm.”

**Sources:**

- [Carl Ludwig Siegel, A Mean Value Theorem in Geometry of Numbers](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969027)

### Character relations locate the orbit

**Remember:** Keep every integer relation satisfied by the step.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a step α on the torus ℝᵈ/ℤᵈ, where points differing by an integer vector coincide. Define H by requiring k·x ∈ ℤ for every integer vector k satisfying k·α ∈ ℤ.

**Problem.** The points nα become uniformly distributed on H. Their averages against every continuous function approach its integral under the translation-invariant probability on H.

**How the definition helps.** The defining relations identify H with the orbit closure by Kronecker’s theorem. Each integer character has a geometric orbit average tending to one for k·α integral and zero otherwise (our own). These are its Haar integrals on H by translation invariance and density of the orbit (our own). Trigonometric approximation extends the equality to continuous functions (our own).

**nLab:** [Haar integral](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Haar+integral). It says: “there exists a unique such integral, up to a scalar multiple.”

**Wikipedia:** [Kronecker's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker%27s_theorem). It says: “the whole Kronecker theorem describes the closure of ⟨P⟩ as the intersection of the kernels”

**Paper or page:** [Metric uniform distribution on analytic curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06909v1). It says: “Then (xₙ) is uniformly distributed mod 1 if and only if for every non-zero v ∈ ℤᵏ,”
