### Uniformly separated frequencies give metric equidistribution

**Remember:** For almost every multiplier, separated frequencies spread uniformly.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Call a real sequence uniformly separated if some g &gt; 0 satisfies \|aₙ − aₘ\| ≥ g whenever n ≠ m.

**Problem.** If a real sequence (aₙ) is uniformly separated, then for almost every real x the sequence aₙx is uniformly distributed modulo one. That is, the fraction of terms landing in each interval approaches its length.

**How the definition helps.** Separation excludes aₙ=1/n, whose multiples converge to zero modulo one (our own). Among the first N frequencies, the jth neighbor on either side lies at distance at least jg (our own). Integrating the squared exponential average over any bounded interval therefore gives O(log N/N) at each nonzero integer frequency (our own). The Davenport–Erdős–LeVeque criterion gives uniform distribution almost everywhere (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Metric uniform distribution on analytic curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06909v1). It says: “Then for almost every x ∈ ℝ the sequence (aₙx) is uniformly distributed modulo 1.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Powered intervals give approximation dimension

**Remember:** Keep the rational centers and shrink each interval by a power.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J83 (Metric theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a&gt;1, define W(a) as the real x satisfying \|x−p/q\|&lt;q⁻²ᵃ for infinitely many coprime integers p,q with q&gt;0. Its intervals keep the Dirichlet centers and raise each radius q⁻² to the power a (our own).

**Problem.** Let a be greater than one. The real numbers approximable infinitely often within the inverse 2a-th power of the denominator have Hausdorff dimension 1/a. Hausdorff dimension measures size by covers at small scales.

**How the definition helps.** Raising the radii to a power puts these intervals in the mass transference principle (our own). Dirichlet’s theorem gives full measure before shrinking, so mass transference gives dimension at least 1/a after shrinking (our own). On each bounded interval there are O(q) relevant fractions per denominator q (our own). Their covering costs sum to a finite number in every dimension above 1/a (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Diophantine approximation in metric space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.06776v1). It says: “Let a &gt; 1 and for a ball B, denote by Bᵃ a ball of the same centre as B and of diameter (diam B)ᵃ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Independent bases prevent power cancellation

**Remember:** Independent bases make irrational algebraic powers survive multiplication.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J86 (Linear forms in logarithms; Baker's method), 11J81. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Positive numbers are multiplicatively independent if no product of their integer powers equals one except with all exponents zero. Use real logarithms to define powers of positive bases. Distinctness of the bases alone does not imply this independence.

**Problem.** Take multiplicatively independent positive algebraic bases and algebraic exponents. If at least one exponent is irrational, the product of those powers is transcendental.

**How the definition helps.** Independence makes the real logarithms rationally independent, hence algebraically linearly independent by Baker’s theorem (our own). If the product were algebraic, its logarithm would belong to their rational span (our own). Otherwise Baker’s theorem would make the enlarged family algebraically linearly independent, contradicting the given expression (our own). Uniqueness would force rational exponents, while dependent bases allow 2<sup>(2√2)</sup>4<sup>(−√2)</sup>=1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Baker's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem). It says: “In particular this number is nonzero, so 1 and λᵢ are linearly independent over the algebraic numbers.”

**Sources:**

- [Alan Baker, Linear forms in the logarithms of algebraic numbers](https://doi.org/10.1112/s0025579300003971)

### Local ratios make approximation projective

**Remember:** Divide out the size of the coordinates at every place.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J87 (Schmidt Subspace Theorem and applications). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Represent a point of projective space over a number field K by a nonzero vector x. Normalize the absolute values \|·\|ᵥ by local degree weights so the product formula holds. Set Mᵥ=maxᵢ\|xᵢ\|ᵥ and define H(x)=∏ᵥ Mᵥ.

**Problem.** Choose d independent K-linear forms in d variables at each of finitely many places. Multiply the ratios \|L(x)\|ᵥ/Mᵥ over every chosen form and place. For fixed ε &gt; 0, the points where this product is below 1/Hᵈ⁺ᵋ lie in finitely many proper projective linear subspaces.

**How the definition helps.** Each ratio removes the choice of coordinates, so the inequality applies directly to projective points (our own). Scaling multiplies the numerator and denominator by the same absolute value (our own). The height also stays fixed by the product formula (our own). The subspace theorem supplies the finite union, and its affine and projective versions are equivalent.

**Paper or page:** [Diophantine approximation and the subspace theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00731v1), [Diophantine approximation and the subspace theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00731v1). It says: “The projective subspace theorem is equivalent to the affine subspace theorem.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### No zero subsums makes unit solutions finite

**Remember:** Remove cancelling groups before counting solutions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J87 (Schmidt Subspace Theorem and applications), 11D61. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An S-unit is a nonzero element of a number field whose principal fractional ideal has prime factors only in a fixed finite set S. A solution of a linear equation in S-units is nondegenerate if no nonempty group of terms on the left sums to zero.

**Problem.** Over a number field, a fixed linear equation in S-units with nonzero coefficients and right side one has finitely many nondegenerate solutions.

**How the definition helps.** The condition removes groups that can vary independently because their terms cancel (our own). Take ℚ with 2 in S (our own). The equation x + y + z = 1 then has solutions (2ᵏ, −2ᵏ, 1) for every positive k (our own). The S-unit theorem, proved using the subspace theorem, carries the finiteness work (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Sum of terms of recurrence sequences and S-units in the solution sets of norm form equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01688v1). It says: “has no vanishing subsums.”

**Sources:**

- [Jan-Hendrik Evertse, Hans Peter Schlickewei and Wolfgang M. Schmidt, Linear Equations in Variables which Lie in a Multiplicative Group](https://doi.org/10.2307/3062133)

### Fourier tests reveal polynomial equidistribution

**Remember:** Polynomial differences make Fourier averages easier to estimate.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K06 (General theory of distribution modulo \\(1\\)), 11K31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Uniform distribution modulo 1 means that the fraction of fractional parts in each interval tends to its length. In the equivalent Fourier test, average exp(2πihx) over the sequence for each nonzero integer h. Require each such average to tend to zero.

**Problem.** The values of a real polynomial at the positive integers are uniformly distributed modulo 1 if some nonconstant coefficient is irrational.

**How the definition helps.** Weyl’s criterion reduces the claim to cancellation of every nonzero integer Fourier mode (our own). Split into residue classes modulo a common denominator of the rational nonconstant coefficients, making those terms constant modulo one (our own). Each remaining phase has irrational leading coefficient, and every fixed positive difference lowers its degree while preserving leading irrationality (our own). The van der Corput inequality gives induction from the linear geometric sum (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Equidistributed sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence). It says: “the sequence p(n) is uniformly distributed modulo 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Hermann Weyl, Über die Gleichverteilung von Zahlen mod. Eins](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01475864)

### Equidistribution makes normal numbers a consequence of ergodicity

**Remember:** A normal number visits intervals at the right frequencies under multiplication by its base.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K16 (Normal numbers, radix expansions, Pisot numbers, Salem numbers, good lattice points, etc.), 37A44. arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A real number x is normal in integer base b ≥ 2 if every length-k block of its digits has frequency 1/bᵏ. Equivalently, the fractional parts of bᵏx are equidistributed. This means their visits to each interval in \[0, 1) have frequency equal to the length of that interval.

**Problem.** For each integer base b ≥ 2, Lebesgue-almost every real number is normal in base b.

**How the definition helps.** The orbit definition makes interval frequencies time averages for multiplication by b modulo one. This map preserves Lebesgue measure and is ergodic (our own). Birkhoff’s theorem gives the required frequencies simultaneously for the countably many intervals with rational endpoints (our own). Approximation by these intervals gives every interval, and the quoted equivalence yields normality (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Normal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number). It says: “A number x is normal in base b if and only if the sequence {\\left( b<sup>k</sup> x \\right) }<sub>k=0</sub><sup>\\infty</sup> is equidistributed modulo 1”

**Sources:**

- [É. Borel, Les probabilités dénombrables et leurs applications arithmétiques, Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo 27 (1909) 247–271](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03019651)

### Block tests expose hidden dependence

**Remember:** Counting blocks catches dependencies that counting single points misses.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K36 (Well-distributed sequences and other variations), 11K06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a fixed length k, form a point in the unit cube from each block of k consecutive fractional parts. Call the sequence completely uniformly distributed if, for every k, the fraction of these points in each box tends to its volume. Ordinary uniform distribution checks only k = 1.

**Problem.** For almost every α &gt; 1, the sequence of positive integer powers of α is completely uniformly distributed modulo 1. For irrational α, its positive integer multiples are uniformly distributed but fail the block test at length two.

**How the definition helps.** One definition tests the distribution of every finite block, so the metric theorem on powers states all block lengths at once. Koksma’s metric uniform distribution theorem applies to each nonzero integer linear combination of the shifted powers (our own). For multiples of an irrational α, adjacent pairs satisfy y=x+α modulo one (our own). Any open box disjoint from that graph receives no pairs, although single terms are equidistributed (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Equidistributed sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence). It says: “is completely uniformly distributed for almost all α &gt; 1”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Continued fraction blocks bound rotation discrepancy

**Remember:** Use return-time blocks so each block contributes only constant count error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an irrational step α, write N in its Ostrowski expansion, the greedy sum of denominators of successive continued fraction approximations to α. Each denominator occurs at most as many times as the next continued fraction entry. Split the first N rotation steps into consecutive blocks of these lengths.

**Problem.** Suppose the continued fraction entries of α are bounded. For the points x+jα modulo one, the greatest absolute difference between arc frequency and arc length is O(log N/N), uniformly in x.

**How the definition helps.** The expansion selects block lengths for which the Denjoy–Koksma inequality bounds the absolute arc count error by two (our own). An arc indicator has total variation two because it jumps once at each endpoint (our own). The denominators at least double every two steps, and bounded entries bound each multiplicity (our own). Thus O(log N) blocks suffice, and adding their errors gives the result after division by N (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Dynamics of multicritical circle maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01153v1), [Limit laws of maximal Birkhoff sums for circle rotations via quantum modular forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07796v1). It says: “Let {qₙ}ₙ∈ℕ be the sequence of return times given by ρ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Fourier cutoffs bound arc discrepancy

**Remember:** Bound the sharp arc count from above and below with short Fourier sums.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an arc I of ℝ/ℤ and integer M≥1, take trigonometric polynomials P₋≤1ᵢ≤P₊ pointwise, of degree at most M. Selberg’s bounds have constant coefficients \|I\|±1/(M+1) and nonconstant coefficients bounded by C/\|k\| at frequency k, with C absolute (our own).

**Problem.** For a circle probability μ, write μ̂(k) = ∫exp(−2πikx) dμ(x). Its arc discrepancy is the supremum of \|μ(I) − \|I\|\| over arcs I. It is at most C times 1/M + ∑ₖ₌₁ᴹ \|μ̂(k)\|/k, with an absolute constant C.

**How the definition helps.** Integrating the two polynomial bounds traps each arc mass using only finitely many Fourier coefficients (our own). The constant terms supply the length and its O(1/M) error (our own). Constructing bounds that hold at every point while controlling all coefficients is the substantive step (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Erdős–Turán inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Tur%C3%A1n_inequality). It says: “where the supremum is over all arcs A ⊂ ℝ/ℤ of the unit circle”

**Sources:**

- [P. Erdős and P. Turán, On a problem in the theory of uniform distribution. I (1948)](https://www.dwc.knaw.nl/DL/publications/PU00018587.pdf)

### Square-summed frequencies bound worst arc error

**Remember:** Square the weighted Fourier errors before choosing the cutoff.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a circle probability μ, its kth Fourier coefficient is μ̂(k) = ∫exp(−2πikx) dμ(x). Define A as the square root of ∑ₖ₌₁∞ \|μ̂(k)\|²/k².

**Problem.** For every arc I, the difference between μ(I) and its length has absolute value at most C times A raised to 2/3. The constant C is universal.

**How the definition helps.** Erdős–Turán bounds the discrepancy by a constant times the sum of 1/M and the first M absolute weighted coefficients (our own). Cauchy–Schwarz bounds that sum of coefficients by √M A (our own). For 0&lt;A≤1, choosing M near A⁻²ᐟ³ balances both errors (our own). If A=0 let M grow, and if A&gt;1 use the trivial bound one (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Erdős–Turán inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Tur%C3%A1n_inequality). It says: “This inequality holds for arbitrary natural numbers m,n”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Gauss averages give denominator growth

**Remember:** The logarithm turns successive reciprocal tails into a sum.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K50 (Metric theory of continued fractions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Gauss map T sends irrational x between 0 and 1 to the fractional part of 1/x. It preserves the probability distribution with density 1/((1 + x) log 2). At each iterate record −log x, evaluated at the current point.

**Problem.** Truncate the continued fraction of x after n digits following the integer part, and let qₙ be the reduced denominator. For almost every x between 0 and 1, (log qₙ)/n tends to π²/(12 log 2).

**How the definition helps.** The reciprocal product of x,Tx,…,Tⁿ⁻¹x equals qₙ+qₙ₋₁Tⁿx, between qₙ and 2qₙ (our own). Its logarithm thus differs from log qₙ by at most log 2 (our own). Gauss-map ergodicity makes the average of −log x converge almost everywhere to its integral against the invariant density. That integral is π²/(12 log 2) (our own).

**nLab:** [continued fraction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/continued+fraction). It says: “then τ is an ergodic transformation with respect to μ”

**Wikipedia:** [Lévy's constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9vy%27s_constant). It says: “The term “Lévy's constant” is sometimes used to refer to π²/(12 ln 2)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Gauss map turns continued fraction digits into ergodic averages

**Remember:** Read each digit as the first digit of the next state.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K50 (Metric theory of continued fractions), 37A44. arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an irrational x in (0, 1), let a₁, a₂, … be its continued fraction digits, obtained by repeatedly taking reciprocals and removing integer parts. The Gauss map T takes x to the fractional part of 1/x. Thus aₙ is the integer part of the reciprocal after n − 1 applications of T.

**Problem.** Khinchin’s theorem says that for Lebesgue-almost every x in (0, 1), the geometric mean of its first n digits tends to the same constant. The constant is about 2.685.

**How the definition helps.** The logarithm of the geometric mean is the time average of log a₁ under the Gauss map (our own). Digit j has Gauss measure O(j⁻²), so log a₁ is integrable (our own). The map is ergodic, and Gauss measure has the same null sets as Lebesgue measure. Birkhoff’s theorem gives the integral as the limit, and exponentiation gives Khinchin’s constant (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Khinchin's constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khinchin%27s_constant). It says: “Moreover, it can be proved that T is an ergodic transformation of the measurable space I endowed with the probability measure μ (this is the hard part of the proof).”

**Sources:**

- [C. Ryll-Nardzewski, On the ergodic theorems (II) (Ergodic theory of continued fractions), Studia Math. 12 (1951) 74–79](https://doi.org/10.4064/sm-12-1-74-79)

### Completion transfers the Weil bound

**Remember:** Fourier modes turn a cut-off inverse phase into complete sums.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For prime p, nonzero b modulo p and unit x, let T(x)=exp(2πibx⁻¹/p), using the inverse modulo p. Set T(0)=0. Replace an interval indicator by its additive Fourier expansion on residues modulo p.

**Problem.** Take an integer a and an interval I containing at most p consecutive integers. The sum of T(x)exp(2πiax/p) over these integers has absolute value at most C√p log(2p) for an absolute constant C.

**How the definition helps.** Fourier expansion of the interval changes only the linear coefficient in each complete Kloosterman sum (our own). A geometric sum bounds the total absolute normalized Fourier coefficients by O(log(2p)) (our own). Weil’s bound gives 2√p for nonzero linear coefficient, while inversion gives −1 for zero coefficient (our own). Multiplication of these bounds proves the estimate (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “Short Kloosterman sums are defined as trigonometric sums of the form”

- [André Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Grouping modulo pʳ isolates stationary residues

**Remember:** Group modulo the square root of the modulus to make the exponent linear.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a prime p and integer r≥1. The Kloosterman sum S(a,b;p²ʳ) sums exp(2πi(ax+bx⁻¹)/p²ʳ) over units x modulo p²ʳ. A class contribution restricts this sum to x≡u modulo pʳ (our own).

**Problem.** Let p be odd and let a,b be integers prime to p. The class of u contributes zero unless au²≡b modulo pʳ. When the congruence holds, it contributes pʳ times the term at any member.

**How the definition helps.** Grouping modulo pʳ makes the exponent linear in the index of the lift. In our own derivation, write x = u + pʳt with 0 ≤ t &lt; pʳ. Modulo p²ʳ its inverse equals u⁻¹ − pʳtu⁻². Summing over t gives zero unless a − bu⁻² vanishes modulo pʳ, and in that case every member has the same term.

**Paper or page:** [Subconvexity for GL₂ × GL₂ L-functions in the depth aspect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18727v1). It says: “Then, S(a,b;pⁿ) = 0 if ab ∉ (ℤₚˣ)².”

**Sources:**

- [Tengyou Zhu, Subconvexity for GL₂ × GL₂ L-functions in the depth aspect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18727v1)

### Hyper-Kloosterman transforms are Gauss powers

**Remember:** A character splits the product constraint into one Gauss sum per variable.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For prime p and integer r≥1, write E(x)=exp(2πix/p). Define Kᵣ(a) by summing E(x₁)⋯E(xᵣ) over nonzero residues whose product equals a modulo p. For a multiplicative character χ modulo p, define G(χ) by summing χ(x)E(x) over nonzero residues (our own).

**Problem.** For every multiplicative character χ, summing χ(a)Kᵣ(a) over nonzero residues a gives G(χ)ʳ.

**How the definition helps.** Summing over a leaves each unrestricted r-tuple of nonzero residues exactly once (our own). Multiplicativity gives χ(a)=χ(x₁)⋯χ(xᵣ), so the sum factors into r copies of G(χ) (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The sixth moment of Dirichlet L-functions at the central point](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01457v1). It says: “where the hyper-Kloosterman sum”

### Joint primitivity prevents oversized sums

**Remember:** Exclude a common factor so the modulus measures the true oscillation.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For integers a,b and q ≥ 2, sum exp(2πi(ax+bx⁻¹)/q) over invertible residues x modulo q. Here x⁻¹ is the inverse modulo q. Write K(a,b;q) for this sum and call the pair jointly primitive when gcd(a,b,q) = 1.

**Problem.** On jointly primitive pairs, \|K(a,b;q)\| ≤ τ(q)√q, where τ counts positive divisors. Without the condition the bound fails, for example when q = 25 and a = b = 0.

**How the definition helps.** Joint primitivity makes the common-divisor factor in the general estimate equal to one. In our own example with q = 25 and a = b = 0, all 20 terms equal one. The proposed upper bound would be 3√25 = 15. The general estimate uses Weil’s prime-modulus bound and separate estimates for prime powers.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “\|K(a,b;m)\| ≤ τ(m) √gcd(a,b,m) √m.”

**Sources:**

- [André Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Smooth weights suppress distant frequencies

**Remember:** Smooth weights let repeated integration by parts remove distant frequencies.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For prime p and b coprime to p, set K(n)=exp(2πibn⁻¹/p) on units modulo p and zero otherwise. Weight n by W(n/N) for N≥1 and a smooth compactly supported function W on ℝ. Use K̂(h)=∑ₓ K(x)exp(2πihx/p) over residues and Ŵ(t)=∫ℝ W(x)exp(−2πitx) dx (our own).

**Problem.** Summing K(n)W(n/N) over all integers gives (N/p)∑ₕ K̂(h)Ŵ(Nh/p), with h over all integers. For H ≥ max(1,p/N), the terms with \|h\| &gt; H contribute at most C√p (p/(NH))ᴬ in absolute value. For each A &gt; 0 the constant depends only on A and W.

**How the definition helps.** Smoothness makes the transformed weight decrease faster than any fixed inverse power of frequency. Our own two-sided formula applies Poisson summation on each residue class. Repeated integration by parts bounds Ŵ, while Weil’s estimate gives \|K̂(h)\| ≤ 2√p. Summing those bounds gives the tail estimate.

**Paper or page:** [On a Finite Field Analogue of van der Corput Differencing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.02525v1). It says: “any even smooth function V compactly supported on ℝ”

### Exponent pairs interpolate

**Remember:** Interpolate two uniform bounds by taking their weighted geometric mean.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A pair (k,l), with 0≤k≤½≤l≤1, is an exponent pair if every s&gt;0 admits R≥1 integral, δ∈(0,1) and C&gt;0 as follows. For N≥1 and T≥Nˢ, suppose \|(f′)⁽ʲ⁾−g⁽ʲ⁾\|≤δ\|g⁽ʲ⁾\| throughout \[N,2N\] for 0≤j&lt;R, where g(x)=T/xˢ. Every subinterval sum of exp(2πif(n)) over integers n must then have magnitude at most C(T/Nˢ)ᵏNˡ (our own).

**Problem.** Every convex combination of two exponent pairs is an exponent pair.

**How the definition helps.** Recording the two powers as coordinates turns interpolation between estimates into a line segment. In our own derivation, take the larger derivative order and the smaller error tolerance. Both estimates then apply, so their weighted geometric mean gives the claimed powers. Proving the initial estimates takes the analytic work.

**Wikipedia:** [Van der Corput's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Corput%27s_method). It says: “The set of exponents pairs is convex.”

### Monotone slopes prevent coherent repetition

**Remember:** Stay away from integer slopes and do not repeatedly retrace the same slopes.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be a continuously differentiable real function on a bounded interval I. Require f′ to be monotone and to stay at least λ &gt; 0 away from every integer throughout I.

**Problem.** The sum of exp(2πif(n)) over integers n in a bounded I is O(1/λ), with an absolute constant. Without monotonicity this bound can fail even with λ = 3/8.

**How the definition helps.** Monotonicity orders the successive phase increments within one integer gap, at least λ from its endpoints (our own). Summation by parts gives O(1/λ) since the reciprocal of exp(2πit)−1 has variation O(1/λ) there (our own). For f(t)=t/2+cos(πt)/(8π), the derivative stays in \[3/8,5/8\] (our own). Each even-odd pair contributes 2i sin(1/4), giving unbounded sums (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On Sárközy's theorem for shifted primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.08001v3). It says: “Let f : I → ℝ be continuously differentiable such that f′ is monotonic and ∥f′(t)∥ ≥ λ on I.”

### Separated phases factor major arcs

**Remember:** Residue classes handle the rational phase and the integral handles the drift.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For positive integers k,N,q and integers a₁,…,aₖ jointly coprime to q, split the phase into A(x)/q+B(x). Here A(x)=∑ⱼaⱼxʲ and B(x)=∑ⱼβⱼxʲ for 1≤j≤k and real βⱼ. Define C as the residue mean of exp(2πiA(x)/q) and I as the integral of exp(2πiB(x)) from zero to N.

**Problem.** The sum of exp(2πi∑ (aⱼ/q+βⱼ)nʲ) over 1 ≤ n ≤ N equals CI plus an error. The error is O(q(1+∑ \|βⱼ\|Nʲ)), with a constant depending only on k.

**How the definition helps.** Each residue class has constant rational phase, so only the smooth factor needs approximation (our own). On each class its sum differs from I/q by O(1+∫₀ᴺ \|B′(x)\| dx), by partial summation (our own). Summing over the q classes gives CI and the stated error (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ maximal estimates for Weyl sums with k ≥ 3 on 𝕋](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15527v1). It says: “S<sub>k</sub>(\\bm {u},N) = q<sup>-1</sup>S<sub>k</sub>(q<sup>-1</sup>\\bm {r};q)I(\\bm {\\xi }) + \\Delta .”

### Vinogradov moments count power sums

**Remember:** Each integral keeps just the tuples with equal sums of powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix positive integers k, N and s. For α ∈ \[0,1\]ᵏ, let F(α) sum exp(2πi∑ⱼ αⱼnʲ) over 1 ≤ n ≤ N, with 1 ≤ j ≤ k. The mean value is the integral of \|F(α)\|²ˢ over this cube.

**Problem.** The mean value counts ordered pairs of lists, each containing s integers from 1 through N. The lists must have equal sums of jth powers for every j from 1 through k.

**How the definition helps.** Our own specialization uses the points (n,n²,…,nᵏ). Expanding the integrand gives one term per ordered pair of lists. Each coordinate integral gives one if the corresponding power sums agree and zero otherwise.

**Paper or page:** [Decoupling estimates in Fourier analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00652v1). It says: “For any finite set A ⊂ ℤᵈ, ∫<sub>\[0,1\]<sup>d</sub></sup> \|f<sub>A</sub>(x)\|<sup>2s</sup> dx = E<sub>s</sub>(A).”

### Reciprocal roots bound polynomial prime sums

**Remember:** Weight each prime power by the degree of its prime.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L20 (Sums over primes), 11T23. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let χ be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character on 𝔽𝓆\[T\], extended by zero off the units modulo its modulus. Define L(u,χ) = ∑ χ(f)u<sup>(deg f)</sup> over monic polynomials f. For each such f, set Λ(f) = deg P if f = Pʲ for monic irreducible P and integer j ≥ 1, and zero otherwise.

**Problem.** Let d be the degree of L(u,χ). For n ≥ 1, the sum of Λ(f)χ(f) over degree-n monic polynomials has modulus at most d√(qⁿ).

**How the definition helps.** The degree weight makes every prime power contribute exactly its coefficient in the logarithmic derivative of the Euler product. Our own calculation factors L into terms 1 − γu. The degree-n coefficient of uL′/L is then minus the sum of the nth powers of the reciprocal roots γ. Weil’s theorem bounds each \|γ\| by √q.

**Paper or page:** [Equidistribution of high traces of random matrices over finite fields and cancellation in character sums of high conductor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01344). It says: “we have \|γᵢ\| ∈ {1, √q} for all 1 ≤ i ≤ d(χ).”

### Conductors isolate primitive correlations

**Remember:** Assign each character to the first modulus where it appears.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L40 (Estimates on character sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Dirichlet character χ modulo q, its conductor is the least divisor d \| q through which χ factors on units. The character is primitive if d = q. For n,m coprime to q, let C(q) sum χ(n) times the conjugate of χ(m) over primitive χ modulo q.

**Problem.** C(q) equals the sum of μ(q/d)φ(d) over divisors d \| q satisfying n ≡ m modulo d. Here μ is the Möbius function and φ is Euler’s totient function.

**How the definition helps.** Grouping characters by conductor expresses the full character sum as a divisor sum of primitive contributions (our own). Each character comes from a unique primitive character. Orthogonality gives φ(d) when n ≡ m modulo d and zero otherwise. Möbius inversion isolates C(q).

**Paper or page:** [Bounds for moments of Dirichlet L-functions to a fixed modulus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00149). It says: “the sum over non-trivial primitive even (respectively odd) characters modulo q.”

### Balanced cutoffs shorten sums

**Remember:** Split the length evenly between the two reflected sums.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For large positive t, choose the same cutoff m = ⌊√(t/(2π))⌋ in both sums that approximate ζ(½ + it). Define θ(t) = Im log Γ(¼ + it/2) − (t/2)log π. Choose the continuous logarithm of the gamma function that is real at t = 0.

**Problem.** Let C(t) sum cos(θ(t) − t log n)/√n for 1 ≤ n ≤ m. Then exp(iθ(t))ζ(½ + it) = 2C(t) + O(t⁻¹⁄⁴) as t tends to infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Equal cutoffs pair terms with the same index, and multiplication by exp(iθ(t)) makes each pair complex conjugates (our own). Each pair therefore contributes twice a cosine divided by √n (our own). The approximate functional equation gives the stated error (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann–Siegel formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Siegel_formula). It says: “an approximation of the zeta function by a sum of two finite Dirichlet series.”

### Integrating the prime count makes the zero sum converge absolutely

**Remember:** One integration gives each distant zero a second denominator.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)), 11N05. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ψ(x) sum log p over prime powers pᵏ ≤ x, with k ≥ 1. Define A(x) = ∫₁ˣ ψ(u) du. Write ζ for the Riemann zeta function and ρ for a zero with 0 &lt; Re ρ &lt; 1.

**Problem.** For x &gt; 1, A(x) equals x²/2 − x log(2π) + ζ′(−1)/ζ(−1) minus two absolutely convergent sums. The first sums exp((ρ + 1) log x)/(ρ(ρ + 1)) over nontrivial zeros with multiplicity. The second sums exp((1 − 2k) log x)/(2k(2k − 1)) over integers k ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** Integration gives each zero a second denominator, so the sum no longer depends on the order of its terms (our own). For fixed x, each term is O(1/\|ρ\|²) as \|ρ\| grows (our own). The count of zeros up to height T is O(T log T), which gives absolute convergence (our own). Moving the integration path past the poles gives the formula and requires bounds for ζ′/ζ on that path (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Explicit formulae for L-functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explicit_formulae_for_L-functions). It says: “This series is also conditionally convergent”

### Logarithmic time enables Wiener–Ikehara

**Remember:** Logarithmic time places each prime power at its logarithm.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)), 11N05. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For y ≥ 0 define A(y) = ψ(exp y). Here ψ(x) sums log p over prime powers pᵏ ≤ x with integer exponent k ≥ 1.

**Problem.** If the Riemann zeta function ζ has no zeros on Re s = 1, then ψ(x)/x tends to 1. Consequently π(x), the number of primes up to x, is asymptotic to x/log x.

**How the definition helps.** The nondecreasing function A has Laplace transform −ζ′(s)/(sζ(s)) for Re s &gt; 1 (our own). Subtracting 1/(s − 1) leaves a function analytic near each point on Re s = 1 under the hypothesis. Wiener–Ikehara gives A(y)/exp(y) → 1. Removing higher prime powers and applying partial summation gives the assertion for π.

**nLab:** [proof of the prime number theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proof+of+the+prime+number+theorem). It says: “The asymptotic statement θ(x) ∼ x implies the prime number theorem.”

**Remember:** For an odd character, multiply by n so opposite integers add.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**How the definition helps.** The extra factor makes the terms at n and −n agree instead of canceling (our own). ### Primitive characters give Dirichlet L-functions a clean functional equation

**Remember:** Strip a character down to its true period before you reflect its L-function.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)), 11L05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Dirichlet character χ modulo q, its conductor is the least divisor d \| q through which its values on units factor. Call χ primitive if its conductor equals q. For Re s &gt; 1, define L(s,χ) = ∑ χ(n)n⁻ˢ over positive integers n.

**Problem.** Let χ be a primitive character modulo q &gt; 1, with δ = 0 if χ(−1) = 1 and δ = 1 otherwise. Put Λ(s,χ) = (q/π) to the power (s+δ)/2, times Γ((s+δ)/2) L(s,χ). Then Λ is entire and Λ(s,χ) = W(χ) Λ(1−s, χ̄) with \|W(χ)\| = 1.

**How the definition helps.** Primitivity removes the extra factors that can break reflection symmetry (our own). For example, inducing the character modulo 3 of conductor 3 to modulus 6 inserts the factor 1 + 2⁻ˢ. Its zeros lie on Re s = 0, while the primitive L-function has no zeros on Re s = 1. For primitive characters, Poisson summation gives the functional equation and the normalized Gauss sum has modulus one.

The contour approaches zero above the positive axis, circles zero counterclockwise within \|x\| &lt; 2π, and returns below the axis. Use the principal branch of log(−x).

**Problem.** The zeta function extends to the whole complex plane with only a simple pole at s = 1.

**How the definition helps.** The fixed contour gives an entire integral, so the gamma factor allows poles only at positive integers (our own). Collapsing the contour for nonintegral s with Re s &gt; 1 recovers the defining series. The series removes the apparent poles at integers above one. Integral comparison gives ζ(s) ∼ 1/(s−1) as real s decreases to one.

### Shifted kernels cancel opposite poles

**Remember:** Combine the shifted terms before letting the shifts meet.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let X(s) = π<sup>(s−½)</sup> Γ((1−s)/2)/Γ(s/2), the factor in the functional equation ζ(s) = X(s)ζ(1−s). For s = ½ + it with t real, the combined shifted kernel is K(z,t) = ζ(1+z) + X(s+z)X(1−s)ζ(1−z).

**Problem.** For real t, the kernel K(z,t) has a removable singularity at z = 0, with value 2γ − X′(s)/X(s), where γ is Euler's constant.

**How the definition helps.** Combining the terms lets their opposite residues cancel before the shifts coincide. Our own calculation uses X(s)X(1−s) = 1 and ζ(1+z) = 1/z + γ + O(z). Expanding X(s+z) to first order gives the stated finite value. The cited theorem identifies the combined expression as the main term in a shifted second moment.

**Remember:** Removing the first prime power leaves a convergent remainder.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The prime zeta function is P(s) = ∑ p⁻ˢ over primes p, for Re s &gt; 1. Compare it with log ζ(s), taken from the Euler product, through the remainder R(s) = P(s) − log ζ(s).

**Problem.** The remainder R extends holomorphically to Re s &gt; ½. So in that half-plane P continues along paths that avoid the zeros and the pole of ζ, with the same logarithmic singularities as log ζ.

**How the definition helps.** Subtracting log ζ cancels every first power in the sum over primes (our own). The logarithm of the Euler product, the product expansion over primes, gives the remaining terms (our own). All have exponent at least two, so their series converges absolutely and locally uniformly for Re s &gt; ½ (our own). This continues the difference beyond the original domain of the series over primes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Prime zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_zeta_function). It says: “with an infinite number of logarithmic singularities”

**Sources:**

- [C.-E. Fröberg, On the prime zeta function (1968)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01933420)

### The Riemann xi function is built to be entire and symmetric

**Remember:** Multiply zeta by its missing factors, and it becomes symmetric and entire.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)), 11M26. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the Riemann xi function by ξ(s) = ½s(s−1)π<sup>(−s/2)</sup>Γ(s/2)ζ(s), taking limits at removable singularities.

**Problem.** The function ξ is entire, real on the real line, and satisfies ξ(1−s) = ξ(s). Its zeros are exactly the nontrivial zeros ρ of ζ. It has the product ξ(s) = ½ ∏ (1 − s/ρ), pairing conjugate zeros and counting multiplicities.

**How the definition helps.** The gamma factor gives the symmetry from the zeta functional equation (our own). The trivial zeros cancel the gamma poles at negative even integers, and s(s−1) removes the poles at zero and one. Hadamard factorization for ξ of order one gives the paired product using the symmetry and ξ(0) = ½.

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann xi function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_xi_function). It says: “In mathematics, the Riemann xi function is a variant of the Riemann zeta function, and is defined so as to have a particularly simple functional equation.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Riemann, Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse, Monatsberichte der Berliner Akademie, 1859](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/HistMath/People/Riemann/Zeta/)

### A product with nonnegative coefficients rules out a zero at one

**Remember:** Multiply by zeta to turn character values into nonnegative divisor sums.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a real nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ, form ζ(s)L(s,χ). For Re s &gt; 1 its Dirichlet coefficient at n is the sum of χ(d) over positive divisors d of n.

**Problem.** For every such character, L(1,χ) is nonzero.

**How the definition helps.** These coefficients are multiplicative (our own). At a prime power they sum successive powers of 0, 1 or −1, giving nonnegative values and at least one on squares. Thus the series diverges at ½. A zero at one would make the product entire, contradicting Landau’s singularity theorem for nonnegative Dirichlet series.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function). It says: “In his proof, Dirichlet showed that L(s,χ) is non-zero at s = 1.”

**Paper or page:** [A note on prime number races and zero free regions for L functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00764v3). It says: “and has a singularity at σ𝒸.”

### A zeta quotient isolates quadratic zeros

**Remember:** Divide out rational zeta to see the quadratic character.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)), 11R11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a quadratic field K of discriminant D, use the quotient ζᴷ(s)/ζ(s) of its Dedekind zeta function by the Riemann zeta function, continued analytically.

**Problem.** On the real interval 0 &lt; s &lt; 1, ζᴷ and L(s,χᴰ) have exactly the same zeros with the same multiplicities. Here χᴰ denotes the primitive quadratic character attached to D.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing out ζ isolates the character factor throughout the interval. The quadratic factorization identifies the quotient with L(s,χᴰ) by matching the prime factors of the two series. Our own check uses the alternating series for ζ to show ζ(s) &lt; 0 for 0 &lt; s &lt; 1. Multiplication by this nonzero factor preserves every zero and its multiplicity.

**Wikipedia:** [Siegel zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_zero). It says: “ζℚ(√D)(s) = ζ(s) L(s,χᴰ)”

### Euler factors preserve Siegel bounds

**Remember:** Bound the primitive value first and put back the missing factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For χ modulo q, its primitive inducing character χ∗ has the least modulus d dividing q that determines χ on units. Its values there agree with χ, and the correction factors are 1−χ∗(p)p⁻ˢ for primes p dividing q.

**Problem.** For every ε &gt; 0 there exists c(ε) &gt; 0 such that every real nonprincipal character χ modulo q satisfies L(1,χ) ≥ c(ε)q<sup>(−ε)</sup>.

**How the definition helps.** The Euler product gives L(1,χ) by multiplying L(1,χ∗) by the correction factors (our own). Their product is at least φ(q)/q since each factor is at least 1−1/p. For each ε &gt; 0, φ(q)/q exceeds a positive constant depending on ε times q<sup>(−ε/2)</sup>. Siegel’s theorem at exponent ε/2 gives the other factor since d ≤ q.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function). It says: “multiplied by only a finite number of factors.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Harmonic subtraction computes L-values

**Remember:** Subtract the same harmonic tail from each residue class.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)), 11M35. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For 0 &lt; u ≤ 1 define H(u) by summing 1/(m+u) − 1/(m+1) over integers m ≥ 0. Every residue class uses the same reference term 1/(m+1).

**Problem.** Let χ be a Dirichlet character modulo q whose values on invertible residues are not all one. Then L(1,χ) = (1/q) ∑ χ(a)H(a/q), summing over 1 ≤ a ≤ q. Also H(u) = −Γ′(u)/Γ(u) − γ, where Γ is Euler’s gamma function and γ is Euler’s constant.

**How the definition helps.** Subtracting the common term makes each residue sum converge separately. Without subtraction each sum diverges like the harmonic series. In our own derivation, summing complete blocks of q terms recovers the original series because the character values sum to zero. Differentiating the logarithm of Euler’s product for Γ gives the displayed formula for H.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function). It says: “linear combinations of the Hurwitz zeta function at rational values.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Logarithmic gaps simplify zero repulsion

**Remember:** Multiply each horizontal gap by log(qT) before comparing zeros.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)), 11M26. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix an integer q ≥ 3 and a real height T ≥ 2. For a zero σ + it of a Dirichlet L-function modulo q, define its scaled distance from Re s = 1 as (1−σ) log(qT).

**Problem.** There exist computable absolute constants 0 &lt; c &lt; 1 and c′ &gt; 0 with the following property. Suppose a quadratic character modulo q has a real zero β with scaled distance δ &lt; c. Every other zero of any Dirichlet L-function modulo q at height \|t\| ≤ T has scaled distance at least c′ log(1/δ).

**How the definition helps.** Using the same unit for both distances makes the gain a single logarithm. Our own rewriting expresses Theorem 3 in these units. The Deuring–Heilbronn theorem supplies the bound on the other zeros.

**Paper or page:** [Condtional Bounds on Siegel Zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01308). It says: “the product over all characters of modulus q including the exceptional one, has no other zero in the domain”

**Sources:**

- [D. R. Heath-Brown, Zero-free regions for Dirichlet L-functions, and the least prime in an arithmetic progression (1992)](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s3-64.2.265)

### Odd parity gives class numbers

**Remember:** For an odd quadratic character, the first residue moment gives the class number.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a prime q &gt; 3 with q ≡ 3 modulo 4. Let χ(a) equal zero on multiples of q, one on nonzero squares modulo q, and minus one on the remaining residues. Its first moment is the sum of aχ(a) over integers 1 ≤ a &lt; q.

**Problem.** The number of ideal classes of ℚ(√(−q)) equals −1/q times this first moment.

**How the definition helps.** Odd parity makes the first moment measure the nonzero value L(0,χ). Our own derivation uses L(0,χ) = −∑ aχ(a)/q and the functional equation L(1,χ) = πL(0,χ)/√q. The class number formula then gives the result. For the quadratic character modulo 5, pairing a with 5−a makes the first moment zero, although L(1,χ) is positive.

**Wikipedia:** [Class number formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_formula). It says: “Dirichlet also showed that the L-series can be written in a finite form”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### One quadratic factor controls abelian exceptions

**Remember:** A quadratic factor can recur in many fields without becoming many exceptions.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)), 11R42. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an abelian number field K, take the Dirichlet characters corresponding to its Galois group via the abelian zeta factorization. Label each by its primitive inducing character, the character of least modulus agreeing on units. Fix Q ≥ 10 and take all such fields of absolute discriminant at most Q.

**Problem.** For some absolute c &gt; 0, suppose a field in this family has a real zeta zero β with 1−c/log Q &lt; β &lt; 1. Exactly one quadratic field F supplies this zero. The fields in the family whose zeta functions vanish at β are precisely those containing F.

**How the definition helps.** The same primitive character labels the same L-factor in every field (our own). The conductor–discriminant formula bounds its modulus by Q. Proposition 6.2 allows at most one exceptional primitive character, which must be quadratic. The abelian zeta factorization includes that character precisely for fields containing its quadratic field.

**Paper or page:** [An explicit version of Bombieri's log-free density estimate and Sárközy's theorem for shifted primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.11123). It says: “there exists a unique primitive quadratic character χ∗ (mod q∗) with q∗ ≤ Q”

### Regulators normalize Siegel’s class bounds

**Remember:** Take the residue at one for every quadratic field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a quadratic field K, define A(K) as the residue of its Dedekind zeta function at s = 1.

**Problem.** For every ε &gt; 0 some c(ε) &gt; 0 satisfies A(K) ≥ c(ε) exp(−ε log ∣D∣) for all quadratic fields K.

**How the definition helps.** The residue puts real and imaginary quadratic fields under one bound. The field's zeta function is the Riemann zeta function times a quadratic Dirichlet L-function (our own). The Riemann zeta function has residue one, so A(K) is the value of that L-function at one (our own). Siegel's theorem supplies the lower bound.

**nLab:** [class number formula](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/class+number+formula). It says: “is proportional the product of the regulator with the class number of K”

**Sources:**

- [C. L. Siegel, Über die Classenzahl quadratischer Zahlkörper (1935)](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-1-1-83-86)

### Removing the exceptional factor bounds derivatives

**Remember:** Remove the exceptional zero before taking the logarithmic derivative.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a real primitive nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ of conductor q and a sufficiently small absolute zero-free region constant c &gt; 0. If L(s,χ) has a real zero β &gt; 1−c/log q, define F(s) = L(s,χ)/(s−β) by continuity at β. Otherwise define F(s) = L(s,χ).

**Problem.** There is an absolute constant C such that \|F′(1)/F(1)\| ≤ C log q. When β exists, L′(1,χ)/L(1,χ) equals 1/(1−β) plus F′(1)/F(1).

**How the definition helps.** Dividing out the simple exceptional zero removes its term from the logarithmic derivative (our own). The explicit formula and classical zero-free region bound the remaining zero contributions at one by comparison with 1+1/log q. The Euler product bounds the logarithmic derivative at that point by O(log q).

**Wikipedia:** [Siegel zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_zero). It says: “classical estimates for the number of non-trivial zeros”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Two quadratic zeros share one pole

**Remember:** Put two candidate zeros into a product with just one pole.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)), 11R11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For distinct primitive quadratic Dirichlet characters χ₁ and χ₂, define F(s) = ζ(s)L(s,χ₁)L(s,χ₂)L(s,χ₁χ₂). The last character multiplies their values at each integer.

**Problem.** Let β₁ and β₂ be real zeros in (0,1) of the respective L-functions, with moduli q₁ and q₂. Then max(1−β₁,1−β₂) ≥ c/log(q₁q₂) for an absolute c &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** The product collects both zeros but has only one pole at one, since χ₁χ₂ is nonprincipal (our own). Every prime-power coefficient of −F′/F contains the nonnegative factor (1+χ₁(n))(1+χ₂(n)). The Landau–Page argument applies the explicit formula to this positive sum to obtain the separation bound.

**Paper or page:** [Condtional Bounds on Siegel Zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01308). It says: “then it is real and associated to a unique, quadratic χ mod q.”

### Continuous angles count zeros

**Remember:** Follow the turn instead of resetting the angle.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let T &gt; 0 avoid all nontrivial zeta zero heights. Starting with argument zero at ζ(2), follow the argument continuously along the segments from 2 to 2+iT to ½+iT. Define S(T) as the final argument divided by π.

**Problem.** The number of zeta zeros with imaginary part strictly between zero and T, counted with multiplicity, equals 1 + θ(T)/π + S(T). Here θ(T) = Im log Γ(¼ + iT/2) − (T/2)log π, using the continuous logarithm real at T = 0.

**How the definition helps.** Following the angle continuously records every full turn along the path (our own). The argument principle counts zeros by the total turn around a closed boundary (our own). The symmetry of the completed zeta function reduces this count to the stated path and the explicit gamma term (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann–Siegel theta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Siegel_theta_function). It says: “the argument is chosen in such a way that a continuous function is obtained”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Cosine gaps exclude zeros

**Remember:** The first cosine must outweigh the constant term.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use a cosine polynomial P(u) = ∑ from j = 0 to m of aⱼ cos(ju) that stays nonnegative on ℝ. Require aⱼ ≥ 0 and a₁ &gt; a₀ &gt; 0. For example, P(u) = (1 + cos u)² has a₁ = 2 and a₀ = 3/2.

**Problem.** For each such P there is a constant c &gt; 0. If \|t\| ≥ 2 and σ ≥ 1 − c/log \|t\|, then ζ(σ + it) is nonzero.

**How the definition helps.** Nonnegativity weights the prime-power expansion of the logarithmic derivatives by nonnegative values (our own). For a zero β+it and σ &gt; 1, the explicit formula gives a₁/(σ−β) ≤ a₀/(σ−1) + O(log \|t\|). The other zero contributions can be discarded because every coefficient is nonnegative. Taking σ−1 to be a sufficiently small multiple of 1/log \|t\| gives the bound since a₁ &gt; a₀.

**Paper or page:** [Optimal Cosine Polynomials for Riemann Zeta Zero-Free Region](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.01385). It says: “Historically, E. Landau used a particular type of non-negative cosine polynomial to construct this region.”

### Fourth powers exclude boundary zeros

**Remember:** Weight five shifts by the coefficients of a fourth power to keep the sum nonnegative.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For Re s&gt;1, let Φ(s) sum log(p) exp(−s log p) over primes p. Fix a real t≠0. Combine Φ(s+irt) for r from −2 to 2 with successive weights 1, 4, 6, 4, 1.

**Problem.** The Riemann zeta function has no zero on Re s = 1.

**How the definition helps.** Each prime gets the nonnegative multiplier (2 cos(t log(p)/2))⁴ for real s &gt; 1 (our own). Comparison with −ζ′/ζ shows that multiplying by s−1 gives limit 6−8μ−2ν as s decreases to one. Here μ and ν are the zero multiplicities at 1+it and 1+2it, with zero denoting a nonzero value. Nonnegativity rules out μ ≥ 1 for every nonzero t.

**nLab:** [proof of the prime number theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proof+of+the+prime+number+theorem). It says: “from which, in conjunction with 1., 2., 3. above, we deduce 0 ≤ 6 − 8μ − 2ν, so that μ = 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Gram signs certify zeros

**Remember:** Test the endpoint signs before trusting a Gram interval.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define θ(t) = Im log Γ(¼ + it/2) − (t/2)log π using the continuous logarithm real at t = 0. Successive Gram points g &lt; h on the increasing branch satisfy θ(g) = nπ and θ(h) = (n+1)π for an integer n. Retain (g,h) if ζ(½+ig) and ζ(½+ih) are both positive.

**Problem.** Every retained interval has a zero ½ + it with g &lt; t &lt; h. The test gives no guarantee about a rejected interval or uniqueness in a retained interval.

**How the definition helps.** At successive Gram points, the factors exp(iθ(t)) have opposite signs. The functional equation makes Z(t) = exp(iθ(t))ζ(½ + it) real for every real t (our own). Positive endpoint values of ζ therefore give opposite signs for Z. Continuity forces an interior zero.

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann–Siegel theta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Siegel_theta_function). It says: “and if this is positive at two successive Gram points, Z(t) must have a zero in the interval.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Integrated gaps certify completeness

**Remember:** A missed zero leaves a gap throughout the later count.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let N(t) count zeta zeros of heights in (0,t\] with multiplicity, and let M(t) count a fixed subset of those occurrences cumulatively. Define S(t) = N(t) − 1 − θ(t)/π, where θ(t) = Im log Γ(¼+it/2) − (t/2)log π. Use the continuous logarithm real at t = 0.

**Problem.** Let 0 &lt; A &lt; B, and let U bound the integral of S over \[A, B\] from above. Let V be the integral of 1 + θ(t)/π − M(t) over that interval. If U + V &lt; B − A, then M(A) = N(A).

**How the definition helps.** Counting all missed zeros cumulatively turns an omission by A into a discrepancy lasting throughout \[A, B\] (our own). Its integral is then at least B − A, even if every later zero is found (our own). By definition that integral is at most U + V (our own). Turing’s method supplies the difficult bound U for the integral of S (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Turing's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing%27s_method). It says: “It was discovered by Alan Turing and published in 1953”

**Sources:**

- [A. M. Turing, Some Calculations of the Riemann Zeta-Function (1953)](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s3-3.1.99)
- [R. S. Lehman, On the Distribution of Zeros of the Riemann Zeta-Function (1970)](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s3-20.2.303)

### Paired zeros cancel exponentials

**Remember:** Center the function and pair the opposite zeros.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define ξ(s) = ½s(s−1)π<sup>(−s/2)</sup>Γ(s/2)ζ(s) by continuity at removable singularities. Its centered form is Ξ(z) = ξ(½+z).

**Problem.** For every z, Ξ(z)/Ξ(0) equals the product of 1 − (z/a)² over one zero from each pair, with multiplicity. This product converges locally uniformly with absolutely summable deviations from 1.

**How the definition helps.** Pairing opposite zeros cancels the exponential factors that each zero needs in the usual product (our own). Hadamard’s theorem gives that product from the growth bound on ξ (our own). The functional equation makes Ξ even, so the remaining exponential has zero linear coefficient (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Completed Riemann Zeta Function has Order One](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Completed_Riemann_Zeta_Function_has_Order_One). It says: “The completed Riemann zeta function ξ has order at most 1.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Riemann, On the Number of Prime Numbers less than a Given Quantity (1859), translated by D. R. Wilkins](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/Wilkins-translation.pdf)

**Remember:** Remove a constant phase speed without moving the zeros.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let F(t) = ζ(½+it)A(½+it), where A is a nonzero Dirichlet polynomial. The phase twist exp(ict)F(t) has the same zeros as F for every real c. On a given interval, choose c to minimize the integral of \|F′ + icF\|².

**How the definition helps.** The phase twist preserves zeros and gives derivative modulus \|F′ + icF\| (our own). Wirtinger’s inequality bounds the square integral on each gap by its derivative square integral times the squared gap divided by π². Summing and minimizing over c gives the bound.

### Phase correction reveals critical zeros

**Remember:** Remove the phase so that a sign change detects a zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For real t define θ(t) = Im log Γ(¼+it/2) − (t/2)log π, choosing the continuous logarithm real at zero. Hardy’s function is Z(t) = exp(iθ(t))ζ(½+it).

**Problem.** On the critical line Re s=1/2, Hardy’s Z takes real values and has the same zeros, with multiplicity, as the Riemann zeta function ζ. Opposite signs at two heights guarantee a zero between them.

**How the definition helps.** The phase factor turns the functional equation into equality with the complex conjugate (our own). The factor never vanishes, so it cannot create or remove zeros (our own). The work moves to the functional equation and to finding points of opposite sign, as in proofs of infinitely many critical zeros (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Z function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z_function). It says: “It follows from the functional equation of the Riemann zeta function that the Z function is real for real values of t.”

### Separated heights avoid poles

**Remember:** Leave a small gap between the contour and every zero.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write ρ for a zero of the Riemann zeta function ζ with 0 &lt; Re ρ &lt; 1. Fix a sufficiently small absolute constant c &gt; 0. Call U separated at scale T if \|U − Im ρ\| ≥ c/log T for every such zero.

**Problem.** For each sufficiently large T there is a separated U in \[T, T + 1\]. At this height (ζ′/ζ)(σ + iU) = O((log T)²) uniformly for −1 ≤ σ ≤ 2.

**How the definition helps.** The gap keeps every denominator σ + iU − ρ away from zero (our own). Only O(log T) zeros have heights between T − 1 and T + 2 (our own). Removing an interval of radius c/log T around each leaves room if c is small enough (our own). In the expansion of ζ′/ζ, each nearby reciprocal is then O(log T), and the distant terms together contribute O(log T) (our own).

### Subtracting the main term reveals a region without zeros

**Remember:** Remove the pole at one to test for other poles.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses), 11N05. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ψ(x) sum log p over prime powers pᵏ ≤ x, and define E(x) = ψ(x) − x. Transform E rather than ψ by setting F(s) = ∫₁∞ E(x) exp(−(s + 1) log x) dx.

**Problem.** If E(x) = O(exp(θ log x)) for some ½ ≤ θ &lt; 1, then ζ has no zeros in Re s &gt; θ. In Re s &gt; 1, sF(s) = −(ζ′/ζ)(s) − s/(s − 1).

**How the definition helps.** Subtracting x from ψ(x) cancels the pole at 1 in the transform identity (our own). Partial summation gives the identity from the series for −ζ′/ζ (our own). The power bound makes the integral converge locally uniformly for Re s &gt; θ, where it defines a holomorphic function (our own). A zeta zero there would produce a pole in the continued identity (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Logarithmic Derivative of Riemann Zeta Function](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Logarithmic_Derivative_of_Riemann_Zeta_Function). It says: “−ζ′(s)/ζ(s) = ∑ₙ≥₁ Λ(n)n⁻ˢ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Subtraction isolates nearby zeros

**Remember:** Subtract at the same height to damp distant zeros.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Compare the logarithmic derivative ζ′/ζ at s = σ + it with its value at 2 + it, at the same height. That is, use D(s) = (ζ′/ζ)(s) − (ζ′/ζ)(2 + it).

**Problem.** Let s = σ + it, with −1 ≤ σ ≤ 2 and \|t\| ≥ 2. Away from zeros, (ζ′/ζ)(s) equals the sum of 1/(s − ρ) over \|Im ρ − t\| ≤ 1, plus O(log \|t\|). Count zeros with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** Subtraction at the same height makes each distant zero contribute a reciprocal difference with quadratic decay (our own). The Hadamard product gives these differences, and the unit-interval count O(log(2+\|u\|)) at height u bounds their total by O(log \|t\|). Nearby subtraction terms obey the same total bound. The Euler product at 2+it and Stirling’s estimate control the remaining terms.

**Paper or page:** [Product Equation for Riemann Zeta Function](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Product_Equation_for_Riemann_Zeta_Function). It says: “∑ρ (1/(s − ρ) + 1/ρ)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The stuffle product makes multiple zeta values an algebra

**Remember:** Interleave the indices and add exponents when summation variables coincide.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 16T30. arXiv math.NT, math.QA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For positive integers k₁,…,kᵣ with k₁ ≥ 2, ζ(k₁,…,kᵣ) sums ∏ᵢ nᵢ<sup>(−kᵢ)</sup> over integers n₁ &gt; ⋯ &gt; nᵣ ≥ 1. The stuffle of two index lists sums all order-preserving interleavings, allowing one entry from each list to share a position. Add the entries at each shared position and count each interleaving separately.

**Problem.** The product of two multiple zeta values is a sum of multiple zeta values. So their ℚ-span 𝒵 is a ring.

**How the definition helps.** Sorting the variables in the product of two convergent sums gives precisely the stuffles (our own). Equal variables contribute the sum of their exponents. Every resulting index starts with an exponent of at least two, so each sum converges. Bilinearity gives closure of the rational span under multiplication.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized quasi-shuffle products](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12386). It says: “For v,w ∈ ℌ⁰ we have ζ(v)ζ(w)=ζ(v∗w). In particular, the space 𝒵 is a ℚ-algebra.”

- [Masataka Satoh, Generalized quasi-shuffle products, arXiv:2303.12386 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12386)

### Word integrals make shuffles multiplicative

**Remember:** Multiplying ordered integrals interleaves their variables.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Encode each positive index s by s−1 zeros followed by one, and concatenate the blocks in order. Read zero as dt/t and one as dt/(1−t), integrating over 1 &gt; t₁ &gt; ⋯ &gt; tₖ &gt; 0. A shuffle sums all interleavings preserving each word’s order, counting each interleaving separately.

**Problem.** For two words starting with zero and ending with one, the product of their multiple zeta values equals the sum of their shuffled integrals.

**How the definition helps.** The integral assigns one region of the product domain to each shuffle. In our own proof, order all the variables together and discard the diagonals, which have measure zero. Each interleaving gives the integral of the shuffled word. The work lies in proving the integral represents the original nested sum.

**Wikipedia:** [Multiple zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_zeta_function). It says: “This result is extremely useful due to a well-known result regarding products of iterated integrals”

**Paper or page:** [Discrete iterated integrals and cyclic sum formulas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16161v2). It says: “(Shuffle product formula) Iγ(xγ; w ⧢ w′; yγ) = Iγ(xγ; w; yγ)Iγ(xγ; w′; yγ).”

**Sources:**

- [Discrete iterated integrals and cyclic sum formulas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16161v2)

### Word reflection gives zeta duality

**Remember:** Reverse the word and swap its letters without changing the value.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Encode positive indices starting with s₁ ≥ 2 by writing s−1 zeros followed by one for each index s. Integrate the resulting word over 1 &gt; t₁ &gt; ⋯ &gt; tₖ &gt; 0, reading zero as dt/t and one as dt/(1−t). The dual word reverses the order and exchanges zero and one.

**Problem.** Every multiple zeta value equals the multiple zeta value of its dual word.

**How the definition helps.** The integral turns duality into a reflection of the integration domain. In our own proof, reverse the variable order and replace each t by 1 − t. This swaps both forms and keeps the ordered domain. The comparison that carries the work identifies the word integral with the nested series.

**Wikipedia:** [Multiple zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_zeta_function). It says: “it is possible to express colored multiple zeta values (and thus their special cases) as certain multivariable integrals.”

**Paper or page:** [Proving dualities for qMZVs with connected sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00058v1). It says: “For every admissible index k, we have ζ(k) = ζ(k∨).”

**Sources:**

- [Discrete iterated integrals and cyclic sum formulas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16161v2)

### Hurwitz zeta cancels character poles

**Remember:** All residue classes have the same pole, so a zero character sum cancels it.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M35 (Hurwitz and Lerch zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a&gt;0 and Re s&gt;1, the Hurwitz zeta function ζ(s,a) sums exp(−s log(n+a)) over integers n≥0. A Dirichlet character χ modulo q is a multiplicative character of the invertible residues, extended by zero elsewhere. Its L-function sums χ(n) exp(−s log n) over positive integers.

**Problem.** If χ differs from one on some invertible residue, its L-function extends holomorphically to the whole complex plane.

**How the definition helps.** Grouping by residues replaces the original series with functions whose sole poles have identical residues (our own). Class r contributes χ(r)ζ(s,r/q) times exp(−s log q), for 1≤r≤q (our own). The character values sum to zero, so the residues cancel (our own). The analytic work lies in continuing each Hurwitz zeta function to the plane with only its simple pole at one.

**Wikipedia:** [Hurwitz zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz_zeta_function). It says: “At s = 1, it has a simple pole with residue 1.”
