### Least factors partition sieve losses

**Remember:** Assign each discarded number to its first prime divisor.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N36 (Applications of sieve methods). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite set A of positive integers, S(A,z) counts its members with no prime factor below z. For each prime p, set Aₚ = {n/p ∣ n ∈ A and p divides n}.

**Problem.** For 2≤z≤y, S(A,y)=S(A,z)−∑ S(Aₚ,p), with the sum over primes z≤p&lt;y. In an interval contained in (√x,x\], taking y&gt;√x makes the surviving numbers exactly the primes at least y.

**How the definition helps.** Sorting by the least prime counts every discarded integer exactly once (our own). Removing that prime p leaves a quotient with no prime factor below p, even if p divides the quotient. Counting all prime divisors would charge 15 to both 3 and 5. Every composite up to x has a prime factor at most √x, giving the interval claim.

**Wikipedia:** [Rough number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough_number). It says: “whose prime factors are all greater than or equal to”

**Sources:**

- [A. Buchstab, Asymptotische Abschätzung einer allgemeinen zahlentheoretischen Funktion, Matematicheskii Sbornik 2 (1937), 1239–1246](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?jrnid=sm&option_lang=eng&paperid=5649&wshow=paper)
- [Runbo Li, The number of primes in short intervals and numerical calculations for Harman's sieve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04458)

### Nearest powers control means

**Remember:** Minimize the prime-weighted distance to imaginary powers over the allowed frequencies.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be multiplicative, so f(ab)=f(a)f(b) for coprime a,b, and assume \|f(n)\| ≤ 1. For real t, sum (1−Re(f(p)exp(−it log p)))/p over primes p ≤ x. Let M be the minimum of this sum for \|t\| ≤ T.

**Problem.** For x ≥ 3, divide the sum of f(n) over n ≤ x by x. For T ≥ 1, the modulus of this average is at most C((1+M)exp(−M)+1/T) with an absolute constant C.

**How the definition helps.** Our own reading is that one minimum replaces a separate comparison with each possible frequency. Halász’s mean value theorem supplies the estimate that turns prime data into a bound for the mean.

**Paper or page:** [Gap problems for integer-valued multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11636). It says: “Let x ≥ 3 and T ≥ 1. Let g ∶ ℕ → 𝕌 be a multiplicative function.”

**Sources:**

- [Gap problems for integer-valued multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11636)
- [Andrew Granville and K. Soundararajan, Decay of Mean Values of Multiplicative Functions (2003)](https://doi.org/10.4153/CJM-2003-047-0)

### The factor at two can erase means

**Remember:** One vanishing local factor can erase the entire mean.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For multiplicative f with \|f(n)\| ≤ 1 and real t, put h(n) = f(n)exp(−it log n). Finite distance at t means ∑ₚ(1−Re h(p))/p converges over primes. Define the local factor at two by B = (1+∑ⱼ≥₁ h(2ʲ)/2ʲ)/2.

**Problem.** Assume f has finite distance from the power at t. The modulus of the average of f(1),…,f(N) tends to a positive limit exactly when B ≠ 0.

**How the definition helps.** Our own local factor replaces the list of all values at powers of two. Its sum can vanish only if h(2ʲ) = −1 for every j ≥ 1, since those weights add to one. Halász’s theorem proves that this is exactly the exceptional case.

**Paper or page:** [Furstenberg systems of pretentious and MRT multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03121). It says: “then there exist a non-zero L ∈ ℂ and a slowly varying sequence”

**Sources:**

- [Furstenberg systems of pretentious and MRT multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03121)

### Wirsing’s factors isolate prime bias

**Remember:** Remove the average prime weight before multiplying local factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be nonnegative and multiplicative with f(1) = 1. Require f(pʲ) ≤ Cjᴬ for fixed C,A &gt; 0, every prime p and every integer j ≥ 1. For ξ &gt; 0 define L(p) = (1−1/p)<sup>ξ</sup> ∑ⱼ≥₀ f(pʲ)/pʲ.

**Problem.** Suppose ∑ₚ≤ₓ f(p) = ξx/log x + O(x/(log x)ʳ) for some 1 &lt; r &lt; 2. Then ∑ₙ≤ₓ f(n) divided by x(log x)<sup>(ξ−1)</sup> tends to ∏ₚ L(p)/Γ(ξ). The prime product converges to a positive number.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, L(p) cancels the average contribution ξ/p in the logarithm of each prime factor. Partial summation converts the prime-sum error into a convergent series. The Wirsing–Odoni theorem identifies the product as part of the leading constant.

**Paper or page:** [Multiplicative complements I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00412). It says: “over the primes is convergent (and positive), and”

**Sources:**

- [Multiplicative complements I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00412)
- [Eduard Wirsing, Das asymptotische Verhalten von Summen über multiplikative Funktionen (1961)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01351892)

### Zeta powers determine logarithmic growth

**Remember:** The zeta power carries the entire leading singularity.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix an integer k ≥ 1 and let a(n) = k raised to ω(n), where ω(n) counts the distinct prime divisors of n. Divide its Dirichlet series by the kth power of the Riemann zeta function: G(s) = ∑ a(n)n⁻ˢ / ζ(s)ᵏ for s &gt; 1.

**Problem.** The sum of a(n) over n ≤ x is asymptotic to G(1)x(log x)ᵏ⁻¹/(k−1)!. Here G(1) is the limit as s decreases to one.

**How the definition helps.** Our own calculation separates the singular factor ζ(s)ᵏ from a product that converges at s=1. At s=1 each remaining prime contributes (1−1/p)ᵏ⁻¹(1+(k−1)/p). Multiplication cancels the term proportional to 1/p. The Selberg–Delange theorem converts the behavior of the series near s=1 into the growth rate of its coefficient sums.

**Paper or page:** [On divisor bounded multiplicative functions in short intervals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08432). It says: “where cₖ is an explicit positive constant.”

**Sources:**

- [On divisor bounded multiplicative functions in short intervals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08432)

### Diverging variance excludes single-prime limits

**Remember:** A bounded prime contribution cannot dominate an infinite total variance.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use a strongly additive real function f, so f(n) is the sum of f(p) over distinct primes dividing n. Require \|f(p)\|≤1 and B(x)²→∞, where B(x)²=∑ f(p)²/p over primes p≤x.

**Problem.** Write A(x)=∑ f(p)/p over primes p≤x. For uniform N from 1 to x, (f(N)−A(x))/B(x) converges in law to a standard normal.

**How the definition helps.** Divergence of B(x) makes every bounded prime contribution negligible after normalization (our own). If only f(2) = 1 is nonzero among the prime values, the normalized values stay at ±1/√2. Each has limiting probability one half. The general Erdős–Kac theorem gives the normal limit under the stated hypotheses.

**Wikipedia:** [Erdős–Kac theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Kac_theorem). It says: “More generally, if f(n) is a strongly additive function”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prime powers factor Erdős–Wintner

**Remember:** Independent prime contributions give one factor each in the limiting transform.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be real and additive, so f(ab)=f(a)+f(b) whenever a and b are coprime. Independently for each prime p, choose a nonnegative integer V with probability (1−1/p)/pᵏ at k. Write Xₚ for f evaluated at p raised to this random exponent.

**Problem.** Suppose ∑ 1/p converges over primes with \|f(p)\|&gt;1. Suppose ∑ f(p)/p and ∑ f(p)²/p converge over the remaining primes. For N uniform on {1,…,x}, f(N) approaches a distribution with characteristic function ∏ E\[exp(itXₚ)\] as x tends to infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Independent prime contributions turn the characteristic function, the mean of exp(it times the random value), into a product (our own explanation). Exponents above one occur at only finitely many primes almost surely, since ∑ 1/p² converges. Kolmogorov’s three-series theorem gives convergence of the independent sum under the three stated conditions. The Erdős–Wintner theorem identifies its distribution with the arithmetic limit.

**Wikipedia:** [Erdős–Wintner theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Wintner_theorem). It says: “It is an analogue of Kolmogorov's three-series theorem.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prime values miss additive variance

**Remember:** A prime square can fluctuate even when every prime value vanishes.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an additive f, use B(x)²=∑ \|f(q)\|²/q over prime powers q=pᵏ≤x with k≥1. Center at A(x)=∑ f(q)(1−1/p)/q over the same prime powers. An additive f satisfies f(ab)=f(a)+f(b) for coprime a and b.

**Problem.** The average of \|f(n)−A(x)\|² over n≤x is at most a constant times B(x)² for every x≥2. No constant works for all additive f if the sum defining B(x)² uses only primes.

**How the definition helps.** Prime-power terms capture variation invisible at primes (our own). Set f(4) = 1 and every other prime-power value to zero, so f(n) indicates divisibility by four but not eight. The mean-square error tends to 7/64, although the prime-only sum vanishes. The Turán–Kubilius inequality gives the bound with all prime powers included.

**Wikipedia:** [Turán–Kubilius inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tur%C3%A1n%E2%80%93Kubilius_inequality). It says: “It is useful for proving results about the normal order of an arithmetic function.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Truncation makes sieve moments Gaussian

**Remember:** Keep enough primes for the variance and few enough for every fixed moment.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a large integer x, put L=log log x and y=exp((log x)/∜L). Choose N uniformly from {1,…,x}. Let T count its distinct prime divisors at most y, and put μ=∑ 1/p over primes p≤y.

**Problem.** For each fixed positive integer k, the kth moment of (T−μ)/√L tends to the kth standard normal moment. Also (ω(N)−L)/√L tends in law to the same normal law, where ω counts all distinct primes.

**How the definition helps.** The cutoff makes yᵏ/x tend to zero for every fixed k (our own). Each joint divisibility probability differs from its independent model by at most 1/x, giving moment error Oₖ(yᵏ/x) after expansion. The independent count has variance asymptotic to L and Gaussian normalized moments. At most ∜L larger primes divide N, and Mertens’ estimate gives μ = L + O(log L), so the normalized difference vanishes.

**Paper or page:** [On an Erdős--Kac-type conjecture of Elliott](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13585v3). It says: “Uniformly for 1 ≤ k ≤ (σℙ)⁽²⁄³⁾ we have”

**Sources:**

- [On an Erdős--Kac-type conjecture of Elliott](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13585v3)
- [Andrew Granville and K. Soundararajan, Sieving and the Erdős–Kac theorem](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4020-5404-4_2)

### Zeta weights make primes independent

**Remember:** Weight by inverse powers and prime divisibility becomes independent.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For s&gt;1, give each positive integer n probability 1/(ζ(s)nˢ), where ζ(s)=∑ 1/nˢ. This replaces a uniform draw from a bounded interval by a power-weighted draw from all integers.

**Problem.** Let ω(N) count distinct prime divisors and put μ(s)=∑ 1/pˢ over all primes. Divisibility by distinct primes gives independent events. As s decreases to 1, (ω(N)−μ(s))/√μ(s) converges in distribution to a standard normal variable.

**How the definition helps.** Summing the weights of multiples of d gives probability d⁻ˢ (our own). For squarefree d this factors over its primes, giving independence. The variance is μ(s)+O(1), and μ(s) diverges as s decreases to one by divergence of the prime harmonic sum. The Lindeberg central limit theorem applies since every centered indicator is bounded by one.

**Paper or page:** [A Generalization of the Erdős-Kac Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06860v1). It says: “Zeta(1+1/aⱼ)-distributed random variables”

**Sources:**

- [A Generalization of the Erdős-Kac Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06860v1)

### Ignoring finitely many exceptions gives Waring's problem its true constant G(k)

**Remember:** Count every target for g and only sufficiently large targets for G.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P05 (Waring's problem and variants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each positive integer k, g(k) is the least s such that every positive integer is a sum of at most s positive kth powers. Define G(k) with the same condition restricted to all integers above some threshold.

**Problem.** Vinogradov's refinements of the circle method give G(k) ≤ k(3 log k + 11). In contrast, a few small numbers force g(k) ≥ 2ᵏ + ⌊(3/2)ᵏ⌋ − 2.

**How the definition helps.** The threshold in G(k) excludes individual small targets that force g(k) upwards (our own). Take n = 2ᵏ⌊(3/2)ᵏ⌋−1, which lies below 3ᵏ and can use only ones and copies of 2ᵏ. Using as many copies of 2ᵏ as possible gives the stated lower bound for k ≥ 2. For k = 1 the bound is immediate, and Vinogradov’s circle method gives the large-target estimate.

**Wikipedia:** [Waring's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem). It says: “G(k) is defined to be the least positive integer s such that every sufficiently large integer (i.e. every integer greater than some constant) can be represented as a sum of at most s positive integers to the power of k.”

**Sources:**

- [G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood, Some problems of 'Partitio Numerorum' IV: The singular series in Waring's problem and the value of the number G(k), Math. Z. 12 (1922) 161–188](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01482074)

### Log weights simplify Vinogradov’s asymptotic

**Remember:** Log weights remove the prime density from the main term.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P32 (Goldbach-type theorems; other additive questions involving primes), 11P55. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each positive integer m, set Λ(m) = log p if m is a power of a prime p, and zero otherwise. Let r(N) sum Λ(a)Λ(b)Λ(c) over ordered triples of positive integers with a+b+c = N.

**Problem.** For odd N tending to infinity and fixed A &gt; 0, Vinogradov’s theorem gives r(N) = ½G(N)N² + O(N²/(log N)ᴬ). Form G(N) by multiplying one factor per prime p. Use 1 − 1/(p−1)² when p divides N and 1 + 1/(p−1)³ otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** In our own comparison, the log weights absorb the changing density of primes, leaving N² as the size of the main term. The prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions estimates the weighted sum near fractions with small denominators. Bounding the sum at the remaining frequencies takes a separate estimate.

**Wikipedia:** [Vinogradov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_theorem). It says: “r(N) = ½G(N)N² + O(N² log⁻ᴬ N)”

**Sources:**

- [I. Vinogradow, Some theorems concerning the theory of primes (1937), Theorem 2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?jrnid=sm&option_lang=eng&paperid=5565&wshow=paper)

### Major arcs expose Vaughan’s saving

**Remember:** Keep small denominators out of the minor arcs.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P32 (Goldbach-type theorems; other additive questions involving primes), 11P55, 11L07. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For large N and B &gt; 0 set L = (log N)ᴮ. The minor arcs are frequencies modulo one farther than 2L/(qN) from every reduced a/q with 1 ≤ q ≤ L. Define S(α) = ∑ₙ≤ᴺ Λ(n)exp(2πiαn) over positive integers, with von Mangoldt weights Λ(n).

**Problem.** For each A &gt; 0, take B &gt; 2A + 8. On the minor arcs \|S(α)\| = O(N/(log N)ᴬ), uniformly in α as N grows.

**How the definition helps.** Minor arcs exclude the small denominators in Dirichlet’s approximation theorem (our own). That theorem gives a reduced a/q with q ≤ ⌊N/L⌋ and error at most 1/(q⌊N/L⌋), forcing q &gt; L. Vaughan’s estimate bounds \|S(α)\| by O((N/√q + N⁴⁄⁵ + √(Nq))(log N)⁴). Both terms involving q are at most N/√L, giving the stated saving.

**Wikipedia:** [Vinogradov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_theorem). It says: “The set of real numbers close to such rational points is usually referred to as the major arcs, the complement forms the minor arcs.”

**Paper or page:** [Almost all primes are not needed in Ternary Goldbach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.08968v1). It says: “Let u ≥ 1, α ∈ ℝ and consider a reduced fraction a/q such that \|α − a/q\| ≤ 1/q².”

**Sources:**

- [R. C. Vaughan, Sommes trigonométriques sur les nombres premiers (1977), pp. 981–983](https://personal.science.psu.edu/rcv4/pubswww.pdf)

### Modulo twenty-four selects five prime squares

**Remember:** Each prime above three has square one modulo twenty-four.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P32 (Goldbach-type theorems; other additive questions involving primes), 11P55, 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Call a target admissible for five squares of primes greater than 3 if its remainder modulo 24 is 5.

**Problem.** Every sufficiently large admissible integer is the sum of five squares of primes greater than 3. No integer outside the class can be such a sum with all five primes greater than 3.

**How the definition helps.** Every prime above three has square one modulo eight and modulo three, hence modulo 24 (our own). Five such squares sum to five modulo 24, excluding all multiples of 24, for example. Liu and Zhan’s near-equal-prime form of the five-square theorem gives representations of sufficiently large admissible targets with every prime above three.

**Paper or page:** [On the density version of quadratic Waring's problem and the quadratic Waring--Goldbach problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14939v3). It says: “for all sufficiently large integers y that are congruent to s mod 24”

**Sources:**

- [Jianya Liu and Tao Zhan, Hua’s Theorem on Prime Squares in Short Intervals (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s101140000077)

### Unit classes isolate Goldbach parity

**Remember:** Count nonzero classes to see the parity obstruction.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P32 (Goldbach-type theorems; other additive questions involving primes), 11P55. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each prime p, let M(p,N) count ordered triples of nonzero residues whose sum equals N modulo p. Define σ(p,N) = pM(p,N)/(p−1)³ and let G(N) be the product of these factors over all primes.

**Problem.** For even N the product G(N) vanishes. For odd N it has a positive lower bound that does not depend on N.

**How the definition helps.** The local factor at two equals zero for even N and two for odd N (our own). Counting nonzero triples gives 1−1/(p−1)² for p dividing N and 1+1/(p−1)³ otherwise. Over odd primes the product of the lower bounds 1−1/(p−1)² is positive since ∑ₚ&gt;₂ 1/(p−1)² converges.

**Wikipedia:** [Vinogradov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_theorem). It says: “If N is odd, then G(N) is roughly 1”

**Sources:**

- [I. Vinogradow, Some theorems concerning the theory of primes (1937), Theorem 2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?jrnid=sm&option_lang=eng&paperid=5565&wshow=paper)

### Dual forms reveal Kloosterman phases

**Remember:** The dual form is the coefficient of the inverse numerator.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11L05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Work modulo an odd prime p in even dimension s. For a symmetric invertible matrix M, define Q(x) = xᵀMx and its dual form D(c) = cᵀM⁻¹c. Write e(t) = exp(2πit/p) for residues t, and define the Kloosterman sum K(m,n) by summing e(ma+na⁻¹) over nonzero residues a.

**Problem.** For an integer N and a vector c modulo p, sum e(a(Q(x)−N)+c·x) over all vectors x and nonzero residues a. The absolute value is pˢ⁄² times \|K(−N,−D(c)/4)\|, with division modulo p.

**How the definition helps.** Completing the square shifts x by (2a)⁻¹M⁻¹c and leaves −D(c)/(4a) as the constant term from c (our own). The quadratic Gauss sum formula gives the shifted vector sum modulus pˢ⁄². Its phase is independent of a because the dimension is even. Summing the remaining phases gives K(−N,−D(c)/4).

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “If a = 0 or b = 0 then the Kloosterman sum reduces to the Ramanujan sum.”

**Paper or page:** [Counting solutions to quadratic polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04328v1). It says: “S(m,n;q) = \\sideset{}{<sup>\*}\\sum\_{x\\bmod{q}}e<sub>q</sub></sup>(mx+n\\overline{x})”

**Sources:**

- [V. Vinay Kumaraswamy, Counting solutions to quadratic polynomials (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04328v1)

### Farey mediants expose Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** At fixed denominator the next Farey denominator is an inverse residue.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11L05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take all reduced fractions in \[0,1\] with denominator at most an integer Q and list them in increasing order. These are the Farey fractions of order Q. For a fraction a/p with right neighbor b/r, end its arc at their mediant, the fraction (a+b)/(p+r).

**Problem.** Fix a prime p ≤ Q, integers m,n with p not dividing m, and β &gt; 0. Sum exp(2πi(ma+na⁻¹)/p) over 1 ≤ a &lt; p whose right endpoint is at least a/p+β, using inverses modulo p. The absolute value is O(√p log p) with an absolute constant.

**How the definition helps.** The mediant endpoint lies 1/\[p(p+r)\] beyond a/p, so the test selects an interval of denominators r (our own). Farey adjacency gives Q−p &lt; r ≤ Q and r ≡ −a⁻¹ modulo p. Completing this interval modulo p costs O(log p) in the sum of absolute normalized Fourier coefficients. Weil’s bound gives at most 2√p for each complete Kloosterman sum since p does not divide m.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “the symbol n\* denotes the congruence class, inverse to n modulo m”

**Sources:**

- [H. D. Kloosterman, On the representation of numbers in the form ax² + by² + cz² + dt² (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02564120)
- [A. Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Numerator-free weights separate Poisson factors

**Remember:** Use one weight for every numerator to get one complete sum.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix Q &gt; 2 and smooth ω supported on \[½,1\] and positive inside, and put C = Q/∑ⱼ≥₁ ω(j/Q). For x &gt; 0 and real y define h(x,y) = ∑ⱼ≥₁ \[ω(xj)−ω(\|y\|/(xj))\]/(xj). For integer polynomial F in s variables, define S(q,c) = ∑ exp(2πi(aF(b)+c·b)/q) over vectors b modulo q and units a modulo q.

**Problem.** For smooth compactly supported W on ℝˢ, set I(q,c) = ∫ W(x)h(q/Q,F(x)/Q²)exp(−2πic·x/q) dx over ℝˢ. The sum of W(x) over integer zeros of F equals (C/Q²)∑ S(q,c)I(q,c)/qˢ over integers q ≥ 1 and vectors c ∈ ℤˢ.

**How the definition helps.** Heath-Brown’s delta identity detects F(x) = 0 with a weight h independent of the unit numerator a (our own). Poisson summation on each residue class b modulo q gives the same integral I(q,c) times exp(2πic·b/q)/qˢ. Summing the phases over b and a produces S(q,c).

**nLab:** [Poisson summation formula](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poisson+summation+formula). It says: “equating a sum or integral of a function over a domain (e.g., a lattice) with a corresponding sum or integral of its Fourier dual over a dual domain”

**Sources:**

- [D. R. Heath-Brown, A New Form of the Circle Method, and its Application to Quadratic Forms (1996)](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid%3Abbd3c62f-f010-44b5-8be5-87e903fb0084/files/m7ec02df6e1b8303a66e7a6015ecb6044)

### Power densities give Waring’s Gamma factor

**Remember:** The power substitution turns the real factor into a beta integral.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For integers k,s ≥ 2, the substitution t = xᵏ on x &gt; 0 gives the density f(t) = t<sup>(1/k−1)</sup>/k for t &gt; 0. Set f(t) = 0 for t ≤ 0. Define the real factor at N as the s-fold convolution of f evaluated at N.

**Problem.** Take N &gt; 0 and integers k,s ≥ 2. The real factor is Γ(1 + 1/k)ˢ times N raised to (s/k − 1), divided by Γ(s/k). For sufficiently large s, this is the real factor in the classical Waring asymptotic.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, using power coordinates turns each convolution into the same beta integral. Write one summand as Nu, so the remaining summands have total N(1−u). Euler’s beta formula evaluates the resulting integral of powers of u and 1−u and cancels the previous gamma denominator. The circle method must still identify this continuous density in the asymptotic count of integer representations.

**nLab:** [Euler beta function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Euler+beta+function). It says: “B(x,y) = \\int<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> t<sup>x-1</sup> (1-t)<sup>y-1</sup> d t = \\frac{\\Gamma(x)\\Gamma(y)}{\\Gamma(x+y)},\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,Re x\\gt 0, \\,\\,\\,\\,Re y \\gt 0,”

**Wikipedia:** [Hardy–Ramanujan–Littlewood circle method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Ramanujan%E2%80%93Littlewood_circle_method). It says: “the singularities, organised into the so-called singular series, predominate”

**Sources:**

- [G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood, Some problems of Partitio Numerorum IV (1922)](https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/download/pdf/PPN266833020_0012/PPN266833020_0012.pdf)

### Power moments count integer solutions

**Remember:** One frequency per degree enforces one equality per degree.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For positive integers N, k and s, let P be a polynomial with no constant term and coefficients α₁ through αₖ. Sum exp(2πiP(n)) over n from 1 to N. The Vinogradov mean value integrates the absolute value of this sum raised to power 2s over the unit cube of coefficients.

**Problem.** Take two ordered s-tuples from 1 to N, and require their jth power sums to agree for every j from 1 to k. The mean value counts exactly these pairs. The full set of equalities survives a common integer translation of the entries.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding the integrand gives one term per ordered pair of tuples (our own). For each degree, integration gives one if its power sums agree and zero otherwise. Thus precisely the required pairs survive. The binomial theorem preserves all these equalities under translation since the system includes every lower degree and both tuples have length s.

**Wikipedia:** [Vinogradov's mean-value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_mean-value_theorem). It says: “An alternative analytic expression for Jₛ,ₖ(X) is”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Primitive phases factor singular series

**Remember:** Use primitive phases once, then multiply the prime contributions.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For r integer polynomials F in s variables and q ≥ 1, sum exp(2πia·F(x)/q) over x modulo q and primitive numerator vectors a. Here x has s coordinates, and a comprises r residues modulo q with gcd(a₁,…,aᵣ,q) = 1. Divide by qˢ to obtain A(q), and sum A(q) over positive q to define the singular series.

**Problem.** Assume the series of \|A(q)\| converges. Then the singular series equals the product over primes p of the sum of A(pʲ) over j ≥ 0.

**How the definition helps.** Primitive numerator vectors split under the Chinese remainder theorem for coprime moduli u and v (our own). Splitting x likewise separates the phase after multiplying each local numerator by a unit. Those multiplications preserve primitivity, giving A(uv) = A(u)A(v). Absolute convergence permits multiplication of the prime factors.

**Paper or page:** [Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09256v2). It says: “In fact, \\\[ \\mathfrak{S}=\\prod\_{p\\textnormal{ prime}}\\chi(p), \\\] where \\\[ \\chi(p)=1+\\sum<sub>k=1</sub><sup>\\infty</sup>A(p<sup>k</sup>). \\\]”

**Sources:**

- [N. Rome and S. Yamagishi, Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations (2026)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.2026.340.179)

### Primitive phases telescope local densities

**Remember:** Grouping phases by their true denominator gives each density increment.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an integer polynomial F in s variables and q ≥ 1, define A(q) = q<sup>(−s)</sup>∑ exp(2πiaF(x)/q). Sum over all vectors x modulo q and all units a modulo q, with A(1) = 1. The density at q is q times the fraction of these vectors satisfying F(x) ≡ 0 modulo q.

**Problem.** For each prime p and integer j ≥ 0, the density at pʲ equals the sum of A(pⁱ) over integers 0 ≤ i ≤ j. If the series converges, its sum equals the limiting density.

**How the definition helps.** Grouping phases by reduced denominator gives one density increment for each prime power (our own). Average ∑ₐ exp(2πiaF(x)/pʲ) over x, using all residues a modulo pʲ. Orthogonality gives pʲ at solutions and zero elsewhere, so the average is the density. Terms of reduced denominator pⁱ contribute A(pⁱ) because every vector modulo pⁱ has equally many lifts.

**Paper or page:** [Solving quadratic forms in restricted variables with the circle method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17949v1). It says: “The weighted p-adic density equals χ̃ₚ(𝒜), i.e. χ̃ₚ(𝒜) = lim \[m → ∞\] pᵐM(pᵐ).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Residue averages separate major arcs

**Remember:** The residue average carries the rational phase and the integral carries the offset.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05, 11L07. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an integer d ≥ 2 write e(t) = exp(2πit) and let S(α) sum e(αnᵈ) over integers 1 ≤ n ≤ X. Define C(q,a) as the average of e(arᵈ/q) over residues r modulo q. Define V(β) as the integral of e(βtᵈ) from zero to X.

**Problem.** For α = a/q + β with a and q coprime, S(α) = C(q,a)V(β) + O(q(1+Xᵈ\|β\|)). The bound is uniform for X ≥ 1, real β and positive integers q at fixed d.

**How the definition helps.** On each residue class the rational phase is constant (our own). Partial summation compares the offset sum on that class with V(β)/q. Its error is at most a constant times one plus the total variation of e(βtᵈ), which is O(Xᵈ\|β\|). Adding over the q classes gives the stated formula.

**Paper or page:** [Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09256v2). It says: “\\sum<sub>1\\le x\\le X</sub> e(\\alpha x<sup>d</sup>) = X q<sup>-1</sup> S(q,a) I(X<sup>d\\beta</sup>) + O\\left(\\frac{q}{\\gcd(q,a)}(1+X<sup>d\|\\beta\|</sup>)\\right).”

**Sources:**

- [N. Rome and S. Yamagishi, Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations (2026)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.2026.340.179)

### Smooth divisor differences detect zero

**Remember:** Subtract the same smooth weight at paired divisors.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix Q &gt; 2 and smooth ω supported on \[½,1\] and positive inside, and set C = Q/∑ⱼ≥₁ ω(j/Q). For x &gt; 0 and real y set h(x,y) = ∑ⱼ≥₁ \[ω(xj)−ω(\|y\|/(xj))\]/(xj). For integers q ≥ 1 and n, let c(q,n) sum exp(2πian/q) over units a modulo q.

**Problem.** For any integer n, C/Q² times ∑ over q ≥ 1 of c(q,n)h(q/Q,n/Q²) is 1 at zero and 0 elsewhere.

**How the definition helps.** Grouping terms by d = qj pairs each divisor with its complementary divisor (our own). The sum of c(q,n) over q dividing d equals d if d divides n and zero otherwise. For nonzero n, substituting d ↦ \|n\|/d swaps the two divisor sums. At zero the second weight vanishes, and the definition of C normalizes the first sum to one.

**Wikipedia:** [Hardy–Ramanujan–Littlewood circle method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Ramanujan%E2%80%93Littlewood_circle_method). It says: “The integral Iₙ is divided up into integrals each on some arc of the circle”

**Sources:**

- [D. R. Heath-Brown, A New Form of the Circle Method, and its Application to Quadratic Forms (1996)](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid%3Abbd3c62f-f010-44b5-8be5-87e903fb0084/files/m7ec02df6e1b8303a66e7a6015ecb6044)

### The dual cone marks large sums

**Remember:** Off the dual cone the inverse phase is nonconstant.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11L05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Q(x) = xᵀMx have even dimension s ≥ 2, with M symmetric and invertible modulo an odd prime p. For the equation Q(x) = 0, call a frequency c off the dual cone if cᵀM⁻¹c is nonzero modulo p.

**Problem.** Sum exp(2πi(aQ(x)+c·x)/p) over all vectors x and nonzero residues a modulo p. Its absolute value is pˢ⁄² off the dual cone and (p−1)pˢ⁄² on it.

**How the definition helps.** Write D = cᵀM⁻¹c and let u represent −D/(4a) modulo p. Completing the square leaves exp(2πiu/p) times a common Gauss factor of modulus pˢ⁄² since s is even (our own). As a ranges over units, the phases sum to −1 for D ≠ 0 and p−1 for D = 0. For example, Q(x,y) = x²−y² has D = 0 at (1,1).

**Paper or page:** [Counting solutions to quadratic polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04328v1). It says: “S(m,n;q) = \\sideset{}{<sup>\*}\\sum\_{x\\bmod{q}}e<sub>q</sub></sup>(mx+n\\overline{x})”

**Sources:**

- [V. Vinay Kumaraswamy, Counting solutions to quadratic polynomials (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04328v1)

### Freiman models prevent false collisions

**Remember:** A usable model preserves both equal sums and unequal sums.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P70 (Inverse problems of additive number theory, including sumsets), 11B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For subsets of abelian groups, a Freiman isomorphism of order eight is a bijection preserving and reflecting all equalities between eight-term sums, allowing repetitions. Write 8A−8A for the set of differences of two such sums from A.

**Problem.** Let A be a finite nonempty set of integers, and let q be prime with q &gt; \|8A − 8A\|. Some subset of A of size at least \|A\|/8 is Freiman isomorphic of order 8 to a subset of ℤ/qℤ.

**How the definition helps.** The definition lets every eight-term equality move between model and original without creating a false one, in our own words. Our own example is {0,1,3} modulo 5, where 0 + 1 and 3 + 3 acquire the same residue. Appending six zeros makes it an eight-term collision as well, in our own example. The hard work is the Ruzsa modeling lemma, which selects a large subset and a suitable map.

**Wikipedia:** [Freiman's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiman%27s_theorem). It says: “By the Ruzsa modeling lemma, there exists a subset A′ of A of cardinality at least \|A\|/8”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Eta shifts give partition inversion

**Remember:** The shifted partition series is the reciprocal of eta.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P82 (Analytic theory of partitions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let P(q) be the generating function for integer partitions, so its coefficient at degree n is the partition count. Set q = exp(2πiτ) with τ in the upper half-plane. Replace P(q) by exp(−πiτ/12)P(q), the reciprocal of the Dedekind eta function.

**Problem.** For t &gt; 0, P(exp(−2πt)) equals √t exp(π(1/t − t)/12) times P(exp(−2π/t)).

**How the definition helps.** The exponential shift turns the partition series into the reciprocal of eta, whose inversion law exchanges t and 1/t. In our own calculation, substitute τ = it in that law to obtain η(i/t) = √t η(it). Substituting the partition series on each side gives the stated factor. The substantive theorem is the inversion law.

**nLab:** [Dedekind eta function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Dedekind+eta+function). It says: “η(τ) = q¹⁄²⁴”

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind eta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_eta_function). It says: “η(−1/τ) = √(−iτ) η(τ).”

**Sources:**

- [G. H. Hardy and S. Ramanujan, Asymptotic Formulaae in Combinatory Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s2-17.1.75)

### Crank classes explain partition congruences

**Remember:** No ones means largest part, otherwise count parts exceeding the ones count, minus ones.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P83 (Partitions; congruences and congruential restrictions), 05A17. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonempty partition without ones, its crank is its largest part. For a partition containing ones, its crank is the number of parts larger than the number of ones, minus the number of ones.

**Problem.** For each integer n ≥ 0, the crank splits the partitions of 5n + 4 equally into five residue classes modulo 5. It does the same for 7n + 5 modulo 7 and 11n + 6 modulo 11. Each partition count is therefore divisible by its modulus.

**How the definition helps.** The crank expresses each congruence as equality of residue-class sizes. Andrews and Garvan’s crank generating function gives these equalities for the three progressions. Adding the equal class sizes gives divisibility (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Crank of a partition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crank_of_a_partition). It says: “M(9, 11, 11n + 6) = M(10, 11, 11n + 6) = p(11n + 6) / 11”

**Sources:**

- [George E. Andrews and F. G. Garvan, Dyson’s crank of a partition](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-1988-15637-6)

### Defining ideal norms by prime factorizations makes them multiply

**Remember:** Raise each residue field size to its prime exponent, then multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers), 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let O be the ring of integers of a number field. For each nonzero integral ideal I = ∏ 𝔭ᵉ, define N(I) = ∏ \|O/𝔭\|ᵉ using its unique prime factorization (our own).

**Problem.** The norm of a product of nonzero integral ideals equals the product of their norms.

**How the definition helps.** With the factorization definition, the norm is multiplicative because exponents add when ideals multiply (our own). The work moves to unique factorization into prime ideals (our own). It also moves to showing that the ring modulo 𝔭ᵉ has N(𝔭)ᵉ elements (our own). The Chinese remainder theorem then gives agreement with the usual definition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 8.4. (Properties of the absolute norm)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “For any other nonzero ideal 𝔟, Norm(𝔞𝔟) = Norm(𝔞)Norm(𝔟).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Determinant field norms of algebraic integers are integers

**Remember:** The field norm takes the determinant of multiplication.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a number field K and α ∈ K, the field norm N(α) is the determinant of multiplication by α on the ℚ-vector space K.

**Problem.** If α satisfies a monic polynomial with integer coefficients, then N(α) is an integer. Such an α is called an algebraic integer.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplication by an algebraic integer α preserves the ring of integers of K (our own). An integral basis therefore gives this map an integer matrix, whose determinant is an integer (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Field norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_norm). It says: “is defined as the determinant of this linear transformation.”

**Paper or page:** [An Infinitely Large Napkin: Alg Nt: Norm Trace](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf), [An Infinitely Large Napkin: Alg Nt: Norm Trace](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “If α is an algebraic integer, its norm and trace are rational integers.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Index checks prevent false ramification

**Remember:** Check the index before reading ramification from polynomial factors.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let θ be an algebraic integer generating a number field K. The subring ℤ\[θ\] has finite index in the full ring of integers. Call it maximal at p if the prime p does not divide that index.

**Problem.** Suppose ℤ\[θ\] is maximal at p. Each distinct irreducible factor of the minimal polynomial modulo p gives one prime ideal above p. Its multiplicity gives that prime’s exponent in the factorization of (p).

**How the definition helps.** The index condition makes the two rings agree after reduction modulo p (our own). The Dedekind–Kummer theorem then reads the prime ideals and their exponents from the polynomial factors. For θ = √5 the index is two, and its polynomial has a double root modulo two (our own). Yet two stays prime because the full ring has generator (1 + √5)/2 with irreducible polynomial modulo two (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Theorem 6.3. (Factoring algorithm / Dedekind-Kummer theorem)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “In particular, if K is monogenic with 𝒪ₖ = ℤ\[θ\] then j=1 and the theorem applies for all primes p.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Lattice-index ideal norms make principal ideal norms absolute field norms

**Remember:** Multiplication scales the lattice by the absolute value of its determinant.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers), 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonzero ideal I in the ring of integers O of a number field, its norm is the additive index \[O:I\] (our own).

**Problem.** The norm of a nonzero principal ideal equals the absolute value of the field norm of its generator.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplication by a nonzero generator a maps the lattice O onto (a) (our own). By Smith normal form, the image has index equal to the absolute determinant (our own). That determinant before taking absolute value is the field norm of a (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 8.4. (Properties of the absolute norm)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “If 𝔞 = (a) is principal, then Norm(𝔞) = \|Normₖ/ℚ(a)\|.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Requiring monic polynomials gives the right ring of algebraic integers

**Remember:** Algebraic integers are roots of integer polynomials with leading coefficient 1.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers), 13F05. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An algebraic integer is a complex number that is a root of a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. A monic polynomial is one whose leading coefficient is 1.

**Problem.** The ring of integers of a number field is a Dedekind domain. Every nonzero proper ideal therefore factors uniquely into nonzero prime ideals.

**How the definition helps.** Including every algebraic integer gives the integral closure of ℤ in the field (our own). For example, ℤ\[√−3\] omits the integral root (1+√−3)/2 of X²−X+1 and fails integral closure (our own). The full ring is also Noetherian and has dimension one by the structure theorem for rings of integers (our own). These properties give the Dedekind ideal factorization theorem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Algebraic integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_integer), [Quadratic integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_integer). It says: “In contrast, Z\[√−3\] is not even a Dedekind domain.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Torus quotients preserve Mahler measure

**Remember:** A surjective torus map carries uniform probability to uniform probability.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The logarithmic Mahler measure m(P) averages log\|P\| over independent, uniformly distributed unit complex numbers. A Laurent polynomial allows negative integer exponents. A monomial map replaces each variable by a product of integer powers of the new variables.

**Problem.** Let q map one product of unit circles onto another by monomials. Then m(P ∘ q) = m(P) for every nonzero Laurent polynomial P.

**How the definition helps.** In our own argument, the averaging definition makes invariance a change of variables. Every rotation of the target lifts through q, so the image probability is uniform. Jensen’s formula connects this integral with the usual one-variable formula in roots. The remaining input is that log\|P\| is integrable even near the zeros of P.

**Paper or page:** [General Boyd-Lawton Theorems with Multivariable Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05910). It says: “In other words, suppose that\~ $q<sub>A</sub> \\colon {\\mathbb {T}}<sup>m</sup> \\to {\\mathbb {T}}<sup>n$</sup> is surjective. Then\\\[  \\int \_{{\\mathbb {T}}<sup>n</sup>} g \\,  d \\tau <sub>n</sub> \\;  = \\;  \\int \_{{\\mathbb {T}}<sup>m}</sup> g \\circ q<sub>A</sub> \\,  d \\tau \_m \\, .  \\\]”

**Sources:**

- [General Boyd-Lawton Theorems with Multivariable Limits, Corollary 5.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05910)

### Regular primes are the primes where Kummer's proof of Fermat works

**Remember:** For regular p, an ideal with principal pth power is principal already.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R18 (Cyclotomic extensions), 11R29, 11D41. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An odd prime p is regular if p does not divide the class number of ℚ(ζₚ), where ζₚ is a primitive pth root of unity.

**Problem.** If p is a regular prime, then xᵖ + yᵖ = zᵖ has no solution in positive integers.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity gives a single class number condition for Kummer’s theorem. It ensures that any ideal class whose pth power is trivial is itself trivial (our own). Kummer’s proof uses this implication after factoring the Fermat equation in the cyclotomic ring (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Regular prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_prime). It says: “In 1850, Kummer proved that Fermat's Last Theorem is true for a prime exponent p if p is regular.”

**Sources:**

- [E. E. Kummer, Allgemeiner Beweis des Fermatschen Satzes, daß die Gleichung xλ+yλ=zλ durch ganze Zahlen unlösbar ist, für alle diejenigen Potenz-Exponenten λ welche ungerade Primzahlen sind und in den Zählern der ersten 1/2(λ) Bernoullischen zahlen als Factoren nicht vorkommen, J. reine angew. Math. 40 (1850), 130–138](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1850.40.130)

### Ignoring finite modules gives a structure theorem for Iwasawa modules

**Remember:** Up to finite error, Iwasawa modules are sums of cyclic pieces.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R23 (Iwasawa theory), 13J05. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Iwasawa algebra of the p-adic integers is the power series ring ℤₚ\[\[T\]\]. A quasi-isomorphism of modules over it is a map with finite kernel and finite cokernel.

**Problem.** Put Λ = ℤₚ\[\[T\]\]. Every finitely generated torsion Λ-module is quasi-isomorphic to a finite direct sum of Λ/(fⁿ), with f prime and n positive. Its characteristic series is unique up to a unit, and its μ and λ invariants are well defined.

**How the definition helps.** Finite kernels and cokernels let the Iwasawa structure theorem describe each module by cyclic factors (our own). For instance, Λ/(p,T) maps to zero with finite kernel (our own). The uniquely determined prime powers give the characteristic series up to a unit and hence determine μ and λ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Iwasawa algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwasawa_algebra). It says: “A quasi-isomorphism of modules is a homomorphism whose kernel and cokernel are both finite groups”

**Sources:**

- [Kenkichi Iwasawa, On Γ-extensions of algebraic number fields, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 65 (1959)](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9904-1959-10317-7)

### Counting infinite places makes the unit rank places minus one

**Remember:** Count each real embedding once and each conjugate pair of nonreal embeddings once.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R27 (Units and factorization). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An infinite place of a number field is a real embedding, or a pair of complex conjugate embeddings, into ℂ. There are r₁ real places and r₂ complex places.

**Problem.** The unit group of the ring of integers is finitely generated with rank r₁ + r₂ − 1. So the rank is the number of infinite places minus one.

**How the definition helps.** Each infinite place supplies one logarithmic coordinate, with weight two at a complex place (our own). The norm of a unit has absolute value one, so the coordinates sum to zero (our own). Dirichlet’s unit theorem gives a full lattice in this hyperplane and a finite kernel (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet's unit theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_unit_theorem). It says: “There will be r + 1 Archimedean places of K, either real or complex.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prime valuations count S-unit rank

**Remember:** Only primes in S may have nonzero exponents.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R27 (Units and factorization). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a finite set S of nonzero prime ideals of the ring of integers of a number field K. An S-unit is an element x ∈ K× whose principal ideal has exponent zero at every prime outside S.

**Problem.** The rank of the S-unit group is the ordinary unit rank plus the number of primes in S.

**How the definition helps.** The exponents in S give a homomorphism to the integer lattice indexed by S, with kernel the ordinary units (our own). Finiteness of the ideal class group gives each prime a principal positive power (our own). Their exponent vectors span a subgroup of full rank, giving \|S\| additional directions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [S-unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S-unit). It says: “An element x of K is an S-unit if the principal fractional ideal (x) is a product of primes in S (to positive or negative powers).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Unit regulators scale by index

**Remember:** Take the logarithmic unit lattice’s fundamental volume and divide by √n for n coordinates.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R27 (Units and factorization). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a number field unit, list its logarithmic absolute values at all real embeddings and one embedding from each nonreal conjugate pair. Double each complex entry (our own). For the resulting lattice with n coordinates, the regulator is its fundamental volume divided by √n.

**Problem.** For a subgroup of the units modulo roots of unity of finite index m, the subgroup regulator is m times the full regulator.

**How the definition helps.** The volume definition tiles a subgroup cell with m translates of a full lattice cell (our own). The common normalization factor cancels (our own). Dirichlet’s unit theorem identifies the logarithmic lattice with units modulo roots of unity (our own). Projecting away one coordinate recovers the usual determinant definition of the regulator (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet's unit theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_unit_theorem). It says: “The volume of a fundamental domain of this lattice is R√(r + 1).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Determinants detect relative integral bases

**Remember:** Split off free summands and take the ideal class of the remaining summand.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let B and A be the rings of integers in a number field and a subfield. As an A-module, B splits into free summands and one nonzero ideal I of A. The Steinitz class is the class of I, where two ideals have the same class if they differ by a scalar.

**Problem.** Consider the ring of integers of a finite number field extension. It has a basis over the base ring of integers exactly when its Steinitz class is trivial.

**How the definition helps.** The decomposition leaves only one ideal summand that could prevent a basis (our own). A trivial class means that one element generates this ideal, completing the basis (our own). Conversely, the top exterior power of a free module is free, and the decomposition identifies that power with I (our own). This replaces a direct search for a basis with the structure theorem for modules over rings of integers (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_domain). It says: “The Steinitz class for P over R is the class \[I\] of I in Cl(R): it is uniquely determined.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Differentials give the monogenic different

**Remember:** Differentiate the defining relation to get the different.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Suppose a ring B comes from a ring A by adjoining x and imposing one monic relation f(x) = 0. Formal differentiation gives the relation f′(x) dx = 0, with all elements of A treated as constants. In this presentation the Kähler different is the ideal generated by the coefficient of dx.

**Problem.** Let L/K be an extension of number fields. Suppose α generates the integers of L over the integers of K and has minimal polynomial f. Then f′(α) generates the different.

**How the definition helps.** The single defining relation gives a one-entry derivative matrix (our own). Its determinant is f′(α) (our own). The work lies in identifying the Kähler different with the usual different for these rings (our own). The usual definition inverts the ideal of elements pairing integrally with all integers under the field trace (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 49.7.4.](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BVZ). It says: “The Kähler different of B over A is the ideal of B generated by det(∂fᵢ/∂xⱼ).”

### Discriminant classes are squared Steinitz classes

**Remember:** The trace pairs two copies of the same line.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For number fields L/K, take the top exterior power of the integers of L over the integers of K. This rank-one module records how determinants change between local bases. Its ideal class, meaning its isomorphism class as a fractional ideal, is the Steinitz class.

**Problem.** The relative discriminant of a number field extension represents the square of the Steinitz class of its ring of integers.

**How the definition helps.** On the top exterior power, the trace determinant pairs two copies of the same module (our own). Its image is the discriminant ideal because local bases give the usual trace determinants (our own). The field trace pairing is nondegenerate, so the induced map from the tensor square is injective (our own). The discriminant ideal therefore represents the square of the module’s ideal class (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “indeed, it is the square of the Steinitz class for O<sub>L</sub> as a O<sub>K</sub>-module.”

### Norms give the discriminant tower law

**Remember:** Take norms of the different tower law.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For number fields L/K the relative discriminant is the ideal norm of the different (our own). The ideal norm acts multiplicatively, sending each prime to the prime below raised to the residue degree (our own).

**Problem.** For a tower of number fields L/K/S, write d(E/F) for the relative discriminant. Then d(L/S) = d(K/S)^\[L:K\] · Nₖ/ₛ(d(L/K)).

**How the definition helps.** Taking ideal norms turns the different tower law directly into the discriminant tower law (our own). Norms compose, and extending an ideal from K to L then taking its norm raises it to the degree of L/K (our own). The work lies in the different tower law and in identifying the norm with the usual discriminant from trace determinants (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Counting extensions of imaginary quadratic fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.09848v1). It says: “Given a tower of number fields L/K/S then the relative discriminant of L/S can be computed as”

### Relative class numbers keep odd characters

**Remember:** Divide by the real class number to keep only odd characters.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11M20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p, let K be the field generated over ℚ by a primitive p-th root of unity. Its real subfield K⁺ consists of the elements fixed by complex conjugation. The relative class number is h⁻ = h(K)/h(K⁺), where h counts ideal classes.

**Problem.** Put n = (p−1)/2, and let R and R⁺ be the regulators of K and K⁺. Then h⁻ = p(√p/π)ⁿ(R⁺/R) times the product of L(1,χ) over the characters χ modulo p with χ(−1) = −1.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing the zeta residues cancels the even characters, which index the factors for K⁺ (our own). The analytic class number formula expresses the remaining product through class numbers, regulators, roots of unity and discriminants (our own). The fields have 2p and 2 roots of unity, and their absolute discriminants have ratio pⁿ (our own). Substitution gives the displayed factor (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Class number formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_formula). It says: “there is a further formulation possible, as shown by Kummer.”

### Root discriminants ignore unramified extensions

**Remember:** The root cancels the extension degree.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a basis of the ring of integers over ℤ, form the matrix of field traces of pairwise basis products. Its determinant is the field discriminant. For a number field of degree n, the root discriminant is the nth root of its absolute discriminant value.

**Problem.** The root discriminant stays constant in extensions unramified at every finite prime. This means that no prime ideal acquires a repeated factor in the larger ring of integers.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the degree root cancels the power in the ordinary discriminant tower law (our own). The relative discriminant is the unit ideal because no finite prime ramifies (our own). The tower law therefore raises the absolute discriminant value to the extension degree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Discriminant of an algebraic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant_of_an_algebraic_number_field). It says: “The relation between relative discriminants in a tower of fields shows that the root discriminant does not change in an unramified extension.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Tameness gives different exponent e − 1

**Remember:** Tame ramification contributes exactly its index minus one.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a number field extension, let e be the exponent of a prime ideal in the factorization of the prime below it. Ramification is tame there if the residue characteristic does not divide e. The different is the inverse ideal of elements whose products with all integers have integral trace.

**Problem.** At a tame prime of ramification index e, the different has exponent e − 1.

**How the definition helps.** Tameness keeps the leading coefficient e of the derivative nonzero in the residue field (our own). After completing and removing the unramified part, the integers have a generator π whose minimal polynomial is Eisenstein of degree e (our own). At π the term eπ<sup>(e−1)</sup> of the derivative has valuation e − 1, strictly below every other term (our own). In the wild extension ℚ₂(√2), the derivative 2√2 has valuation three although e = 2 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “The precise exponent to which a ramified prime P divides δ is termed the differential exponent of P and is equal to e − 1 if P is tamely ramified”

### The different ideal shows exactly which primes ramify

**Remember:** Take the trace dual of the integers, then invert that ideal.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R32. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let O be the integers of a number field L. Its inverse different consists of x ∈ L with Trₗ/ℚ(xy) ∈ ℤ for every y ∈ O. The different is the inverse of this fractional ideal (our own).

**Problem.** A prime ideal of L is ramified when it appears to a power above 1 in the factorization of the prime below. This happens exactly when it divides the different.

**How the definition helps.** The different is an ideal upstairs, so divisibility singles out individual primes above a rational prime (our own). The local different exponent theorem gives exponent zero at unramified primes and positive exponent at ramified primes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “Pi divides the relative different δL / K if and only if Pi is ramified, that is, if and only if the ramification index e(i) is greater than 1.”

### The narrow class group decides which primes a norm form represents

**Remember:** Signs matter for norm forms, so count ideals with positive generators.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R11, 11E16. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An element of a number field is totally positive when it is positive under every embedding into the real numbers. The narrow class group is the group of fractional ideals modulo principal ideals with a totally positive generator. The ordinary class group allows any generator.

**Problem.** Let K = ℚ(√d) have trivial narrow class group and discriminant D, and let q be the norm form of an integral basis. A prime p equals q(x,y) for some integers exactly in three cases. Either p divides D, or p = 2 and D ≡ 1 mod 8, or p is odd and (D/p) = 1.

**How the definition helps.** Triviality of the narrow class group supplies a totally positive generator for every prime ideal of norm p (our own). Its field norm is p, so its integral coordinates represent p (our own). Conversely, an element of norm p generates a prime ideal of norm p (our own). The quadratic splitting criterion gives exactly the listed cases for such an ideal (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Narrow class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow_class_group). It says: “However, this statement is false if we focus only on p and not −p (and is in fact even false for p = 2), because the narrow class group is nontrivial.”

### Trace determinants square lattice indices

**Remember:** A basis change enters a trace determinant twice.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An order in a number field is a subring containing 1 that has full rank inside the ring of integers. Choose a ℤ-basis of the order. Its discriminant is the determinant of the matrix of field traces of pairwise basis products.

**Problem.** If one order has index m in another order of the same field, its discriminant is m² times the larger order’s discriminant.

**How the definition helps.** Using the trace matrix makes the basis change appear twice in one determinant (our own). If C expresses the smaller basis in the larger basis, the matrix changes from T to CᵀTC (our own). The lattice index theorem identifies the absolute determinant of C with m (our own). This avoids computing how each entry in the alternative matrix of field embeddings changes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Discriminant of an algebraic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant_of_an_algebraic_number_field). It says: “The discriminant of an order in K with integral basis b₁,…,bₙ is defined in the same way.”

### Trace duals multiply in towers

**Remember:** Trace maps compose, so trace duals multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For number fields L/K, the trace dual consists of x ∈ L with Trₗ/ₖ(xy) ∈ Oₖ for every y ∈ Oₗ. Here O denotes the corresponding ring of integers, and the different is the inverse fractional ideal (our own).

**Problem.** In a tower L/K/F, the different of L/F is the product of the different of L/K and the extended different of K/F.

**How the definition helps.** Trace transitivity tests x against Oₗ by requiring every Trₗ/ₖ(xy), y ∈ Oₗ, to belong to the K/F trace dual (our own). Indeed, one may multiply y by every integer of K in the combined test (our own). Locally the K/F dual has one generator, which factors out and leaves the L/K dual (our own). Inverting the product gives the tower law (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “In a tower of fields L/K/F the relative differents are related by δL/F = δL/K δK/F.”

### Unit signs explain narrow classes

**Remember:** The only signs that disappear come from units.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fractional ideals are ideals with denominators allowed. In the ordinary class group, two such ideals represent the same class if one is a nonzero scalar multiple of the other. In the narrow class group, the scalar must also be positive under every real embedding.

**Problem.** Forgetting positivity maps narrow classes onto ordinary classes. Its kernel is the group of sign patterns at the real embeddings modulo the signs of units.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping positivity in the quotient leaves only the signs of a principal generator to track (our own). Two generators differ by a unit, so their signs agree modulo unit signs (our own). Weak approximation, which lets one prescribe signs at all real embeddings, gives every sign pattern (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Narrow class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow_class_group). It says: “where now Pₖ⁺ is the group of totally positive principal fractional ideals”

### Decomposition groups turn counting prime factors into orbit counting

**Remember:** Primes above p form one orbit; the stabilizer is the decomposition group.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L over K be Galois with group G and P a prime of L above p. The decomposition group of P is the set of elements of G that send P to itself. The inertia group is the part that acts trivially on the residue field.

**Problem.** In a finite Galois extension of number fields, all primes above a nonzero prime p have the same ramification index e and residue degree f. Their number g equals \|G\|/\|D\| for the decomposition group D of any one of them, and the extension degree equals efg.

**How the definition helps.** The Galois group acts transitively on primes above p, so orbit-stabilizer gives g = \|G\|/\|D\| (our own). Conjugation preserves e and f, and the fundamental degree identity sums ef over those g primes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Splitting of prime ideals in Galois extensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splitting_of_prime_ideals_in_Galois_extensions). It says: “the decomposition group of Pj, is the subgroup of elements of G sending a given Pj to itself.”

### Frobenius as a conjugacy class makes Chebotarev's theorem statable

**Remember:** Each prime picks a conjugacy class; classes are hit in proportion to size.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory), 11R45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix an unramified rational prime p in a finite Galois extension L/ℚ and a prime P above p. Its Frobenius is the unique automorphism preserving P that induces x ↦ xᵖ on the residue field (our own). The Frobenius class of p is its conjugacy class.

**Problem.** Let L/ℚ be a finite Galois extension with group G, and let C be a conjugacy class of G. The unramified primes whose Frobenius class is C have density \|C\|/\|G\|.

**How the definition helps.** Changing P conjugates its Frobenius, so the conjugacy class depends only on p. Chebotarev’s density theorem gives the density of primes with that class (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem). It says: “The statement of the more general Chebotarev density theorem is in terms of the Frobenius element of a prime (ideal), which is in fact an associated conjugacy class C of elements of the Galois group G.”

- [Nikolai Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören, Mathematische Annalen 95 (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01206606)

### Frobenius defined by a pth-power congruence restricts to Frobenius below

**Remember:** Restrict the same power map to the smaller residue field.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L/ℚ be finite Galois and let 𝔓 lie above an unramified rational prime p. Its Frobenius is the unique σ ∈ Gal(L/ℚ) satisfying σ(x) ≡ xᵖ modulo 𝔓 for every x ∈ Oₗ (our own).

**Problem.** Let L ⊃ K be number fields, both Galois over ℚ, and let 𝔓 in L lie over 𝔭 in K, both unramified. The Frobenius of 𝔓 restricts on K to the Frobenius of 𝔭.

**How the definition helps.** The restriction to K satisfies the defining congruence there (our own). For x ∈ Oₖ the difference σ(x) − xᵖ lies in both 𝔓 and Oₖ, hence in 𝔭 (our own). Uniqueness at the unramified prime 𝔭 identifies the restriction (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Theorem 6.1. (Restrictions of Frobenius elements)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “Assume L/ℚ and K/ℚ are both Galois. Let 𝔓 and 𝔭 be unramified as above.”

### Restricted products put Poitou–Tate duality in one sequence

**Remember:** Almost everywhere unramified makes the infinite product locally compact.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois module M over a number field k, consider families with one entry in H¹(kᵥ,M) at each place v. The restricted product requires all but finitely many entries to vanish on inertia at finite places (our own). Its topology makes the product of the unramified subgroups at finite places open with its product topology, including unrestricted archimedean factors (our own).

**Problem.** For M and its twisted dual M′ = Hom(M, μ), Poitou–Tate duality gives a nine-term exact sequence through restricted products of local cohomology. Here μ is the group of roots of unity, and the sequence uses modified cohomology at archimedean places (our own). Summing local pairings perfectly pairs the degree-one restricted products.

**How the definition helps.** The restriction makes the product locally compact, so Pontryagin duality applies to it (our own). Global classes are unramified almost everywhere, so they land in the restricted product (our own). The work went into the global duality theorems of Poitou and Tate.

**Wikipedia:** [Tate duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_duality). It says: “where ∏′ denotes a restricted product with respect to the unramified cohomology groups.”

### Artin and Hecke factors agree

**Remember:** The same Frobenius value gives both factors wherever the units act trivially.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11S40. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite-order one-dimensional Galois character χ of a number field, its Hecke character is χ composed with the global reciprocity map on idele classes. Normalize reciprocity so local uniformizers map to arithmetic Frobenius modulo inertia (our own).

**Problem.** At every finite place of a number field, the Artin and Hecke Euler factors of these characters agree. An Euler factor is the local term in the product defining an L-function.

**How the definition helps.** Compatibility of local and global reciprocity gives the same character on each local multiplicative group (our own). Local units map onto inertia, so a character nontrivial there gives factor one on both sides (our own). Otherwise both factors use the character’s value on arithmetic Frobenius (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_reciprocity). It says: “connects Artin L-functions associated to abelian extensions of a number field with Hecke L-functions”

**Problem.** Take two finite abelian extensions of the same number field inside one algebraic closure. The norms on idele classes from their compositum form the intersection of their two norm subgroups.

**How the definition helps.** The kernel description turns the norm identity into a fixed field test (our own). An automorphism fixes the compositum exactly when it fixes both fields (our own). Global reciprocity supplies the hard step by identifying each kernel with the image of the idele class norm (our own).

### Brauer reciprocity forces even ramification

**Remember:** Each nonsplit place contributes one half to a zero sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11S45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At each completion of ℚ, a quaternion algebra either becomes a matrix algebra or remains a division algebra. Call the former place split and the latter ramified. The local Brauer invariant records these cases by zero and one half respectively, modulo the integers.

**Problem.** A quaternion algebra over ℚ ramifies at an even number of places, counting the real place when it is nonsplit.

**How the definition helps.** The invariant converts a parity question into addition modulo the integers (our own). Only finitely many places ramify, and global Brauer reciprocity makes the sum of all local invariants zero (our own). Each ramified place contributes one half, so their number is even (our own). Reciprocity supplies the global step (our own).

**Remember:** One automorphism generates the whole cyclic Galois group.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite Galois extension L/K is cyclic if some σ ∈ Gal(L/K) generates Gal(L/K). The norm of x ∈ L× is the product of τ(x) over all τ ∈ Gal(L/K) (our own).

**Problem.** An element of a number field that is a local norm everywhere from a finite cyclic extension is a global norm.

**How the definition helps.** Cyclicity lets one test the norm equation by checking each completion. For a cyclic extension, the norm equation has a solution exactly when its associated cyclic algebra is a matrix algebra (our own). The local-global theorem for these algebras supplies the hard step (our own). Hasse found that 3 is a local norm everywhere from ℚ(√−3, √13) but is not a global norm.

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse norm theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_norm_theorem). It says: “Hasse gave the counterexample that 3 is a local norm everywhere for the extension ℚ(√−3, √13)/ℚ but is not a global norm.”

**Remember:** Divide the size in Tate degree zero by the size in degree one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 20J06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite cyclic group G acting on a module A, write Ĥⁱ(G,A) for Tate cohomology. If the groups in degrees zero and one are finite, define h(A) = \|Ĥ⁰(G,A)\|/\|Ĥ¹(G,A)\| (our own).

**Problem.** For a cyclic extension L/K of number fields of degree n, the idele class group of L has Herbrand quotient n. So the index of the norm group in the idele class group of K is at least n.

**How the definition helps.** The quotient is multiplicative and ignores finite modules, so one may cut the idele class group into S-units and local unit groups (our own). Each cohomology group alone is hard to find, but the quotient for the S-units follows from Dirichlet's unit theorem (our own). The degree 0 group is the norm index, which gives the inequality.
