### Oddness excludes nonmodular real representations

**Remember:** Complex conjugation must have opposite signs in the two directions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The absolute Galois group of ℚ consists of the automorphisms of its algebraic closure fixing ℚ. A two-dimensional representation of this group is odd if complex conjugation has determinant −1. In odd characteristic its eigenvalues are then 1 and −1.

**Problem.** Take a continuous odd representation over a finite field of odd characteristic that stays irreducible over the algebraic closure. Serre’s modularity theorem says it arises from a cuspidal modular eigenform, a modular form vanishing at the cusps and diagonalizing the Hecke operators.

**How the definition helps.** Oddness excludes totally real examples with trivial complex conjugation (our own argument). The irreducible cubic x³−4x+1 has positive nonsquare discriminant 229, hence a totally real S₃ splitting field. Its permutation action on the coordinate-sum-zero plane over 𝔽₅ is absolutely irreducible but even. Serre’s modularity theorem supplies modularity under the stated oddness and irreducibility hypotheses.

**Wikipedia:** [Serre's modularity conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%27s_modularity_conjecture). It says: “Additionally, assume ρ is odd, meaning the image of complex conjugation has determinant -1.”

**Sources:**

- [Khare and Wintenberger, Serre’s modularity conjecture (I)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-009-0205-7)
- [Khare and Wintenberger, Serre’s modularity conjecture (II)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-009-0206-6)

### Prismatic F-crystals over a p-adic integer ring are crystalline Galois lattices

**Remember:** Crystalline lattices are F-crystals on all prisms at once, with no choices.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let 𝒪 be the integer ring of a p-adic field K. A prismatic F-crystal assigns each prism (A,I) over 𝒪 a finite projective A-module M compatibly with base change. It carries compatible isomorphisms from φ\*M to M after inverting I, where φ is the prism’s Frobenius.

**Problem.** Prismatic F-crystals over 𝒪 are equivalent to Galois-stable ℤₚ-lattices in crystalline representations of Gal(K̄/K).

**How the definition helps.** The F-crystal uses every prism and no chosen uniformizer, so it describes crystalline lattices integrally and canonically. Kisin's earlier Breuil–Kisin module depends on a uniformizer and its Eisenstein polynomial. Du and Liu's Theorem 4.1.10 says that this module is the value of the crystal at one prism, the Breuil–Kisin prism. The work went into the proof of Bhatt and Scholze, and Du and Liu give a second proof.

**Paper or page:** [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240), [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240). It says: “There is an equivalence of the category of prismatic F-crystals in finite locally free 𝒪\_Δ-modules over (𝒪<sub>K</sub>)\_Δ and the category of Galois stable lattices in crystalline representations of G<sub>K</sub>.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Bhatt and P. Scholze, Prismatic F-crystals and crystalline Galois representations, Cambridge Journal of Mathematics 11 (2023)](https://doi.org/10.4310/cjm.2023.v11.n2.a3)
- [M. Kisin, Crystalline representations and F-crystals, in Algebraic Geometry and Number Theory, Progress in Mathematics](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-8176-4532-8_7)

### Rational Hodge–Tate crystals compute Galois cohomology of nearly Hodge–Tate representations

**Remember:** Reduce modulo the prism ideal, invert p, and require base change.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S25. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K be a p-adic field with integer ring 𝒪, completed algebraic closure C and Galois group G = Gal(K̄/K). A rational Hodge–Tate crystal assigns each prism (A,I) over 𝒪 a finite projective (A/I)\[1/p\]-module compatibly with base change. Nearly Hodge–Tate means every Sen weight belongs to ℤ+E′(π)⁻¹𝔪<sub>C</sub>, with π a uniformizer, E its Eisenstein polynomial and 𝔪<sub>C</sub> the maximal ideal of 𝒪<sub>C</sub>.

**Problem.** Evaluation at Fontaine's perfect prism for C, Witt vectors of the tilt of 𝒪(C), gives an equivalence. It goes from rational Hodge–Tate crystals over 𝒪 to nearly Hodge–Tate C-representations, and matches prismatic cohomology with continuous Galois cohomology.

**How the definition helps.** The crystal's one operator plays the role of the Sen operator (our own reading), so Sen theory gets a canonical home on the prismatic site. Sen's classification by linear operators assumes an algebraically closed residue field and is not canonical, as Theorem 8.6 recalls. The work went into Sen theory over the Kummer tower, through locally analytic vectors (Theorem 7.12).

**Paper or page:** [Hodge--Tate prismatic crystals and Sen theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07024), [Hodge--Tate prismatic crystals and Sen theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07024), [Hodge--Tate prismatic crystals and Sen theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07024), [Hodge--Tate prismatic crystals and Sen theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07024). It says: “There exists a natural quasi-isomorphism RΓ((𝒪<sub>K</sub>)\_Δ,\*, 𝕄) ≃ RΓ(G<sub>K</sub>, W) where the right hand side is Galois cohomology.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Gao, Y. Min and Y. Wang, Hodge–Tate prismatic crystals and Sen theory, preprint (2023), arXiv:2311.07024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07024)
- [S. Sen, Continuous cohomology and p-adic Galois representations, Inventiones Mathematicae 62 (1980) 89–116](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01391665)

### Reducibility ideals locate split traces

**Remember:** One ideal detects every quotient with a split trace.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let T be a two-dimensional Galois pseudocharacter over a complete local ring with 2 invertible and residual trace χ₁+χ₂ for distinct characters. Its reducibility ideal is the least ideal J for which T modulo J is a sum of characters lifting χ₁ and χ₂.

**Problem.** In the cited family of Galois traces attached to modular forms, the reducibility ideal equals the maximal ideal. Among nonzero quotient rings, only the residue field gives a split trace.

**How the definition helps.** The smallest ideal turns a search for two characters into an inclusion test on ideals (our own). A quotient gives a split trace exactly when its defining ideal contains the reducibility ideal (our own). The hard step is the cited calculation of that ideal.

**Paper or page:** [Eisenstein degeneration of Euler systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02078v2). It says: “The reducibility ideal of the pseudo-character t𝐟 is exactly 𝔪.”

**Sources:**

- [Eisenstein degeneration of Euler systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02078v2)

### Requiring an étale Frobenius makes φ-modules match Galois representations

**Remember:** Invertible linearized Frobenius excludes multiplication by p.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11S20, 14F30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K be a finite extension of ℚₚ, K∞ the field K with all p-power roots of unity, and 𝐀(K) Fontaine's ring for K. An étale φ-module over 𝐀(K) is a finite free module M with a Frobenius-semilinear map whose linearization is an isomorphism. Without the word étale one allows, for example, M = 𝐀(K) with Frobenius x ↦ p·φ(x).

**Problem.** Let 𝐀 be Fontaine's larger completed ring. Taking Frobenius-fixed vectors in M ⊗ 𝐀 is an equivalence from étale φ-modules over 𝐀(K) to ℤₚ-representations of Gal(K̄/K∞).

**How the definition helps.** Fontaine’s equivalence identifies the scalar extension of an étale module with that of its fixed lattice (our own explanation). For the excluded map x ↦ pφ(x), any fixed vector lies in pⁿ𝐀 for every n and hence vanishes. This loses rank one. The quoted Lubin–Tate theorem specializes to the cyclotomic case with coefficient field ℚₚ.

**Paper or page:** [Prismatic F-crystals and Lubin-Tate (φq,Γ)-modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07620). It says: “The functors Mod\_𝐀<sub>K</sub><sup>φ<sub>q</sub>,et</sup> → Rep\_𝒪<sub>L</sub>(G<sub>K∞</sub>), M ↦ (M⊗\_𝐀<sub>K</sub> 𝐀)<sup>φ = 1</sup>, (T⊗\_𝒪<sub>L</sub> 𝐀)<sup>G<sub>K∞</sub></sup> ↤ T form an equivalence of exact tensor categories.”

**Sources:**

- [J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations p-adiques des corps locaux (1ère partie), Modern Birkhäuser Classics (2007 reprint)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-8176-4575-5_6)
- [M. Kisin and W. Ren, Galois representations and Lubin–Tate groups, Documenta Mathematica 14 (2009) 441–461](https://doi.org/10.4171/dm/278)

### The self-product prism gives a one-line criterion for crystalline lattices

**Remember:** Crystalline means τ stays inside the self-product prism.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a p-adic integer ring 𝒪 with residue field k, choose a uniformizer π with Eisenstein polynomial E. Set A = W(k)\[\[u\]\] with φ(u)=uᵖ, and let A⁽²⁾ be the prismatic self-product of (A,(E)) over 𝒪. Thus two maps from this prism into a common prism over 𝒪 induce a unique map from the self-product ring (our own description).

**Problem.** Liu’s (φ,Ĝ)-modules classify lattices in semistable representations with bounded Hodge–Tate weights. Choose the Kummer generator τ acting on compatible roots of π and fixing p-power roots of unity. The associated lattice is crystalline exactly when its underlying Kisin module 𝔐 satisfies τ(𝔐) ⊆ A⁽²⁾ ⊗<sub>A</sub> 𝔐.

**How the definition helps.** Crystalline lattices come from F-crystals on all prisms, and A⁽²⁾ is where such crystals glue, so crystallinity becomes a ring condition on τ. Semistable lattices need a larger ring built from A⁽²⁾ (our own reading). The work went into Du and Liu's prismatic construction of (φ,Ĝ)-modules.

**Paper or page:** [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240). It says: “Select τ ∈ Ĝ as the above. Then T̂(𝔐̂) is crystalline if and only if τ(𝔐) ⊂ A<sup>(2)</sup>⊗<sub>A</sub> 𝔐.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Du and T. Liu, A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals, preprint (2023), arXiv:2107.12240](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240)
- [T. Liu, A note on lattices in semi-stable representations, Mathematische Annalen 346 (2010) 117–138](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00208-009-0392-y)

### Alternation forces a square order

**Remember:** A perfect alternating pairing puts the finite group into pairs.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11G40. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A bilinear pairing b on an abelian group A with values in ℚ/ℤ is alternating if b(x,x) = 0 for every x ∈ A.

**Problem.** If the Tate–Shafarevich group of an elliptic curve over a number field is finite, its order is a square.

**How the definition helps.** Alternation rules out an unpaired cyclic factor of order two (our own). Skew symmetry alone allows the generator of a group of order two to pair with itself to ½ modulo ℤ (our own). For elliptic curves, Cassels proves alternation, and duality makes the pairing perfect when the group is finite (our own). A finite group with a perfect alternating pairing splits into pairs of cyclic factors of equal order, so its order is a square (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Tate–Shafarevich group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate%E2%80%93Shafarevich_group). It says: “if the order of Ш is finite then it is a square.”

**Sources:**

- [Cassels, Arithmetic on Curves of Genus 1. IV. Proof of the Hauptvermutung](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1962.211.95)
- [Poonen and Stoll, The Cassels–Tate Pairing on Polarized Abelian Varieties](https://doi.org/10.2307/121064)

### Relaxed Selmer conditions pair with strict ones

**Remember:** Opposite local conditions make the two dimension jumps add to half the local dimension.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11R34. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix an elliptic curve over a number field and a prime p. Its p-Selmer group consists of global Galois cohomology classes on the points killed by p that locally come from dividing curve points by p. At one finite prime, the relaxed group allows every local class and the strict group requires zero. Both keep the usual conditions elsewhere.

**Problem.** The relaxed dimension minus the strict dimension equals half the dimension of local first cohomology at the chosen prime. All dimensions use the field of p elements.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing everything and allowing zero give opposite local conditions under the local duality pairing (our own). The usual condition pairs to zero with itself and has half the local dimension (our own). The two global dimension jumps give images in the usual local condition and its dual (our own). The cited orthogonality theorem makes these images exact annihilators, so their dimensions add to the dimension of the usual condition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Increasing the p-Selmer rank by twisting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09207v3). It says: “The images of the two right-hand maps in the following exact sequences are orthogonal complements of each other under the sum of the local Tate pairings.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Exterior powers give determinant characters

**Remember:** Take the top exterior power before passing to the Galois action.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a rank-r Drinfeld module E with associated A-motive M, its determinant is the rank-one Drinfeld module whose motive is ∧ʳM. The cited exterior-power theorem gives existence and uniqueness up to isomorphism.

**Problem.** At a prime different from the characteristic, the Galois action on the determinant module’s Tate module equals the determinant of the original Galois action. The Tate module records compatible points killed by powers of that prime.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, a linear transformation acts on the top exterior power by its determinant. The cited theorem realizes the resulting motive by a unique rank-one Drinfeld module up to isomorphism. Applying the linear calculation to torsion also requires the comparison between motives and Tate modules to preserve exterior powers.

**Paper or page:** [Pour une définition commune des courbes elliptiques et modules de Drinfeld](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13160). It says: “Le $A$-motif $\\underline{D}$ provient d'un $A$-module de Drinfeld de rang $1$ et de caractéristique $\\delta<sub>E</sub>$. Ce module de Drinfeld est unique à isomorphisme près, et on le note $\\det E$.”

**Sources:**

- [Quentin Gazda and Damien Junger, Pour une définition commune des courbes elliptiques et modules de Drinfeld](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13160)

### Frobenius determinants measure Drinfeld points

**Remember:** Take the determinant of one minus Frobenius to measure rational torsion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let A = 𝔽q\[T\]. A finite A-module splits into cyclic modules A/(h) with monic polynomials h. Use the product of these polynomials to measure the module, giving the monic generator of its Fitting ideal.

**Problem.** For a Drinfeld module over a finite field, this polynomial measure of its rational points equals the Frobenius polynomial at one, scaled to be monic. Here the Frobenius polynomial is the characteristic polynomial of the field-size power map on the Tate module at a prime away from the characteristic.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the polynomial measure records determinants of presentations and therefore lets one state a polynomial point-count formula. Rational points are the points fixed by Frobenius. Away from the characteristic, the quotient by one minus Frobenius on compatible torsion gives the corresponding part of the rational point module. The cited theorem gives the full polynomial, including its characteristic factor.

**Paper or page:** [Convolutions of Goss and Pellarin L-series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14931). It says: “Then\\\[  \\bigl\[ E(\\mathbb {F}<sub>f</sub>) \\bigr\]\_{\\mathsf{A}} = \\gamma \\cdot \\Char (\\tau ^d,T<sub>\\lambda </sub>(E),1),  \\\]where $\\gamma \\in \\mathbb {F}<sub>q</sub><sup>\\times </sup>$ forces the right-hand expression to be monic in\~ $t$.”

**Sources:**

- [Wei-Cheng Huang and Matthew A. Papanikolas, Convolutions of Goss and Pellarin L-series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14931)

### Frobenius polynomials classify Drinfeld isogeny classes

**Remember:** The Frobenius polynomial determines the isogeny class over a finite field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix A = 𝔽q\[T\]. A Drinfeld module lets A act by additive polynomials, and its characteristic ideal is the kernel of the scalar map to the base field. At a different prime, collect compatible points killed by powers of that prime and invert the prime to form the rational Tate module. Define the Frobenius polynomial as the characteristic polynomial of the field-size power map on this space.

**Problem.** Take two Drinfeld modules of the same rank and characteristic over the same finite field. Their Frobenius polynomials agree exactly when an isogeny, a nonzero map respecting both actions, exists over that field.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, one polynomial lets us state the classification as equality of two computable invariants. An isogeny identifies the rational Tate modules and carries one Frobenius action to the other. Conversely, Frobenius acts semisimply, so its polynomial determines the rational representation. The Tate isogeny theorem turns this linear comparison into an isogeny.

**Paper or page:** [Traces of Hecke operators on Drinfeld modular forms for 𝔽q\[T\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04555). It says: “Then cφ(X) = cψ(X) if and only if φ is isogenous to ψ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ideal classes classify rank one Drinfeld modules

**Remember:** At rank one, period lattices become fractional ideals up to scaling.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.), 11R58. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a smooth projective curve over a finite field and a place at infinity, and let A be the functions regular elsewhere. Over the completed algebraic closure at infinity, the period lattice of a Drinfeld module is the kernel of its exponential. In rank one this is a projective A-module of rank one.

**Problem.** The ideal class group acts freely and transitively on the rank one Drinfeld modules up to isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** A basis for the lattice’s span over the fraction field identifies the lattice with a fractional ideal of A (our own argument). Changing basis scales that ideal, leaving its ideal class. Drinfeld uniformization identifies module isomorphisms with lattice homotheties, so ideal multiplication acts freely and transitively on the resulting classes.

**Paper or page:** [Drinfeld Module and Weil pairing over Dedekind domain of class number two](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.16919). It says: “The set of isomorphism classes of A-Drinfeld modules is the principle homogeneous space of the class group of A”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Lattice enlargement composes ideal isogenies

**Remember:** Ideal isogenies enlarge the period lattice by inverse ideals.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a Drinfeld module, an action of a curve’s coefficient ring A by additive polynomials. Here A consists of functions regular away from a chosen place at infinity. Over the completed algebraic closure at infinity, let Λ denote the kernel of the module’s exponential. For a nonzero ideal I of A, define the quotient using the larger lattice I⁻¹Λ.

**Problem.** Taking the quotient for I and then for J gives the quotient for IJ up to isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, enlarging the lattice twice gives J⁻¹I⁻¹Λ, exactly the lattice for IJ. Uniformization identifies the inclusion with an isogeny, a map of modules with finite kernel. Its kernel consists of the points killed by I. Normalizing the polynomial for this map can scale the target lattice, as the cited formula shows.

**Paper or page:** [Drinfeld Module and Weil pairing over Dedekind domain of class number two](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.16919). It says: “Then we have Λψ = Λφ · ∂(λ) I⁻¹.”

**Sources:**

- [Chuangqiang Hu and Xiao-Min Huang, Drinfeld Module and Weil pairing over Dedekind domain of class number two](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.16919)

### Forgetting signs lets twists share j

**Remember:** A modular curve sees torsion bases only up to curve automorphisms.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G18 (Arithmetic aspects of modular and Shimura varieties), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let H be an open subgroup of GL₂ over the profinite integers. Above j in characteristic zero, X(H) identifies full torsion bases that differ by H or by an automorphism of the elliptic curve. For j outside {0,1728}, this identifies bases precisely up to the group ±H generated by H and negation (our own formulation).

**Problem.** Take an algebraic number j different from 0 and 1728 and an elliptic curve over ℚ(j) with that invariant. Some point of X(H) above j is rational over ℚ(j) exactly when a conjugate of ±H contains the curve’s Galois image on torsion.

**How the definition helps.** Identifying opposite bases allows a basis class to be fixed even when Galois changes its sign (our own). A rational point requires some fixed class, which accounts for the choice of conjugate (our own). A quadratic twist changes the torsion action by signs, so it gives the same test (our own). Identifying the geometric points above j with basis classes supplies the geometric input (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Degrees of points with rational j-invariant on X₀(n) and X₁(n)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13199v1). It says: “there exists a point x ∈ Xᴴ(ℚ(j)) such that j(x) = j if and only if 𝒢ⱼ ≤ ±ℋ.”

**Sources:**

- [Degrees of points with rational j-invariant on X₀(n) and X₁(n)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13199v1)

### Component graphs count torus rank

**Remember:** Each independent loop supplies one multiplicative direction in the Jacobian.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a split semistable curve model, the dual graph has one vertex per irreducible component of the special fibre. Each node gives an edge joining the components containing its two branches, with a loop when they coincide.

**Problem.** Take a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of positive genus over ℚ with split semistable reduction at a prime. Its Jacobian, which parametrizes divisor classes of degree zero, has torus rank equal to the number of independent loops in this graph. This rank counts multiplicative group factors in the connected part of its reduced group model.

**How the definition helps.** Line bundles glue across each node by one nonzero scalar (our own explanation). Rescaling on components changes the scalars, with common rescaling acting trivially. This leaves edges minus vertices plus one independent parameters for the connected graph. The description of the Jacobian’s Néron model identifies these gluing parameters with its torus.

**Paper or page:** [Normal distribution of bad reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15874v1). It says: “the toric rank of Jac(C) is equal to m − c + 1”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ramification scales node thickness

**Remember:** An edge length is a valuation, so ramification multiplies it.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14G20. arXiv math.AG, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A split semistable curve model has a reduced special fiber whose only singularities are crossings with two branches over the residue field. Draw a vertex for each component and an edge for each crossing. In completed local coordinates, write a crossing as xy = a. Give its edge length v(a), where the valuation v counts powers of a generator of the maximal ideal.

**Problem.** Start with such a model over a complete discrete valuation ring. After a finite totally ramified extension of index e, the pulled-back model has the same graph with every length multiplied by e.

**How the definition helps.** The pulled-back node still has equation xy = a, so its length is the new normalized valuation of a (our own calculation). This valuation restricts to e times the old one. Total ramification preserves the residue field, hence the special fibre and its graph.

**Paper or page:** [Models of Bihyperelliptic Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09730v1). It says: “with the same dual graph as 𝒞, but with the lengths of all edges multiplied by e.”

**Sources:**

- [Models of Bihyperelliptic Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09730v1)

### Under semistability, invariant valuations determine the reduction graph of hyperelliptic curves

**Remember:** Require semistability before reading a reduction graph from invariants.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14H45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A hyperelliptic curve has a degree-two map to the projective line. It is semistable if it has a proper flat model over the ring of integers whose special fibre is reduced, with only ordinary double points. The dual graph of the special fibre has a vertex for each component and an edge for each double point.

**Problem.** Let C be a hyperelliptic curve of genus g ≥ 2 over a local field K of odd residue characteristic. The paper gives a finite list of invariants that depends only on g. If C is semistable, their valuations determine the dual graph of its minimal regular model over the maximal unramified extension of K.

**How the definition helps.** Semistability removes the curves whose graph the invariants cannot see, so the valuations then determine the graph. The paper shows by a counterexample that, for genus at least two, no list of invariants works for curves that are not semistable. The result is the analog of Tate’s algorithm, where ord(j) gives the graph of a semistable elliptic curve. The work is the explicit method that reads the graph from the valuations.

**Paper or page:** [Invariants recovering the reduction type of a hyperelliptic curve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08487v3). It says: “They also determine the dual graph of the special fibre of the minimal regular model of C/Kᵘⁿʳ if C/K is semistable.”

**Sources:**

- [Lilybelle Cowland Kellock, Elisa Lorenzo, Invariants recovering the reduction type of a hyperelliptic curve, arXiv:2502.08487v3 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08487v3)

### Serre–Frobenius groups separate ordinary and supersingular curves

**Remember:** Close the powers of the normalized Frobenius tuple inside a torus.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G25 (Varieties over finite and local fields), 11G10, 11G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an abelian variety over 𝔽q, let u be the tuple of complex Frobenius eigenvalues divided by √q. Its Serre–Frobenius group is the closure of {uⁿ : n ∈ ℤ} in the product of unit circles.

**Problem.** Normalized Frobenius traces are equidistributed for the image of Haar probability measure under the coordinate sum. For elliptic curves the group is a circle exactly in the ordinary case. The supersingular case gives exactly the cyclic orders 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12.

**How the definition helps.** Powers of a topological generator equidistribute for Haar measure, and summing coordinates gives the traces (our own explanation). For elliptic curves the two coordinates are inverses, so one determines the group. The classification of elliptic Frobenius eigenvalues gives the listed root-of-unity orders in the supersingular case and an infinite, hence dense, circle subgroup otherwise.

**Paper or page:** [Frobenius distributions of low dimensional abelian varieties over finite fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02237), [Frobenius distributions of low dimensional abelian varieties over finite fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02237). It says: “This group, which we call the Serre--Frobenius group, encodes the possible multiplicative relations between the Frobenius eigenvalues.”

**Sources:**

### Regular dessins descend to moduli fields

**Remember:** A regular cover can move any chosen sheet to any other.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G32 (Arithmetic aspects of dessins d'enfants, Bely? theory), 14H57. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A dessin is a connected cover of the sphere branched only over 0, 1 and ∞. Call it regular if its symmetries over the sphere act transitively on each unbranched fiber. Its field of moduli consists of the algebraic numbers fixed by every Galois automorphism preserving its isomorphism class.

**Problem.** Every regular dessin admits defining equations over its field of moduli.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity makes the deck group act simply transitively above the rational unbranched value 2 (our own argument). Mark a point there and use the unique deck transformation adjusting each conjugate isomorphism to preserve the marking. Uniqueness gives the cocycle condition, so Weil descent gives equations over the field of moduli.

**Wikipedia:** [Dessin d'enfant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dessin_d%27enfant). It says: “Due to the Galois correspondence between subgroups of Γ and algebraic number fields, the stabilizer corresponds to a field, the field of moduli of the dessin.”

### Zero-cycles with modulus give class field theory

**Remember:** The modulus D bounds ramification along the boundary, as a conductor does.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G45 (Geometric class field theory), 19F05, 14C25. arXiv math.AG, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a proper variety X and effective Cartier divisor D, start with the free abelian group on closed points outside D. Quotient by pushed-forward principal divisors from normalizations of integral curves in X meeting the complement. Use rational functions congruent to one modulo the pulled-back divisor, retaining its multiplicities.

**Problem.** Let U be smooth, connected and quasi-projective over a finite field with normal proper compactification X. Assume the boundary supports an effective Cartier divisor, and let D range over effective Cartier divisors with that support. Reciprocity identifies π₁ᵃᵇ(U) with the inverse limit of CH₀(X\|D) ⊗ ℤ/m over D and positive integers m.

**How the definition helps.** Increasing the multiplicities allows increasing ramification along the same boundary (our own explanation). The reciprocity theorem identifies the resulting finite quotients in the inverse limit, using Bloch’s formula with modulus.

It says: “The reciprocity maps {ρ₍X,D₎}\|D\|⊂C induce an isomorphism of pro-finite topological groups ρU : lim D,m CH₀(X\|D) ⊗ ℤ/m ≅ π₁ᵃᵇ(U).”

### Invariant metrics scale heights exactly

**Remember:** An invariant metric turns pullback into exact multiplication of heights.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G50 (Heights), 14G40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f be an endomorphism of a projective variety over a number field. Fix an ample line bundle L and an isomorphism from f\*L to its qth tensor power for some integer q &gt; 1. A continuous adelic metric on L is invariant if this isomorphism preserves the metrics at every place.

**Problem.** For such a map, invariant norms exist, and the height h that they define satisfies h(f(P)) = qh(P).

**How the definition helps.** The invariant norms make pullback multiply the height exactly, in our own explanation. Arbitrary norms on the same bundle generally give this relation only up to bounded error. Heights pull back with maps and add when bundles are tensored. The existence theorem constructs the compatible norms by repeated pullback and normalization, starting with norms from an integral model outside finitely many places.

**Paper or page:** [Specialization of canonical heights on abelian varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07664v1). It says: “In particular, there exists a canonical height”

### Alternating Kummer products give symmetric powers

**Remember:** Alternating the relative product makes the Kummer tensors symmetric.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Work over the rational affine line with 0 and 1 removed, using coordinate z. The Kummer motive K records degree-one cohomology of the multiplicative line relative to the points 1 and 1/z. Take degree-n relative cohomology of its n-fold product, marking every face where a coordinate equals either point. Select the part where exchanging two coordinates acts by minus one.

**Problem.** This part of the relative cohomology motive is the symmetric tensor power Symⁿ(K).

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, selecting the sign cancels the sign already contributed by exchanging two degree-one cohomology factors. The relative product theorem identifies the whole group with a tensor power and explains this extra sign. The selected part therefore corresponds to symmetric tensors. This realizes the abstract symmetric power by an explicit product of marked lines.

### Clean polylogarithms erase product terms

**Remember:** Project away products before taking a single-valued period.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Represent a multiple polylogarithm by its formal iterated integral, with weight equal to the number of integrations. Take its de Rham image, which retains its algebraic differential data. Apply the Dynkin projection, a linear operator whose kernel in positive weight consists of sums of products of positive-weight elements. Evaluate the single-valued period and take its real part in odd weight or its imaginary part in even weight.

**Problem.** Suppose a rational linear combination of formal integrals of the same positive weight equals a sum of products of positive-weight elements. The corresponding clean functions then sum to zero with the same coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** The projection kills the entire sum before numerical evaluation. Our own comparison is with ordinary single-valued evaluation, which preserves multiplication and can retain nonzero products. The substantive step identifies the kernel of the Dynkin projection.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344), [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344). It says: “The kernel of Π is generated by all non-trivial products”

### Clean polylogarithms reverse interior letters

**Remember:** After products vanish, reversal preserves odd lengths and negates even lengths.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a formal iterated integral with fixed endpoints, apply the Dynkin projection to its de Rham image and evaluate its single-valued period. The clean value takes the real part in odd length and the imaginary part in even length.

**Problem.** In a clean iterated integral of length n &gt; 0, reversing the interior letters multiplies it by (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ without exchanging endpoints.

**How the definition helps.** The shuffle antipode identity expresses the word plus (−1)ⁿ times its reversal as a sum of products from nonempty proper cuts (our own explanation). The Dynkin projection kills those products. Evaluating the remaining two terms gives the claimed sign with unchanged endpoints.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344). It says: “Iᶜˢᵛ(x₀; xₙ, …, x₁; xₙ₊₁) = (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ Iᶜˢᵛ(x₀; x₁, …, xₙ; xₙ₊₁).”

### Clean projection gives tetralogarithm reduction

**Remember:** Remove all products, then fix the constant on real inputs.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 33B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write I₃,₁(x,y) for the nested integral from 0 to 1 with successive poles x,0,0,y, using the paper’s clean evaluation. This evaluation first projects formal integrals of weight four along products of integrals of smaller weight. It then takes the imaginary part of their single-valued evaluation. Write L₄ for the same evaluation of the fourth polylogarithm.

**Problem.** For x,y∉{0,1}, with y∉{x,1−x} and all displayed arguments of L₄ outside {0,1}, I₃,₁(1−x,y)+I₃,₁(x,y)=L₄((1−x)/(1−y))−L₄((1−y)/x)−3L₄(y/(1−x))−3L₄(y/x)+L₄(y/(y−1))−L₄((1−x)y/(x(1−y)))/2−L₄(xy/((1−x)(1−y)))/2+L₄((1−y)y/((1−x)x))/2.

**How the definition helps.** The clean projection removes the lower-weight products and taking the imaginary part fixes the constant on real inputs. The work goes into Gangl’s matching of the symbols, which record the successive logarithmic differentials, modulo products.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344v2). It says: “This constant must be 0 since each side vanishes on the real line, as we take the imaginary part in the definition of the functions.”

### Cobrackets rule out classical tetralogarithms

**Remember:** A nonzero two-by-two split rules out a classical expression.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Give each polylogarithm symbol a weight equal to its tensor length. Quotient positive-weight symbols by sums of products of positive-weight symbols. For a weight-four symbol, split after its second position and subtract the result with the two halves exchanged. Take both halves modulo products to obtain the weight-(2,2) cobracket.

**Problem.** The weight-(2,2) cobracket vanishes on every rational sum of classical tetralogarithm symbols modulo products. Thus a nonzero value rules out any such expression.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, this test selects the split where the classical tetralogarithm has a repeated logarithm in its second half. That two-letter tensor is half the shuffle square of the logarithm, so it vanishes modulo products. Linearity gives the same result for any rational sum. Applying this obstruction to a particular function requires computing its cobracket.

**How the definition helps.** In our own comparison, the diamond product turns two period calculations into one equality between formal sums of points. Bloch’s formula evaluates each period by applying the same real-valued function, the elliptic dilogarithm, to that sum. The elliptic dilogarithm changes sign under negation, so it respects the imposed relation. The formula supplies the link with integration.

### Five-term relations give a regulator

**Remember:** The five-term identity lets the dilogarithm act on classes of symbols.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a subfield F of ℂ, start with formal integer sums of symbols \[x\], where x belongs to F and differs from 0 and 1. For distinct such x and y impose \[x\]−\[y\]+\[y/x\]−\[(1−x⁻¹)/(1−y⁻¹)\]+\[(1−x)/(1−y)\]=0. The resulting quotient is the pre-Bloch group.

**Problem.** The Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D gives a homomorphism \[x\] ↦ D(x) from the pre-Bloch group to ℝ.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation uses the quotient to replace checking every change of representative with checking one family of relations. The analytic five-term identity says exactly that D sends each defining relation to zero.

### Integrable symbols exclude path dependence

**Remember:** Adjacent wedge tests remove the local obstruction to path independence.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a smooth complex variety, remove the zeros and poles of the rational functions under consideration. Represent each function f by the differential form df/f, and represent ordered lists of these forms by tensors. For each adjacent pair, replace its two forms by their exterior product, leaving the other positions intact. A sum of tensors is integrable when every such replacement gives zero after summing.

**Problem.** An integrable tensor gives a homotopy-invariant linear combination of logarithmic iterated integrals. Homotopies fix both endpoints and stay in the open variety.

**How the definition helps.** Chen’s variation formula has only adjacent wedge terms here, since logarithmic differentials are closed (our own explanation). Integrability makes each such term vanish. For dx/x followed by dy/y, move from (1,1) to (2,2) along coordinate segments. Moving first in x gives (log 2)², while the homotopic path moving first in y gives zero (our own example).

**Remember:** The antipode inverts the whole variation matrix.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Arrange the formal coefficients of multiple polylogarithms in their triangular variation matrix V, with ones on the diagonal. Write W for its transpose. The coproduct splits Wᵢⱼ into the sum of Wᵢₖ ⊗ Wₖⱼ over intermediate indices k.

**Problem.** The antipode, the operation undoing a coproduct under multiplication, sends V entry by entry to V⁻¹.

**How the definition helps.** The matrix coproduct turns the antipode axiom into S(W)W = I (our own calculation). Hence S(W) = W⁻¹, and transposition gives S(V) = V⁻¹ since the coefficient algebra is commutative. The substantive input is the coproduct formula for the variation matrix.

### Multiplication identifies torsion logarithm fibers

**Remember:** Multiplication sends torsion to zero and rescales each graded piece invertibly.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let π be the fundamental group of a complex elliptic curve at zero. In its rational group ring, let I be the ideal of sums whose coefficients add to zero. Keep terms through degree n by taking the quotient by Iⁿ⁺¹. The pointed logarithm system transports this vector space along loops by group multiplication and marks the element 1 at zero.

**Problem.** For N ≥ 1, multiplication by N identifies this system with its pullback, whose fiber at P is the original fiber at NP. Thus every point killed by N has a canonical identification of its fiber with the fiber at zero.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplication by N sends each loop γ to γᴺ and hence induces a map on the truncated group ring (our own argument). This map preserves the marked unit and intertwines transport with pullback transport. On degree k of the associated graded ring it acts by Nᵏ, so it is invertible over ℚ. At a point P killed by N the pullback fibre is the fibre at zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Represent an iterated integral by a word listing its integration forms between two endpoints. The second multiplies the integrals between successive selected positions, counting both endpoints as boundaries.

**Problem.** Splitting the first factor again gives the same three-factor sum as splitting the second factor again.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, both expansions list exactly the same pairs of nested subsequences. One expansion chooses the larger subsequence first. The comparison with the coproduct defined by periods still requires the theorem identifying it with the cut formula.

### Rational Bloch regulators are injective

**Remember:** Rational coefficients remove classes that every real regulator must kill.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F be a number field, a finite extension of ℚ. Form rational sums of symbols \[x\] for x in F other than 0 and 1, subject to the dilogarithm’s five-term relations. The rational Bloch group consists of classes with Σa\[x\] mapping to zero under \[x\] ↦ x ∧ (1−x). Here ∧ denotes the alternating product on the multiplicative group of F with rational coefficients.

**Problem.** Choose one embedding σ from each conjugate pair of nonreal embeddings of F. Evaluating the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D gives an injective map with coordinates ΣaD(σ(x)).

**How the definition helps.** Rational coefficients remove elements of finite order, which every homomorphism to a real vector space kills. Our own explanation uses Borel’s regulator theorem to establish injectivity after this step. The comparison with the dilogarithm regulator identifies its coordinates.

**nLab:** [Bloch group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Bloch+group). It says: “Now the point is that restricted to the Bloch group proper the Borel regulator is injective.”

**Sources:**

- [Don Zagier, Polylogarithms, Dedekind zeta functions, and the algebraic K-theory of fields (1990)](https://people.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/zagier/files/scanned/PolylogsDedekindZetaAndKTheory/fulltext.pdf)
- [A. A. Suslin, K₃ of a field, and the Bloch group (1990)](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/tm1914)

### Regulator forms kill Steinberg relations

**Remember:** The dilogarithm turns the Steinberg relation into an exact differential.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19D45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a smooth complex curve, take rational functions f and g without zeros or poles on an open set U. Set η(f,g) = log\|f\| d arg g − log\|g\| d arg f, where d arg records angular change. A Steinberg symbol {f,g} turns multiplication in either entry into addition and satisfies {f,1−f} = 0 whenever both entries qualify.

**Problem.** Sending {f,g} to the class of η(f,g) gives a well-defined map from Steinberg symbols to closed real 1-forms on U, modulo differentials of single-valued functions.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, passing to classes checks all closed-path integrals at once. Roy proves that η is closed and turns multiplication into addition in each entry. He also identifies η(f,1−f) as the differential of the single-valued Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D(f). Its class therefore vanishes, exactly as the Steinberg relation requires.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601). It says: “\\eta \\left(x, 1-x\\right) = d D\\left(x\\right).”

**Sources:**

- [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials, Lemma 2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601)

### Residues identify elliptic polylogarithms

**Remember:** Once the residue is fixed, there is no class left to add.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a complex elliptic curve, remove the D² points killed by multiplication by an integer D ≥ 2. Use the logarithm system of coefficients, which transports truncated power series in two loop variables along paths. At each removed point the residue measures the local cohomology class around that puncture. Define the elliptic polylogarithm as the compatible sequence of degree-one classes with scalar residue D²−1 at zero and −1 at every other puncture.

**Problem.** There is exactly one compatible sequence of degree-one classes with these residues, so the elliptic polylogarithm is well defined. The residues are read through the splitting at each removed point given by multiplication by D, and they have zero components in all positive degrees.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, defining the class by residues replaces comparison of global representatives by local calculations at finitely many points. Sprang’s exact sequence shows that residues determine the class after taking all truncations together. It also shows that the specified residues occur, since their scalar components sum to zero. Sprang computes these residues for explicit differential forms from the Poincaré line bundle, proving that they represent the polylogarithm.

**nLab:** [Poincaré line bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poincar%C3%A9+line+bundle). It says: “The canonical line bundle on the product of an abelian group (abelian variety) and its dual Picard scheme.”

**Sources:**

- [Sprang, The algebraic de Rham realization of the elliptic polylogarithm via the Poincaré bundle, Definition 3.2 and Theorem 5.8](https://doi.org/10.2140/ant.2020.14.545)

### Steinberg symbols yield elliptic identities

**Remember:** One Steinberg relation gives a whole sum of elliptic dilogarithm values.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19D45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a rational function f, its divisor div(f) lists its zeros and poles with signed multiplicities. The diamond product ⋄ replaces each pair of divisor points P,Q by P−Q and multiplies their multiplicities. Add the results, with a point and its negative carrying opposite signs. A Steinberg symbol {f,g} is additive under multiplication in either entry and obeys {f,1−f} = 0.

**Problem.** Take a nonconstant rational function f on an elliptic curve over ℚ. Assume its zeros, its poles and all points where f equals one are rational. Applying the elliptic dilogarithm linearly to div(f) ⋄ div(1−f) gives zero.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the symbol definition replaces a sum of special function values with one defining relation. Bloch’s formula identifies that sum with the regulator of {f,1−f}, a period integral depending additively on the symbol. The defining relation makes the symbol zero, and its period therefore vanishes.

**Paper or page:** [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974). It says: “r<sub>E</sub>(\\{ f,g\\} )\[\\gamma \]=D<sup>E</sup>((f)\\diamond (g)), \\end{align\*}where $\[\\gamma \]$ is a generator of $H<sub>1</sub>(E,\\mathbb {Z})<sup>-$</sup>.”

**Sources:**

- [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family, Lemma 2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974)
- [Yang, Liu and Tang, A Mahler Measure Identity Involving a Genus 2 Family, Section 1](https://ccj.pku.edu.cn/Article/DownLoad?id=364490499&type=ArticleFile)

### Three terms compute next-to-Milnor cohomology

**Remember:** Next to Milnor degree, only three terms affect the answer.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19E15. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F be a field of characteristic zero, m ≥ 3, and V = F× ⊗ ℚ. In degree m−1, Goncharov’s complex uses B₂(F) ⊗ Λᵐ⁻²V, where B₂(F) is the rational space of dilogarithm symbols modulo their functional relations. The differential sends \[x\]₂ ⊗ β to (1−x) ∧ x ∧ β.

**Problem.** Quotient the kernel by the span of \[x\]₂ ⊗ (x ∧ α) for x ∈ F outside {0,1} and α ∈ Λᵐ⁻³V. This quotient gives rational motivic cohomology of F in degree m−1 and weight m, also defined using algebraic cycles.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the symbol complex reduces this description to one kernel and one family of boundaries. Each incoming relation is the image of a trilogarithm symbol tensored with α. Computing cohomology here needs only these two arrows. Identifying the answer with the group defined using algebraic cycles requires Bolbachan’s comparison theorem.

**Wikipedia:** [Goncharov conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goncharov_conjecture). It says: “Goncharov defined the following complex called Γ(F,n) placed in degrees \[1,n\]”

**Paper or page:** [On Goncharov's conjecture in next to Milnor degree](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06271). It says: “is true when i = m − 1 and m ∈ ℤ, m ≥ 2.”

**Sources:**

- [On Goncharov's conjecture in next to Milnor degree](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06271)

### Top polylogarithm cohomology gives Milnor K-theory

**Remember:** The last differential lists exactly the relations of Milnor K-theory.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19D45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an infinite field F, put V = Fˣ ⊗ ℚ and fix m ≥ 2. Goncharov’s last differential maps B₂(F) ⊗ Λᵐ⁻²V to ΛᵐV, where B₂(F) is the rational dilogarithm symbol space modulo five-term relations. It sends each \[x\] ⊗ α to (1 − x) ∧ x ∧ α for x ∈ F outside {0,1}.

**Problem.** For m ≥ 2, the top cohomology of this complex is the rational Milnor K-group of F in degree m.

**How the definition helps.** The displayed images span precisely the Steinberg relations in the exterior-power presentation of rational Milnor K-theory (our own). Top cohomology takes the quotient of ΛᵐV by their span.

**Wikipedia:** [Goncharov conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goncharov_conjecture). It says: “Goncharov defined the following complex called Γ(F,n) placed in degrees \[1,n\]”

**Sources:**

- [A. B. Goncharov, Geometry of configurations, polylogarithms, and motivic cohomology](https://doi.org/10.1006/aima.1995.1045)

### Truncated cuts vanish in lower depth

**Remember:** A surviving cut needs one depth letter in every factor.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A formal iterated integral class has depth at most d if words with at most d nonzero interior letters represent it modulo products and linearity. The truncated cobracket discards all terms of the ordinary cobracket with a weight-one factor.

**Problem.** For k ≥ 2, this k-factor operation vanishes on classes of depth at most k − 1. On depth k its value therefore depends only on the class modulo lower depth.

**How the definition helps.** Every surviving factor needs a nonzero interior letter because depth-zero integrals are powers of logarithms and products vanish (our own). Truncation removes the remaining weight-one logarithms. The cut formula bounds total depth by input depth, so k surviving factors require depth at least k.

**Paper or page:** [Cluster Polylogarithms I: Quadrangular Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01564). It says: “For $k\\geq 2$ iterated truncated coproduct $\\overline{\\Delta }<sup>\[k-1\]</sup>$ vanishes on $\\mathcal{D}<sub>k-1</sub>\\mathcal{L}\_\\bullet (\\mathrm{F})$”

### Weight frames split the dilogarithm

**Remember:** The dilogarithm has just one intermediate weight to cut.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Represent the dilogarithm by its period matrix, a triangular matrix encoding the integral and its lower-weight logarithms. Frames specify the generators at the bottom and top weights. The reduced coproduct splits a frame at each intermediate weight, pairing a basis with its dual.

**Problem.** For z ∈ ℂ outside {0,1}, the reduced coproduct is log(1 − z) ⊗ log z. Each logarithm represents a class modulo 2πiℤ in the integral normalization.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, framing makes the single intermediate basis vector supply the only term. Reading the two adjacent entries in units of their diagonal periods gives log(1 − z) and log z. The scalar dilogarithm alone does not record both entries. Constructing the period matrix and proving basis independence supply the substantive work.

**Paper or page:** [Chern-Simons invariants of hyperbolic three-manifolds, mixed Tate motives, and motivic path torsor of augmented character varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11950), [Chern-Simons invariants of hyperbolic three-manifolds, mixed Tate motives, and motivic path torsor of augmented character varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11950). It says: “log(1 − z) ⊗ log(z)”

### Weight-one symbols multiply by shuffling

**Remember:** The symbol shuffles the lists of weight-one entries.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In the graded Hopf algebra of formal polylogarithms, the symbol of a weight-n element is its n-fold coproduct projected to weight one in every factor. The shuffle product sums all interleavings of two tensors that preserve the order within each.

**Problem.** The symbol of a product equals the shuffle product of the two symbols.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplicativity of the coproduct makes each weight-one position take weight one from one input and zero from the other (our own). The counit removes the scalar positions. Choosing the positions supplied by the first input gives every shuffle with its multiplicity.

**Paper or page:** [Hopf algebras of multiple polylogarithms, and holomorphic 1-forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08337). It says: “Δ₁,…,₁ is a morphism of graded Hopf algebras.”

### Fourier signs bound lattice packing

**Remember:** One sign controls the lattice and the other controls its dual.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H31 (Lattice packing and covering (number-theoretic aspects)), 11H60. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix r &gt; 0 and use the Fourier kernel exp(−2πix·ξ) on ℝⁿ. An admissible function is a real radial Schwartz function f with f(x) ≤ 0 whenever ‖x‖ ≥ r. Require f̂(ξ) ≥ 0 for every ξ and f(0) = f̂(0) &gt; 0.

**Problem.** If such a function exists, any lattice packing by balls of radius r/2 has density at most the volume of one such ball. For a unit-covolume lattice with shortest length r, the bound is sharp.

**How the definition helps.** The signs give ∑ᵥ f(v) ≤ f(0) on the packing lattice and ∑ᵤ f̂(u) ≥ f̂(0) on its dual (our own). Poisson summation equates the first sum to the second divided by the lattice covolume. The covolume is therefore at least one, with equality giving the claimed density.

**Paper or page:** [Algebraic proof of modular form inequalities for optimal sphere packings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14659v3). It says: “f(0) = f̂(0) &gt; 0”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Short vectors encode Littlewood’s conjecture

**Remember:** Diagonal scaling turns small products into short lattice vectors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H46 (Products of linear forms), 11J13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For real α and β, let Λ consist of all (qα − p, qβ − r, q) with p,r,q ∈ ℤ. Its forward orbit consists of diag(a,b,1/(ab))Λ for all a,b ≥ 1.

**Problem.** Let d(t) denote the distance to the nearest integer. The lower limit of q·d(qα)·d(qβ) over positive integers q is zero exactly when this orbit has noncompact closure.

**How the definition helps.** The lattice records both approximation errors and their common denominator, and each diagonal map preserves their product (our own). The dynamical correspondence for Littlewood’s conjecture equates lower limit zero with arbitrarily short nonzero vectors in the forward orbit. Mahler’s compactness theorem identifies this condition with noncompact orbit closure.

**Wikipedia:** [Littlewood conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlewood_conjecture). It says: “failure of Littlewood's conjecture corresponds to relative compactness of the orbit”

### Shortest vectors test extreme packings

**Remember:** Shortest vectors fix the form and balance its volume.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H55 (Quadratic forms (reduction theory, extreme forms, etc.)), 11H31. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a positive definite form with matrix Q, let S contain vvᵀ for every nonzero integer vector v minimizing vᵀQv. The form is perfect if S spans the real symmetric matrices of the same size. It is eutactic if Q⁻¹ is a linear combination of all members of S with strictly positive coefficients.

**Problem.** A lattice packing has locally maximal density among lattice packings exactly when its form is perfect and eutactic.

**How the definition helps.** Perfection and eutaxy replace comparisons with nearby packings by two linear tests on the shortest vectors (our own). Perfection rules out a nonzero change of the matrix that leaves all their squared lengths fixed (our own). Eutaxy expresses the inverse matrix using positive weights on those same vectors (our own). Voronoi’s theorem proves that together these tests characterize a local density maximum.

**Paper or page:** [The lattice packing problem in dimension 9 by Voronoi's algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20719v1). It says: “is extreme if and only if it is perfect and eutactic.”

### Critical lattices detect Dirichlet improvement

**Remember:** Better uniform approximation keeps the moving lattice away from the critical locus.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J13 (Simultaneous homogeneous approximation, linear forms), 11H06. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a plane norm ν and give ℝ³ the norm η(u,t) = max(ν(u),\|t\|). At time s ≥ 0, use the lattice of all (exp(s)(p − qx),exp(−2s)q) with p ∈ ℤ² and q ∈ ℤ. The critical locus consists of unit-covolume lattices maximizing the η-length of a shortest nonzero vector.

**Problem.** Call x uniformly improvable if some c below the sharp universal bound works for every sufficiently large T. This requires integers 1 ≤ q ≤ T and p ∈ ℤ² satisfying Tν(qx − p)² ≤ c. Uniform improvement holds exactly when the moving lattice eventually avoids a neighborhood of the critical locus.

**How the definition helps.** The scaled lattice turns two size bounds into one shortest-vector test (our own). Mahler’s compactness theorem makes the lattices with shortest lengths bounded below a compact set (our own). Avoiding a neighborhood of the maximizers then leaves a uniform gap (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Abundance of Dirichlet-improvable pairs with respect to arbitrary norms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.10298v2), [Abundance of Dirichlet-improvable pairs with respect to arbitrary norms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.10298v2). It says: “x ∈ DIν if and only if the forward aₛ-orbit of Λₓ eventually avoids an open neighborhood of ℒη”

**Remember:** The modulus cutoff becomes a horizontal height cutoff for geodesic tops.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a squarefree integer D &gt; 1 with D ≢ 1 modulo 4. For each positive m and each solution r² ≡ D modulo m, draw the semicircle with endpoints (r ± √D)/m. Take its highest point and read its horizontal coordinate modulo one.

**Problem.** Take the fractions r/m with 1 ≤ m ≤ X, one representative 0 ≤ r &lt; m per solution, counted with repetition. As X grows, the fraction of them in each fixed arc approaches the length of the arc.

**How the definition helps.** The semicircle represents r/m as a position and the cutoff m ≤ X as a minimum height √D/X (our own). Theorem 5.1 identifies the roots with lifts of finitely many closed geodesics on the modular surface, the quotient of the hyperbolic plane by SL₂(ℤ). Corollary 2.7 counts the tops above a given height with leading term proportional to arc length. Dividing by the total count cancels that constant (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Fine-scale distribution of roots of quadratic congruences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.02854v3), [Fine-scale distribution of roots of quadratic congruences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.02854v3). ### Independent coordinate functions prevent diagonal concentration

**Remember:** No nonzero character sees a constant polynomial phase.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Call real polynomials p₁, …, pₖ independent modulo constants if no nonzero real linear combination of them is constant.

**Problem.** Let p₁, …, pₖ be independent modulo constants and let aₙ be distinct integers. For almost every real x, the fraction of the vectors (aₙp₁(x), …, aₙpₖ(x)) modulo one in each box approaches the volume of the box.

**How the definition helps.** Independence excludes equal coordinates, which would confine the vectors to the diagonal (our own). Every nonzero integer combination gives a nonconstant polynomial P. The scalar metric theorem applies to aₙP(x) almost everywhere because P has local differentiable inverses away from finitely many critical points. Weyl’s criterion combines the conclusions for countably many integer combinations.

**Paper or page:** [Metric uniform distribution on analytic curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06909v1). It says: “The set {1, p₁, …, pₖ} is linearly independent over ℝ.”

### Macroscopic pair counts detect uniformity

**Remember:** Averaging all pair differences squares the magnitude of each Fourier coefficient.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For N points on the circle, give each of the N² ordered differences modulo one mass 1/N². Keep the test arcs fixed as N grows.

**Problem.** The fraction of ordered differences in every arc approaches its length exactly when the original sequence has the same property. Omitting pairs with equal indices gives the same equivalence.

**How the definition helps.** At every integer frequency, averaging the character over differences gives the squared magnitude of its average over points (our own). Thus both averages tend to zero together. Weyl’s criterion tests precisely this limit at every nonzero frequency. Equal-index pairs have mass 1/N, so omitting them preserves the limits.

### Period torsors bound transcendence degree

**Remember:** The group dimension caps the number of independent periods.

*True by definition.* MSC 11J81 (Transcendence (general theory)), 14C15, 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a Nori motive over ℚ, consider the comparisons between its cohomology from differential forms and its rational topological cohomology. Allow only comparisons that respect maps and tensor operations in the category generated by the motive. They form a torsor, a space on which the comparison symmetries act freely and transitively after extending scalars.

**Problem.** The number of algebraically independent entries of the actual comparison matrix is at most the dimension of the motivic Galois group of the motive.

**How the definition helps.** The torsor presents the period integrals as values of coordinate functions at a single complex point. In our own argument, their transcendence degree cannot exceed the dimension of the space containing that point. Tensor reconstruction identifies the comparison space as a torsor for the motivic Galois group, so the two dimensions agree.

**Definition.** Fix a pure motive M over ℚ̄ in Ancona and Fratila’s graded category with good reduction at a chosen prime above p. Its period space parametrizes embeddings of specialized algebraic cycle classes into the de Rham cohomology of the corresponding objects before reduction. Require these embeddings to respect all maps and tensor products in the category generated by M.

**Problem.** The transcendence degree of André’s p-adic periods over ℚ̄ is at most dim GdR − dim Gcrys. These groups describe tensor symmetries of de Rham cohomology before reduction and crystalline cohomology after reduction.

**How the definition helps.** The period space makes the numerical periods values of algebraic functions at the comparison point. In our own argument, no point can yield more algebraically independent coordinates than the dimension of its space. The homogeneous-space theorem computes that dimension by subtracting the dimension of the stabilizer Gcrys from that of the acting group GdR.

### Relative periods isolate moving relations

**Remember:** Fix the constant motives before testing relations among moving periods.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J81 (Transcendence (general theory)), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a finitely generated extension k of ℂ and a Zariski-dense real analytic arc on a model of k extending past both endpoints. Relative comparisons are tensor isomorphisms between de Rham and Betti realizations that agree with the usual comparison on every constant object. The relative formal period ring is the coordinate ring of these comparisons.

**Problem.** Evaluation identifies the relative formal period ring with the ring of analytic period germs. A germ records a function only near the chosen arc point.

**How the definition helps.** Fixing the constant comparisons lets injectivity express exactly which relations hold among the varying periods, in our own interpretation. A formal relation holds whenever its evaluation vanishes. Bakker and Tsimerman prove injectivity using their functional transcendence theorem.

### Counting only reduced fractions frees multiplicative Khintchine from monotonicity

**Remember:** Count each rational point once, and monotonicity is no longer needed.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J83 (Metric theory), 11J13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Approximate a vector α in ℝᵏ by fractions p₁/q, …, pₖ/q with one common denominator q. Require every numerator pᵢ to be coprime to q. Measure the error as the product of the k coordinate errors \|αᵢ − pᵢ/q\|.

**Problem.** Let ψ map positive integers to \[0,1/2\]. Almost every α admits infinitely many reduced approximations of product error at most ψ(q)/qᵏ exactly when ∑<sub>q≥1</sub> ψ(q)(φ(q)/q)ᵏ(log(q/(φ(q)ψ(q))))ᵏ⁻¹ diverges. Here φ is Euler’s totient function, and denominators with ψ(q) = 0 contribute zero.

**How the definition helps.** Coprimality counts distinct rational coordinates and leaves φ(q) residue classes per coordinate (our own). This gives the totient weight in the multiplicative Duffin–Schaeffer theorem. Its overlap estimates establish divergence without assuming monotonicity.

**Paper or page:** [The Duffin-Schaeffer Conjecture for multiplicative Diophantine approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11257v1). It says: “The recent result of Koukoulopoulos and Maynard provides an elegant way of removing monotonicity when only counting reduced fractions.”

### Reduced fractions remove monotonicity from Khintchine's theorem

**Remember:** Count each fraction once, in lowest terms, and monotonicity is not needed.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J83 (Metric theory), 11J04. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a positive function f on the positive integers. A reduced approximation to α is p/q with q positive, gcd(p,q) = 1 and \|α−p/q\| &lt; f(q)/q. Its test series is ∑<sub>q≥1</sub> φ(q)f(q)/q, where φ(q) counts residues coprime to q.

**Problem.** For every f, almost every real α has infinitely many coprime solutions exactly when the totient series diverges. Khintchine’s test needs f to be monotone, since Duffin and Schaeffer found a non-monotone f whose series diverges while almost no α is approximable.

**How the definition helps.** Coprimality leaves φ(q) distinct reduced centers per unit interval at denominator q (our own). Their radii f(q)/q give the totient series. The Duffin–Schaeffer theorem of Koukoulopoulos and Maynard proves the divergence implication for arbitrary f.

**Wikipedia:** [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duffin–Schaeffer<sub>theorem</sub>](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/https%3A//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duffin%E2%80%93Schaeffer_theorem). It says: “has infinitely many solutions in coprime integers p,q with q &gt; 0 if and only if”

**Paper or page:** [General Duffin--Schaeffer-type counterexamples in diophantine approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16565), [Independence inheritance and Diophantine approximation for systems of linear forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03929). It says: “Duffin and Schaeffer provided a famous counterexample to show that Khintchine's theorem fails without monotonicity assumption.”

**Sources:**

- [Sam Chow, Manuel Hauke, Andrew Pollington, Felipe A. Ramírez, General Duffin--Schaeffer-type counterexamples in diophantine approximation, arXiv:2504.16565 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16565)
