### Unshifted pair correlations force uniformity

**Remember:** At zero shift the density pairs with itself.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K06 (General theory of distribution modulo \\(1\\)), 11K38. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix circle points x₁,x₂,… and a shift γ. Count ordered pairs of distinct indices i,j ≤ N with xᵢ−xⱼ within circular distance s/N of γ. Correlation is Poissonian at γ if this count divided by N tends to 2s for every s &gt; 0.

**Problem.** Poissonian pair correlation at zero forces uniform distribution. Each interval receives a limiting fraction of points equal to its length. For every nonzero shift modulo 1, some sequence has Poissonian pair correlation at that shift and fails uniform distribution.

**How the definition helps.** The shift parameter lets one statistic express both assertions (our own). The unshifted pair correlation theorem gives uniform distribution at zero. The cited shifted counterexample theorem supplies a nonuniform sequence for each nonzero shift.

**Paper or page:** [On Inhomogeneous Poissonian Pair Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16542v1), [On Inhomogeneous Poissonian Pair Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16542v1). It says: “that has γ-PPC but is not uniformly distributed.”

**Sources:**

- [On Inhomogeneous Poissonian Pair Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16542v1)

### Anchored variation gives exact quadrature error

**Remember:** A single box tests the sharpness of the integration bound.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On \[0,1)ᵈ, represent f as a constant plus a mixture of box indicators against a finite signed measure ν on (0,1\]ᵈ. The indicator at t tests whether x lies below t in every coordinate. Define variation as the infimum of the total unsigned mass of ν over all such representations.

**Problem.** The supremum of the absolute integration error over functions of variation at most one equals the star discrepancy. Integration error means sample average minus uniform integral. Star discrepancy is the supremum of the absolute frequency error over these boxes.

**How the definition helps.** The representation expresses integration error as an integral of box errors against ν (our own). Each box error is bounded in magnitude by star discrepancy, so taking the infimum gives the upper bound. A unit mass at each individual box recovers its error, giving the reverse bound upon taking the supremum.

**Wikipedia:** [Low-discrepancy sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-discrepancy_sequence). It says: “The Koksma–Hlawka inequality is sharp in the following sense”

**Sources:**

- [C. Aistleitner and J. Dick, Functions of bounded variation, signed measures, and a general Koksma–Hlawka inequality (2015)](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa167-2-4)

### Dual digital nets retain exactly surviving frequencies

**Remember:** A Walsh frequency survives precisely when its induced input frequency is zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A binary digital net takes every u ∈ {0,1}ᵐ once and uses Cⱼu modulo two as coordinate j’s digits, followed by zeros. A Walsh mask k selects binary digits, giving value (−1) raised to their sum. The dual net consists of masks with ∑ⱼ Cⱼᵀkⱼ = 0 modulo two, using only digit positions present in each matrix.

**Problem.** The sample average of a Walsh function equals one for dual masks and zero otherwise. For an absolutely convergent series of Walsh functions, sample average minus uniform integral equals the sum of coefficients at nonzero dual masks.

**How the definition helps.** A dual mask gives even parity on every input (our own). Otherwise, flipping an input bit with nonzero coefficient pairs opposite signs. Absolute convergence permits termwise averaging, and only the constant Walsh function has nonzero uniform integral.

**Paper or page:** [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1). It says: “and where 𝒟 is the so-called dual net”

**Sources:**

- [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1)

### Extreme discrepancy removes lower-dimensional Haar terms

**Remember:** Taking differences of both box ends discards terms that ignore a coordinate.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F(t) be the sample fraction in \[0,t) minus its volume, where membership requires every coordinate to be below its threshold. Start with F and, one coordinate at a time, subtract the current function’s average in that coordinate. Call the result G.

**Problem.** For a box \[a,b), take its error as the sample fraction minus the volume. The integral of the squared error over all endpoint pairs with a ≤ b in every coordinate equals ∫\|G(t)\|² dt over the unit cube.

**How the definition helps.** Endpoint differences in all coordinates recover the box error and cancel every term removed by centering (our own). For mean-zero g, integrating \|g(b)−g(a)\|² over a ≤ b gives ∫\|g\|² by symmetry and expansion. Apply this identity in each coordinate to G, whose coordinate averages vanish.

**Paper or page:** [Point sets with optimal order of extreme and periodic discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.05781v1). It says: “and D its anchored discrepancy function with Haar coefficients”

**Sources:**

- [Point sets with optimal order of extreme and periodic discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.05781v1)

### Greedy squared error gives uniform distribution

**Remember:** Uniform averaging cancels the cross term before you choose the next point.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For each box \[0,t) in the unit cube, subtract N times its volume from its count among the first N points. Here \[0,t) contains points below t in every coordinate. Choose the next point to minimize the integral over t of the resulting squared error.

**Problem.** From any fixed nonempty finite starting list, the root mean square count error divided by N is O(N⁻¹⁄²). The fraction of points in each box approaches its volume.

**How the definition helps.** Squaring the error makes the cross term disappear when we average over a uniformly chosen next point (our own). At each box the random count increment minus its expected value has mean zero and absolute value at most one (our own). The minimum therefore increases the integrated squared error by at most one per step (our own). The cited theorem gives the resulting uniform distribution.

**Paper or page:** [Uniformly distributed sequences generated by a greedy minimization of the L² discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06298v4). It says: “is uniformly distributed modulo 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Uniformly distributed sequences generated by a greedy minimization of the L² discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06298v4)

### Index coordinates transfer discrepancy bounds

**Remember:** A box in the new coordinate selects a block of the old sequence.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Attach j/N to the jth point of a list indexed from zero. For any half-open box, subtract the expected count under uniform sampling from its actual count. Extreme L² discrepancy is the square root of the integral of this squared error over coordinatewise ordered endpoint pairs.

**Problem.** For every infinite sequence in the d-dimensional unit cube, infinitely many prefixes have extreme L² discrepancy at least c(d)(log N)ᵈ⁄². Here N is the prefix length and c(d) is positive.

**How the definition helps.** An interval in the added coordinate selects the difference of two prefixes (our own). Rounding its endpoints to indices changes the expected count by at most two (our own). The triangle inequality bounds the lifted discrepancy by twice the largest prefix discrepancy plus two (our own). The finite point theorem in dimension d+1 forces this maximum to grow at least as fast as (log N)ᵈ⁄² (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Exact order of extreme Lᵖ discrepancy of infinite sequences in arbitrary dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06461v1), [Point sets with optimal order of extreme and periodic discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.05781v1). It says: “for infinitely many N ∈ ℕ.”

**Sources:**

- [Exact order of extreme Lᵖ discrepancy of infinite sequences in arbitrary dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06461v1)

### Interlaced digits raise digital net order

**Remember:** Interlacing pushes the largest input digits up by nearly a factor α.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a binary digital net, a dual mask selects digit positions whose sum is even for every input. Its order-α weight sums the largest α selected positions per coordinate, using all positions when fewer occur. Interlacing groups α coordinates by moving position j in coordinate r to position α(j−1)+r, for 1 ≤ r ≤ α.

**Problem.** Suppose every nonzero dual mask of the original αd-dimensional net has order one weight greater than m−t′. Every nonzero dual mask of the interlaced d-dimensional net then has order α weight greater than αm−αt′−dα(α−1)/2.

**How the definition helps.** Splitting an output dual mask by these positions gives an input dual mask with the same parity test (our own). Each input coordinate’s leading position j moves to αj−(α−r). Each group’s largest α positions sum to at least the sum of those moved leaders. The loss per group is at most α(α−1)/2.

**Paper or page:** [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1). It says: “is an order 1 digital (t′, αd)-sequence over ℤ₂”

**Sources:**

- [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1)

### Low discrepancy forces mesoscopic counts

**Remember:** At a wider scale, each point sees the expected number of neighbors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix 0 &lt; β &lt; 1 and s &gt; 0. Among the first N points of a circle sequence, count ordered pairs of distinct indices at circular distance at most s/Nᵝ. Divide by N raised to 2 − β.

**Problem.** Suppose the largest absolute difference between sample fraction and length over all arcs is o(N⁻ᵝ). Then the normalized count tends to 2s for every fixed s &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** The chosen radius makes each test arc longer than the discrepancy error, uniformly over its center (our own). Each center therefore sees 2sN¹⁻ᵝ + o(N¹⁻ᵝ) points including itself (our own). Summing over centers counts ordered pairs, and removing the N self-pairs does not affect the limit (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Weak Poissonian box correlations of higher order](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.11105v2). It says: “Then the sequence has (k, β)-Poissonian box correlations”

**Sources:**

- [Weak Poissonian box correlations of higher order](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.11105v2)

### Normalized height lets roots reflect

**Remember:** Reflect through the unit circle without changing angles or normalized height.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a monic polynomial P with P(0) ≠ 0, use the height h(P) = ∫₀¹ log⁺(\|P(exp(2πit))\|/√\|P(0)\|) dt. Here log⁺ means the positive part of the logarithm.

**Problem.** Replace each root r outside the unit disk by 1/r̄ and take the monic polynomial with the resulting roots. This preserves height and every angular sector count. Thus the degree-N angular count bound 4√(Nh(P)/π) reduces to the case of roots in the closed unit disk.

**How the definition helps.** For \|z\| = 1, reflection preserves \|z−r\|/√\|r\| and the argument of r (our own). Multiplying these factors preserves the normalized boundary modulus and hence its height. Reflection also preserves every angular count with multiplicity, so the estimate inside the disk applies.

**Paper or page:** [Hilbert transforms and the equidistribution of zeros of polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00105v4). It says: “If P is a monic polynomial of degree N with P(0) ≠ 0, then 𝒟(P) ≤ (4/√π)√(N h(P)).”

**Sources:**

- [E. Carneiro et al., Hilbert transforms and the equidistribution of zeros of polynomials (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfa.2021.109199)
- [K. Soundararajan, Equidistribution of Zeros of Polynomials (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1080/00029890.2019.1546078)

### Pure eigenvalues bound hyper-Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** The sum is a signed trace of r eigenvalues of the same size.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a prime p, an integer r ≥ 3 and a ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ. The hyper-Kloosterman sum Kᵣ(a) sums exp(2πi(x₁+⋯+xᵣ)/p) over all tuples in (𝔽ₚˣ)ʳ with product a. A Frobenius action is pure of weight w if every eigenvalue has complex absolute value p raised to w/2.

**Problem.** The absolute value of Kᵣ(a) is at most r times p to the power (r−1)/2.

**How the definition helps.** The trace formula expresses the sum through eigenvalues, so their number and sizes give a bound. Deligne’s theorem supplies the difficult facts about this vector space, called cohomology with compact support. Only degree r−1 contributes, its dimension is r, and every eigenvalue has absolute value p to the power (r−1)/2. In our own final step, the signed trace satisfies the triangle inequality.

**Paper or page:** [The sixth moment of Dirichlet L-functions at the central point](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01457v1). It says: “where the hyper-Kloosterman sum”

**Sources:**

- [Pierre Deligne, Applications de la formule des traces aux sommes trigonométriques, SGA 4½, section 7 (1977)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0091523)

### Rank and purity bound Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** Rank counts the eigenvalues and purity bounds their sizes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations), 11T23, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite field 𝔽𝓆 and nontrivial additive character ψ, the rank-r Kloosterman sum at a ∈ 𝔽𝓆ˣ sums ψ(x₁+⋯+xᵣ) over tuples with product a. Purity of weight w means every Frobenius eigenvalue at a rational point has complex modulus q raised to w/2.

**Problem.** For r ≥ 2 the sum has modulus at most r times q raised to (r − 1)/2.

**How the definition helps.** The sheaf expresses every sum as a signed trace, so its rank and the sizes of its eigenvalues give one uniform bound. Our own deduction uses Deligne’s theorem that the sheaf has rank r and every Frobenius eigenvalue has modulus q raised to (r − 1)/2. The triangle inequality finishes the estimate.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “Geometrically the sum is taken along a 'hyperbola' XY = ab”

**Sources:**

- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 11](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/ik-ant-exp-sums.pdf)

### Symmetric powers bound Kloosterman angles

**Remember:** Chebyshev polynomials remove the invariant part of ordinary moments.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations), 11T23, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For odd prime p, nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽ₚ and a ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ, put K(a) = ∑ₓ ψ(x+a/x) over x ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ. Define θ(a) ∈ \[0,π\] by 2cos θ(a) = −K(a)/√p. Define Uₘ(cos θ) = sin((m+1)θ)/sin θ by continuity at both endpoints.

**Problem.** For each fixed integer m ≥ 1, the sum of Uₘ(cos θ(a)) over a ≠ 0 has modulus O(√p). The constant depends only on m.

**How the definition helps.** The polynomial Uₘ turns each angle into the trace on degree-m symmetric tensors, which have no invariant vector for the determinant-one group SL(2). Our own calculation adds the eigenvalues exp(i(m − 2j)θ) for 0 ≤ j ≤ m. Katz identifies the geometric symmetry group of the normalized Kloosterman system as SL(2). The trace formula and Deligne’s bound then give the stated cancellation.

**Wikipedia:** [Chebyshev polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_polynomials). It says: “Similarly, the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind Uₙ are defined by”

### Zeta roots bound Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** The first coefficient is the negative sum of the two reciprocal roots.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a prime p and a,b ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ. For every r ≥ 1, let S(r) sum exp(2πiTr(ax+b/x)/p) over x ∈ 𝔽ₚʳˣ, using the trace to 𝔽ₚ. The associated L-function is the formal series L(t) = exp(∑<sub>r≥1</sub> S(r)tʳ/r).

**Problem.** There are complex numbers α and β of absolute value √p such that L(t) = (1−αt)(1−βt). Consequently \|S(1)\| ≤ 2√p.

**How the definition helps.** The generating series puts the original sum in its linear coefficient. Weil’s work on the curve yᵖ−y = ax+b/x gives the factorization and the sizes of α and β. In our own coefficient comparison, S(1) = −α−β. The triangle inequality gives the estimate.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “A fundamental technique of Weil reduces the estimate \|K(a,b;p)\| ≤ 2√p, when ab ≠ 0 to his results on local zeta-functions.”

**Sources:**

- [André Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Cube-free moduli ensure square-root bounds

**Remember:** A prime cube can support a sum larger than the square-root bound.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a fixed k ≥ 3, call q cube-free if no prime cube divides it. Let f be an integer polynomial of degree at most k whose nonconstant coefficients have no common factor with q.

**Problem.** For cube-free q, the complete sum of exp(2πif(x)/q) over x modulo q is O(q to the power ½+ε) for every ε &gt; 0. The constant depends on k and ε. At q = p³ with prime p &gt; 3, the phase x³ instead gives the sum p².

**How the definition helps.** Cube-freeness leaves only primes and prime squares in the standard complete-sum estimate (our own). Modulo p³, group the cubic phase by residue classes modulo p². Each class of units cancels by additive character orthogonality, while each of the p² multiples of p contributes one.

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ maximal estimates for Weyl sums with k ≥ 3 on 𝕋](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15527v1). It says: “q₂ ≥ 1 is cube free,”

**Sources:**

### One critical moment controls all

**Remember:** Below the critical moment use Hölder, and above it use the maximum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For positive integers k,N and α ∈ \[0,1\]ᵏ, put F(α) = ∑<sub>n=1</sub>ᴺ exp(2πi∑<sub>j=1</sub>ᵏ αⱼnʲ). Its moment M(p) is the integral of \|F(α)\|ᵖ over the unit cube. The critical order is 2K with K = k(k+1)/2.

**Problem.** Suppose M(2K) ≤ Cε Nᴷ⁺ᵋ for every ε &gt; 0. Then M(2s) ≤ C Nᵐ⁺ᵋ for every fixed s &gt; 0 and ε &gt; 0, where m = max(s,2s−K). Constants may depend on k, ε and the chosen order.

**How the definition helps.** At the critical order the two predicted powers of N coincide, so one estimate covers both ranges. In our own reduction, Hölder’s inequality on a cube of volume one bounds M(2s) by M(2K) to the power s/K below that order. Above it, bound the extra factors using \|F\| ≤ N. The deep mean-value theorem supplies the critical estimate.

**Paper or page:** [Decoupling estimates in Fourier analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00652v1). It says: “N<sup>1/2</sup> + N<sup>{1</sup> - \\frac{k(k+1)}{2p}}”

**Sources:**

- [Jean Bourgain, Ciprian Demeter and Larry Guth, Proof of the main conjecture in Vinogradov’s Mean Value Theorem for degrees higher than three (2016)](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2016.184.2.7)

### Reduced phases exclude constant counterexamples

**Remember:** Over the prime field, remove powers of p before using the degree.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over the field with p elements, replace each monomial degree that is positive and divisible by p by that degree divided by p. Repeat until no such degree remains and combine equal powers. Call the resulting polynomial reduced and exclude constant reduced polynomials.

**Problem.** If the reduced phase has degree d ≥ 1, the complete sum of exp(2πif(x)/p) has absolute value at most (d−1)√p. A nonconstant original phase need not qualify, since xᵖ−x gives sum p.

**How the definition helps.** Over 𝔽ₚ, xᵖ = x preserves each monomial’s values under reduction (our own). Thus xᵖ−x reduces to zero and the nonconstant-degree requirement excludes it. Every surviving leading degree is coprime to p, so Weil’s estimate applies.

**Wikipedia:** [Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_little_theorem). It says: “aᵖ ≡ a (mod p).”

**Sources:**

- [André Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Exceptional weights isolate prime obstructions

**Remember:** Separate ordinary character weights before seeking power savings over primes.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L20 (Sums over primes), 11T23. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a pointwise pure weight-zero middle-extension sheaf on the affine line over 𝔽ₚ whose geometric representation is a sum of copies of one irreducible representation. Call it exceptional when that irreducible sheaf is geometrically a product of a Kummer character sheaf and a linear Artin–Schreier character sheaf. Either character may be trivial.

**Problem.** Let K be the Frobenius trace function of a nonexceptional system and V a fixed smooth function supported in \[1/2, 2\]. For 0 &lt; η &lt; 1/24, summing K(l)V(l/p) over primes l gives a bound of order p raised to (1 − η). The constant depends on η, V and the conductor, which measures the rank and ramification of the system.

**How the definition helps.** The exception removes character products for which the uniform estimates over primes can fail. Our own example is the constant function one. For nonnegative nonzero V, the prime number theorem gives a sum of order p/log p. Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel prove the saving for the remaining systems using estimates for sums in two variables.

**Wikipedia:** [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem). It says: “The first such distribution found is π(N) \~ N/log(N)”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel, Algebraic trace functions over the primes](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/weights-over-primes.pdf)

### Root power sums give multiplicative weights

**Remember:** Root power sums add when monic polynomials multiply.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L20 (Sums over primes), 11T23. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix k ≥ 1 and a nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽𝓆. For every monic f over 𝔽𝓆, define χ(f) = ψ(∑ᵣ rᵏ), summing over all roots in an algebraic closure with multiplicity. Frobenius permutes the roots, so the sum belongs to 𝔽𝓆.

**Problem.** Set Λ(Pʲ) = deg P for monic irreducible P and j ≥ 1, and set Λ(f) = 0 otherwise. For n ≥ 1, the sum of Λ(f)χ(f) over degree-n monic polynomials has modulus at most √(qⁿ) gcd(k,qⁿ − 1).

**How the definition helps.** Taking all roots makes χ multiplicative and turns the prime-power sum into one sum over elements of the degree-n field extension. Our own explanation groups extension elements by their minimal polynomial P. Each P contributes deg P elements, and their field traces repeat each root exactly as often as the corresponding power of P requires. Multiplicative character orthogonality counts kth powers, and the Gauss sum bound gives the estimate.

**Paper or page:** [Equidistribution of high traces of random matrices over finite fields and cancellation in character sums of high conductor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01344). It says: “\|∑ (f ∈ ℳₙ,𝓆) Λ(f)χₖ,ψ(f)\| ≤ qⁿᐟ² gcd(k, qⁿ − 1).”

**Sources:**

- [Equidistribution of high traces of random matrices over finite fields and cancellation in character sums of high conductor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01344)

### Complex shifts generate derivative moments

**Remember:** Differentiate independent shifts to get both derivative factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let ζ denote the Riemann zeta function, A a Dirichlet polynomial and w a nonnegative integrable weight of compact real support. Set B(t) = \|A(½+it)\|²w(t) and fix 0 &lt; r &lt; ¼. Define J(z₁,z₂) as the real-line integral of ζ(½+it+z₁)ζ(½−it+z₂)B(t).

**Problem.** The integral of \|ζ′(½+it)\|²B(t) over the real line equals the mixed derivative of J at (0,0), taken once in each shift. So it is at most r⁻² times the maximum of \|J\| on \|z₁\| = \|z₂\| = r.

**How the definition helps.** Independent shifts let the mixed derivative differentiate each zeta factor once (our own). Compact support and separation from the pole justify differentiation under the integral. At zero the derivatives are conjugates, and Cauchy’s integral formula on both circles gives the bound.

**Paper or page:** [Upper bounds for fractional joint moments of the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.00165). It says: “F(z<sub>1</sub>,z<sub>2</sub>) = \\sum <sub>h,k \\leq T<sup>\\theta</sup> </sub> \\frac {a<sub>h</sub> \\overline {a<sub>k</sub>}}{\[h,k\]} \\frac {(h,k)<sup>z<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>2</sub></sup>}{h<sup>z<sub>1</sub></sup> k<sup>z<sub>2</sub></sup>},”

**Sources:**

- [Michael J. Curran, Upper bounds for fractional joint moments of the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.00165)

### Factoring poles regularizes reciprocal moments

**Remember:** Remove the prime term before multiplying the local factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For k &gt; 0, define μₖ(n) by ζ(s)⁻ᵏ = ∑<sub>n≥1</sub> μₖ(n)n⁻ˢ on Re s &gt; 1, using the branch positive for real s &gt; 1. For real s &gt; 1, the normalized square sum is ζ(s) raised to −k² times ∑<sub>n≥1</sub> μₖ(n)²n⁻ˢ.

**Problem.** The resulting quotient tends to a positive finite limit as s decreases to 1. The original square sum is asymptotic to that limit times (s−1) to power −k².

**How the definition helps.** Dividing out the zeta power cancels the first-order term in every prime factor. In our own proof, the power series for (1−z) raised to k gives μₖ(p) = −k at each prime p. So the normalized factor differs from one by O(p⁻²), uniformly for real s ≥ 1, and every limiting factor is positive. The simple pole of ζ then gives the claimed growth.

**Paper or page:** [Negative moments of the Riemann zeta-function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.07226). It says: “where μₖ(n) denotes the nth Dirichlet coefficient of ζ(s)⁻ᵏ.”

**Sources:**

- [Hung M. Bui, Alexandra Florea, Negative moments of the Riemann zeta-function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.07226)

### Inverse log shifts cap kernels

**Remember:** Keep the height cutoff when two shifts nearly coincide.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write ζ for the Riemann zeta function. For T ≥ 3 and real d set K(T,d) = \|ζ(1+1/log T+id)\|.

**Problem.** Fix θ &gt; −1 and 0 ≤ β ≤ 1, and take \|h₁\|, \|h₂\| ≤ (log T) raised to θ. Set Y(t) = \|ζ(½+i(t+h₁))ζ(½+i(t+h₂))\|. Its mean after raising to 2β on \[T,2T\] lies between constant multiples of (K(T,h₁−h₂) log T) raised to 2β².

**How the definition helps.** The displacement 1/log T gives one finite comparison even when the shifts coincide. Our own check uses the simple pole of ζ at 1. At equal shifts, the displaced factor grows like log T, while the undisplaced factor has a pole. The cited theorem proves both bounds for sufficiently large T, uniformly over the allowed shifts.

**Paper or page:** [Freezing transition and moments of moments of the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.10634). It says: “\\frac {1}{T}\\int \_T<sup>2T</sup> \|\\zeta (\\tfrac {1}{2} + i t + ih<sub>1</sub>)\\zeta (\\tfrac {1}{2} + i t + ih<sub>2</sub>)\|<sup>2\\b </sup> \~dt \\ll (\\log T)<sup>2\\b ^2</sup> \|\\zeta (1 + i (h<sub>1</sub> - h<sub>2</sub>) + 1/\\log T)\|<sup>2\\b ^2</sup>.”

**Sources:**

- [Michael J. Curran, Freezing transition and moments of moments of the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.10634)

### Matching parity folds central moments

**Remember:** Match the weight to the character’s gamma factor.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a primitive nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ modulo q, set h = ¼ for even χ and h = ¾ for odd χ. For x &gt; 0 define W(x) by integrating Γ(h+u/2)² exp(−u log x)/(uΓ(h)²) upwards along Re u = 2 and dividing by 2πi.

**Problem.** Let L(s,χ) denote the continuation of ∑ χ(n) exp(−s log n) from Re s &gt; 1. Put C(a,b) = χ(a) times the conjugate of χ(b). Then \|L(½,χ)\|² equals twice the sum of C(a,b)W(πab/q)/√(ab) over positive integers a,b.

**How the definition helps.** The matching gamma factors make the completed product invariant under u ↦ −u by the functional equation (our own). Shifting the contour past zero picks up the residue \|L(½,χ)\|². Reflection identifies the two contributions, and expanding the Dirichlet series gives the stated double sum.

**Paper or page:** [Bounds for moments of Dirichlet L-functions to a fixed modulus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00149). It says: “\|L(\\tfrac {1}{2}, \\chi )\|<sup>2</sup> = 2 \\sum <sup>\\infty </sup><sub>a, b=1</sub> \\frac{\\chi (a) \\overline{\\chi }(b)}{\\sqrt{ab}} \\mathcal{W}\_{\\mathfrak {a}} \\left(\\frac{\\pi ab}{q}\\right),”

**Sources:**

- [Peng Gao, Bounds for moments of Dirichlet L-functions to a fixed modulus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00149)

### Mellin weights turn logarithms into poles

**Remember:** A logarithmic power becomes a higher pole.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)), 44A15. arXiv math.NT, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write ζ for the Riemann zeta function. For Re s &gt; 1 define Z(s) by integrating \|ζ(½+it)\|⁴ exp(−s log t) over 1 ≤ t &lt; ∞.

**Problem.** The function Z extends meromorphically to Re s &gt; 7/8, meaning it is holomorphic there except for poles. Its only pole there has order five at s = 1. The coefficient of (s−1)⁻⁵ is 12/π².

**How the definition helps.** The Mellin integral sends (log t)ʲ to j!/(s−1)ʲ⁺¹ with measure t⁻ˢdt on \[1,∞) (our own). Heath-Brown’s integrated fourth moment is T times a quartic in log T with leading coefficient 1/(2π²) and error O(T⁷⁄⁸⁺ᵋ). Integration by parts gives leading coefficient 4!/(2π²), while the error integral is holomorphic for Re s &gt; 7/8.

**nLab:** [Mellin transform](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Mellin+transform). It says: “its Mellin transform is the function given by the integral expression”

**Sources:**

- [D. R. Heath-Brown, The Fourth Power Moment of the Riemann Zeta Function, Proc. London Math. Soc. 38 (1979), 385–422](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s3-38.3.385)

### One prime blocks exceptional conductors

**Remember:** Remove one prime to remove every multiple of the bad conductor.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)), 11N13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix Q ≥ 100 and a sufficiently small absolute c &gt; 0. Call a Dirichlet character exceptional if its conductor is at most Q and its L-function has a real zero above 1 − c/log Q. Set B = 1 if no exceptional character exists, and otherwise let B be the largest prime factor of its conductor.

**Problem.** Take any q ≤ Q coprime to B. Every zero σ+it of every Dirichlet L-function modulo q satisfies 1−σ ≥ c′/log(Q(1+\|t\|)) for an absolute c′ &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** Landau–Page and the standard zero-free region leave at most one exceptional primitive character (our own). Every modulus inducing it is divisible by its conductor and therefore by B. Passing to an imprimitive character adds zeros only on Re s = 0.

**Paper or page:** [Recent results on large gaps between primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07176v2). It says: “whenever L(σ + it, χ) = 0 and χ is a character of modulus at most Q”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Vandermonde contours handle colliding shifts

**Remember:** Keep the shifts inside the contour rather than in separate denominators.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M06 (\\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Put k shifts inside a positively oriented circle Γ, and set P(w) = ∏ₘ(w−αₘ) and Δ(z) = ∏<sub>r&lt;s</sub>(zₛ−zᵣ). For 1 ≤ j ≤ k, take G holomorphic near the j-fold product of the closed disk. Integrate G(z)Δ(z)²/∏ᵣP(zᵣ) along Γ in each variable and divide by (2πi)ʲ.

**Problem.** For distinct shifts, the Vandermonde contour integral equals the sum of G(u)Δ(u)²/∏ᵣP′(uᵣ) over ordered j-tuples u of different shifts. So this sum extends holomorphically to shifts that meet inside Γ.

**How the definition helps.** Interior collisions leave the integrand holomorphic in the shifts because the contour denominators stay nonzero. For distinct shifts, residues select tuples of roots, and Δ² kills repeated selections. With two shifts, j = 1 and G = 1, the two singular residues cancel (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Averages of quadratic twists of long Dirichlet polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01783). It says: “\\frac{1}{(2\\pi i)<sup>j}</sup> \\int \_\\Gamma \\cdots \\int \_\\Gamma \\frac{G(z) \\Delta (z)<sup>2}{\\Delta</sup> (z;A)}\\,  d<sup>j</sup> z = \\sum \_{u<sub>1</sub>,...,u<sub>j</sub> \\in A \\atop \\textrm{distinct}} \\frac{G(u<sub>1</sub>,...,u<sub>j</sub>)}{\\Delta (u; A-u)},”

**Sources:**

- [Brian Conrey, Brad Rodgers, Averages of quadratic twists of long Dirichlet polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01783)

### Exponential weights quantify zero repulsion

**Remember:** A zero near one leaves less weight for the other zeros.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix Q ≥ 10 and collect zeros β+iγ of all primitive Dirichlet L-functions of conductor at most Q. Keep β ≥ ½ and \|γ\| ≤ Q, counting multiplicities. Give each retained zero the weight exp(−323905(1−β)log Q).

**Problem.** For some absolute λ₁ &gt; 0, at most one such zero satisfies (1−β)log Q &lt; λ₁. If present, this zero β₁ is real. The other weights then sum to at most C(1−β₁)log Q for an absolute C.

**How the definition helps.** The weights express repulsion from one as a bound on all remaining zeros together. Proposition 6.5 bounds their total weight by a constant times one minus the exceptional zero’s weight. Our own final step uses 1−exp(−u) ≤ u for u ≥ 0.

**Paper or page:** [An explicit version of Bombieri's log-free density estimate and Sárközy's theorem for shifted primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.11123). It says: “If there is an exceptional zero ρ∗ at scale Q, then”

### Random Euler products factor moments

**Remember:** Independent local signs turn each moment into a product over primes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For each prime p choose X(p) independently. Give each sign ±1 probability p/(2(p+1)), and give zero probability 1/(p+1). Define Z as the limit of the products of 1/(1−X(p)/p) over primes in increasing order.

**Problem.** Choose either sign and average over quadratic field discriminants D of that sign with \|D\| ≤ Y. For each positive integer t, the average of L(1,χᴰ)ᵗ tends to the expectation of Zᵗ as Y grows. Here χᴰ is the quadratic character attached to D.

**How the definition helps.** Independent prime factors turn each random moment into a product of local averages. Our own expansion cancels the odd powers of each sign and gives the prime factors in Corollary 6.13. Bounded moments of order 2t justify passing expectations to the limit. The corollary supplies the arithmetic average, and counting discriminants supplies its normalization.

**Paper or page:** [Counting quadratic points on Fano varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17940). It says: “the set of positive, and ℱ₋ the set of negative fundamental discriminants.”

**Sources:**

- [Francesca Balestrieri, Kevin Destagnol, Julian Lyczak, Jennifer Park, Nick Rome, Counting quadratic points on Fano varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17940)

### Short Euler products approximate L-values

**Remember:** For most conductors, only small primes are needed at one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); results on \\(L(1, \\chi)\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a quadratic Dirichlet character χ, the short Euler product P(y,χ) is the product of 1/(1−χ(p)/p) over primes p ≤ y. For Q ≥ 3 and fixed α &gt; 2, take y = exp(8α² log log Q).

**Problem.** Consider the nonprincipal quadratic characters χ of conductor at most Q, each taken modulo its conductor. For all of them except those of at most exp((2/α) log Q) conductors, \|L(1,χ)/P(y,χ)−1\| ≤ C(α) exp(−α log log Q).

**How the definition helps.** The cutoff expresses a uniform approximation using only the character values at small primes. Proposition 2.1 bounds both the error and the number of exceptional conductors. In our own interpretation, estimates counting zeros near one control which conductors can obstruct this approximation.

**Paper or page:** [Amicable pairs and aliquot cycles on average](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5810). It says: “not in ℰα(Q), then”

**Sources:**

### Fourier cutoffs shorten prime sums

**Remember:** Compact frequency support cuts the prime sum off exactly.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses), 11N05. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix A &gt; 0 and choose a real even smooth function φ that decreases rapidly with all its derivatives. Require its Fourier transform φ̂(u) = ∫ over real v of φ(v) exp(−2πiuv) dv to vanish for \|u\| &gt; A.

**Problem.** Assume the Riemann hypothesis and write the nontrivial zeros as ½ + iγ, repeated with multiplicity. For T ≤ t ≤ 2T, the sum of φ((γ − t) log T/(2π)) equals φ̂(0) − 2D(t)/log T + O(1/log T). Here D(t) sums (log p)φ̂(log n/log T) cos(t log n)/√n over prime powers n = pᵏ ≤ exp(A log T).

**How the definition helps.** The Fourier transform vanishes beyond A, so prime powers with log n &gt; A log T contribute exactly zero (our own). A Gaussian would leave terms at arbitrarily large prime powers (our own). The explicit formula relating zeros to prime powers supplies the identity and its error term.

**Paper or page:** [Selberg's Central Limit Theorem weighted by Linear Statistics of Zeta Zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04150). It says: “Nφ(t) = φ̂(0) + Sφ(t) + O(1/log T)”

**Sources:**

- [Selberg's Central Limit Theorem weighted by Linear Statistics of Zeta Zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04150)

### Gaussian weights permit interpolation

**Remember:** Analytic weights let one interpolate between lines.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix α,T &gt; 0 and X &gt; 1, and put M(s) = ∑<sub>n≤X</sub> μ(n)n⁻ˢ using the Möbius function. Define H(s) = ((s−1)/s)exp(α(s/T)²)ζ(s)M(s), filling in its removable singularity at one.

**Problem.** Let B(σ) be the integral of \|H(σ + it)\|² over all real t. Then log B is a convex function of σ on \[½, ∞).

**How the definition helps.** A Gaussian factor supplies decay at both ends of every vertical line without cutting the integral off at height T (our own). The factor s − 1 cancels the pole of ζ at 1 (our own). Fourier transformation in t turns horizontal shifts into multiplication by real exponentials (our own). Plancherel’s identity and Hölder’s inequality then give the stated bound for the integrals (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Explicit zero density for the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.12263), [Explicit zero density for the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.12263). It says: “g(s) = ((s − 1)/s) exp(α(s/T)²).”

**Sources:**

- [H. Kadiri, A. Lumley, and N. Ng, Explicit zero density for the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.12263)

### Li’s variable circles critical zeros

**Remember:** The critical line becomes the unit circle, and zeros become poles of a logarithmic derivative.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let ξ denote the entire completion of the Riemann zeta function, whose zeros are precisely the nontrivial zeta zeros. Set φ(z)=ξ(1/(1−z)). Expand φ′(z)/φ(z) in a Taylor series about zero.

**Problem.** The Riemann hypothesis holds exactly when this Taylor series has radius at least 1.

**How the definition helps.** The change of variable sends each zero to 1−1/ρ, whose modulus is below 1 exactly when Re ρ &gt; 1/2 (our own). A zero there gives a pole of the logarithmic derivative, with nonzero residue (our own). The work uses the functional equation to pair zeros on opposite sides of the critical line (our own). Li’s stronger positivity criterion also needs the formula for the coefficients in terms of zeros (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Li's criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li%27s_criterion). It says: “Hence, φ′(z)/φ(z) is holomorphic on the unit disk \|z\| &lt; 1”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Minimization gives the prime error scale

**Remember:** Minimize over height to find the scale of the error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses), 11N05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write s = σ + it and let η be continuous and decreasing from \[0, ∞) into (0, ½\]. Define ω(x) as the infimum of η(t) log x + log t over t ≥ 1.

**Problem.** Suppose ζ has no zeros where σ &gt; 1 − η(\|t\|). For every ε &gt; 0, ψ(x) − x = O(x exp(−(1 − ε)ω(x))). Here ψ sums log p over prime powers up to x, and the constant may depend on ε and η.

**How the definition helps.** One infimum combines the effects of the width of the region and the height of a possible zero (our own). The same expression therefore states the error bound for different boundary shapes (our own). Pintz’s theorem supplies the estimate relating that expression to the prime count.

**Paper or page:** [On the connection between zero-free regions and the error term in the Prime Number Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13780). It says: “Then for every ε &gt; 0, ψ(x) − x ≪ε x exp(−(1 − ε)ω(x)).”

**Sources:**

- [J. Pintz, On the remainder term of the prime number formula II. On a theorem of Ingham (1980)](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-37-1-209-220)

### Squared sinc bounds multiplicities

**Remember:** Majorize coincidence with a weight whose frequencies are controlled.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of \\(\\zeta (s)\\) and \\(L(s, \\chi)\\); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Measure the difference between two zero heights in units of 2π/log T, and call the result u. Give the pair weight r(u) = (sin(πu)/(πu))², with r(0) = 1.

**Problem.** Assume the Riemann hypothesis, which places every nontrivial zeta zero on Re s = ½. Among zeros at heights in (0,T\], let P(T) be the proportion with multiplicity one, counting every occurrence in the denominator. Then lim inf P(T) ≥ ⅔ as T tends to infinity.

**How the definition helps.** The squared sinc majorizes coincidence and its Fourier transform vanishes outside \[−1,1\] (our own). Montgomery’s pair correlation formula applied to r(au), followed by a ↑ 1, bounds the equal-height pair count by (4/3+o(1)) times the zero count. A zero of multiplicity m contributes m² ordered pairs. Since m² ≥ 2m for m ≥ 2, repeated zeros account for at most a third asymptotically.

**Wikipedia:** [Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery%27s_pair_correlation_conjecture). It says: “proved under the Riemann hypothesis, that for \|α\| ≤ 1 this function converges uniformly”

**Sources:**

- [H. L. Montgomery, The Pair Correlation of Zeros of the Zeta Function (1973)](https://public.websites.umich.edu/~hlm/paircor1.pdf)

### Coproduct stabilizers give double shuffle groups

**Remember:** Symmetries of one coproduct compose and invert.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.QA, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For the corrected Ihara action on the harmonic module, let Δ denote the harmonic coproduct. Its stabilizer inside 𝒢 consists of every g ∈ 𝒢 satisfying (g ⊗ g)Δ = Δg in the induced module action.

**Problem.** The normalized double shuffle solutions with parameter zero form a group under Ihara multiplication.

**How the definition helps.** The stabilizer description makes closure follow from composition of transformations. In our own proof, transformations fixing the coproduct still fix it after composition or inversion. These operations also preserve the subgroup 𝒢. The identification theorem proves that the intersection of that subgroup with the stabilizer equals the normalized solutions.

### Counting threes lowers coaction level

**Remember:** An odd cut changes the parity of the number of threes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Encode each motivic zeta index 2 by 10 and each 3 by 100. The level of such a word counts its 100 blocks, and Fₗ spans the corresponding motivic values of level at most l over ℚ. Set F₋₁ = 0 and let Dₘ denote the infinitesimal coaction cutting m letters.

**Problem.** For odd m ≥ 3, Dₘ sends Fₗ into tensors whose second factors belong to Fₗ₋₁.

**How the definition helps.** Counting threes makes a decrease in level visible after an odd cut. The cut formula shows that surviving words still use the two allowed blocks and have no more threes than before. In our own count, weight equals twice the number of blocks plus the number of threes. Removing an odd number of letters changes the parity of the number of threes, so that number decreases.

### Cyclotomic words give Fibonacci dimensions

**Remember:** Counting weighted words gives the dimensions without counting relations among integrals.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For motivic iterated integrals on the letters 0, 1 and a fixed primitive sixth root of unity, weight counts integrations. The graded word model has basis pairs consisting of a word and a nonnegative power of the weight-one generator for 2πi. There is one letter of each integer weight ≥ 2, and weights add.

**Problem.** The dimensions at weights zero and one are both one. Each subsequent dimension is the sum of the previous two.

**How the definition helps.** Deligne’s basis theorem identifies the dimensions with counts of these pairs. In our own count, the letters contribute t²/(1−t), so arbitrary words contribute (1−t)/(1−t−t²). The powers of the weight-one generator multiply this by 1/(1−t). Comparing coefficients of 1/(1−t−t²) gives both initial values and the recurrence.

**Paper or page:** [The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04289v2), [The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04289v2). It says: “If N ∈ {2, 6} then d₍N,n₎ is the Fibonacci sequence”

### Depth quotients expose parity vanishing

**Remember:** Opposite weight and depth parity leaves only products and shallower terms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A multiple zeta value has depth equal to the number of exponents and weight equal to their sum. Fix weight w and depth r ≥ 2. In the space spanned by values of weight w and depth at most r, identify elements whose difference is a polynomial in shallower values.

**Problem.** A convergent multiple zeta value of weight w and depth r ≥ 2 represents zero in this quotient whenever w + r is odd.

**How the definition helps.** The quotient turns reduction to a polynomial in shallower values into vanishing of one class. In our own description, each term that the parity theorem produces already lies in the algebra we divide out. The parity theorem supplies the reduction itself.

**Paper or page:** [The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04289v2). It says: “if $n<sub>d</sub>+\\ldots+n<sub>1</sub>+d$ is odd.”

### Double shuffle coordinates are polynomial

**Remember:** One polynomial family of solutions identifies each fiber with the group at zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The formal multiple zeta algebra is the rational shuffle algebra of words modulo normalization and the regularized double shuffle relations. It is the coordinate ring of the normalized solution scheme, with parameter λ given by ζᶠ(2).

**Problem.** The formal multiple zeta algebra over ℚ is a polynomial algebra, without assuming completeness of the relations for numerical values.

**How the definition helps.** Racinet’s torsor theorem and a polynomial family of solutions identify the scheme with the parameter line times its parameter-zero group. In our own explanation, the graded exponential identifies this prounipotent group with its Lie algebra degree by degree. The resulting coordinate ring is polynomial.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “The algebra 𝒵ᶠ of formal multiple zeta values is a free polynomial algebra.”

### Endpoint labels prevent forest integral divergence

**Remember:** Start every total order with label one and end it with zero.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let a nonempty finite rooted forest order its vertices with each root above its descendants. Label vertices by 0 or 1, with minimal vertices labelled 1 and maximal vertices labelled 0. Integrate over times in (0,1) increasing along the order, using dt/t for 0 and dt/(1 − t) for 1.

**Problem.** The resulting integral converges and is a finite sum of ordinary multiple zeta values, counted with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** The labels exclude divergent chains such as two consecutive ones ending at the upper endpoint. Sorting the integration times partitions the domain up to measure zero into regions indexed by compatible total orders (our own). Each order begins with one and ends with zero, so its word integral is a convergent multiple zeta value.

**Paper or page:** [Generalisations of multiple zeta values to rooted forests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00611v4). It says: “The flattening map fl maps convergent forests to convergent words”

### First-letter deletion isolates the kernel

**Remember:** First-letter deletion detects every word unless its first letter uses the whole weight.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Brown’s graded word model uses words in odd letters f₃,f₅,… multiplied by nonnegative powers of a commuting variable f₂, with subscripts giving weights. For each odd r ≥ 3, deletion removes the first letter if it equals fᵣ and returns zero otherwise. Extend deletion linearly, leaving the f₂ power as a factor whenever deletion succeeds.

**Problem.** At weight N ≥ 2, the operators for odd letters of weight below N have a one-dimensional common kernel. The single motivic zeta value ζᵐ(N) spans it.

**How the definition helps.** The word model turns the kernel into a count of words that no deletion can detect. In our own proof, monomials beginning with a fixed letter have distinct remainders, so their coefficients cannot cancel. Only the single weight-N letter for odd N, or the power of f₂ for even N, remains. The work lies in identifying the motivic coaction with the shuffle model and normalizing the single zeta values.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “\\ker(D<sub>&lt;N</sub>) \\cap \\mathcal{U}<sup>\\mathsf{f}<sub>N</sub></sup> = \\mathbb{Q} \\,s<sub>N</sub>.”

### Formal zeta symbols parametrize solutions

**Remember:** The quotient records the relations that every solution must satisfy.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Start with the rational two-letter shuffle algebra, whose product sums all order-preserving interleavings. Quotient by the ideal generated by the one-letter words and the regularized double shuffle relations. The formal zeta symbol ζᶠ(w) is the class of the word w in this quotient.

**Problem.** For every commutative ℚ-algebra R, maps of ℚ-algebras into R from this quotient correspond to normalized double shuffle solutions over R. Imposing ζᶠ(2) = λ selects the solutions with parameter λ.

**How the definition helps.** The quotient represents solutions without requiring numerical linear independence. In our own proof, a map from the quotient is exactly a shuffle evaluation that kills the regularized relations. The work lies in Racinet’s comparison with the series conditions, including the correction to the stuffle series. The numerical algebra is a quotient and is not known to coincide with this formal algebra.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “the algebra 𝒵ᶠ of formal multiple zeta values.”

### Missing barred ones kill weight-one cuts

**Remember:** Without a barred one, no nonzero weight-one cut survives.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an Euler index (m₁,…,mᵣ) in increasing summation order, each exponent mᵢ has a sign εᵢ ∈ {−1,1}. Its integral word concatenates blocks consisting of εᵢ⋯εᵣ followed by mᵢ−1 zeros. A barred one is a position with mᵢ = 1 and εᵢ = −1.

**Problem.** Let D₁ sum the one-letter cuts of the word, recording each cut separately from its remainder. For convergent motivic Euler sums without a barred 1, D₁ gives zero.

**How the definition helps.** The one-letter cut formula requires adjacent opposite nonzero signs for a surviving logarithm (our own). Include the final endpoint 1 when testing adjacency. Consecutive sign letters require mᵢ = 1, and their ratio is εᵢ. Opposite signs therefore require a barred one.

**Paper or page:** [On Some Unramified Families of Motivic Euler Sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06925v3). It says: “If 1̅ does not appear in s then D₁ζₐᵐ(s) = 0”

### Odd single zeta values have a two-term coaction

**Remember:** One letter 1 leaves no nontrivial proper coaction term.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Encode ζᶠ(k) by 1 followed by k−1 zeros between endpoints 0 and 1. The formal coaction sums over retained subwords, putting the intervening blocks in the left factor after the projection a setting ζᶠ(2) to zero.

**Problem.** For odd k ≥ 3, Δζᶠ(k) = a(ζᶠ(k)) ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ ζᶠ(k).

**How the definition helps.** The cut formula leaves only the two extreme terms because each nonempty proper cut vanishes (our own). A proper block containing the one begins at the first letter and has both endpoints zero. Every other nonempty block contains only zeros, so regularization kills its integral as well.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “ΔGon(ζᶠ(2n+1)) = a(ζᶠ(2n+1)) ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ ζᶠ(2n+1).”

### Parity alphabets locate ordinary zeta values

**Remember:** With the parity basis, ordinary zeta values occupy the odd-letter words.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** At level N, cyclotomic motivic iterated integrals use zero and Nth roots of unity as letters. The parity basis takes conjugation eigencomponents of Deligne’s generators, using the real or purely imaginary component prescribed by weight. Its f-alphabet expresses motivic values in the resulting graded word coordinates.

**Problem.** For N equal to 2, 3, 4 or 6, the ordinary motivic multiple zeta values use only the letters of odd weight at least three. Their algebra is exactly the rational span of these words multiplied by even powers of 2πi.

**How the definition helps.** The parity basis makes membership in the ordinary algebra a test on words. The ordinary algebra uses only the integration letters zero and one. Panzer and Schnetz prove that the parity coordinates respect conjugation and identify precisely the stated subalgebra. In our own reading, this comparison theorem does the work of excluding all the other letters.

**Paper or page:** [The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04289v2), [The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04289v2). It says: “be the sub-algebra of words in letters of odd weights ≥ 3 times even powers of 2πi.”

### Path reversal gives zeta duality

**Remember:** Read the path backward and swap the two endpoints.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Encode a convergent integral from 0 to 1 by its forms from innermost to outermost, using 0 for dt/t and 1 for dt/(1−t). An admissible nonempty word starts with 1 and ends with 0. Its dual reverses the word and exchanges 0 with 1.

**Problem.** A convergent word and its dual give the same motivic multiple zeta value.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation uses the path description to replace a nested-sum identity by a symmetry of the interval. Reversing the path reverses the word and contributes one minus sign per letter. Substituting t ↦ 1 − t exchanges the letters, contributes the same signs again, and restores the original endpoints and their tangent directions. Brown’s motivic integral identities justify both operations before numerical evaluation.

**nLab:** [iterated integral](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/iterated+integral). It says: “Iterated integrals include nested integration of differential forms of the kind as it appears in the formulation of parallel transport”

### Projected coactions give derivations

**Remember:** Keep one positive-weight factor and discard products of two.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Motivic multiple zeta values are algebraic versions of nested sums that retain information about their symmetries. Their coaction Δ records these symmetries in a left factor A and keeps the values in a right factor H. For r &gt; 0, define D by taking left weight r and discarding products of two positive-weight left factors.

**Problem.** The projected map satisfies the product rule D(uv) = (1 ⊗ u)D(v) + (1 ⊗ v)D(u).

**How the definition helps.** In Δ(u)Δ(v), projection kills every term with two positive-weight left factors (our own). The left weight-zero parts of Δ(u) and Δ(v) are 1 ⊗ u and 1 ⊗ v. Multiplicativity of Brown’s coaction therefore leaves exactly the two displayed terms.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630). It says: “is a derivation with respect to ∗”

### Projection removes single-valued period products

**Remember:** Project first and products drop out of the relation.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 33B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In the graded de Rham Hopf algebra let S be the antipode and Y multiply each homogeneous element by its weight. On weight n &gt; 0, the clean projector sends x to ∑ S(x₁)Y(x₂)/n, writing Δx = ∑ x₁ ⊗ x₂.

**Problem.** If a rational linear combination of motivic multiple polylogarithms equals a sum of products of positive weights, its clean single-valued combination vanishes.

**How the definition helps.** The clean definition projects away products before evaluating, so product terms in the original identity contribute zero (our own). Ordinary single-valued evaluation can retain such products (our own). The projector kills them because the degree operator satisfies the product rule and the Hopf inverse cancels the coproduct on positive degrees (our own). The construction then applies single-valued evaluation and selects the real or imaginary part prescribed by the weight (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344). It says: “for every linear combination of motivic MPL’s that can be reduced to products,”

### Regularizing divergent Hurwitz-type multiple zeta values lets their two products be compared

**Remember:** Keep the divergent part as a variable, then compare the polynomials.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 11M35. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix the base shift used to normalize the divergent single index of weight one. A stuffle regularization extends convergent μ-multiple Hurwitz zeta evaluation to an algebra map into polynomials in T and sends that index to T. A shuffle regularization imposes the corresponding conditions on the integral words.

**Problem.** An explicit linear map on polynomials in T converts stuffle regularization into shuffle regularization for each μ-multiple Hurwitz zeta index. With both base shifts equal to one, the comparison formula is independent of μ.

**How the definition helps.** Both regularizations take values in a common polynomial space, so a linear comparison makes sense even for divergent indices (our own). Corollary 4.29 computes the map. With both base shifts equal to one, its shift corrections vanish.

### Separate regularizations avoid incompatible values

**Remember:** The two products need different values for the first divergent pair.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On indices in decreasing summation order, shuffle interleaves integral words and stuffle interleaves index entries with optional pairwise merges by addition. For each product, a regularization is a rational algebra map into real polynomials in T extending convergent zeta evaluation and sending (1) to T.

**Problem.** Both extensions exist uniquely. They give T²/2 and (T² − ζ(2))/2 respectively for the index (1,1), so one extension cannot preserve both products.

**How the definition helps.** Separate extensions allow the two products to assign different values to the divergent index (1,1). In our own calculation, shuffling (1) with itself yields two copies of (1,1). Stuffling adds the merged index (2), which has nonzero value. Existence and uniqueness use the polynomial description of each index algebra over its convergent part.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “Let T be a commutative variable and extend the stuffle product ∗ by ℚ\[T\]-linearity”

### Stable ideals preserve the coaction

**Remember:** Impose only period relations that remain relations under the coaction.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let W be the two-letter shuffle algebra with its motivic coaction Δ and numerical period map per given by tangentially regularized integration. A graded ideal I is eligible if I ⊆ ker(per) and Δ(I) ⊆ A ⊗ I, where A is the coacting algebra. Take the quotient of W by the sum of all eligible ideals.

**Problem.** The quotient carries both the coaction and the map to numerical periods.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation is that stable relations let the coaction pass to the quotient. Requiring numerical vanishing also preserves evaluation. The sum of all eligible ideals is still eligible, so a largest one exists. Brown constructs the coaction before imposing these relations.

### Symmetric zeta sums lose their parameter

**Remember:** Reversal makes the common regularization shift cancel.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let Z(w;t) be the harmonic regularization of a descending multiple zeta index w with Z((1);t) = t and Z(∅;t) = 1. For each split w = uv, multiply Z(reverse(u);T+πi/2) by Z(v;T−πi/2) and by (−1) raised to the weight of u. Sum over every split, including empty parts.

**Problem.** This signed sum is independent of T.

**How the definition helps.** A common translation introduces inverse factors at the join between the reversed prefix and suffix (our own). Translating by h multiplies the regularized word series on the left by exp(hy), where y represents index one. Signed reversal moves this multiplier to the right and changes its sign in the exponent. The two factors cancel.

**Remember:** At greatest depth, no letters have merged.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A word in positive integers has depth equal to its length. Stuffle interleaves words while allowing paired letters from different inputs to merge by addition. Stage d spans all words of length at most d, so the associated graded product keeps only terms of full combined length.

**Problem.** The associated graded algebra of the stuffle word algebra for this filtration is the shuffle algebra on the same alphabet.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping only the longest terms removes every merge from the product. In our own proof, a merge takes two input letters and produces one output letter. Exactly the interleavings have length equal to the sum of the input lengths. The cited theorem treats a larger alphabet whose positive-index letters give this product.

### Word weights count motivic dimensions

**Remember:** Odd letters form arbitrary words, and the even variable contributes its own powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Motivic multiple zeta values are algebraic versions of nested sums, graded by the sum of their exponents. Brown gives a model with one letter in each odd weight starting at three and an independent polynomial variable of weight two. A basis consists of every ordered word, including the empty word, times each power of that variable.

**Problem.** The series whose coefficient of tⁿ counts the dimension in weight n equals 1 ∕ (1 − t² − t³).

**How the definition helps.** Brown’s word model makes the dimension equal to a basis count (our own). The one-letter series is L = t³/(1−t²), so all words contribute 1/(1−L). Powers of the weight-two generator contribute 1/(1−t²), giving the stated series.

### Selberg factors telescope to Ruelle

**Remember:** A shift by one cancels every geodesic factor except the first.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M36 (Selberg zeta functions and regularized determinants; applications to spectral theory, Dirichlet series, Eisenstein series, etc. (explicit formulas)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented hyperbolic surface, let ℓ run over lengths of primitive oriented closed geodesics, counted once per geodesic. Selberg’s Z(s) multiplies 1−exp(−(s+n)ℓ) over these geodesics and integers n ≥ 0. The Ruelle product R(s) takes just the n = 0 factor for each geodesic.

**Problem.** The Ruelle product is Z(s)/Z(s+1) for Re s &gt; 1 and extends meromorphically by that quotient.

**How the definition helps.** Writing the Ruelle product as a quotient cancels every factor indexed by n≥1 (our own). Absolute convergence justifies this cancellation for Re s&gt;1 (our own). The quotient then gives continuation from Selberg’s theorem for Z, a step the original Ruelle product alone cannot justify (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_zeta_function). It says: “where p runs over conjugacy classes of prime geodesics (equivalently, conjugacy classes of primitive hyperbolic elements of Γ)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Finite-field cancellation truncates Goss values

**Remember:** Summing over each free coefficient kills high-degree terms at negative integers.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M38 (Zeta and \\(L\\)-functions in characteristic \\(p\\)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Use polynomials over the field with q elements. In the degree expansion for Goss zeta, group the monic polynomials, those with leading coefficient one, by degree. At a negative integer −k, the degree d coefficient sums the kth powers of all monic polynomials of degree d.

**Problem.** For k ≥ 1, only degrees at most k/(q−1) contribute to the Goss zeta value at −k.

**How the definition helps.** The sum over monic polynomials of degree d sums independently over d free coefficients (our own). In the expanded kth power, a coefficient sum vanishes unless its exponent is a positive multiple of q−1. A surviving term thus needs d(q−1) ≤ k. Goss’s continuation theorem identifies the resulting finite sum with the zeta value.

**Wikipedia:** [Goss zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goss_zeta_function). It says: “is an analogue of the Riemann zeta function for function fields.”

**Sources:**

- [Jeffrey T. Sheats, The Riemann Hypothesis for the Goss Zeta Function for 𝔽q\[T\] (1998)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jnth.1998.2232)

### Conductor survives gamma regrouping

**Remember:** The conductor keeps the linear term of the gamma growth.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a nonzero Selberg-class function F, write its completing factor as γ(s) = Qˢ∏Γ(λs+μ), with Q and all slopes λ positive. Put d = 2∑λ. Define the conductor q as (2π)ᵈQ² times the product of exp(2λ log λ) over all factors.

**Problem.** The conductor of F has the same value for every allowed completion. The exponential base Q alone can change when a gamma factor splits into several factors.

**How the definition helps.** The definition recovers the conductor from two growth coefficients of the completing factor (our own). Stirling’s formula gives log\|γ(x)\| = (d/2)x log x + Bx + O(log x), where B = log Q + ∑λ log λ − d/2. Uniqueness up to a constant preserves both d and B, which determine q.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class). It says: “the same gamma factor can be expressed in many different ways, involving different numbers of gamma functions with different constants.”

**Sources:**

- [Kaczorowski and Perelli, On the structure of the Selberg class, IV: basic invariants](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa104-2-1)

### In the Selberg class, degree below 2 means a Dirichlet L-function

**Remember:** Double the sum of gamma slopes to obtain the Selberg degree.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Problem.** In the Selberg class, only F = 1 has degree below one. From degree one up to but excluding two, the functions are ζ(s) and L(s+iθ,χ) for real θ and nonprincipal primitive Dirichlet characters χ.

### The Euler axiom excludes nonconstant degree-zero polynomials

**Remember:** At degree zero, a nonconstant local polynomial violates the Euler bound.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In the Selberg class, the degree is twice the sum of the positive slopes λ in the factors Γ(λs+μ). The Euler axiom requires log F to have coefficients only at prime powers pʳ. Their absolute values must be bounded by a constant times p raised to rθ for some θ &lt; ½.

**Problem.** Only 1 has degree zero in the Selberg class. Without the Euler axiom, F(s) = 1 + √p/pˢ gives a degree-zero example for each prime p.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the Euler bound keeps each local factor free of zeros for Re s &gt; θ. The degree-zero classification reduces F to a Dirichlet polynomial, which multiplicativity splits into local polynomials with all zeros at real part at most θ. Reflection would place a partner zero to the right of ½, so no local polynomial can have a zero and each must be constant. For the example, exp(s log(p)/2) completes F and gives reflection with no gamma factor.

### Admissible tuples are the prime patterns that sieve theorems can reach

**Remember:** If a pattern covers every class mod p, one entry is always divisible by p.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes), 11N36. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An admissible k-tuple consists of distinct integers h₁,…,hₖ whose residues miss at least one class modulo every prime p. Only primes p ≤ k need checking.

**Problem.** For every positive integer m, some k ensures that every admissible k-tuple has at least m prime entries n+hᵢ for infinitely many integers n.

**How the definition helps.** Admissibility expresses all local congruence conditions in one hypothesis (our own). For example, (0,2,4) covers every class modulo three, so at least one translated entry is always divisible by three. Maynard’s sieve theorem gives the claimed m primes in admissible tuples.

**Wikipedia:** [Prime k-tuple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_k-tuple). It says: “A k-tuple that includes every possible residue modulo p is said to be inadmissible modulo p.”

**Sources:**

- [G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood, Some problems of 'Partitio numerorum' III: On the expression of a number as a sum of primes, Acta Math. 44 (1923) 1–70](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02403921)
