- [N. Rome and S. Yamagishi, Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations (2026)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.2026.340.179)

### Disjoint supports multiply local sums

**Remember:** Functions on disjoint pieces vary independently, so their averages multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a curve over a finite field K, a finite closed subscheme Z specifies finitely many points, possibly with multiplicities. Write R for its finite K-algebra of functions and λ for a K-linear map from R to K. Given an integer k ≥ 1, define S(Z,λ) as the average of ψ(λ(xᵏ)) over x in R. Here ψ maps addition in K to multiplication of complex numbers of modulus one and is not identically one.

**Problem.** If Z is the disjoint union of Z₁ and Z₂, then S(Z,λ) = S(Z₁,λ₁)S(Z₂,λ₂), where λᵢ applies λ to functions on Zᵢ extended by zero. Moreover, λ is nondegenerate, meaning that it factors through no proper quotient of R, exactly when λ₁ and λ₂ are nondegenerate.

**How the definition helps.** The function ring is a product, so choosing a uniform function chooses two independent uniform components (our own explanation). Powers act componentwise, λ adds the outputs, and ψ turns their sum into a product. Thus the averages multiply, as in Sawin’s lemma for the trivial line bundle. Each ideal also splits componentwise, so the kernel contains a nonzero ideal exactly when some component kernel does (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The asymptotic in Waring's problem over function fields via singular sets in the circle method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14053v1). It says: “Then we have \\\[ S<sub>Z</sub>(\\overline{\\alpha})=S<sub>Z<sub>1</sub></sub>(\\overline{\\alpha}<sub>Z<sub>1</sub></sub>)S<sub>Z<sub>2</sub></sub>(\\overline{\\alpha}<sub>Z<sub>2</sub></sub>) \\\]”

**Sources:**

- [W. Sawin, The asymptotic in Waring's problem over function fields via singular sets in the circle method (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14053v1)

### Real solution density makes positivity local

**Remember:** A smooth zero with positive weight sends positive mass near zero.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F map ℝˢ smoothly to ℝʳ, and let w be a nonnegative smooth function with compact support. Integrate w over points whose images lie in a cube of side 2ε centered at zero. The real solution density is the limit of this integral divided by the cube’s volume as ε decreases to zero, when the limit exists.

**Problem.** Assume F has derivative of rank r at every zero in the support of w. Then the normalized mass has a finite limit, which is positive if w is positive at any zero.

**How the definition helps.** Near each relevant zero the rank assumption gives coordinates in which F selects the first r coordinates (our own proof). Integrating in the remaining coordinates gives a continuous density, positive at zero wherever the chart contains a zero with positive weight. A finite partition of unity near the compact zero set combines the local limits. The remaining compact support maps away from zero.

**Paper or page:** [Solving quadratic forms in restricted variables with the circle method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17949v1). It says: “can be interpreted as a local density over the reals inside the compact set 𝔅.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Residues modulo sixteen select sums of twelve fourth powers

**Remember:** Modulo sixteen, a fourth power records whether its base is odd.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Call a positive integer admissible if its remainder modulo 16 lies between 1 and 12 inclusive. Consider representations by exactly twelve positive fourth powers with at least one odd base.

**Problem.** Every sufficiently large admissible integer is a sum of twelve fourth powers of positive integers. No integer outside the admissible classes is such a sum with an odd base.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the remainder records exactly how many of the twelve bases are odd. An even fourth power is zero modulo 16, and an odd fourth power is one. Thus a remainder of zero forces all twelve bases to be even, while remainders 13 through 15 are impossible. Brüdern and Wooley prove existence for every sufficiently large admissible integer in Corollary 1.3.

**Wikipedia:** [Waring's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem). It says: “any sufficiently large number congruent to 1 through 14 mod 16 could be written as a sum of 14 fourth powers”

**Sources:**

- [J. Brüdern and T. D. Wooley, On smooth Weyl sums over biquadrates and Waring’s problem (2022)](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~twooley/publ/20220507smbiq.pdf)

### Smooth cutoffs suppress Poisson tails

**Remember:** Smooth weights remove boundary terms in repeated integration by parts.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11L07. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F₁ and F₂ be fixed quadratic forms in s real variables and W a smooth function of compact support. Define I by integrating W(x/P)exp(2πi\[β₁F₁(x)+β₂F₂(x)−c·x/q\]) over ℝˢ. Here β = (β₁,β₂) is real, c is a real vector and q is a positive integer.

**Problem.** Fix δ &gt; 0 and take P sufficiently large. If \|c\| ≥ (q/P)(1+P²\|β\|)Pᵟ, then \|I\| ≤ C(A)Pˢ/(P\|c\|/q)ᴬ for each integer A ≥ 1. The constants may depend on the forms, W and δ.

**How the definition helps.** Smooth compact support removes boundary terms at every integration by parts (our own explanation). A sharp cutoff on \[0,1\] gives Fourier magnitude 1/(πt) at positive half-integers t. After scaling by P, the derivative along c has magnitude comparable to P\|c\|/q throughout the support. Repeated integration by parts in that direction gives the stated decay.

**Paper or page:** [A two-dimensional delta symbol method and its application to pairs of quadratic forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11355v1). It says: “I<sub>q</sub>(\\vec{\\mathrm{w}},\\mathbf{u})\\ll<sub>N</sub> P<sup>s</sup>(P\|\\mathbf{u}\|/q)<sup>-N</sup>\\ll P<sup>s-N\\delta</sup>”

**Sources:**

- [J. Li, S. L. Rydin Myerson and P. Vishe, A two-dimensional delta symbol method and its application to pairs of quadratic forms](https://www.maths.dur.ac.uk/users/pankaj.vishe/2dDelta.pdf)

### Subcritical moments bound minor arcs

**Remember:** A good moment below twelve leaves a factor for the arc saving.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05, 11L15. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let g(α) sum exp(2πiαx⁴) over positive integers x ≤ P whose prime factors are at most R. The moment of order t is the integral of \|g(α)\|ᵗ over \[0,1\]. Call Δ admissible if this moment is O(P raised to (t−4+Δ)). The bound must hold uniformly for 1 ≤ R ≤ P raised to η for some fixed η &gt; 0.

**Problem.** Brüdern and Wooley prove that zero is admissible for t = 11.95597. Suppose \|g\| ≤ εP on a measurable subset E of \[0,1\], with R in the allowed range. Then the integral of \|g\|¹² over E is O(P⁸ times ε raised to (12−t)).

**How the definition helps.** Admissibility with Δ=0 gives a global moment bound of order P raised to t−4, by Theorem 1.2. On E, each of the remaining 12−t powers contributes at most εP (our own calculation). Multiplying the bounds gives the claimed power of ε and P⁸.

**Wikipedia:** [Hardy–Ramanujan–Littlewood circle method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Ramanujan%E2%80%93Littlewood_circle_method). It says: “one takes a sufficiently high power of the generating function”

**Sources:**

### Bailey pairs generate identity chains

**Remember:** Keep the relation, and each new pair can start the next step.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P84 (Partition identities; identities of Rogers-Ramanujan type), 11B65. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write (x;q)ₘ for the product of 1−xqʲ over integers 0≤j&lt;m. Sequences α and β form a Bailey pair relative to a if βₙ=∑ᵣ αᵣ/((q;q)ₙ₋ᵣ(aq;q)ₙ₊ᵣ) for every integer n≥0. The sum runs over integers 0≤r≤n, and all denominators must be nonzero.

**Problem.** Bailey’s lemma turns each Bailey pair into another Bailey pair relative to the same a, with free parameters for which the denominators do not vanish. So one may iterate the limiting transformation to produce a chain of finite sum identities.

**How the definition helps.** A Bailey pair records the exact relation that each successive application of the lemma requires. The lemma gives formulas for two new sequences and proves that they satisfy the same relation. The work lies in that finite summation identity. In our own reading, preservation of the relation explains why every output can serve as the next input.

**Wikipedia:** [Bailey pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailey_pair). It says: “This process can be iterated to produce an infinite sequence of Bailey pairs, called a Bailey chain.”

**Paper or page:** [Truncated theta series from the Bailey lattice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11608v2). It says: “If (αₙ, βₙ) is a Bailey pair relative to a, then so is (α′ₙ, β′ₙ)”

**Sources:**

- [W. N. Bailey, Identities of the Rogers-Ramanujan Type](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s2-50.1.1)

### Centered Blaschke products preserve Mahler measure

**Remember:** The image of uniform boundary measure stays uniform if the center stays fixed.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A finite Blaschke product B multiplies factors (z − a)/(1 − āz), with \|a\| &lt; 1, by a constant of modulus one. Require B(0) = 0. The logarithmic Mahler measure m(P) averages log\|P\| over independent uniform points on the unit circle.

**Problem.** For every nonzero complex polynomial P(x,y), replacing x by B(x) preserves m(P). Here y denotes any number of additional variables.

**How the definition helps.** If B fixes zero, composing a harmonic extension with B preserves its center value and hence its boundary average (our own proof). Testing continuous functions shows that B preserves uniform circle measure, so it preserves integrals of integrable logarithms. For B(z)=(z+½)/(1+z/2), the center moves to ½. The average of log\|z−2\| changes from log 2 to log(3/2) under this substitution (our own example).

**Paper or page:** [An invariant property of Mahler measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00125). It says: “We denote by $\\widetilde{P}$ the rational function obtained by replacing $x$ by $f(x)/g(x)$ in $P$. Then\\\[  \\mathrm{m}(P)=\\mathrm{m}(\\widetilde{P}).  \\\]”

**Sources:**

- [An invariant property of Mahler measure, Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00125)

### Constant terms count lattice walks

**Remember:** The constant coefficient keeps exactly the walks that return to the origin.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over ℂₚ, the completed algebraic closure of the p-adic numbers, put S=x+x⁻¹+y+y⁻¹. For \|c\|ₚ&gt;1, define the p-adic Mahler measure of c+S as the constant coefficient of logₚ c+logₚ(1+S/c). The logarithm series converges under this strict inequality.

**Problem.** Let Bⱼ denote the binomial coefficient of 2j over j. For \|c\|ₚ&gt;1, the measure of c+S equals logₚ c minus the sum of Bⱼ²/(2j c²ʲ) over j≥1.

**How the definition helps.** The constant coefficient of Sⁿ counts walks of n unit steps returning to the origin (our own calculation). In coordinates u+v and u−v, each step chooses two signs independently. A return requires equal sign counts in each coordinate, giving Bⱼ² walks in 2j steps and none in odd length. Substitution in the logarithm series gives the formula, using Katagiri’s comparison with root-of-unity averages.

**Paper or page:** [A note on p-adic higher Mahler measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05724). It says: “m<sub>p</sub>(f)=\\log \_p c -\\frac{2}{c<sup>2}</sup> {}<sub>4F</sub><sub>3</sub>\\left(\\frac{3}{2}, \\frac{3}{2}, 1, 1 ; 2, 2, 2 ; \\frac{16}{c<sup>2}\\right</sup>).”

### Constant terms preserve p-adic measures

**Remember:** An injective exponent map cannot turn a nonconstant monomial into a constant.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f be a Laurent polynomial over ℂₚ with no zero where every coordinate has absolute value one. Write f=atᵘ(1+g), where atᵘ is its dominant monomial and all coefficients of g have absolute value below one. For each integer k≥1, its kth p-adic Mahler measure is the constant coefficient of (logₚ a+logₚ(1+g))ᵏ.

**Problem.** For k ≥ 1, every square integer monomial substitution with nonzero determinant preserves the k-th p-adic Mahler measure.

**How the definition helps.** In our own argument, the constant coefficient survives because the substitution sends only exponent zero to zero. Substitution respects the convergent logarithm series and its powers. Katagiri’s comparison with averages over roots of unity justifies the constant-coefficient formula. Those averages use orders coprime to p.

**Paper or page:** [A note on p-adic higher Mahler measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05724). It says: “For any $n \\times n$ matrix $S \\in M<sub>n</sub>(\\mathbb {Z}) \\cap {\\rm GL}n(\\mathbb {Q})$, we have $m{p, k}(f(t<sup>S</sup>))=m<sub>p, k</sub>(f(t))$.”

### Cyclotomic factors characterize zero measure

**Remember:** One monomial pulls ordinary cyclotomy onto the whole torus.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For each integer n≥1, the nth cyclotomic polynomial is monic with simple roots precisely at the complex roots of unity of exact order n. An extended cyclotomic factor substitutes a nonconstant Laurent monomial with coefficient one into such a polynomial. Units in the integer Laurent polynomial ring are the signed monomials.

**Problem.** A nonzero Laurent polynomial over ℤ has logarithmic Mahler measure zero exactly when it is a product of these factors and a unit.

**How the definition helps.** One monomial substitution describes each factor in Boyd’s theorem in any dimension (our own explanation). A nonconstant monomial with coefficient one sends uniform circle variables to a uniform circle variable. Jensen’s formula therefore gives each factor measure zero. Boyd proves the converse for integer polynomials, and a monomial clears negative exponents without changing the measure.

**Wikipedia:** [Mahler measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler_measure). It says: “Then M(F)=1 if and only if F is an element of Kₙ.”

### Dilogarithms evaluate triangular Mahler measure

**Remember:** An exact regulator form makes the endpoints carry the whole integral.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For \|z\|&lt;1, set Li₂(z)=∑ₙ≥₁ zⁿ/n². For 0&lt;\|z\|&lt;1, define D(z)=Im Li₂(z)+arg(1−z)log\|z\|, using the principal argument. Extend D continuously to zero and the unit circle.

**Problem.** The uniform circle average of log\|1 + x + y\| over x and y equals D(exp(πi/3))/π. This average is the logarithmic Mahler measure.

**How the definition helps.** Roy’s differential identity turns the remaining circle integral into an endpoint difference (our own calculation). Jensen’s formula keeps the arc \|1+x\|≥1, where x runs counterclockwise from exp(−2πi/3) to exp(2πi/3). There dD(−x)=−log\|1+x\| d arg x. The endpoint values of D(−x) are D(exp(πi/3)) and its negative, giving the stated average.

**Wikipedia:** [Mahler measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler_measure). It says: “m(1+x+y)=3√3/(4π) L(χ₋₃,2)”

**Paper or page:** [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601). It says: “\\eta \\left(x, 1-x\\right) = d D\\left(x\\right).”

**Sources:**

- [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials, Lemma 2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601)

### Dominant coefficients exclude p-adic zeros

**Remember:** One strictly largest term cannot cancel on the p-adic unit torus.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Use ℂₚ, the completed algebraic closure of the p-adic numbers. A Laurent polynomial allows negative integer exponents. Call one coefficient dominant if its p-adic absolute value strictly exceeds every other coefficient’s absolute value. The unit torus consists of points whose coordinates all have absolute value one.

**Problem.** A nonzero Laurent polynomial has no zero on this torus exactly when it has a dominant coefficient.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the largest term stays strictly larger than every other term throughout the torus. The p-adic triangle inequality then prevents cancellation. The converse uses the lemma’s factorization into a monomial times one plus a polynomial with coefficients smaller than one in absolute value. Our own example 1 − t has tied coefficients and vanishes at t = 1.

It says: “Then $f$ does not vanish in any point of $T<sub>p</sub><sup>n$</sup> if and only if we have\\begin{align}  f(t<sub>1</sub>, \\cdots , t<sub>n</sub>)=at<sub>1</sub><sup>l<sub>1</sub></sup>\\cdots t<sub>n</sub><sup>l<sub>n</sub></sup>(1+g(t<sub>1</sub>, \\cdots , t<sub>n</sub>)) \\end{align}for some $a \\in \\mathbb {C}<sub>p</sub><sup>\\times </sup>, (l<sub>1</sub>, \\cdots , l<sub>n</sub>) \\in \\mathbb {Z}<sup>n$</sup> and $g \\in \\mathfrak {m}<sub>p</sub>\[t<sub>1</sub><sup>\\pm 1</sup>, \\dots ,t<sub>n</sub><sup>\\pm 1</sup>\]$.”

### Exact symbols give boundary integrals

**Remember:** Each term supplies a primitive, so only the boundary remains to integrate.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Work on the smooth locus of an irreducible polynomial surface P(x,y,z)=0, away from zeros and poles of the functions used. Take the third exterior power of its rational function field’s multiplicative group and allow rational coefficients. Require x∧y∧z to be a finite rational linear combination of f∧(1−f)∧g.

**Problem.** Over \|x\| = \|y\| = 1, collect the roots with \|z\| ≥ 1, counting multiplicities and orienting by the angles θ, φ of x,y. Assume they form a piecewise smooth chain Γ in this open set, including its boundary. Then the logarithmic Mahler measure minus that of the leading coefficient in z equals a boundary integral.

**How the definition helps.** Trieu’s regulator identities give primitives for the terms of the decomposition. On Γ their weighted sum is a one-form β satisfying dβ=log\|z\| dθ∧dφ (our own explanation). Jensen’s formula expresses the difference of measures as the integral of dβ over Γ divided by (2π)². Stokes’ theorem replaces that integral by the integral of β over the oriented boundary.

**Paper or page:** [The Mahler measure of exact polynomials and special L-values of K3 surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00893). It says: “\\mathrm{m}(P) - \\mathrm{m}(\\tilde P) = \\dfrac {(-1)<sup>n-1</sup>}{(2\\pi i)<sup>n-1</sup>} \\int <sub>\\partial \\Gamma </sub> \\rho (\\xi ).”

### Exterior roots give regulator integrals

**Remember:** Jensen keeps the exterior roots, and the regulator form reads their logarithms.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let P(x,y) = 0 define an elliptic curve, and let P\* be the leading coefficient in y. As x travels counterclockwise around the unit circle, follow the roots y outside that circle, counting multiplicities. Together these oriented paths form γ.

**Problem.** Assume γ consists of finitely many smooth paths on the curve. Write m(P) for the average of log\|P\| with both variables uniform on the unit circle. Then m(P) − m(P\*) equals −1/(2π) times the integral along γ of η = log\|x\| d arg y − log\|y\| d arg x.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the path selects exactly the root terms in Jensen’s formula for the circle average in y. On γ, log\|x\| vanishes, leaving only −log\|y\| times the angular change of x. Integrating this expression gives the stated sign and factor.

### Short relation bounds imply equidistribution

**Remember:** Every fixed nonconstant character disappears from the average once the height is large enough.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Problem.** Fix the target and let the Boyd heights tend to infinity. Then the source averages of each continuous target function composed with these maps approach its uniform target average. The same conclusion holds for log\|P\| for each fixed nonzero Laurent polynomial P, giving convergence of logarithmic Mahler measures.

**How the definition helps.** In our own argument, the height bound ensures that every fixed nonconstant monomial eventually stays nonconstant. Its uniform average is then zero. Finite sums of monomials approximate every continuous function on the target uniformly. For log\|P\| the Boyd–Lawton theorem also controls the contribution near zeros, where uniform approximation fails.

### Tempered faces prevent tame obstructions

**Remember:** Cyclotomic edge roots make every boundary tame symbol torsion.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 19D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a polynomial allowing negative exponents in two variables, take the convex hull of its exponent vectors. Along each edge, list its coefficients in successive lattice positions, including zeros at missing positions. Use that list as coefficients of a one-variable polynomial. Call the original polynomial tempered if every nonzero root of every edge polynomial is a root of unity.

**Problem.** Take an irreducible tempered polynomial over ℚ whose exponent polygon has positive area. On its smooth complete curve, every tame symbol of the coordinate functions x and y is a root of unity. Thus their symbol has no boundary obstruction after allowing rational coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** Each boundary tame symbol is a signed power of an edge root (our own calculation). With uniformizer t, write x=tᵐa and y=tⁿb for units a,b, giving symbol (−1)ᵐⁿaⁿ/bᵐ at the point. For (m,n)≠(0,0), the lowest-order terms cancel along one edge, making the leading unit in its primitive direction an edge root. Temperedness makes its powers torsion, excluding x+y+2, whose symbol at x=0 is −1/2 (our own example).

**Paper or page:** [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974). It says: “Qₖ(x,y) and Qₖ(x−1,y) are tempered polynomials.”

**Remember:** For monic polynomials, compare the rings, not the norm forms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R09 (Polynomials (irreducibility, etc.)), 11R54. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

Its norm form sends n coordinates to the determinant of multiplication by the element with those coordinates in R (our own description). Two such polynomials are Hermite equivalent if an invertible integer change of coordinates identifies their norm forms.

**Problem.** Let f and g be monic integer polynomials with nonzero discriminant. They are Hermite equivalent exactly when the rings ℤ\[X\]∕(f) and ℤ\[X\]∕(g) are isomorphic.

**How the definition helps.** The invariant order replaces a comparison of forms in many variables with a comparison of rings. In our own explanation, a ring isomorphism maps one integer basis to another and keeps norms, so the norm forms agree. The hard direction recovers the ring from its norm form, which the paper proves for general orders.

### Euclidean ideal classes force cyclic class groups

**Remember:** Let the Euclidean algorithm run on ideals, and the class group becomes cyclic.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 13F07, 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let R be the ring of integers of K and E the fractional ideals containing R. A nonzero integral ideal C is Euclidean if some map ψ from E to a well-ordered set satisfies this condition. For every I∈E and x∈IC outside C, some y∈C satisfies ψ((x−y)⁻¹IC)&lt;ψ(I) (our own formulation).

**Problem.** A number field with a Euclidean ideal class has cyclic class group. Suppose K is Galois over ℚ, its Hilbert class field is abelian over ℚ, and its unit rank is at least four. Then a class is Euclidean exactly when it generates the class group.

**How the definition helps.** Each decreasing division step multiplies the ideal class by \[C\], so descent expresses every class as a power of \[C\] (our own explanation). Lenstra proved this implication. Murty and Graves prove the converse under the stated field and unit hypotheses.

### Pólya groups equal strongly ambiguous classes, giving short proofs

**Remember:** Galois-fixed ideals are products over whole fibres, so the groups agree.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R32, 11R34. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let L/K be a Galois extension of number fields with group G. The class group of L is its group of ideals modulo principal ideals. The relative Pólya group Po(L/K) is the subgroup generated by the classes of the products of all primes of L above one prime of K. A strongly ambiguous class is an ideal class that contains an ideal fixed by G.

**Problem.** Po(L/K) equals the group of strongly ambiguous classes. Its order is h(K)∏ᵥ eᵥ/\|H¹(G,U(L))\|, where v ranges over the finite primes of K. Here eᵥ is the ramification index, h(K) the class number, and U(L) the unit group of L.

**How the definition helps.** G acts transitively on the primes above each finite prime of K (our own argument). A fractional ideal is fixed exactly when its exponents are constant on each such orbit. Its class is therefore a product of integer powers of the Pólya generators, each represented by a fixed ideal. Corollary 2.3 obtains the order from the Brumer–Rosen and Zantema exact sequence.

**Paper or page:** [Ostrowski quotients for finite extensions of number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00442). It says: “For L/K a finite Galois extension of number fields, the relative Pólya group Po(L/K) coincides with the group of strongly ambiguous ideal classes in L/K.”

**Sources:**

### Galois sets identify completions

**Remember:** Restrict the Galois action to read the local field factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let L be a finite Galois extension of ℚ with group G. For an intermediate field K fixed by H, the cosets H∖G represent the embeddings of K into L. For a prime of L above p, its decomposition group D consists of the automorphisms preserving that prime.

**Problem.** For two intermediate fields, form the products of their completions above p. These products are isomorphic as ℚₚ-algebras exactly when their coset sets are isomorphic with the action of D.

**How the definition helps.** Restricting the coset action to D records the local fields and their multiplicities together (our own). Each orbit supplies one completion, the field fixed by a point stabilizer inside the chosen completion of L (our own). The converse uses the correspondence between finite separable algebras and finite sets with Galois action (our own). The cited proposition applies this argument to fields whose coset actions have equal fixed-point counts for every element of G (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Stronger arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4). It says: “if and only if \[H₁∖G\] and \[H₂∖G\] are isomorphic as D𝔭-sets.”

**Sources:**

### Locally integrally equivalent number fields have isomorphic class groups

**Remember:** Keep integer information at every prime, and the class group survives.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R33 (Integral representations related to algebraic numbers; Galois module structure of rings of integers), 11R29, 11R42. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K₁ and K₂ be number fields with a common Galois closure L, and let Hᵢ = Gal(L∕Kᵢ) in G = Gal(L∕ℚ). The group G permutes the cosets of H₁ and of H₂, and this gives two permutation modules. The fields are locally integrally equivalent if these modules are isomorphic over the ℓ-adic integers for every prime ℓ.

**Problem.** Locally integrally equivalent number fields have isomorphic ideal class groups. They also have the same zeta function and the same regulator.

**How the definition helps.** Local integral equivalence gives an isomorphism of the ℓ-primary class groups for every ℓ by the paper’s class-group theorem (our own explanation). Combining these isomorphisms gives the full class-group result. Rational equivalence gives the common zeta function, and the analytic class number formula yields equal regulators using the common arithmetic invariants. Equal zeta functions alone permit different class numbers (our own comparison).

**Paper or page:** [Stronger arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4). It says: “In addition to having the same Dedekind zeta function (the usual notion of arithmetic equivalence), number fields that are equivalent in any of these stronger senses must have the same class number”

**Sources:**

### Cartesian conditions preserve Selmer torsion

**Remember:** Pull back the local tests to get the same test on torsion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take T finite free over R/(πᵐ) with continuous Galois action, where π generates the maximal ideal of a discrete valuation ring R. At each place choose a subgroup of H¹(Kᵥ,T), and define the Selmer group by requiring all global restrictions to belong to these subgroups. Cartesian conditions on T\[πⁱ\] pull back those subgroups under inclusion, and multiplication by πᵐ⁻ⁱ identifies T/πⁱT with T\[πⁱ\].

**Problem.** Suppose the Galois group of the number field fixes no nonzero element of T modulo π. For 1 ≤ i ≤ m, both smaller Selmer groups identify with the subgroup killed by πⁱ in the Selmer group on T.

**How the definition helps.** Pulling the tests back makes membership on the smaller module exactly membership of its image on T (our own). The absence of fixed vectors gives the needed injections through the exact sequences of Galois cohomology (our own). These sequences identify the image with the classes killed by πⁱ (our own). The cited theorem verifies the Cartesian property for a particular family of tests.

**Paper or page:** [Bipartite Euler Systems for certain Galois Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05181v1). It says: “The Selmer structure ℱ(𝔫) is cartesian for any 𝔫 ∈ 𝒩.”

**Sources:**

### Ext into units extends Artin–Verdier duality

**Remember:** Pair against the units, and every constructible sheaf gets a dual.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11R37, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let X be the spectrum of the ring of integers of a totally imaginary number field. A ℤ-constructible étale sheaf F is locally constant with finitely generated abelian stalks on each piece of a finite locally closed stratification. The duality pairing uses the groups Extʲ(F,𝔾ₘ), with 𝔾ₘ the étale sheaf of units.

**Problem.** For a constructible sheaf F on X, Deninger's theorem identifies the dual of Hʳ(X, F) with Ext³⁻ʳ(F, 𝔾ₘ) for r = 0, 1. For r = 2, 3 it identifies Hʳ(X, F) with the dual of that Ext group.

**How the definition helps.** Ext into 𝔾ₘ makes sense for every sheaf, so the duality needs no torsion hypothesis. For F = ℤ and r = 2, H²(X, ℤ) is the dual of the Galois group of the Hilbert class field (our own). The group Ext¹(ℤ, 𝔾ₘ) is the class group, so this case says that this Galois group is the class group (our own). That is unramified class field theory.

**Wikipedia:** [Artin–Verdier duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Verdier_duality). It says: “proved Artin–Verdier duality for constructible, but not necessarily torsion sheaves. For such a sheaf F, the above pairing induces isomorphisms”

### Tate-modified compact supports make Artin–Verdier duality hold

**Remember:** Tate cohomology at real places removes the 2-torsion that never stops.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let U be a nonempty open subset of the integer spectrum of a number field K. Take the restriction map from the étale cochain complex on U to the sum of local complexes at the omitted places, including infinity. Use complete Tate complexes at archimedean places and ordinary local cochains elsewhere. The mapping cone shifted by −1 defines modified compactly supported cohomology.

**Problem.** Let F be a constructible sheaf on U, one that is locally constant with finite stalks on the pieces of a finite partition. Then the Tate-modified compactly supported cohomology Ĥⁱc(U, F) is finite, is dual to Ext³⁻ⁱ(F, 𝔾ₘ) for every i, and vanishes for i ≥ 4.

**How the definition helps.** The Tate restriction cancels the persistent high-degree contribution at real places (our own explanation). For example, ordinary cohomology of the integer spectrum of ℚ with coefficients ℤ/2 persists in arbitrarily high degrees (our own). Modified Artin–Verdier duality gives finiteness and the pairing, and negative Ext groups vanish.

**Wikipedia:** [Artin–Verdier duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Verdier_duality). It says: “The sum is taken over all places of K, which are not in U, including the archimedean ones.”

**Paper or page:** [Special values of L-functions on regular arithmetic schemes of dimension 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00811). It says: “If F is constructible, all groups are finite and the Artin-Verdier arrow is an isomorphism.”

### Unit cohomology detects capitulation

**Remember:** A generator upstairs records the lost class through its conjugates.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois extension K/F, choose a finite set S containing all infinite places and all ramified finite primes of F. Form ideal classes using only prime factors outside S and identifying ideals differing by a principal ideal outside S. An S-unit is a nonzero element with prime exponent zero outside S. Upstairs, use the primes above S.

**Problem.** The kernel of extension on S-ideal classes is the first cohomology of the Galois group acting on the S-units of K.

**How the definition helps.** Ratios of conjugates turn a generator upstairs into an S-unit cocycle (our own argument). For a generator a outside S, replacing a by an S-unit multiple changes the cocycle c(g)=g(a)/a by a coboundary. Hilbert’s Theorem 90 gives such an a for every S-unit cocycle. Its ideal outside S descends because its prime exponents are invariant and all ramification lies in S.

**Paper or page:** [The S-relative Pólya groups and S-Ostrowski quotients of number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.09362v1). It says: “0 → Ker(ε<sub>K/F,S</sub>) → H¹(G,U<sub>K,S</sub>)”

### A torus detects common scales

**Remember:** One cohomology class records whether all norms share a scale.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take finite separable extensions of a number field K. Map a tuple of nonzero extension elements and one nonzero base scalar to their field norms multiplied by that common scalar. Let T be the kernel as an algebraic group over K. It is a torus, meaning it becomes a product of multiplicative groups over a separable closure.

**Problem.** Suppose a tuple of nonzero base elements becomes a tuple of norms after common rescaling at each completion of K. The projective Hasse norm principle asks whether one scalar in K suffices. It holds exactly when the map from first Galois cohomology of T to the product of its local counterparts is injective.

**How the definition helps.** The kernel torus assigns one obstruction class to the entire tuple, retaining the requirement of a common scalar (our own). The connecting map in Galois cohomology assigns this class, which vanishes exactly when the tuple has a preimage (our own). Hilbert’s theorem 90 shows that every class arises this way, both globally and locally (our own). Thus injectivity says that vanishing at every completion forces global vanishing (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Projective Twist on the Hasse Norm Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11159v1). It says: “{PHNP} \_K(L<sub>1</sub>, L<sub>2</sub>, \\ldots , L<sub>n</sub>) is true if and only if H<sup>1</sup>(L/K, \\mathbf {T}(L)) \\to \\prod <sub>w\\mid v</sub> H<sup>1</sup>(L<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>v</sub>, \\mathbf {T}(L<sub>w</sub>)) is injective.”

*True by definition.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a number field K, factor each nonzero integral ideal into prime ideals. Give it weight 1 for an even number of factors and −1 for an odd number, counting repeats.

**Problem.** Sum these weights over ideals of norm at most x, where the norm counts residue classes modulo the ideal. If the sum divided by x tends to zero, the number of prime ideals up to norm x is asymptotic to x/log x.

**How the definition helps.** In our own formulation, the sign turns balance between even and odd factor counts into cancellation in one sum. Burgin proves that this cancellation implies the prime ideal theorem and establishes the required cancellation.

**Paper or page:** [A New Elementary Proof of Landau's Prime Ideal Theorem, and Associated Results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08565v4). It says: “i.e., that Ω is equidistributed modulo 2.”

**Sources:**

- [Alex Burgin, A New Elementary Proof of Landau's Prime Ideal Theorem, and Associated Results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08565v4)

### Null boundaries permit infinite Chebotarev

**Remember:** A boundary of measure zero lets finite quotients approximate the prime density.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Galois group G of an infinite Galois extension is the inverse limit of its finite Galois groups. Give G its translation-invariant probability measure, called Haar measure. Choose a set X stable under conjugation whose boundary has measure zero.

**Problem.** Let L be a possibly infinite Galois extension of a number field K, ramified at only finitely many primes. The proportion of primes with Frobenius in X tends to its Haar measure as the residue field size bound grows.

**How the definition helps.** A boundary of measure zero lets finite quotient conditions approximate X from inside and outside with arbitrarily small differences in measure. Our own argument applies finite Chebotarev to both approximations. In our own counterexample, the cyclotomic ℤ₃-extension of ℚ has Galois group the additive group of 3-adic integers. The countable set of prime Frobenius elements has measure zero but contains the Frobenius of every unramified prime.

**Wikipedia:** [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem). It says: “Let X be a subset of G that is stable under conjugation and whose boundary has Haar measure zero.”

**Sources:**

- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Odd torsion removes norm obstructions

**Remember:** Odd torsion cannot see an obstruction of order two.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R70 (\\(K\\)-theory of global fields), 19D50. arXiv math.KT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite extension L/F of number fields, viewing each L-vector space as an F-vector space gives a map on K-groups called the norm. The p-primary torsion subgroup consists of elements killed by some power of the prime p.

**Problem.** For i ≥ 1 and odd p, the norm in degree 2i maps onto the p-primary torsion of F from that of L. For ℚ(i) over ℚ, surjectivity fails on the 2-primary torsion in degree two.

**How the definition helps.** Restricting to odd-primary torsion removes the obstruction at real embeddings, in our own explanation. Lim proves the surjectivity statement. In our own example, the product symbol {−1,−1} formed from two negative units in K₂(ℚ) has order two and remains nonzero over ℝ. The norm from ℂ gives zero under the real sign symbol, so this class cannot come from ℚ(i).

**Paper or page:** [Norm principle for even K-groups of number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06482). It says: “is surjective for every odd prime p.”

**Sources:**

- [Meng Fai Lim, Norm Principle for Even K-groups of Number Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40840-022-01413-x)

### Exceptional local field extensions give the ramification bound for exceptional covers

**Remember:** An exceptional cover gives a bijection over infinitely many finite extensions.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let X→Y be a finite separable cover of smooth geometrically integral curves over 𝔽q. It is exceptional if the induced map on 𝔽qᵏ-points is bijective for infinitely many positive integers k.

**Problem.** For an exceptional cover X→Y over 𝔽q, the ramification index at each 𝔽q-rational point of X is coprime to q−1. This theorem of Guralnick and Müller generalizes a result of Lenstra that settled conjectures of Carlitz and Wan.

**How the definition helps.** Completing at a rational point produces an exceptional local extension by Theorem 3.3. Its degree is the ramification index because the residue fields agree (our own explanation). Theorem 2.1 makes that degree coprime to q−1.

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional extensions of local fields and the Carlitz--Wan conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12877v1). It says: “As a consequence, we obtain three new proofs, using quite different tools, of a theorem of Guralnick and Müller about ramification indices in exceptional maps between curves over 𝔽q.”

### Logarithmic coordinates diagonalize graded differentiation

**Remember:** In the basis dt/t, differentiating a pole multiplies its coefficient by minus its order.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In the Laurent series field k((t)), let k be a perfect field of characteristic p, so every element has a pth root. Write continuous differentials as multiples of dt/t. Filter both functions and differentials by allowing their coefficients to have poles of order at most n.

**Problem.** On the quotient that retains only the coefficient of pole order n, differentiation acts by multiplication by −n in the basis dt/t.

**How the definition helps.** Using dt/t keeps the coefficient at the same pole order (our own calculation). Differentiating t⁻ⁿ gives −n times t⁻ⁿ dt/t, so the induced map vanishes when p divides n. The basis dt would shift the order by one. The cited lemma also proves that the identification on these quotients is independent of the parameter.

**Paper or page:** [Ramification groups of some finite Galois extensions of maximal nilpotency class over local fields of positive characteristic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07928v4). It says: “The derivation d induces a morphism ∂ : Grₙ K → Grₙ Ω¹ₖ. We have ∂ = −n ⋅ μ.”

**Sources:**

### Drinfeld division points detect norms

**Remember:** A zero symbol means the norm residue action fixes the division point.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over a local field of positive characteristic, a formal Drinfeld module uses additive power series for scalar multiplication. Assume stable reduction of height one, as in the cited proposition, and that L contains all points killed by the chosen division map. For α in the maximal ideal, choose a division point ξ mapping to α. For nonzero β in L, the symbol subtracts ξ from its image under the automorphism assigned to β by local reciprocity.

**Problem.** The formal Drinfeld norm residue symbol is zero exactly when β is a norm from the field obtained by adjoining ξ.

**How the definition helps.** Defining the symbol as a difference replaces an explicit formula with a test for fixing one point (our own). The conjugates of ξ differ from ξ by division torsion, which already lies in L (our own). The Galois group therefore acts by translations and is abelian (our own). Local reciprocity says the elements acting trivially on L(ξ) are precisely its norms (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The norm residue symbol for formal Drinfeld modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10368v1). It says: “β is a norm from L(ξ)”

**Sources:**

- [Marwa Ala Eddine, The norm residue symbol for formal Drinfeld modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10368v1)

### Drinfeld symbols commute with norms

**Remember:** An Artin action upstairs restricts to the action of the norm downstairs.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over a local field of positive characteristic, a formal Drinfeld module uses additive power series for scalar multiplication. Assume stable reduction of height one, as in the cited proposition, and that L contains all points killed by the chosen division map. For α in the maximal ideal, choose a division point ξ mapping to α. For nonzero β in L, the symbol subtracts ξ from its image under the automorphism assigned to β by local reciprocity.

**Problem.** Let M/L be finite separable, let α belong to the maximal ideal of L, and let β be nonzero in M. The symbol over M equals the symbol over L evaluated at α and the norm of β.

**How the definition helps.** Using the same division point in both fields replaces comparison of explicit symbol formulas by restriction of automorphisms (our own). Local reciprocity says the automorphism attached to β restricts to the automorphism attached to its field norm (our own). Their displacements of ξ therefore agree (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The norm residue symbol for formal Drinfeld modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10368v1). It says: “Then (\\alpha ,\\beta )<sub>M,n</sub> =(\\alpha ,\\operatorname {N}<sub>M\|L</sub>(\\beta ))<sub>L,n</sub>.”

**Sources:**

- [Marwa Ala Eddine, The norm residue symbol for formal Drinfeld modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10368v1)

### Deleting one factor restores continuity

**Remember:** Remove the factor whose exponent behaves discontinuously in the p-adic distance.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S40 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions), 11M41. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix an odd prime p. For every positive multiple n of p−1, define the corrected value A(n)=(1−pⁿ⁻¹)ζ(1−n). Measure distances using \|a−b\|ₚ=p⁻ᵛ, where v is the exponent of p in a−b for a≠b.

**Problem.** These corrected values extend continuously in the p-adic variable n away from n=0, where the extension has a pole. For p=5, the original values have no continuous extension at n=4.

**How the definition helps.** Kubota–Leopoldt interpolation gives the corrected values a continuous extension away from the pole (our own explanation). For p=5, the integers n=4+4·5ᵏ tend 5-adically to 4, while 5ⁿ⁻¹ tends to zero. Thus ζ(1−n) tends to A(4)=(1−5³)ζ(−3). Since ζ(−3)≠0, this differs from ζ(−3) (our own calculation).

**Wikipedia:** [P-adic L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_L-function). It says: “except that the Euler factor at p is removed, otherwise it would not be p-adically continuous.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regularization bounds Bernoulli weights

**Remember:** Subtract the rescaled Bernoulli weight to cancel the denominator N.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, \\(p\\)-adic integration, etc.)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix an odd prime p and positive integers d and c, with c ≥ 2 coprime to dp. At modulus N = dpⁿ, give each least nonnegative representative a the weight w(a) = a/N − 1/2. Let b represent c⁻¹a modulo N in the same range. The corrected weight is w(a) − cw(b).

**Problem.** For odd p the regularized distribution is a bounded p-adic measure, even though the original Bernoulli distribution is not.

**How the definition helps.** The congruence cb≡a modulo N makes (a−cb)/N integral (our own calculation). The corrected weight adds (c−1)/2, also p-adically integral for odd p. Bernoulli weights add under subdivision, and multiplication by c permutes the subdivisions, so the bounded corrected weights still add correctly. For d=a=1 the original weights have unbounded p-adic magnitude (our own example).

**Paper or page:** [Dirichlet Series Expansions of p-adic L-Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02851v3). It says: “Let p be a prime, c, d ∈ ℕ, and c ≥ 2 such that (c, dp) = 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Dirichlet Series Expansions of p-adic L-Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02851v3)

### Convolution lifts Gaussian periods

**Remember:** Fourier transformation turns the lift of periods into a power of Gauss sums.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11T22 (Cyclotomy), 11T24. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let e≥2 divide q−1 and identify the cyclic quotient of 𝔽q× by its eth powers with the additive group ℤ/eℤ. The Gaussian period at each index sums a fixed nontrivial additive character ψ over the corresponding coset. In extensions, label elements by their norms’ indices and use the additive character ψ composed with the trace.

**Problem.** Over the degree n extension, the Gaussian period function equals the n-fold cyclic convolution of the base function times the sign (−1)ⁿ⁻¹.

**How the definition helps.** The Fourier transform of the period function consists of Gauss sums (our own explanation). Davenport–Hasse lifts each sum to its nth power times (−1)ⁿ⁻¹. Since Fourier transformation turns cyclic convolution into multiplication, inversion gives the stated convolution power.

**Paper or page:** [Davenport and Hasse's theorems and lifts of multiplication matrices of Gaussian periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14872). It says: “is the n-fold product of ηᵣ with respect to the convolution product.”

### Conductor bounds complete trace errors

**Remember:** One conductor controls both the size and the number of error terms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F be a middle-extension ℓ-adic sheaf on the affine line over 𝔽q, with ℓ prime to q. Its conductor is its generic rank plus ∑ₓ(1+Swanₓ(F)) over geometric singular points on the projective line. At each singular point the middle extension takes the local inertia invariants, and Swanₓ measures wild ramification.

**Problem.** Assume all Frobenius eigenvalues at closed points of the largest locally constant open set U have complex modulus one. Sum the Frobenius traces of F over the whole affine line over 𝔽q. This differs from the Frobenius trace on second compactly supported geometric cohomology of U with coefficients F by O(c²√q), with an absolute constant.

**How the definition helps.** The conductor controls both the number of omitted points and the number of eigenvalues in the error term. Our own explanation uses the Euler characteristic formula for a curve to bound the dimension of first compactly supported cohomology. Deligne bounds the modulus of each of its eigenvalues by √q. Each omitted fiber contributes at most the rank.

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “Taking logarithmic derivatives of both formal power series produces a statement on sums of traces for each finite field extension E of the base field k:”

### Disjoint characters preserve hypergeometric purity

**Remember:** Disjoint lists prevent a character from canceling a parameter.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take two length-n lists of multiplicative characters on 𝔽𝓆, with n ≥ 1. Call them disjoint when no character occurs in both. For nonzero tuples x and y with ∏xᵢ = t∏yᵢ, multiply the first characters on xᵢ and the inverse second characters on yᵢ. Multiply by ψ(Σxᵢ − Σyᵢ), where ψ is a nontrivial additive character, and sum over these tuples.

**Problem.** For disjoint lists and t different from zero and one, the sum is a signed trace of n eigenvalues. Each eigenvalue has modulus q raised to (2n − 1)/2, so the sum has modulus at most n times that number.

**How the definition helps.** Disjointness prevents a matching character from canceling between the lists and changing the predicted eigenvalue size. Our own example takes both lists to contain just the trivial character. For t different from zero and one, the sum becomes the sum of ψ((t − 1)y) over nonzero y, which equals −1. Katz’s hypergeometric sheaf theorem gives the rank and absolute values for disjoint lists.

**Paper or page:** [Traces of Hecke Operators via Hypergeometric Character Sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02918). It says: “are algebraic numbers and have the same absolute value”

**Sources:**

### Fourier sheaves exclude completion spikes

**Remember:** Exclude additive characters to keep Fourier mass spread out.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 11L26. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Start with a coefficient system on the affine line over 𝔽ₚ, extended across missing points by taking locally invariant vectors. Assume its Frobenius eigenvalues on the regular part have complex absolute value one. Call it a Fourier sheaf if none of its irreducible pieces over the algebraic closure comes from an additive character x ↦ ψ(ax). Include a = 0 in this test.

**Problem.** Write K for the function giving the Frobenius trace at each point. The conductor c adds the rank to the sum of 1 + Swan over all singularities, including any at infinity. On each integer interval of length at most p, the sum of K has modulus O(c²√p log p), with an absolute constant.

**How the definition helps.** Excluding additive characters removes the constituents whose Fourier transforms concentrate at a single frequency. Our own counterexample is the constant function, whose sum on a full interval equals p. The applied cohomology lectures bound the other Fourier coefficients and sum them against those of the interval. Here Swan measures ramification from the field characteristic.

**Wikipedia:** [Quadratic residue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_residue). It says: “for any nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ(n) modulo q and any integers M and N,”

### Frobenius traces give Kloosterman recurrences

**Remember:** A Kloosterman sum over an extension is the negative trace of a Frobenius power.

*True by definition.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a nonzero a∈𝔽q and a nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽q. In the degree n extension, define S(n) as the sum of ψ(Tr(ax+1/x)) over all nonzero x, using the trace to 𝔽q. Use first compactly supported geometric cohomology of the punctured line with the Artin–Schreier sheaf attached to ψ and x↦ax+1/x (our own description).

**Problem.** Write S(n) for the sum in degree n. For n ≥ 1, it satisfies S(n+2) = −S(1)S(n+1) − bS(n), where b = (S(1)² + S(2))/2.

**How the definition helps.** In our own deduction, the cohomology description gives all extension sums as negative traces of powers of one two-dimensional operator F. The cited calculation gives dimension two in degree one and zero elsewhere. The cohomological trace formula identifies each sum with −tr(Fⁿ), replacing a separate calculation in every field. The characteristic polynomial of F then gives the recurrence, with b equal to its determinant.

**Paper or page:** [Matrix Kloosterman sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00762). It says: “\\\[\\dim H<sup>i<sub>c</sub></sup>(\\mathbb {A}<sup>1\\setminus</sup> \\mathbb {A}<sup>0</sup>,f\_\\alpha )=\\left \\{\\begin {array}{ll}2, &amp; \\mathrm {if\~} i=1,\\\\ 0, &amp; \\mathrm {if\~} i\\neq 1\\end {array}\\right .\\\]”

**Sources:**

### Geometric nonisomorphism forces small correlations

**Remember:** Compare sheaves after extending the field to detect the main term.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On an open subset U of the affine line over 𝔽𝓆, take two locally constant systems of vector spaces F and G. Use ℓ-adic coefficients for a prime ℓ different from the characteristic. Assume both systems stay irreducible over the algebraic closure, meaning neither has a proper nonzero invariant subspace there. Call them geometrically distinct if they remain nonisomorphic there.

**Problem.** Assume both systems have weight zero, meaning all pointwise Frobenius eigenvalues have complex absolute value one. For geometrically distinct systems, sum the trace of F times the conjugate trace of G over U(𝔽𝓆). The modulus is O(√q), with constant depending on the ranks, omitted points and local ramification.

**How the definition helps.** Geometric distinction excludes invariant maps, by Schur’s lemma (our own explanation). For example, two constant rank-one systems with Frobenius scalars 1 and −1 give a correlation of modulus q on the affine line. They become isomorphic over the algebraic closure. Deligne’s bound controls the remaining trace-formula terms when the systems are geometrically distinct (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “where the cohomology groups are replaced by cohomology with coefficients in the sheaf.”

### Good twists erase boundary terms

**Remember:** A good twist leaves no cohomology at zero or infinity.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F be a locally constant system of r-dimensional ℓ-adic vector spaces on the line with zero removed over 𝔽𝓆, with ℓ prime to q. Twist F by the one-dimensional system associated to a multiplicative character χ through the power covering of the nonzero line. Call χ good if extension by zero agrees with derived direct image on the projective line for this twist. These extensions differ only through local cohomology at zero and infinity.

**Problem.** Over any finite extension field, at most 2r multiplicative characters fail this test. For every good character, ordinary cohomology of the twist agrees with its cohomology with compact supports.

**How the definition helps.** Agreement of the two extensions gives identical cohomology on the projective line (our own explanation). For the constant system the trivial twist leaves nonzero boundary invariants. A bad twist must cancel a local tame character on the subspace fixed by wild inertia. At each of the two boundary points that subspace has dimension at most r, giving the count.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**How the definition helps.** The face test allows the Adolphson–Sperber theorem to concentrate cohomology in one degree with dimension equal to normalized volume (our own explanation). **Remember:** An odd number of standard symplectic factors cannot contain a fixed vector.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

Assume only the identity fractional linear map over the algebraic closure preserves F up to a rank-one twist. For a normal list, the product of transformed traces sums to O(√p) over finite inputs away from poles.

Repeating the identity twice instead allows the symplectic pairing to contribute an invariant. Independence for distinct transforms and Deligne’s bound give the estimate, with the constant depending on list length, rank and ramification.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.
