### Almost uniform convergence gives Egorov’s theorem one exceptional set

**Remember:** Discard one set of arbitrarily small measure to get uniform convergence.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Convergence is almost uniform if, for every ε &gt; 0, convergence is uniform outside some measurable set of measure less than ε.

**Problem.** On a finite measure space, suppose real measurable functions converge to a real measurable limit outside a set of measure zero. Then they converge almost uniformly.

**How the definition helps.** Almost uniform convergence lets one exceptional set absorb the errors at every accuracy (our own). For each k, the points where some error after index N exceeds 1/k form sets that decrease to measure zero as N grows (our own). Finite total measure makes their measures tend to zero, so one N per k can be chosen with measures summing to less than ε (our own). Outside the union of these sets, convergence is uniform (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Egorov's Theorem](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Egorov's_Theorem). It says: “Then fₙ converges a.u. to f.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Borel sets on the target make measurable functions compose

**Remember:** Pull back only Borel sets, so a Borel map after it is safe.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 28A05. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Lebesgue measurable function f goes from ℝ with the Lebesgue sets to ℂ with the Borel sets. The preimage of each Borel set must be Lebesgue measurable. So the σ-algebra on the source is large, but the one on the target is only the Borel sets.

**Problem.** If f is Lebesgue measurable and g is Borel measurable, then g ∘ f is Lebesgue measurable. In particular, continuous functions of measurable functions, and sums and products of measurable functions, are measurable.

**How the definition helps.** For each Borel B, g⁻¹(B) is Borel, so f⁻¹(g⁻¹(B)) is Lebesgue measurable (our own). A pair of measurable functions is measurable because open rectangles from a countable basis have measurable preimages (our own). Addition and multiplication are continuous functions of this pair (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Measurable function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_function). It says: “Indeed, two Lebesgue-measurable functions may be constructed in such a way as to make their composition non-Lebesgue-measurable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Completeness preserves measurability after changes on a null set

**Remember:** A complete measure lets you change a function anywhere on a null set.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A complete measure makes every subset of a measurable set of measure zero measurable. An incomplete measure need not include those subsets in its domain.

**Problem.** On a complete measure space, a real function that agrees with a measurable function outside a null set is measurable.

**How the definition helps.** For each Borel set, its new inverse image combines the old inverse image outside the null set with a subset inside it (our own). Completeness makes that subset measurable (our own). Without completeness, the indicator of a nonmeasurable subset of a measurable null set agrees almost everywhere with zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lebesgue measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_measure). It says: “However, as a measure on only the Borel sets, it is not complete: a subset of a Borel set of measure zero need not itself be Borel.”

**Paper or page:** [Function A.E. Equal to Measurable Function in Complete Measure Space is Measurable](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Function_A.E._Equal_to_Measurable_Function_in_Complete_Measure_Space_is_Measurable). It says: “Then g is Σ-measurable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Finite test sets give local convergence in measure

**Remember:** Measure the bad sets one finite piece at a time.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Local convergence in measure tests each measurable set of finite measure. On that set, the measure where the error exceeds any fixed positive threshold must tend to zero. Global convergence tests the whole space at once.

**Problem.** Almost everywhere convergence of real measurable functions implies local convergence in measure on any measure space.

**How the definition helps.** A finite test set lets us use continuity of measure for decreasing sets (our own). Within it, take the union of all error sets from index n onward (our own). These unions decrease to a null set, so their measures tend to zero (our own). On ℝ the indicators of \[n, n+1\] tend pointwise to zero, yet each interval has measure one (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence in measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_in_measure). It says: “if (fₙ) converges to f almost everywhere, then (fₙ) converges to f locally in measure.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Measurable level sets stay measurable under pointwise limits

**Remember:** For a strict limit bound, leave a little room above the threshold.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A real-valued function is measurable if every set where its value exceeds a rational threshold is measurable. This is equivalent to testing inverse images of all Borel sets.

**Problem.** If real-valued measurable functions converge pointwise to a real-valued function, then their limit is measurable.

**How the definition helps.** The threshold test expresses a limit level set using only countable unions and intersections (our own). The limit exceeds t exactly when all sufficiently late terms exceed some rational q &gt; t (our own). The generator theorem does the work of equating the threshold test with the test on all Borel sets (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Pointwise Limit of Measurable Functions is Measurable](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Pointwise_Limit_of_Measurable_Functions_is_Measurable). It says: “Then the pointwise limit limₙ→∞ fₙ: X → ℝ̄ is also Σ-measurable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The subsequence test makes continuous functions preserve convergence in measure

**Remember:** Follow each almost everywhere convergent subsequence through the continuous function.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Convergence in measure means that for each positive threshold, the measure where the absolute error exceeds that threshold tends to zero. On a finite measure space, an equivalent test requires every subsequence to have a further subsequence converging to the same limit almost everywhere.

**Problem.** On a finite measure space, suppose real measurable functions fₙ converge in measure to a real measurable function f. For every continuous real function h, the functions h(fₙ) converge to h(f) in measure.

**How the definition helps.** Continuity preserves ordinary limits at every point where the further subsequence converges (our own). The work moves to the subsequence criterion, which uses a choice of indices with summable error-set measures (our own). The usual definition instead tracks the measure of sets on which the error exceeds a fixed threshold (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence in measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_in_measure). It says: “converges to f locally in measure if and only if every subsequence has in turn a subsequence that converges to f almost everywhere.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Counting measure turns nonnegative series into integrals

**Remember:** Counting measure gives each term of the series weight one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Counting measure on ℕ gives a finite set its number of elements and an infinite set measure ∞. Each singleton thus has mass one.

**Problem.** For any nonnegative function on ℕ, its integral for counting measure equals the sum of its values, even when the sum is infinite.

**How the definition helps.** On a finite set, each value contributes exactly once because its singleton has mass one (our own). Monotone convergence does the work of passing from finite initial segments to the whole sum (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Integral of Positive Function with respect to Counting Measure on Natural Numbers](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Integral_of_Positive_Function_with_respect_to_Counting_Measure_on_Natural_Numbers). It says: “Then: ∫ f dμ = ∑ₙ₌₁<sup>∞</sup> f(n)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Differences of positive integrals make the signed integral linear

**Remember:** Add the nonnegative pieces before subtracting their integrals.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a real measurable f with finite integral of \|f\|, define ∫f as ∫f⁺ − ∫f⁻. Here f⁺ = max(f, 0) and f⁻ = max(−f, 0).

**Problem.** The Lebesgue integral is linear on real integrable functions. If f = a − b with nonnegative integrable a and b, then ∫f = ∫a − ∫b.

**How the definition helps.** Using arbitrary differences of nonnegative integrable functions avoids finding the positive and negative parts of each sum (our own). If f = a − b, then a + f⁻ = b + f⁺ (our own). Additivity for nonnegative integrals gives the same integral from either representation (our own). Add or scale the two terms separately, exchanging them when the scalar is negative (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Integral of Integrable Function is Homogeneous](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Integral_of_Integrable_Function_is_Homogeneous), [Integral of Integrable Function is Additive](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Integral_of_Integrable_Function_is_Additive). It says: “Then λf is μ-integrable, and: ∫ λf dμ = λ ∫ f dμ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Large-power norms find essential suprema

**Remember:** Large powers detect every height that occurs on positive measure.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The essential supremum of \|f\| is the infimum of all extended nonnegative bounds M for which \|f\| ≤ M almost everywhere. For finite p ≥ 1, the p-norm of f is the pth root of ∫\|f\|ᵖ.

**Problem.** On a probability space, the p-norms of a measurable function tend to the essential supremum of its absolute value as p tends to infinity. Both norms and limit may equal infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Ignoring sets of measure zero removes peaks that no integral can detect (our own). For example, the indicator of one point in \[0, 1\] has supremum one but every p-norm zero (our own). Each height below the essential supremum is exceeded on a set of positive measure, and the pth root of that measure tends to one (our own). The essential supremum bounds every norm because the space has measure one (our own).

**nLab:** [essential supremum](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/essential+supremum). It says: “But we ignore things that happen only on a null set.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Tail infima prove Fatou

**Remember:** Take the infimum before integrating, then let the tail move.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a sequence of extended real numbers, the limit inferior is its smallest subsequential limit. Equivalently, take the infimum of each tail, then the supremum of these infima.

**Problem.** For nonnegative measurable functions, the integral of their pointwise limit inferior is at most the limit inferior of their integrals.

**How the definition helps.** The tail formula gives increasing measurable functions without choosing a subsequence at each point (our own). Each tail infimum has integral at most the infimum of the integrals over that tail (our own). Monotone convergence identifies the limit of these integrals with the integral of the pointwise limit inferior (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Fatou's Lemma for Integrals/Positive Measurable Functions](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Fatou's_Lemma_for_Integrals/Positive_Measurable_Functions). It says: “∫ lim inf fₙ dμ ≤ lim inf ∫ fₙ dμ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Testing a density on every measurable set makes it unique

**Remember:** Test where one density is larger than the other.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A density of a finite measure ν relative to μ is a nonnegative measurable function. Its integral over each measurable set equals the ν-measure of that set. Matching only the total mass does not define a density.

**Problem.** Two densities of the same finite measure relative to the same measure μ are equal outside a μ-null set.

**How the definition helps.** Testing where one density exceeds the other rules out a positive difference on a set of positive measure (our own). There the integrals agree and are finite, so the nonnegative difference vanishes almost everywhere (our own). Exchange the two densities to rule out the opposite difference (our own). Testing total mass alone would give the same answer for the indicators of either half of the unit interval (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Radon-Nikodym Theorem](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Radon-Nikodym_Theorem). It says: “then: g₁ = g₂ μ-almost everywhere.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Lebesgue integral lets limits pass inside the integral

**Remember:** Measure each level of a simple function, then approximate from below.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For nonnegative measurable f, take the supremum of the integrals of all nonnegative simple functions s ≤ f. Integrate a simple function by summing each distinct positive value times the measure of its level set. For an integrable real function, subtract the integral of its negative part from that of its positive part (our own).

**Problem.** If nonnegative measurable functions increase pointwise to f, their integrals tend to ∫f. If measurable real functions converge pointwise to f under a common integrable absolute bound, their integrals tend to ∫f.

**How the definition helps.** Measurability passes to pointwise limits, and the hypotheses ensure that each limit has a defined integral (our own). The monotone convergence theorem handles increasing nonnegative functions, and the dominated convergence theorem handles the common integrable bound (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lebesgue integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral), [Dominated convergence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominated_convergence_theorem). It says: “The main purpose of the Lebesgue integral is to provide an integral notion where limits of integrals hold under mild assumptions.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Lebesgue, Intégrale, longueur, aire, Ann. Mat. Pura Appl. 7 (1902), 231–359, doi:10.1007/BF02420592](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02420592)
- [H. Lebesgue, Leçons sur l'intégration et la recherche des fonctions primitives, Gauthier-Villars, Paris, 1904](https://archive.org/details/leconegrarecher00leberich)

### The lower-sum definition makes the Lebesgue integral monotone

**Remember:** A higher function admits every lower test of a smaller one.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a nonnegative measurable function, define its integral as the supremum of integrals of nonnegative simple functions below it. A simple function takes finitely many values, with a measurable set of points for each value.

**Problem.** If nonnegative measurable functions f and g satisfy f ≤ g, then ∫f dμ ≤ ∫g dμ.

**How the definition helps.** Every simple function below f also lies below g, so the supremum for g includes every test for f (our own). Defining the integral by limits instead requires proving that all increasing simple approximations give the same limit (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Integral of Positive Measurable Function is Monotone](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Integral_of_Positive_Measurable_Function_is_Monotone). It says: “This can be summarized by saying that ∫ · dμ is monotone.”

### The lower-test integral makes Markov’s bound a single comparison

**Remember:** Use the threshold as a lower bound wherever the function reaches it.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a nonnegative measurable function, the Lebesgue integral is the supremum of integrals of nonnegative simple functions below it. A simple function takes only finitely many values on measurable sets.

**Problem.** For a nonnegative measurable function f and any t &gt; 0, the measure of {f ≥ t} is at most (∫f dμ)/t. In particular, convergence in Lᵖ implies convergence in measure for every finite p ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** The function equal to t on {f ≥ t} and zero elsewhere is one of the simple functions below f (our own). Its integral already gives the required bound, without taking limits along simple approximations (our own). The equivalence of the two integral constructions justifies using either one (our own). Applying the bound to the pth power of the absolute error gives convergence in measure (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Markov's Inequality](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Markov's_Inequality). It says: “μ({x ∈ A : \|f(x)\| ≥ t}) ≤ (1/t) ∫ₐ \|f\| dμ”

### Absolute integrability rules out conflicting orders in Fubini’s theorem

**Remember:** Integrate the absolute value before trusting a change of order.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 28A25. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A real measurable function is Lebesgue integrable if its absolute value has finite integral. A measure space is σ-finite if countably many sets of finite measure cover it.

**Problem.** For an integrable function on a product of two σ-finite measure spaces, almost every slice in either direction is integrable. Both orders of integration give the integral over the product.

**How the definition helps.** Absolute integrability makes both parts finite, so Tonelli’s theorem lets us integrate the positive and negative parts separately. On pairs of positive integers with counting measure, put 1 at (i,i), −1 at (i,i+1), and zero elsewhere (our own). Every row sums to zero, but the first column sums to one and all later columns sum to zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Fubini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem). It says: “Use the condition that the functions are integrable to write them as the difference of two positive integrable functions and apply Tonelli's theorem to each of these.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Measurable rectangles make every section of a product set measurable

**Remember:** Taking a section commutes with complements and countable unions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The product σ-algebra is the smallest σ-algebra containing all rectangles with measurable sides. A σ-algebra is a nonempty family closed under complements and countable unions. A vertical section fixes the first coordinate.

**Problem.** Every vertical or horizontal section of a set in the product σ-algebra is measurable in the corresponding factor.

**How the definition helps.** Rectangles have measurable sections, and taking sections preserves complements and countable unions (our own). Thus the sets with measurable sections form a σ-algebra containing every rectangle (our own). Completion can break this conclusion for individual sections (our own). In the plane, every subset of a vertical line is Lebesgue measurable, even one whose vertical section is nonmeasurable (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Vertical Section of Measurable Set is Measurable](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Vertical_Section_of_Measurable_Set_is_Measurable). It says: “where Eₓ is the x-vertical section of E.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Requiring σ-finite measures makes Tonelli's theorem true

**Remember:** σ-finite spaces can be cut into countably many finite pieces.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A measure space is σ-finite when it is a countable union of sets of finite measure.

**Problem.** For two σ-finite measure spaces, consider a nonnegative function measurable for the product σ-algebra. Its two iterated integrals both equal its integral against the product measure.

**How the definition helps.** Countably many finite pieces let Tonelli’s theorem pass from finite spaces to the full product by monotone convergence (our own). Give \[0, 1\] Lebesgue measure in one factor and counting measure in the other. Counting measure here is not σ-finite. The diagonal indicator has iterated integrals zero and one, so they cannot both equal its product integral.

**Wikipedia:** [Fubini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem). It says: “This shows that Tonelli's theorem can fail for spaces that are not σ-finite no matter which product measure is chosen.”

### Testing box volumes identifies the product as Lebesgue measure

**Remember:** A product of boxes is a box, and their volumes multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Borel Lebesgue measure on Euclidean space is the unique measure that gives each half-open box its volume. A product measure gives a measurable rectangle the product of the measures of its sides.

**Problem.** The product of Borel Lebesgue measures on ℝᵐ and ℝⁿ is Borel Lebesgue measure on ℝᵐ⁺ⁿ.

**How the definition helps.** Each half-open box splits into a box in each factor, so the product measure gives it the prescribed volume (our own). Uniqueness from box volumes replaces a comparison of arbitrary box covers (our own). This uses the fact that the product of the Borel σ-algebras is the Euclidean Borel σ-algebra (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Product measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_measure). It says: “the completion procedure is needed to extend the Borel measure into the Lebesgue measure, or to extend the product of two Lebesgue measures to give the Lebesgue measure on the product space.”

**Paper or page:** [Existence and Uniqueness of Lebesgue Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Existence_and_Uniqueness_of_Lebesgue_Measure). It says: “Then Lebesgue measure, the extension of λⁿ to the Borel σ-algebra ℬ(ℝⁿ), exists and is unique.”

### Standard Borel spaces always have conditional distributions

**Remember:** Standard Borel spaces are the measurable spaces of Polish spaces.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, \\(\\sigma\\)-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 60A10, 60B05. arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measurable space is standard Borel if its σ-algebra is the Borel σ-algebra of some Polish topology. A Polish topology is one given by a complete separable metric. Up to isomorphism, the standard Borel spaces are the countable discrete spaces and ℝ.

**Problem.** On a standard Borel probability space, every sub-σ-algebra admits a regular conditional distribution of the identity. Given an input probability, every Markov kernel between standard Borel spaces has a Bayesian inverse, unique almost surely under the output law.

**How the definition helps.** The regular conditional distribution theorem applies to standard Borel outcome spaces for any conditioning sub-σ-algebra (our own). Apply disintegration to the joint law from the input probability and kernel to obtain the inverse (our own). A countable generating class makes its uniqueness simultaneous outside one output null set (our own).

It says: “They provide a setting for many constructions in probability theory, including conditional probability, disintegration, and countable products.”

### The partition definition of total variation makes it the least dominating measure

**Remember:** A dominating measure pays for every partition at once.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions), 28A25. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each finite measurable partition of A, sum the absolute values of its pieces’ signed or complex masses. The supremum of these sums is the total variation \|μ\|(A) (our own).

**Problem.** Always \|μ(A)\| ≤ \|μ\|(A). Every positive measure ν with \|μ(A)\| ≤ ν(A) for all measurable A satisfies \|μ\|(A) ≤ ν(A).

**How the definition helps.** The partition containing only A gives \|μ(A)\| ≤ \|μ\|(A) (our own). If ν dominates \|μ(B)\| on every measurable B, each partition sum is bounded by the sum of the ν-masses (our own). That sum equals ν(A), so taking the supremum proves the second inequality (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Total Variation is Smallest Measure exceeding Modulus of Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Total_Variation_is_Smallest_Measure_exceeding_Modulus_of_Measure). It says: “\|μ(A)\| ≤ ν(A) for each A ∈ Σ.”

### Total variation adds both signs

**Remember:** Count both signs as positive mass.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Choose a measurable partition P, N of the space for a finite signed measure μ. Require every measurable subset of P to have nonnegative mass and every measurable subset of N to have nonpositive mass. Define \|μ\|(A) = μ(A ∩ P) − μ(A ∩ N) for measurable A (our own).

**Problem.** The total variation of a finite signed measure is a nonnegative measure.

**How the definition helps.** The formula adds two nonnegative measures, so it gives a measure. The Hahn decomposition theorem supplies P and N (our own). The triangle inequality bounds every sum of absolute masses over a finite measurable partition of A by this formula (our own). Splitting A along P and N attains the bound, so the value is independent of the decomposition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Variation of Signed Measure is Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Variation_of_Signed_Measure_is_Measure). It says: “Then \|μ\| is a measure.”

### Finite mass controls small sets

**Remember:** With finite mass, control at zero also controls nearby values.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let μ and ν be measures on the same measurable space, with ν finite. Absolute continuity means that ν vanishes on every measurable set of μ-mass zero.

**Problem.** Suppose ν is finite and absolutely continuous with respect to μ. For every ε &gt; 0, some δ &gt; 0 ensures ν(A) &lt; ε for every measurable A with μ(A) &lt; δ.

**How the definition helps.** Finite total mass makes ν continuous on decreasing sequences of sets. In our own proof, if the bound fails for some ε, choose sets Aₙ with μ(Aₙ) ≤ 2⁻ⁿ and ν(Aₙ) ≥ ε. The unions of the tails decrease to a set of μ-measure zero but keep ν-measure at least ε, a contradiction. Our own counterexample without finiteness takes ν as counting measure on the positive integers and μ({n}) = 2⁻ⁿ.

**Paper or page:** [Characterization of Absolutely Continuous Measures](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Characterization_of_Absolutely_Continuous_Measures). It says: “for each ε &gt; 0 there exists δ &gt; 0 such that for each A ∈ Σ with μ(A) &lt; δ, we have ν(A) &lt; ε.”

### Truly continuous measures give Radon–Nikodym without σ-finiteness

**Remember:** Truly continuous means absolute continuity controlled by one set of finite measure.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A25. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ν be a real finitely additive set function on the measurable sets of a measure space with measure μ. True continuity requires, for every ε &gt; 0, a measurable E of finite μ-measure and a number δ &gt; 0. Every measurable F with μ(E ∩ F) &lt; δ must then satisfy \|ν(F)\| &lt; ε.

**Problem.** A real finitely additive ν has an integrable density with respect to μ exactly when ν is truly continuous with respect to μ. A density f satisfies ν(E) = ∫<sub>E</sub> f dμ for every measurable E.

**How the definition helps.** True continuity supplies the finite-measure control in the Radon–Nikodym theorem for arbitrary measure spaces (our own). Counting measure on an uncountable space has no nonempty null sets. On the countable–cocountable σ-algebra, the probability assigning zero to countable sets is absolutely continuous. It fails the finite-set test because the complement of each finite E has probability one (our own).

**nLab:** [Radon–Nikodym derivative](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon%E2%80%93Nikodym+derivative). It says: “The following example shows that the condition of being truly continuous is necessary in the non-σ-finite case.”

### Measure densities multiply

**Remember:** Changing the reference measure twice multiplies the two weights.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A15 (Abstract differentiation theory, differentiation of set functions), 28A25. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A density dν/dμ is a nonnegative measurable function whose integral against μ over each measurable set equals its ν-measure. A measure is σ-finite if countably many measurable sets of finite measure cover its space.

**Problem.** Let ν, μ and λ be σ-finite positive measures on one measurable space. Suppose ν vanishes on every set of μ-measure zero and μ vanishes on every set of λ-measure zero. Then dν/dλ equals (dν/dμ)(dμ/dλ) outside a set of λ-measure zero, using finite versions of the densities.

**How the definition helps.** The integral definition allows the second weight to replace integration against the intermediate measure (our own). Check that substitution on indicators, then extend it to nonnegative functions by monotone convergence (our own). Apply it to the first weight restricted to any measurable set (our own). Existence and uniqueness of the resulting weight belong to the Radon–Nikodym theorem (our own).

### Continuous sections keep substitution measurable

**Remember:** Approximate the input by countably many values before substituting it.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 26B40. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Ω be an open subset of Euclidean space and let W(x, y) be real-valued, with y in a Euclidean space. A Carathéodory function is Lebesgue measurable in x for each y. Outside one set of x of measure zero, it is continuous in y.

**Problem.** For each Lebesgue measurable map u from Ω into the space of y values, x ↦ W(x, u(x)) is Lebesgue measurable.

**How the definition helps.** Continuity in y preserves pointwise limits after substitution outside a fixed null set (our own). Approximate u by countably valued measurable maps, whose substitutions are measurable by the condition on x (our own). For a nonmeasurable A ⊂ ℝ, take W to be the indicator of {(a, a) ∣ a ∈ A} (our own). Each section is measurable, but substituting u(x) = x gives the indicator of A (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Carathéodory function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory_function). It says: “the mapping ξ ↦ W(x, ξ) is continuous for almost every x ∈ Ω.”

### Defining convergence in measure by truncated distances makes it metrizable

**Remember:** Cap each pointwise error at one, then integrate.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 46E30. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For real measurable functions f and g, integrate min{\|f − g\|, 1} over each measurable set E of finite measure. These pseudometrics define the topology of local convergence in measure.

**Problem.** On a finite measure space, convergence in measure comes from one metric on measurable functions, once functions equal almost everywhere are identified.

**How the definition helps.** On a finite measure space, the whole-space pseudometric dominates every other one in the family. Its value is zero exactly when the functions agree almost everywhere, so it induces a metric on the quotient (our own). Splitting the integral at any positive error threshold gives the usual convergence-in-measure test (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence in measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_in_measure). It says: “When μ(X) &lt; ∞, we may consider only one metric ρ<sub>X</sub>, so the topology of convergence in finite measure is metrizable.”

**Remember:** Add up the areas of the horizontal slabs.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 26A42. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Problem.** Let f be nonnegative and measurable. Its integral equals the integral over t from 0 to ∞ of μ{f &gt; t}, also when both are infinite.

**How the definition helps.** With the slice definition, this formula is the definition itself, and Wikipedia says the integral may be defined this way. The work is proving that the slice integral agrees with the simple-function integral, in our own account. One checks it for simple functions and then passes to increasing limits with the monotone convergence theorem, in our own account.

### Bounded mass controls vague tests

**Remember:** A uniform mass bound keeps small tails small in the integral.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Measures converge vaguely if their integrals converge against every continuous function that is zero outside a compact set. A function on the line vanishes at infinity if it tends to zero as \|x\| grows. Require a single finite upper bound on all total masses.

**Problem.** Suppose finite positive Borel measures on the line converge vaguely to a finite measure and have uniformly bounded masses. Their integrals converge against every continuous function vanishing at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** A compactly supported test can approximate a vanishing test uniformly, and the mass bound controls every integral error. In our own proof, multiply the test by a cutoff that equals one on a large interval and dies away outside it. In our own counterexample, mass n at n converges vaguely to zero. Its integral against f(x) = 1/(1 + \|x\|) tends to one.

### Lipschitz tests bound closed-set masses

**Remember:** Fade a closed set’s indicator to zero just beyond its boundary.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures). arXiv math.PR, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Lipschitz test is a real function f on a metric space with a finite constant L. For all x and y it satisfies \|f(x) − f(y)\| ≤ Ld(x,y). A bounded test also has bounded range.

**Problem.** Suppose Borel probabilities on a metric space converge against every bounded Lipschitz test to a Borel probability P. For every closed C, their masses on C have limit superior at most P(C).

**How the definition helps.** Bounded Lipschitz tests include functions that decrease to the indicator of any closed set C, such as max(0, 1 − n·dist(x, C)) (our own). For fixed n, the integral bounds the mass of C from above and converges by hypothesis (our own). Letting n grow and applying bounded convergence to the limit measure gives the bound (our own). The equivalence with all bounded continuous tests is part of the Portmanteau theorem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence of measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_measures). It says: “lim sup Pₙ(C) ≤ P(C) for all closed sets C of space S”

**Remember:** Countably many finite rectangles let their masses determine the whole product.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measure is σ-finite if countably many measurable sets of finite mass cover its space. The product σ-algebra is the smallest collection containing measurable rectangles and closed under complements and countable unions.

For our own counterexample, take length and counting measure on \[0, 1\]. Summing the lengths of horizontal sections gives the diagonal mass zero. Adding length along the diagonal gives it mass one but leaves every rectangle's mass unchanged.

**Remember:** Measure each slice, then integrate the slice measures.

### Fiber averages contract integral norms

**Remember:** Average over each fiber before taking the norm.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A50 (Integration and disintegration of measures). arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ν be the image of m under φ. A disintegration is a probability kernel mᵧ carried by φ⁻¹({y}) for ν-almost every y and satisfying ∫mᵧ(A) dν(y) = m(A) for every Borel A. The fiber average of f is ∫f dmᵧ wherever defined (our own).

**Problem.** Let a Borel map carry a probability on one complete separable metric space to its image law on another. For 1 ≤ p &lt; ∞, the Lᵖ norm of the fiber average is at most the original Lᵖ norm.

**How the definition helps.** Jensen’s inequality on each fiber bounds the absolute average raised to p by the average of \|f\|ᵖ (our own). Integrating against the image law recovers ∫\|f\|ᵖ dm by disintegration (our own). Taking pth roots proves the bound (our own).

### New densities reweight fiber laws

**Remember:** Weight each fiber, then move its total weight to the image law.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A50 (Integration and disintegration of measures). arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A disintegration of m along φ is a probability kernel mᵧ carried by φ⁻¹({y}) for almost every y under the image law ν. It satisfies ∫mᵧ(A) dν(y) = m(A) for every Borel A. A probability density is a nonnegative measurable function with integral one (our own).

**Problem.** Let m be a probability on a complete separable metric space, φ a Borel map into another, and ρ a probability density. The image of ρm has density equal to the fiber average of ρ against the image of m. Where this average is positive and finite, the new conditional law is ρ times the old one, divided by the average.

**How the definition helps.** The image density is h(y) = ∫ρ dmᵧ because integrating h over any image event gives its reweighted probability (our own). Where 0 &lt; h(y) &lt; ∞, the probability ρmᵧ/h(y) stays on the same fiber (our own). Integrating it against hν cancels h and recovers ρm (our own). All remaining fibers have zero mass under hν (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Disintegration theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disintegration_theorem). It says: “for every Borel-measurable function f : Y → \[0,∞\]”

### Shared fibers glue couplings

**Remember:** Take products within fibers and average over the shared coordinate.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A50 (Integration and disintegration of measures). arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A coupling is a joint probability with prescribed coordinate laws. Given adjacent couplings, disintegrate both over their shared middle law. At almost every middle value, take the product of the two conditional laws, retain the middle coordinate, and average over its law (our own).

**Problem.** Two couplings on complete separable metric spaces with a common middle law have a joint law on three coordinates. The joint law has the original couplings as its adjacent marginals.

**How the definition helps.** Each conditional factor has total mass one, so integrating out either outer coordinate leaves the other conditional law (our own). Averaging over the middle coordinate recovers the corresponding original coupling (our own). The disintegration theorem supplies the measurable conditional laws (our own).

### Standard probability spaces make every measure-algebra map come from a point map

**Remember:** Standard spaces have enough points, so set maps come from point maps.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A60 (Measures on Boolean rings, measure algebras), 60A10. arXiv math.PR, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A probability space is standard if, after removing null sets, it is isomorphic to one of three things. These are an interval with Lebesgue measure, a countable set of atoms, or a disjoint union of both. The measure algebra is the Boolean algebra of measurable sets, with sets that differ by a null set treated as equal.

**Problem.** Between standard probability spaces, every probability-preserving Boolean homomorphism of measure algebras comes from inverse images under a measure-preserving point map. The point map is determined up to null sets.

**How the definition helps.** The spatial realization theorem represents each probability-preserving event map on standard spaces by inverse images under a point map (our own). The perforated interval has inner measure zero and outer measure one, and its induced measure algebra matches the interval’s. A point map realizing this identification would agree almost everywhere with the identity, although the perforated set contains no measurable set of full length (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Standard probability space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_probability_space). It says: “It may seem that every homomorphism of measure algebras has to correspond to some measure preserving map, but it is not so. However, for standard probability spaces each F corresponds to some f.”

**Sources:**

- [V. A. Rokhlin, On the fundamental ideas of measure theory, Mat. Sbornik 25 (67) (1949), 107–150; English translation, AMS Translations 71 (1952), 1–54](http://ma.huji.ac.il/~matang02/rohlin.pdf)

### Flat norms contract boundaries

**Remember:** Take a boundary and only the small remainder survives.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Euclidean k-current T, consider all decompositions T = R + ∂S with finite-mass currents R of dimension k and S of dimension k+1. The flat norm is the infimum of mass(R) + mass(S) over these decompositions, taking ∞ if none exists (our own).

**Problem.** The boundary operator is a contraction for the flat norm on Euclidean currents of finite flat norm.

**How the definition helps.** For each decomposition T = R + ∂S, the identity ∂² = 0 gives ∂T = ∂R (our own). Thus R fills ∂T, so its flat norm is at most mass(R) (our own). Taking the infimum over decompositions gives the contraction (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Current (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current_%28mathematics%29). It says: “they are close in the flat norm if they coincide up to a small deformation.”

**Sources:**

- [Herbert Federer and Wendell H. Fleming, Normal and Integral Currents (1960)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970227)

### Lipschitz charts preserve rectifiability

**Remember:** A Lipschitz map composes with charts and preserves Hausdorff null sets.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A countably m-rectifiable set is covered, except for an m-dimensional Hausdorff null set, by countably many Lipschitz images from subsets of ℝᵐ. One can instead use smooth charts in Euclidean space.

**Problem.** A Lipschitz map between metric spaces sends a countably m-rectifiable set to a countably m-rectifiable set, for m ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** Composing each chart with the given map gives another Lipschitz chart (our own). An L-Lipschitz map multiplies each covering diameter by at most L, so the exceptional set still has zero m-dimensional Hausdorff measure (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Rectifiable set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectifiable_set). It says: “Equivalently, the fᵢ may be taken to be Lipschitz continuous without altering the definition.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Normal components count boundary crossings

**Remember:** The projected area factor turns a boundary integral into a crossing count.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set has finite perimeter when the distributional derivative of its indicator is a finite vector measure. Its variation measures its size without cancellation. The reduced boundary consists of points where the derivative divided by its variation on shrinking centered balls is defined and approaches a unit normal.

**Problem.** Let E be a bounded set of finite perimeter in ℝⁿ. Integrate the absolute last component of its normal over the reduced boundary with respect to (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure. This equals the integral, over horizontal coordinates, of the number of reduced boundary points on each vertical line.

**How the definition helps.** The reduced boundary provides the normal needed to state the projection formula even for sets without a smooth boundary. Our own derivation uses De Giorgi’s theorem, which gives a tangent plane at almost every reduced boundary point. Projecting that plane horizontally scales area by the absolute last component of the normal. The area formula integrates this factor and counts each point in each fiber.

**Paper or page:** [The Petty projection inequality for sets of finite perimeter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07103v1). It says: “\\int\_{\\partial<sup>\\ast</sup>E}g(x)\|\\nu<sup>E<sub>y</sub></sup>(x)\|d\\mathcal{H}<sup>n-1</sup>(x)=\\int\_{\\mathbb{R}<sup>n-1</sup>}dx<sup>\\prime</sup>\\int\_{(\\partial<sup>\\ast</sup>E)\_{x<sup>\\prime</sup>}}g(x<sup>\\prime</sup>,y)d\\mathcal{H}<sup>0</sup>(y).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced boundaries ignore null holes

**Remember:** Removing a null set does not change the measured boundary.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.CA, math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set has finite perimeter if the distributional derivative of its indicator is a finite vector measure. This derivative tests the indicator by integration against derivatives of smooth functions. Its total variation measures the size of the derivative without cancellation. At a reduced boundary point, the derivative divided by its variation on shrinking centered balls is defined and tends to a unit vector.

**Problem.** Changing a set of finite perimeter on a Lebesgue null set preserves its reduced boundary. Its perimeter measure equals normalized (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure restricted to that boundary in ℝⁿ.

**How the definition helps.** The reduced boundary uses only the derivative measure, which ignores changes on null sets. Our own example removes a countable dense subset from an open ball. Every point inside the ball then belongs to the topological boundary, but the reduced boundary stays on the sphere. De Giorgi’s structure theorem identifies surface measure there with perimeter for general sets of finite perimeter.

**Paper or page:** [Rectifiability; a survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00540v3). It says: “Let E ⊂ ℝⁿ be a set of finite perimeter. Then ∂∗E is (n−1)-rectifiable”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Covering fixes packing premeasure

**Remember:** Pack each piece, then take the cheapest countable cover.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For s &gt; 0 and δ &gt; 0, take disjoint balls centered in E with diameters at most δ. The packing premeasure is the limit as δ decreases to zero of the supremum of sums of their diameters raised to s. Packing measure takes the infimum of sums of these premeasures over all countable covers of E.

**Problem.** Packing measure is countably subadditive and gives countable sets zero measure in every positive dimension. Packing premeasure need not do either.

**How the definition helps.** Joining nearly optimal covers with summable errors proves countable subadditivity (our own). A singleton admits at most one packing ball, so its premeasure vanishes for s &gt; 0 (our own). Covering by singletons therefore gives every countable set packing measure zero (our own). In \[0,1\], equally spaced rational centers admit arbitrarily fine disjoint balls of total diameter at least one-half, giving positive one-dimensional premeasure (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Packing dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packing_dimension). It says: “the packing measure of S is the infimum of the packing pre-measures of countable covers of S.”

**Sources:**

- [Claude Tricot, Two definitions of fractional dimension (1982)](https://doi.org/10.1017/s0305004100059119)

### Diameter powers reveal dimension

**Remember:** On small sets, raising the exponent makes every cover cheaper.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures), 28A80. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For s ≥ 0, cover the set by countably many nonempty sets of diameter at most δ. Take the infimum of the sums of their diameters raised to s, charging one per set when s = 0. Let δ decrease to zero to obtain the unnormalized Hausdorff measure at exponent s. The Hausdorff dimension is the infimum of exponents where this measure vanishes.

**Problem.** For a subset of Euclidean space, Hausdorff measure is infinite below its dimension and zero above it. At the dimension itself, it can be zero, finite positive, or infinite.

**How the definition helps.** The same cover compares costs at two exponents (our own). For t &lt; s, the cost at s is at most the cost at t times δ raised to s − t (our own). Thus finite measure at t forces zero measure at s (our own). This gives one cutoff without first computing any of the measures (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Strictly Positive Hausdorff Measure implies Infinite Lower Dimensional Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Strictly_Positive_Hausdorff_Measure_implies_Infinite_Lower_Dimensional_Measure). It says: “ℋˢ(F) &gt; 0 ⇒ ∀ t ∈ \[0, s) : ℋᵗ(F) = +∞”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Frostman bounds force positive measure

**Remember:** If each covering set carries little mass, the whole cover must cost enough.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An s-Frostman probability on E is a Borel probability μ giving E mass one. Some finite C bounds μ(B(x,r)) by Crˢ for every center x and radius r &gt; 0 (our own).

**Problem.** A Borel subset of Euclidean space carrying a Frostman probability of exponent s &gt; 0 has positive s-dimensional Hausdorff measure.

**How the definition helps.** Each nonempty cover member of diameter d &gt; 0 lies in a ball of radius 2d, costing at most C(2d)ˢ in mass (our own). Singletons have zero mass by the ball bound (our own). Every countable cover of E must cover mass one, so the sum of diameter powers is at least 1/(2ˢC) at every scale (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Study Guide to "Kaufman and Falconer estimates for radial projections"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11847v1). It says: “If a Borel set X supports an s-Frostman probability measure μ, then ℋˢ(X) &gt; 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Hausdorff dimension respects countable unions

**Remember:** A countable union of sets of measure zero still has measure zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At each scale δ, take the infimum of sums of s-th powers of diameters over countable covers with diameters at most δ. Letting δ decrease to zero gives s-dimensional Hausdorff measure up to normalization. Hausdorff dimension is the infimum of exponents giving zero measure. Box dimension instead counts boxes of one size at a time.

**Problem.** The Hausdorff dimension of a countable union is the supremum of the dimensions of its members.

**How the definition helps.** Above the supremum, every member has measure zero, so the union has measure zero. In our own proof, monotonicity gives the reverse inequality. Countable subadditivity comes from joining the countable covers with a summable error budget. In our own comparison, each singleton has box dimension zero, but the rationals in \[0, 1\] have box dimension one.

**Wikipedia:** [Hausdorff dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_dimension). It says: “If X=\\bigcup<sub>i\\in I</sub>X<sub>i</sub> is a finite or countable union, then \\dim\_{\\operatorname{Haus}}(X) =\\sup<sub>i\\in I</sub> \\dim\_{\\operatorname{Haus}}(X<sub>i</sub>).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Mass bounds give dimension bounds

**Remember:** A cover must pay enough to carry all the mass.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each countable cover, add the s-th powers of its set diameters. Take the infimum over covers with diameters at most δ, then let δ decrease to zero. This defines s-dimensional Hausdorff measure up to normalization. Hausdorff dimension is the infimum of exponents giving zero measure.

**Problem.** Suppose a finite measure gives a Borel set F on the line positive mass. For some C and s &gt; 0, each sufficiently small closed interval has mass at most C times its diameter to power s. Then F has Hausdorff dimension at least s.

**How the definition helps.** The interval bound compares the mass of F directly with the cost of every sufficiently fine cover (our own). Enclose each nonempty covering set in a closed interval of the same diameter (our own). Summing gives a cost of at least μ(F)/C, so the s-dimensional measure is positive and the dimension is at least s (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Constructing self-similar subsets within the fractal support of Lacunary Wavelet Series for their multifractal analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17712). It says: “μ(U) ≤ c \|U\|ᵗ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Packing dimension respects countable unions

**Remember:** Cover each piece first, then put all the covers together.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures), 28A80. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a bounded nonempty set, let N(r) count the fewest radius-r balls that cover it. Its upper box dimension is the limit superior of log N(r) divided by log(1/r) as r decreases to zero. For each countable cover by bounded sets, take the supremum of their upper box dimensions. In Euclidean space the infimum over these covers equals packing dimension, usually defined using disjoint balls.

**Problem.** The packing dimension of a countable union of subsets of Euclidean space equals the supremum of their packing dimensions.

**How the definition helps.** Combining countably many countable covers gives one countable cover of the union (our own). Above the supremum of the packing dimensions, each piece admits a cover whose upper box dimensions stay below that bound (our own). Monotonicity gives the reverse inequality (our own). The theorem identifying modified upper box dimension with packing dimension justifies the cover formula.

**Wikipedia:** [Packing dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packing_dimension). It says: “the packing dimension of S is equal to the upper modified box dimension of S”

**Sources:**

- [Claude Tricot Jr., Two definitions of fractional dimension (1982)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100059119)

### Disjoint pieces give unique addresses

**Remember:** The first place where two addresses differ puts them in disjoint pieces.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A80 (Fractals), 37B10. arXiv math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Consider finitely many injective contractions on a compact metric space. Their attractor is the unique nonempty compact set A equal to the union of its images. Strong separation means those images are pairwise disjoint. An address is an infinite list of maps whose successive compositions, applied to A with the first map outermost, contain the point.

**Problem.** If the space and the family are nonempty and strong separation holds, each point of A has exactly one address.

**How the definition helps.** Disjoint images determine the first map uniquely, and injectivity determines the point to use at the next step. Our own proof repeats this choice inside A to construct the entire address. The contraction mapping theorem supplies the attractor. Without separation, the two half-size copies of \[0,1\] meet at 1/2, giving our own example of two addresses.

**Paper or page:** [Applications of the Tarski-Kantorovitch Fixed-Point Principle to the study of Infinite Iterated Function Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.04650v1). It says: “the canonical projection π : Λ(I) → A is bijective.”

**Sources:**

- [Applications of the Tarski-Kantorovitch Fixed-Point Principle to the study of Infinite Iterated Function Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.04650v1)

### Graph norms let closed operators commute with integrals

**Remember:** Integrate the point and its image together.

*True by definition.* MSC 28B05 (Vector-valued set functions, measures and integrals). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let T be a linear operator from part of one Banach space into another. Suppose its graph is closed in the product space. Give its domain the graph norm ‖x‖ + ‖Tx‖. The Bochner integral uses approximations by measurable functions with finitely many values, with error measured by the integral of the norm.

**Problem.** If f takes values in the domain of T and both f and Tf are Bochner integrable, T commutes with integration. In particular, the integral of f belongs to the domain.

**How the definition helps.** The graph norm makes T bounded on its domain even when the original norm does not. Our own proof integrates the pair (f, Tf) in the product space. Its integral belongs to the closed graph because simple approximations can take their values there. The two coordinates of the integral therefore satisfy the required identity.

**Paper or page:** [A Representation of Matrix-Valued Harmonic Functions by the Poisson Integral of Non-commutative BMO Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11752v2). It says: “T\\left(\\int \_E f(x)\\, d\\mu (x) \\right)=\\int \_E T(f(x))\\, d\\mu (x),”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Separable range rules out invisible vectors

**Remember:** A separable range lets scalar tests detect strong measurability.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28B05 (Vector-valued set functions, measures and integrals). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Banach-valued function is weakly measurable if every continuous linear functional gives a measurable scalar function. It is essentially separably valued if its values outside a null set lie in a separable subspace. Strong measurability means it is an almost everywhere norm limit of simple functions.

**Problem.** Pettis's theorem says that weak measurability gives strong measurability when the range is essentially separable.

**How the definition helps.** A separable subspace has a countable dense set, which lets scalar tests yield measurable simple approximations in Pettis’s theorem. Our own example on the Lebesgue interval sends t to the unit vector at coordinate t in ℓ²(\[0,1\]). Each continuous linear functional has only countably many nonzero coordinates, so its value is zero almost everywhere. Distinct unit vectors have distance √2, so a separable subspace contains only countably many of them.

**Paper or page:** [Kernel-Summability Methods and the Silverman-Toeplitz Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06770v3). It says: “A function v : E → X is strongly measurable if, and only if, the two following conditions are satisfied: v is weakly measurable; v is essentially separably valued.”

**Sources:**

- [B. J. Pettis, On integration in vector spaces (1938)](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1938-1501970-8)

### Stone's condition lets an abstract Daniell integral come from a measure

**Remember:** Truncate at height one, and the integral finds its measure.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C05 (Integration theory via linear functionals (Radon measures, Daniell integrals, etc.), representing set functions and measures), 28A12. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Daniell starts from a vector lattice T₀ of functions, closed under maximum and minimum, and a positive linear functional I on it. The functional must be continuous under monotone limits: if φₙ decreases to 0, then I(φₙ) tends to 0. Stone's condition asks that min(φ, 1) is in T₀ whenever φ is.

**Problem.** Under Stone’s condition, some measure μ on a σ-algebra of subsets of X represents I. Every φ in T₀ is μ-measurable and satisfies I(φ) = ∫φ dμ.

**How the definition helps.** Truncation produces indicator approximations inside the lattice (our own). For nonnegative φ in T₀, min(nφ, 1) increases to the indicator of {φ &gt; 0} (our own). The Daniell–Stone theorem extends the integral and supplies the representing measure.

**Paper or page:** [The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1), [The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1). It says: “with the property that χX ∧ φ ∈ T₀ whenever φ ∈ T₀. Let I be an I-integral on T₀. Then there is a σ-algebra 𝒜 on X and a measure μ on 𝒜”

**Sources:**

- [Adriaan de Clercq, The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure, arXiv:2211.14964 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1)

### Compatible finite quotient averages give Haar measure on profinite groups

**Remember:** On each finite quotient, average with equal weight for every point.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 20E18. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A profinite group is an inverse limit of finite discrete groups. For each open normal subgroup N, integrate a function factoring through G/N by averaging its values over that finite quotient (our own).

**Problem.** These finite averages determine Haar probability measure on any profinite group, without using Haar’s general existence theorem.

**How the definition helps.** The finite averages make translation invariance immediate because translations permute each finite quotient (our own). Passing to a finer quotient does not change the average, since each fibre has the same number of points (our own). Functions from finite quotients are uniformly dense in the continuous functions, so the averages extend to a positive linear functional (our own). The Riesz representation theorem makes it integration against a regular Borel probability measure (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_group). It says: “In the profinite case there are many subgroups of finite index, and Haar measure of a coset will be the reciprocal of the index.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining Haar measure on Baire sets makes the regularity conditions unnecessary

**Remember:** On Baire sets, invariant measures are regular for free.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 43A05. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a locally compact Hausdorff group, compact sets that are countable intersections of open sets generate the Baire σ-algebra. A left Haar measure there is a nonzero left-invariant Baire measure finite on compact Baire sets.

**Problem.** Every locally compact Hausdorff group has a left Haar measure, unique up to a positive constant. On the Baire sets this can be stated without any regularity condition.

**How the definition helps.** Automatic regularity for locally finite Baire measures removes the separate regularity hypothesis. Haar’s theorem supplies existence and uniqueness up to a positive factor (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “Some authors define a Haar measure on Baire sets rather than Borel sets. This makes the regularity conditions unnecessary as Baire measures are automatically regular.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Haar, Der Massbegriff in der Theorie der kontinuierlichen Gruppen, Annals of Mathematics 34 (1933)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968346)

### Left invariant volume forms give Haar measure on Lie groups

**Remember:** Translate a volume form at the identity to get invariant volume everywhere.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 22E15. arXiv math.DG, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On an n-dimensional Lie group, choose a nonzero alternating n-linear form on the tangent space at the identity. Move it by left translation to get a smooth volume form ω on the group. Its absolute value defines a measure by integration. The general definition of left Haar measure asks for a nonzero regular Borel measure unchanged by left translation.

**Problem.** Every Lie group has a left Haar measure, given by its left invariant volume form.

**How the definition helps.** The volume form makes invariance automatic because left translation preserves the form. Integrating its absolute value then gives a positive measure on nonempty open sets and a finite measure on compact sets (our own). Standard integration of a smooth density gives regularity, which means approximation by open and compact sets (our own). This replaces Haar’s general existence proof with the construction and integration of a smooth form.

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “On an n-dimensional Lie group, Haar measure can be constructed easily as the measure induced by a left-invariant n-form. This was known before Haar's theorem.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Haar, Der Massbegriff in der Theorie der kontinuierlichen Gruppen, Annals of Mathematics 34 (1933)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968346)

### The Haar scaling definition makes compact groups unimodular

**Remember:** Left translation cannot rescale the finite mass of the whole group.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 22C05. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a right Haar measure ν on a locally compact Hausdorff group. For each g, its modular factor Δ(g) is the unique positive number satisfying ν(g⁻¹S) = Δ(g)ν(S) for every Borel S. The group is unimodular if every factor equals one.

**Problem.** The modular function is multiplicative. Every compact Hausdorff group is unimodular.

**How the definition helps.** Defining Δ by scaling makes multiplicativity a composition law, since two translations multiply their scaling factors (our own). For compact G, the whole group has finite positive Haar measure, and a translation leaves it unchanged. So Δ(g) = 1. The usual argument instead needs Δ to be a continuous homomorphism into the positive reals, which have no nontrivial compact subgroup (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “Thus, by uniqueness up to a constant scaling factor of the Haar measure, there exists a function Δ from the group to the positive reals, called the Haar modulus, modular function or modular character”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Inner regularity is what Kolmogorov's extension theorem needs beyond Euclidean spaces

**Remember:** Compact sets inside every event let finite laws glue into one process.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 60G05, 28A35. arXiv math.PR, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measure on a topological space is inner regular if each set has measure equal to the supremum over the compact sets inside it. A consistent family gives a probability measure on each finite product. These measures agree under the projections between products.

**Problem.** Consider consistent inner regular probability laws on the finite products of Hausdorff spaces. They extend uniquely to a probability measure on the product σ-algebra of the infinite product. Borel probabilities on Polish spaces are inner regular, so Euclidean spaces require no extra regularity assumption.

**How the definition helps.** Inner regularity lets the proof use compact sets. Nested compact sets with the finite intersection property have a common point, which gives countable additivity. Without such a condition the extension can fail; a known example is due to Andersen and Jessen (our own). The measure lives only on the product σ-algebra, so events that depend on uncountably many coordinates stay outside it.

**Wikipedia:** [Kolmogorov extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov_extension_theorem). It says: “In fact, any collection of measurable spaces together with a collection of inner regular measures defined on the finite products of these spaces would suffice, provided that these measures satisfy a certain compatibility relation.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Kolmogoroff, Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung, Springer, 1933](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-49888-6)

### Measures that respect directed unions of open sets have a support

**Remember:** Measure a directed open union by taking the supremum of its members’ measures.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 28A12. arXiv math.FA, math.GN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A nonempty family of open sets is directed if any two members lie in a third member. A Borel measure is τ-additive if each such family’s union has measure equal to the supremum of its members’ measures.

**Problem.** Every τ-additive Borel measure has a support, a smallest closed set of full measure.

**How the definition helps.** τ-additivity says directly that the union of the null open sets is null, because the null open sets form a directed family. The complement of that union is the support. For a general Borel measure, the union of all null open sets can fail to be null. Every Radon measure on a Hausdorff space is τ-additive, so the definition covers the usual examples.

**nLab:** [tau-additive measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tau-additive+measure), [valuation (measure theory)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/valuation+%28measure+theory%29), [correspondence between measure and valuation theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/correspondence+between+measure+and+valuation+theory). It says: “the union of all null open sets is null”

**Sources:**

- [Tobias Fritz, Paolo Perrone, Sharwin Rezagholi, Probability, valuations, hyperspace: Three monads on Top and the support as a morphism (2019); arXiv:1910.03752](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.03752)

### Proper maps keep Radon measures locally finite

**Remember:** Compact inverse images keep mass finite near every target point.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)). arXiv math.GN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Radon measure is locally finite and approximates Borel sets from inside by compact sets. A proper continuous map has compact inverse images of compact sets. Its pushforward assigns each Borel set the measure of its inverse image.

**Problem.** A proper continuous map between locally compact Hausdorff spaces sends a Radon measure to a Radon measure in the inner-regular convention.

**How the definition helps.** Properness makes the inverse image of a compact neighborhood compact, so the image measure stays locally finite. Our own proof approximates the inverse image of a Borel set from inside by compact sets. Their images give compact subsets of the target set with at least as much image measure. Our own counterexample sends the whole real line to one point, which receives infinite Lebesgue mass under the pushforward.

**nLab:** [Radon measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon+measure). It says: “is a Borel measure m on X such that m is locally finite and inner regular on all Borel subsets.”

### Proper maps preserve Radon measures

**Remember:** Compact sets cannot collect infinite mass from far away.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A proper map has compact inverse images of compact sets. On locally compact metric spaces, use Radon measures that are finite on compact sets and approximate Borel sets from inside by compact sets.

**Problem.** A continuous proper map between locally compact metric spaces sends a Radon measure to a Radon measure.

**How the definition helps.** A compact target set has compact inverse image and therefore finite pushforward mass (our own). Approximate the inverse image of any Borel set from inside by compact sets (our own). Their images are compact subsets of the target set and capture at least the same mass (our own). Without properness, a constant map sends the entire length of the real line to one point (our own).

**nLab:** [Radon measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon+measure). It says: “The pushforward measure H∗μ is a Radon measure on Y defined as follows.”
