**Definition.** Fix c ∈ ℝ and set g(x) = exp(cx)f(exp(x)). Define the normalized Mellin transform at c+iξ as the unitary Fourier transform of g at −ξ, using the negative Fourier phase.

**Problem.** Suppose ∫₀∞ \|f(r)\|² exp(2c log r) dr/r is finite. The integral of the squared transform over ξ equals this same number.

**How the definition helps.** The substitution r = exp(x) turns the weighted input integral into ∫ \|g(x)\|² dx (our own). Fourier Plancherel says the unitary Fourier transform preserves this integral (our own). Substitution in the ordinary Mellin integral identifies the two transforms, first on smooth inputs of compact support (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Well-Posedness and Regularity of the Heat Equation with Robin Boundary Conditions in the Two-Dimensional Wedge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04651v2). It says: “For every $\\beta \\in \\mathbb {R}$ the map \\eqref{mellin-iso} is an isometric isomorphism.”

**Sources:**

- [Well-Posedness and Regularity of the Heat Equation with Robin Boundary Conditions in the Two-Dimensional Wedge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04651v2)

### Matching bases makes Bargmann unitary

**Remember:** Match orthonormal bases to preserve lengths.

*True by definition.* MSC 44A15 (Special integral transforms (Legendre, Hilbert, etc.)). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Bargmann–Fock space consists of entire functions square integrable for the plane measure exp(−\|z\|²) dA(z)/π, with dA denoting area. For f with normalized Hermite coefficients cₙ, define its Bargmann transform by the sum of cₙzⁿ/√(n!) over n ≥ 0.

**Problem.** The Bargmann transform is a unitary map onto the space of entire functions square integrable for the complex Gaussian weight.

**How the definition helps.** The two bases give the same squared norm as a sum of squared coefficients (our own). The work lies in proving that both systems are complete and that the Gaussian integral acts this way on Hermite functions (our own).

**nLab:** [Bargmann-Segal transform](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Bargmann-Segal+transform). It says: “The classical Bargmann-Segal transform is a unitary transformation from the Hilbert space of Lebesgue square integrable functions L²(ℝⁿ) to the Bargmann-Fock space of analytic functions with certain growth condition.”

**Sources:**

- [Valentine Bargmann, On a Hilbert space of analytic functions and an associated integral transform, part I (1961)](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.3160140303)

### Radial Fourier transforms explain Hankel inversion

**Remember:** Reflection leaves every radial function unchanged.

*True by definition.* MSC 44A15 (Special integral transforms (Legendre, Hilbert, etc.)). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix an integer d ≥ 2 and a profile h square-integrable against rᵈ⁻¹ dr on (0,∞). Its radial Hankel transform is the radial profile of the unitary Fourier transform of x ↦ h(\|x\|) on ℝᵈ.

**Problem.** Applying this transform twice recovers every radial profile square-integrable with respect to r to the power d − 1 times dr.

**How the definition helps.** Two Fourier transforms reflect the input, and our own observation is that reflection leaves radial functions unchanged. The work moves to Fourier inversion and to identifying the radial Fourier kernel with the Bessel formula (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hankel transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hankel_transform). It says: “The Hankel transform appears when one writes the multidimensional Fourier transform in hyperspherical coordinates”

**Paper or page:** [The Wˢ,ᵖ-boundedness of stationary wave operators for the Schrödinger operator with inverse-square potential](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01969v2). It says: “\\mathscr H<sub>\\nu k</sub>\\mathscr H{\\nu \_k}&amp; =I”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Stieltjes boundary values recover atoms

**Remember:** The scaled kernel tends to the indicator of a single point.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 44A15 (Special integral transforms (Legendre, Hilbert, etc.)), 44A60. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite positive measure on ℝ, define its Stieltjes transform by integrating 1/(t − z) against the measure for nonreal z. This includes measures assigning positive mass to individual points, called atoms.

**Problem.** As ε decreases to zero, ε times the imaginary part of the transform at x + iε tends to the mass at x. This holds even at a nonisolated point of the support.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing measures makes the mass at a single point visible in the transform (our own). At z = x + iε, the imaginary part of the kernel times ε equals ε²/((t − x)² + ε²) (our own). As ε decreases to zero, this quantity stays between zero and one and tends to the indicator of {x} (our own). Dominated convergence gives the result (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Stieltjes transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stieltjes_transformation). It says: “If instead the measure has a point mass at x, then the limit as ε → 0⁺ of the integral diverges”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Stieltjes imaginary parts smooth measures

**Remember:** The negative imaginary part divided by π gives a unit-mass averaging kernel.

*True by definition.* MSC 44A15 (Special integral transforms (Legendre, Hilbert, etc.)). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define G(z) by integrating 1/(z − t) against a finite positive measure μ on the real line. For ε &gt; 0, set pε(x) = −Im G(x + iε)/π.

**Problem.** The measures with density pε approach μ as ε decreases to zero. This means their integrals against every continuous compactly supported function approach its integral against μ.

**How the definition helps.** The negative imaginary part gives convolution with the probability density Pε(u) = ε/\[π(u²+ε²)\] (our own). Its mass outside every fixed neighborhood of zero tends to zero. Averaging a continuous compactly supported test function therefore recovers its value pointwise with a uniform bound. Fubini’s theorem and bounded convergence give convergence against μ.

**Wikipedia:** [Stieltjes transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stieltjes_transformation). It says: “the smaller the value of ε, the less smoothing is applied.”

**Sources:**

- [Matthew J. Colbrook, Computing Spectral Measures and Spectral Types (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-021-04072-4)

### Product grids preserve Laplace uniqueness

**Remember:** Independent sample coordinates let you apply one-variable uniqueness repeatedly.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 44A30 (Multiple integral transforms). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Choose a countable sequence of complex numbers with positive real parts for each coordinate. The product grid contains every tuple formed by choosing one number from each sequence. Call samples determining if their Laplace transform values distinguish integrable functions up to equality almost everywhere.

**Problem.** On a finite product of nonnegative half-lines, the grid is determining exactly when every coordinate sequence is determining on its half-line.

**How the definition helps.** Independent coordinate choices let us test one variable while keeping all other samples fixed (our own). The exponential weight factors, so Fubini’s theorem gives successive one-variable integrals (our own). Countability lets us discard one null set for all remaining sample choices at each step (our own). If one sequence fails, multiply its undetected function by nonzero integrable functions of the other variables (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Uniqueness sequences for multidimensional vector-valued Laplace transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17485v1). It says: “are the uniqueness sequences for the one-dimensional Laplace transform if and only if”

**Sources:**

- [Uniqueness sequences for multidimensional vector-valued Laplace transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17485v1)

### Logarithms transfer Young’s inequality

**Remember:** The logarithm turns division into subtraction and dx/x into ordinary length.

*True by definition.* MSC 44A35 (Convolution as an integral transform). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the Mellin convolution h(x) by integrating f(x/y)g(y) against dy/y over positive y. Compute each integral norm with the same measure dx/x.

**Problem.** Let f and g be smooth with compact support in (0, ∞). Choose finite p, q, r ≥ 1 with 1/r = 1/p + 1/q − 1. The r-norm of h is at most the p-norm of f times the q-norm of g.

**How the definition helps.** Choosing dx/x makes logarithmic coordinates preserve both convolution and all three norms (our own). Indeed, u = log x gives du = dx/x and turns division into subtraction (our own). Young’s inequality for ordinary convolution on the real line supplies the bound (our own).

**Paper or page:** [From Schwartz space to Mellin transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.10706v1). It says: “Let p, q, r ∈ \[1, ∞) be such that 1/r = 1/p + 1/q − 1.”

**Sources:**

- [From Schwartz space to Mellin transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.10706v1)

### Quadratic-phase convolution becomes multiplication

**Remember:** Put the same phase into both inputs before convolving.

*True by definition.* MSC 44A35 (Convolution as an integral transform), 44A15. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let q(x) = exp(iax²) for real a. Define Tf(ξ) by integrating q(x)f(x)exp(−ixξ) over ℝ. Define the adapted convolution of f and g as the ordinary convolution of qf and qg divided pointwise by q.

**Problem.** For integrable f and g on ℝ, applying T to their adapted convolution gives the pointwise product of Tf and Tg.

**How the definition helps.** Applying T restores the phase removed by the adapted convolution (our own). The ordinary Fourier convolution theorem then turns convolution into multiplication (our own). Our own convention omits the paper’s output phase and uses an unscaled Fourier integral. Those choices account for the extra factor in the quoted formula.

**Paper or page:** [The windowed quadratic phase Fourier transform: structure, convolution theorem and application](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03911v2). It says: “(𝒬Λ(f ⊗ₐ g))(ω) = e⁻ⁱ⁽ᶜω²⁺ᵉω⁾ F̃(ω) G̃(ω)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Convolution quotients make integration invertible

**Remember:** Taking fractions gives integration an inverse and gives convolution a unit.

*True by definition.* MSC 44A40 (Calculus of Mikusi?ski and other operational calculi). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For continuous functions on \[0,∞), define (f∗g)(t) = ∫₀ᵗ f(t−s)g(s) ds. A convolution fraction f/g consists of two such functions with g not identically zero. Identify f/g with h/k when f∗k = h∗g, and multiply fractions by convolving numerators and denominators.

**Problem.** The constant kernel 1 has an inverse in the convolution fraction field. Its product with that inverse is the unit, even though no continuous convolution kernel acts as the unit.

**How the definition helps.** The fraction construction gives every nonzero kernel an inverse, including the constant kernel that represents integration (our own). Titchmarsh’s convolution theorem supplies cancellation, which makes these fractions well defined (our own). No continuous kernel acts as the identity because convolution always gives zero at time zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Convolution quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolution_quotient). It says: “a convolution quotient is to the operation of convolution as a quotient of integers is to multiplication”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Exponential moments ensure moment uniqueness

**Remember:** Exponential control lets the moment series identify the law.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 44A60 (Moment problems), 44A10. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Require the integral of exp(ε\|x\|) against the probability measure to be finite for some ε &gt; 0. This is stronger than requiring every polynomial moment to be finite.

**Problem.** If a probability measure on ℝ has an exponential moment, its nonnegative integer moments determine it among all probability measures on ℝ.

**How the definition helps.** An exponential moment makes the Laplace transform analytic on a strip around the imaginary axis (our own). Any measure with matching moments integrates cosh(εx) by monotone convergence, so its transform is analytic there too. Their Taylor coefficients agree at zero, hence analytic continuation and Fourier uniqueness identify the laws. Without exponential integrability the lognormal law shares all moments with other laws.

**Wikipedia:** [Log-normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution). It says: “However, the log-normal distribution is not determined by its moments.”

**Sources:**

- [C. C. Heyde, On a Property of the Lognormal Distribution (1963)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1963.tb00521.x)

### Shifted moments detect negative support

**Remember:** Test squares after multiplying by the support coordinate.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 44A60 (Moment problems). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a real sequence starting with m₀ = 1, set L(xⁿ) = mₙ and extend L linearly to polynomials. Test both L(p²) and L(xp²) for every nonzero real polynomial p.

**Problem.** The sequence gives the moments of a probability measure with infinite support in \[0,∞) exactly when both tests are strictly positive.

**How the definition helps.** The second test puts the sign of x into an integral of a square (our own). A uniform measure on \[−2,−1\] passes every first test but gives L(x) &lt; 0 (our own). The two tests assert positive definiteness of the ordinary and shifted moment matrices (our own). The Stieltjes existence theorem supplies the measure.

**Wikipedia:** [Stieltjes moment problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stieltjes_moment_problem). It says: “det(Δₙ) &gt; 0 and det(Δₙ⁽¹⁾) &gt; 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Unit-interval moments have nonnegative differences

**Remember:** On the unit interval, taking a moment difference inserts a nonnegative factor.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 44A60 (Moment problems). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Hausdorff moment sequence consists of the integrals of 1, x, x², and all higher powers against one finite positive measure on \[0, 1\]. Form a difference sequence by subtracting each term’s successor from that term.

**Problem.** A real sequence is a Hausdorff moment sequence exactly when every term of every difference sequence is nonnegative. Include the original sequence as the difference of order zero.

**How the definition helps.** Restricting x to \[0, 1\] makes every difference insert the nonnegative factor 1 − x into the moment integral (our own). A unit mass at 2 gives first difference 1 − 2, so the half-line permits a counterexample (our own). The converse needs a separate theorem. Bernstein polynomial approximation and the representation of positive linear functionals by measures provide the reverse implication (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Chapter 12: The moment problem on compact semi-algebraic sets (revised version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10052v1). It says: “s is a Hausdorff moment sequence on \[0, 1\]ᵈ.”

**Sources:**

- [Chapter 12: The moment problem on compact semi-algebraic sets (revised version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10052v1)
- [Felix Hausdorff, Summationsmethoden und Momentfolgen. I (1921)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01378337)

### Compact support removes light ray ambiguity

**Remember:** Compact support lets visible Fourier data determine the missing frequencies.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 44A12 (Radon transform). arXiv math.AP, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In at least two space dimensions, define the scalar light ray transform by integrating along every straight spacetime line with unit spatial speed. Restrict the input to smooth functions that vanish outside a bounded set.

**Problem.** All light ray integrals together determine a smooth compactly supported function. The same data need not determine a smooth rapidly decreasing function.

**How the definition helps.** Compact support gives a real analytic Fourier transform, so its values on any open frequency region determine it everywhere (our own). Fourier transformation of the line integrals gives those values where the absolute time frequency is less than the spatial frequency length (our own). For our own counterexample, choose a nonzero smooth frequency bump supported where the reverse strict inequality holds. Its inverse Fourier transform decays rapidly and has zero line integrals (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The Momentum Light Ray Transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18450v1). It says: “Let $n\\ge 2$, $m\\geq 0$, and $f<sup>(m)</sup>\\in C<sub>c</sub><sup>\\infty </sup>(\\mathbb {R}<sup>1+n</sup>;S<sup>m</sup>)$. Suppose that $ \\Tilde {L}<sup>m,m</sup>f<sup>(m)</sup>((t,x),\\omega )=0 \\quad \\forall \\omega \\in \\S <sup>n-1</sup>, (t,x) \\in \\mathbb {R}<sup>1+n</sup>,$ then\\begin{align\*}  f<sup>(m)</sup>&amp; =\\begin{cases}  i\_{g\_{\\frac{1}{c}}}f<sup>(m-2)</sup> \\quad \\mbox{for some} \\quad f<sup>(m-2)</sup> \\in C<sub>c</sub><sup>\\infty </sup>(\\mathbb {R}<sup>1+n</sup>;S<sup>m-2</sup>) \\quad \\mbox{when $m\\ge 2$,} \\\\ 0 \\hspace{1.4cm}\\quad \\mbox{when}\\quad m=0,1. \\end{cases}\\end{align\*}”

**Sources:**

- [The Momentum Light Ray Transform, Theorem 2 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18450v1)

### Filtered Radon data localize ridges

**Remember:** Opposite directions share the profile, with reversed offsets.

*True by definition.* MSC 44A12 (Radon transform). arXiv math.FA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a unit vector θ and finite measure r on ℝ, define the ridge distribution u by ⟨u,f⟩ = ∫ Rf(θ,t) dr(t). Here Rf integrates the Schwartz test f over each hyperplane x·θ = t. Its filtered Radon data act on each range test g = Rf by ⟨u,R⁻¹g⟩.

**Problem.** For a finite measure profile, the filtered transform has an even measure representation. It places half the profile at θ and half its reflection at −θ.

**How the definition helps.** Testing through the inverse transform recovers the data at the ridge direction without integrating the ridge over hyperplanes (our own). Reversing both direction and offset describes the same hyperplane, so averaging the two descriptions gives the even measure (our own). The work lies in characterizing which smooth data arise from hyperplane integrals and inverting the transform there (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Ridges, Neural Networks, and the Radon Transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02543v1). It says: “be the ridge with profile r ∈ 𝒮′(ℝ) and direction ξ₀ ∈ 𝕊ᵈ⁻¹.”

**Sources:**

- [Ridges, Neural Networks, and the Radon Transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02543v1)

### Positive backprojections transfer Radon bounds

**Remember:** Pull the positive test back to the measured side.

*True by definition.* MSC 44A12 (Radon transform). arXiv math.FA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Radon transform Rh integrates h over each hyperplane in ℝⁿ. A positive backprojection represents a weight w by a nonnegative measure on hyperplanes. For every nonnegative measurable h, integrating wh over space must equal integrating Rh against that measure.

**Problem.** Let p &gt; 1 and let φ and ψ be continuous, even, nonnegative functions in L¹ and Lᵖ on ℝⁿ. Suppose Rφ ≤ Rψ on every hyperplane and φᵖ⁻¹ has a positive backprojection representation. Then ‖φ‖ₚ ≤ ‖ψ‖ₚ.

**How the definition helps.** The representation turns an inequality on hyperplanes into a comparison of ordinary integrals (our own). Testing with φ and ψ gives ∫φᵖ ≤ ∫φᵖ⁻¹ψ, and Hölder’s inequality gives the norm bound (our own). Finding a positive representation for a particular function remains a separate problem (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Comparison Problems for Radon Transforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17796v1). It says: “if p &gt; 1 and φᵖ⁻¹ is an intersection function”

**Sources:**

- [Comparison Problems for Radon Transforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17796v1)

### Reflections select Hilbert modes

**Remember:** Odd and even reflections select exactly the required half-integer modes.

*True by definition.* MSC 44A15 (Special integral transforms (Legendre, Hilbert, etc.)), 42A50. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For T &gt; 0, extend f on (0,T) by odd reflection about zero and even reflection about T to a 4T-periodic function. Apply the negative periodic Hilbert transform and restrict the result to (0,T). Use the convention that the periodic Hilbert transform sends each positive-frequency sine to minus its cosine.

**Problem.** This reflected transform sends each sine with frequency (j + ½)π/T to the cosine of the same frequency, for every nonnegative integer j.

**How the definition helps.** The reflection leaves each stated sine unchanged as a periodic sine on the extended interval (our own). The negative periodic Hilbert transform therefore gives its cosine (our own). The usual series definition replaces every sine in this interval basis by its cosine (our own). Completeness of the basis and boundedness of the periodic transform identify the two definitions for all square-integrable inputs (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Some properties of a modified Hilbert transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02609v1). It says: “where φ̃ is the periodic reflection”

**Sources:**

- [Some properties of a modified Hilbert transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02609v1)

### Stieltjes products add orders

**Remember:** Multiply the transforms and add their orders.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 44A15 (Special integral transforms (Legendre, Hilbert, etc.)). arXiv math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix α &gt; 0 and a finite positive measure on \[0,∞). Its Stieltjes transform of order α integrates the reciprocal αth power of z + t against that measure in t, for z &gt; 0.

**Problem.** On positive real arguments, the product of two generalized Stieltjes transforms of finite positive measures is another such transform. Its order is the sum of the two orders.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing every positive order gives the product a place in the same family (our own). The beta integral expresses the product of two kernels as an average of kernels of the summed order (our own). Integrating that average against both measures gives the new finite positive measure (our own).

**Paper or page:** [To the theory of generalized Stieltjes transforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03474v2). It says: “If μ₁ and μ₂ are positive, then μ is positive too.”

**Sources:**

- [To the theory of generalized Stieltjes transforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03474v2)

## 45 Integral equations

### Volterra integration limits give uniqueness at every coupling

**Remember:** Past-only integration puts a factorial under each iterate.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 45D05 (Volterra integral equations). arXiv math.CA, math.AP. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A linear Volterra equation of the second kind on \[0,T\] has the form u(t) = f(t) + λ∫₀ᵗ K(t,s)u(s) ds. The given kernel K weights only times s ≤ t.

**Problem.** On \[0,T\], assume the known function is continuous and K is continuous for 0 ≤ s ≤ t ≤ T. Each scalar λ gives exactly one continuous solution.

**How the definition helps.** The ordered integration times give each power of the integral operator a factorial denominator (our own). Our own proof uses this bound to sum the series for the inverse at every coupling. Our own counterexample is the fixed-limit equation u(x) − ∫₀¹ u(y) dy = 0, which every constant solves.

**Wikipedia:** [Volterra integral equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volterra_integral_equation). It says: “A linear Volterra equation of the second kind is x(t) = f(t) + ∫ₐᵗ K(t,s)x(s) ds.”

**Paper or page:** [The Non-zonal Rossby-Haurwitz Solutions of the 2D Euler Equations on a Rotating Ellipsoid](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.17854v1). It says: “Then the unique solution g ∈ C(\[−π/2, 0\]) of the Volterra integral equation”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Finite-rank Fredholm series terminate

**Remember:** A sampled kernel cannot have more rank than its separated terms.

*True by definition.* MSC 45B05 (Fredholm integral equations). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A kernel K on J×J has separated rank at most r if K(x,y) = ∑ⱼ₌₁ʳ aⱼ(x)bⱼ(y) throughout J×J. In the Fredholm determinant for I−λK, the coefficient of λⁿ is (−1)ⁿ/n! times the integral of det\[K(xᵢ,xⱼ)\] over Jⁿ.

**Problem.** For a continuous separated kernel of rank at most r on a compact interval, the Fredholm determinant is a polynomial of degree at most r.

**How the definition helps.** Each product contributes a matrix of rank at most one, so every coefficient above degree r vanishes (our own). The eigenvalue definition gives another proof by counting nonzero eigenvalues with multiplicity (our own). Fredholm’s solvability theorem identifies what the zeros of this series mean for the integral equation (our own).

**nLab:** [Fredholm determinant](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Fredholm+determinant). It says: “d is an entire function of λ such that d(λ) ≠ 0 iff the integral equation has a unique solution.”

**Sources:**

- [Ivar Fredholm, Sur une classe d’équations fonctionnelles (1903)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02421317)

### Positive kernels give convergent Mercer expansions

**Remember:** Positive kernels turn the diagonal expansion into a sum of squares.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 45C05 (Eigenvalue problems for integral equations), 45P05. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Call a continuous symmetric kernel positive definite if every matrix of its values at finitely many points has a nonnegative quadratic form.

**Problem.** On a closed bounded interval, expand a continuous symmetric positive definite kernel in eigenfunctions of its integral operator. The series converges absolutely and uniformly to the kernel.

**How the definition helps.** Positivity makes the diagonal partial sums increase, while the cited indefinite kernel can fail to converge even pointwise. Mercer’s diagonal identity gives their pointwise limit K(x,x) (our own outline). Dini’s theorem gives uniform convergence on the compact interval. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds each absolute off-diagonal tail by the geometric mean of the two diagonal tails.

**Paper or page:** [Extending Mercer's expansion to indefinite and asymmetric kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.16453v2). It says: “there exists a continuous symmetric indefinite kernel Kₚₜ: \[a, b\] × \[a, b\] → ℝ with a Mercer's expansion that does not converge pointwise.”

**Sources:**

- [Sungwoo Jeong, Alex Townsend. Extending Mercer's expansion to indefinite and asymmetric kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.16453v2)

### Resolvent kernels handle every forcing

**Remember:** Find one kernel and reuse it for every forcing.

*True by definition.* MSC 45D05 (Volterra integral equations). arXiv math.CA, math.AP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write j ∗ u for the integral of j(t − s)u(s) from 0 to t. In the equation u + j ∗ u = g, the known function g may vary. Define one resolvent kernel r by r + j ∗ r = j.

**Problem.** Assume j, r and g are integrable on every interval \[0,T\]. Then g − r ∗ g is the unique locally integrable solution up to equality almost everywhere.

**How the definition helps.** The identity r + j∗r = j cancels the extra terms when composing the two solution rules (our own). Associativity and commutativity of scalar convolution give the same cancellation in both orders. Thus subtracting convolution by r inverts addition of convolution by j.

**Paper or page:** [Comparison between the Cauchy problem and the scattering problem for the Landau damping in the Vlasov-HMF equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.15932v2). It says: “The solution f is then given by f(t) = g(t) − r ∗ g(t).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Finite parts differentiate Cauchy integrals

**Remember:** Differentiate the simple pole to define the squared pole.

*True by definition.* MSC 45E05 (Integral equations with kernels of Cauchy type), 46F10. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a smooth density f on \[a,b\], integrate f(t)/(t − x) after excluding equal lengths on each side of the interior point x. Call the limit the Cauchy principal value. Define the finite part for the squared denominator as the derivative of that principal value with respect to x.

**Problem.** On the interior of a bounded interval, the derivative equals the limit of the squared-pole cutoff integral after subtracting 2f(x)/ε. Here ε is the length cut out on each side.

**How the definition helps.** Differentiating the cutoff integral gives the squared-pole integral minus (f(x−ε)+f(x+ε))/ε from its moving endpoints (our own). Taylor expansion replaces this endpoint term by 2f(x)/ε with error O(ε). The omitted symmetric principal value equals ∫₀ᵋ (f(x+s)−f(x−s))/s ds. Its derivative is locally O(ε) by smoothness, justifying differentiation of the limit.

**Wikipedia:** [Hadamard regularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadamard_regularization). It says: “exists, then it may be differentiated with respect to x to obtain the Hadamard finite part integral as follows:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Frequency halves invert Hilbert equations

**Remember:** Divide separately on the two frequency halves.

*True by definition.* MSC 45E05 (Integral equations with kernels of Cauchy type), 44A15. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For f ∈ L²(ℝ), define Hf by multiplying its Fourier transform by −i on positive frequencies and by i on negative frequencies. The multiplier value at zero does not affect the L² function.

**Problem.** Take complex constants a and b and consider aI + bH on square-integrable functions on the line. It is invertible exactly when a − ib and a + ib are both nonzero.

**How the definition helps.** The multiplier definition splits the equation into two scalar equations (our own). When both scalars are nonzero, their reciprocals give a bounded inverse (our own). A zero scalar kills every function supported in frequency on that half-line (our own). The work lies in proving the integral and multiplier definitions agree and that the Fourier transform preserves the norm (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_transform). It says: “the phase of the negative frequency components of u(t) by +90°”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Total mass fixes Hilbert ambiguity

**Remember:** Prescribe the mass to fix the otherwise invisible arcsine term.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 45E05 (Integral equations with kernels of Cauchy type), 42A50. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On (−1,1), use densities p(t)/√(1 − t²) with polynomial numerator p. Record both the integral of the density and its finite Hilbert transform. The transform integrates the density against 1/(x − t), taking the limit after omitting equal lengths on both sides of x.

**Problem.** Fix an integer n ≥ 0, a real mass m, and a real polynomial g of degree at most n. Exactly one polynomial p of degree at most n+1 gives a density p(t)/√(1−t²) with mass m and finite Hilbert transform g.

**How the definition helps.** Recording the mass determines the constant numerator that the transform cannot detect, since the transform annihilates 1/√(1 − t²). In our own calculation, a monic numerator of degree d ≥ 1 transforms to a polynomial of degree d − 1 with leading coefficient −π. So coefficient comparison determines all nonconstant terms, and the mass fixes the constant, which changes the mass by π times its value.

**Paper or page:** [On the Local Regularity of the Hilbert Transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.11947v3). It says: “p.v. ∫₋₁¹ 1/(√(1−t²) (x−t)) dt = 0 if \|x\|&lt;1,”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Sonine pairs invert convolution

**Remember:** One partner undoes the other after one ordinary derivative.

*True by definition.* MSC 45E10 (Integral equations of the convolution type (Abel, Picard, Toeplitz and Wiener-Hopf type)). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For positive time, convolution of k and h means integrating k(t − s)h(s) from 0 to t. Call the kernels Sonine partners if their convolution equals 1 almost everywhere. The unknown input enters the integral equation through convolution with k.

**Problem.** Assume both kernels and the input are integrable on every interval \[0,T\]. Convolving the output with h and differentiating its absolutely continuous representative recovers the input almost everywhere.

**How the definition helps.** The two kernels combine to ordinary integration, so our own proof ends by differentiating that integral. The work moves to finding a partner and justifying associativity by Fubini's theorem (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Trends, Directions for Further Research, and Some Open Problems of Fractional Calculus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.04241v1). It says: “\\begin{equation}   (\\mathbb {D}<sub>(k)</sub>\\,  \\mathbb {I}<sub>(\\kappa )</sub>\\,  f) (t) = f(t),\\  f\\in C<sub>-1</sub>(0,+\\infty ),\\  t&gt;0,\\end{equation}”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Squared radii simplify Abel inversion

**Remember:** Two half integrals give one ordinary integral.

*True by definition.* MSC 45E10 (Integral equations of the convolution type (Abel, Picard, Toeplitz and Wiener-Hopf type)), 44A15. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write u = r² and let h(u) be the radial profile at radius √u. In squared distance v, define Ah(v) by integrating h(u)/√(u − v) over u &gt; v. This replaces the radial kernel containing both r and the observation radius.

**Problem.** For smooth compactly supported h, applying A twice gives π times the integral of h over \[v,∞). Differentiating and multiplying by −1/π recovers h(v).

**How the definition helps.** Squaring the radius turns the kernel into a function of one difference (our own). Fubini’s theorem reduces its double application to the beta integral, whose value is π (our own). The remaining work is matching the radial projection to this kernel by the squared-radius change of variable (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Abel transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_transform). It says: “The Abel transform of a function f(r) is given by”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Exponential norms contract Volterra iteration

**Remember:** Discount later errors and long histories no longer obstruct contraction.

*True by definition.* MSC 45G10 (Other nonlinear integral equations), 45D05, 47H09. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On continuous functions on \[0,T\], use the supremum of exp(−at)\|u(t)\|, with a &gt; 0, in place of the usual supremum norm. Define the integral map by adding to f(t) the integral of G(t,s,u(s)) from zero to t.

**Problem.** Assume f and G are continuous and \|G(t,s,v) − G(t,s,w)\| ≤ L\|v − w\| whenever 0 ≤ s ≤ t ≤ T. For a &gt; L, iteration from any continuous input converges geometrically to the unique fixed point.

**How the definition helps.** The exponential weight inserts exp(−a(t−s)) into the error integral (our own). Its integral over 0 ≤ s ≤ t is at most 1/a, giving contraction factor L/a. The weighted norm is equivalent to the complete supremum norm. Banach’s fixed-point theorem gives uniqueness and geometric convergence.

**Wikipedia:** [Banach fixed-point theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_fixed-point_theorem). It says: “the most difficult part is typically to define X properly so that T(X) ⊆ X.”

**Sources:**

- [Mihály Bessenyei and Zsolt Páles. Applications of the Bielecki renorming technique.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11784-020-00845-x)

### Normalization separates shape from scale

**Remember:** Fix a value to find the shape, then recover the scale.

*True by definition.* MSC 45G10 (Other nonlinear integral equations), 45M20. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On \[0,1\], let H(u)(x) integrate K(x,y)u(y)ᵏ over 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, with continuous K &gt; 0 and integer k ≥ 2. For positive continuous u with u(0) = 1, set N(u) = H(u)/H(u)(0).

**Problem.** Dividing each positive fixed point of H by its value at zero gives a bijection onto the fixed points of N.

**How the definition helps.** Normalization turns the unknown scale into one positive number. In our own calculation, N(u) = u means H(u) = cu with c = H(u)(0) &gt; 0. Homogeneity gives H(su) = sᵏcu. The equation s⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾c = 1 determines the unique positive scale that turns u into a fixed point of H.

**Paper or page:** [On positive fixed points of operator of Hammerstein type with degenerate kernel and Gibbs Measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08496v1). It says: “has a nontrivial positive solution iff the Hammerstein’s operator Hₖ has a nontrivial positive fixed point,”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Separable kernels give cubic systems

**Remember:** The kernel’s output functions give all the unknowns you need.

*True by definition.* MSC 45G10 (Other nonlinear integral equations), 45M20. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On \[0,1\], let H(u)(x) integrate K(x,y)u(y)³ over y. Write the continuous kernel as a finite sum of products aⱼ(x)bⱼ(y), using linearly independent functions aⱼ. Represent a candidate fixed point by its coefficients in these functions.

**Problem.** The fixed points correspond exactly to the solutions of a finite system of cubic equations. For positive fixed points, retain the vectors whose reconstructed functions are positive.

**How the definition helps.** The separated kernel puts every fixed point in the span of the independent output functions aⱼ (our own). Writing u = ∑ cᵢaᵢ gives the cubic equations cⱼ = ∫₀¹ bⱼ(y)(∑ cᵢaᵢ(y))³ dy. Conversely, each solution reconstructs a fixed point, whose coordinates are unique by independence.

**Paper or page:** [On positive fixed points of operator of Hammerstein type with degenerate kernel and Gibbs Measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08496v1). It says: “The Hammerstein’s operator H₃ has a nontrivial positive fixed point iff the cubic operator P has a nontrivial positive fixed point,”

**Sources:**

- [I. M. Mavlonov, Kh. N. Khushvaktov, G. P. Arzikulov, F. H. Haydarov. On positive fixed points of operator of Hammerstein type with degenerate kernel and Gibbs Measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08496v1)

### Skew coupling preserves monotonicity

**Remember:** The two cross terms cancel when you test the product operator.

*True by definition.* MSC 45G10 (Other nonlinear integral equations), 47H05. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a real Hilbert space, call F monotone if ⟨F(u) − F(w),u − w⟩ ≥ 0 for every u,w. For maps F and K on this space, introduce v = F(u). Replace u + K(F(u)) = 0 by the zero equation for A(u,v) = (F(u) − v,K(v) + u).

**Problem.** Monotone F and K give a monotone A for the product inner product. Suppose each map M ∈ {F,K} satisfies ⟨M(u)−M(w),u−w⟩ ≥ η<sub>M</sub>‖u−w‖² for every u,w, with η<sub>M</sub> &gt; 0. Then A satisfies the same bound on the product space with constant min{η<sub>F</sub>,η<sub>K</sub>}.

**How the definition helps.** The opposite signs cancel the two cross terms in the pairing for A. In our own calculation, only the original pairings for F and K remain. Their lower bounds add. The remaining task is to solve the product equation using these separate bounds.

**Paper or page:** [Algorithm for equations of Hammerstein type and applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.07117v1). It says: “Then A is a (p, η)-strongly monotone mapping, where η := min{η₁, η₂}.”

**Sources:**

- [M. O. Aibinu, S. C. Thakur, S. Moyo. Algorithm for equations of Hammerstein type and applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.07117v1)

### Quadrature weights preserve convolution composition

**Remember:** Multiply the generating functions and the discrete convolutions compose.

*True by definition.* MSC 45L05 (Theoretical approximation of solutions to integral equations), 45E10, 65R20. arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a time step h &gt; 0. For a kernel with Laplace transform K analytic near 1/h, expand K((1 − z)/h) in powers of z. Use the coefficients as weights for discrete convolution, which sums weighted past inputs.

**Problem.** Suppose two scalar Laplace transforms are analytic near 1/h. Composing their discrete convolution maps gives the map defined by the product transform.

**How the definition helps.** A common substitution turns the product of two transforms into the product of their weight series. In our own calculation, coefficient multiplication gives exactly the weights for composing the discrete maps. This avoids approximating the two successive integrals independently. Proving accuracy for the underlying integrals requires separate estimates.

**Wikipedia:** [Cauchy product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy_product). It says: “the Cauchy product of these two power series is defined by a discrete convolution as follows:”

**Sources:**

- [C. Lubich, Convolution quadrature and discretized operational calculus. I (1988)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01398686)

### Continuous diagonals recover traces

**Remember:** Continuity pins down the diagonal that integration can otherwise ignore.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 45P05 (Integral operators), 47B10. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A continuous kernel for T on L²(\[a,b\]) is a continuous K on \[a,b\]² satisfying (Tf)(x) = ∫ₐᵇ K(x,y)f(y) dy almost everywhere for every f. The operator is trace class if the sum of its singular values is finite.

**Problem.** For a trace-class integral operator with a continuous kernel, the trace equals ∫ₐᵇ K(x,x) dx.

**How the definition helps.** Continuity makes the diagonal integral a limit of traces of compressions to functions constant on small intervals (our own). Uniform continuity controls the difference between each square average and its diagonal values. The projections approach the identity strongly, so the compressed trace-class operators converge in trace norm. A kernel equal to one only on the diagonal represents zero but has diagonal integral b−a.

**Paper or page:** [Numerical Fredholm determinants for matrix-valued kernels on the real line](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22875v1). It says: “Then Tr(𝒦) = ∫ₐᵇ K(x,x) dx.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Schur weights handle divergent rows

**Remember:** Measure each row and column against a weight it can integrate.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 45P05 (Integral operators). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonnegative measurable kernel K, Schur weights are strictly positive finite measurable functions p and q satisfying two bounds for finite A,B ≥ 0. Require ∫K(x,y)q(y)dy ≤ Ap(x) for almost every x and ∫K(x,y)p(x)dx ≤ Bq(y) for almost every y.

**Problem.** Integrating K(x,y)f(y) in y defines an operator of norm at most √(AB) on square-integrable functions. For K(x,y) = 1/(x + y) on the positive half-line, choose p(x) = 1/√x and q(y) = 1/√y.

**How the definition helps.** Weights make finite estimates possible even where unweighted row or column integrals diverge (our own). Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz and Tonelli’s theorem prove the bound (our own). The work in the example is evaluating the weighted integral by scaling, which gives A = B = π (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Schur test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_test). It says: “Such functions p(x), q(y) are called the Schur test functions.”

**Sources:**

- [Issai Schur, Bemerkungen zur Theorie der beschränkten Bilinearformen mit unendlich vielen Veränderlichen (1911)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1911.140.1)

### Actual ranges characterize attained fits

**Remember:** Projecting onto the closure finds the target, not necessarily an input.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 45Q05 (Inverse problems for integral equations), 45B05. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a bounded integral operator K between Hilbert spaces, write R for its actual range. Define the domain of least-squares inversion as R + R⊥, where R⊥ consists of vectors perpendicular to every output.

**Problem.** A vector u minimizing ‖Ku − f‖ exists exactly when f belongs to this domain.

**How the definition helps.** The actual range condition ensures that some input attains the closest output. In our own proof, project f onto the closure of R; this projection has a preimage exactly when it lies in R. Our own example maps g in L²(\[0,1\]) to its integral from zero to x. Its range is dense, but no output equals the constant one almost everywhere, so the constant one has no least-squares solution.

**Paper or page:** [Fredholm integral equations for function approximation and the training of neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.05262v3). It says: “Assume that F ∈ R(𝒢) + R(𝒢)⊥ ⊂ L²(X).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Quadratic penalties stabilize Fredholm inversion

**Remember:** The penalty puts a positive floor under the normal operator.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 45Q05 (Inverse problems for integral equations), 47A52. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a bounded integral operator between Hilbert spaces. For data f and λ &gt; 0, define the regularized solution as the minimizer of ‖Ku − f‖² + λ‖u‖².

**Problem.** The regularized solution exists uniquely for any data. Its change is at most 1/(2√λ) times the norm of the data change.

**How the definition helps.** Adding λI to K\*K makes the normal operator invertible, even for K = 0, where unregularized minimizers are arbitrary. In our own proof, the normal equation for data difference g and solution difference v gives ‖Kv‖² + λ‖v‖² = Re⟨Kv,g⟩. Completing the square gives λ‖v‖² ≤ ‖g‖²/4.

**Paper or page:** [Moore-Penrose inverse and applications to linear equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01332v3). It says: “has a unique global minimizer”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Nonzero diagonals ensure Abel uniqueness

**Remember:** Keep the diagonal so differentiation can expose the input.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 45E10 (Integral equations of the convolution type (Abel, Picard, Toeplitz and Wiener-Hopf type)), 45D05. arXiv math.FA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix finite a &lt; b and 0 &lt; β &lt; 1. Require K and its first partial derivative in p to be continuous on a ≤ t ≤ p ≤ b, with K(p,p) always nonzero. The Abel operator integrates K(p,t)f(t)/(p − t)ᵝ from a to p for almost every p.

**Problem.** These integrals determine any square-integrable solution up to equality almost everywhere.

**How the definition helps.** A second integration and one differentiation expose f(p) with a nonzero coefficient proportional to K(p,p). Dividing by that coefficient leaves an equation involving only earlier values, for which the standard uniqueness theorem applies. For our own counterexample, let K(p,t) equal a smooth function of t that vanishes on a subinterval. Every input supported there gives zero data.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized Abel equations and applications to translation invariant Radon transforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08180v1). It says: “K(p,p) is non-zero, for p ∈ \[a,b\].”

**Sources:**

- [Generalized Abel equations and applications to translation invariant Radon transforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08180v1)

### Divided differences preserve discrete inversion

**Remember:** Use divided differences of the inverse symbol to undo the discrete convolution.

*True by definition.* MSC 45L05 (Theoretical approximation of solutions to integral equations), 45E10, 65R20. arXiv math.NA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take distinct positive nodes x₀,…,xₙ with K nonzero at each node. Start with D(j,j) = K(xⱼ) and set D(i,j) = (D(i,j+1) − D(i−1,j))/(xᵢ − xⱼ) for j &lt; i. Define A(K) as lower triangular with entries (−1)ⁱ⁻ʲ⁺¹D(i,j) for j ≤ i.

**Problem.** The lower triangular matrix for 1/K is the inverse of the matrix for K.

**How the definition helps.** The divided-difference product rule sums over the same splits as triangular matrix multiplication. Our own sign check gives A(K)A(L) = −A(KL). Taking L = 1/K gives the identity because A(1) = −I.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized convolution quadrature based on the trapezoidal rule](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11134v1). It says: “the relation φₙ = ∑ⱼ₌₀ⁿ (−1)ⁿ⁻ʲ⁺¹ gⱼ ⟨xⱼ,…,xₙ⟩ 𝒦 can be inverted”

**Sources:**

- [Lehel Banjai, Matteo Ferrari. Generalized convolution quadrature based on the trapezoidal rule](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11134v1)

### Iterated collocation transfers a smoothed error bound

**Remember:** The extra integral smooths the collocation error.

*True by definition.* MSC 45L05 (Theoretical approximation of solutions to integral equations), 65R20. arXiv math.NA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For u = f + Ku on a bounded interval, let P interpolate at nodes with spacing h. First solve v = P(f + Kv) in the interpolation space. Define the improved approximation w = f + Kv by applying the integral operator once more.

**Problem.** Suppose I − KP has uniformly bounded inverses as h decreases. If ‖K(u − Pu)‖∞ ≤ Chᵖ, then the maximum error of w is bounded by a constant times hᵖ.

**How the definition helps.** The last integral puts the interpolation error inside K. In our own calculation, v = Pw gives (I − KP)(u − w) = K(u − Pu). Applying the bounded inverse proves the estimate. The paper obtains an improved rate by bounding the right side for its particular kernels and smooth solutions.

**Paper or page:** [A note on improvement by iteration for the approximate solutions of second kind Fredholm integral equations with Green's kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12343v2). It says: “Then ‖φ − φₙᶜ‖∞ = O(h²ʳ⁺¹), ‖φ − φₙˢ‖∞ = O(h²ʳ⁺²).”

**Sources:**

- [Gobinda Rakshit, Shashank K. Shukla, Akshay S. Rane. A note on improvement by iteration for the approximate solutions of second kind Fredholm integral equations with Green's kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12343v2)

## 46 Functional analysis

### For 0 &lt; p ≤ 1, dropping the p-th root gives a metric

**Remember:** For small p, drop the root and the triangle inequality comes back.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 46B20 (Geometry and structure of normed linear spaces), 54E35. arXiv math.FA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For 0 &lt; p ≤ 1, let ℓᵖ consist of scalar sequences x with ∑ᵢ \|xᵢ\|ᵖ finite. Define d(x,y) = ∑ᵢ \|xᵢ − yᵢ\|ᵖ.

**Problem.** The function d is a metric on ℓᵖ. For 0 &lt; p &lt; 1, taking its p-th root breaks the triangle inequality.

**How the definition helps.** Our own proof adds the coordinate inequalities \|a + b\|ᵖ ≤ \|a\|ᵖ + \|b\|ᵖ. Symmetry and separation follow term by term. For distinct coordinate unit vectors, the rooted distance is 2¹⁄ᵖ, while the route through zero has length two.

**nLab:** [p-norm](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/p-norm). It says: “A variant definition for 0 &lt; p ≤ 1 (which agrees with the usual definition for p = 1, preserving continuity in p) leaves out the pth root; then the result satisfies the triangle inequality (and indeed is a metric)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Pythagoras is trivial in an inner product space

**Remember:** Define perpendicular and length by one inner product; Pythagoras is expanding a square.

*True by definition.* MSC 46C05 (Hilbert and pre-Hilbert spaces: geometry and topology (including spaces with semidefinite inner product)), 51F20. arXiv math.FA, math.MG. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** An inner product space is a real vector space with a symmetric, positive definite bilinear form ⟨−,−⟩. The length of v is \|v\| = √⟨v,v⟩. The vectors v and w are perpendicular, written v ⊥ w, when ⟨v,w⟩ = 0.

**Problem.** In an inner product space, if v ⊥ w then \|v + w\|² = \|v\|² + \|w\|².

**How the definition helps.** Perpendicularity and length both come from one inner product, so the theorem is one line of algebra. Expand \|v + w\|² = \|v\|² + \|w\|² + 2⟨v,w⟩, and the cross term is zero when v ⊥ w. The nLab notes that the real work moves elsewhere: one must show that Euclidean geometry carries an inner product structure.

**nLab:** [Pythagorean theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Pythagorean+theorem). It says: “That the Pythagorean Theorem holds in an inner product space is trivial; all that matters is establishing that one is, in fact, working in an inner product space.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Continuity makes the integral of \|x\| a norm, with no identification needed

**Remember:** A continuous function that is nonzero somewhere is nonzero on a whole interval.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 46E05 (Lattices of continuous, differentiable or analytic functions), 46B20, 26A42. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For real a &lt; b, C\[a,b\] consists of all continuous real functions on \[a,b\]. Define ‖x‖₁ as the integral of \|x\| over \[a,b\].

**Problem.** On C\[a, b\], ‖x‖₁ = ∫ₐᵇ \|x(t)\| dt is a norm. On all integrable functions it is only a seminorm.

**How the definition helps.** Continuity rules out nonzero functions that the integral cannot see. Our own sketch: if x(t₀) ≠ 0, then \|x\| &gt; \|x(t₀)\|/2 on some interval, so the integral of \|x\| is positive. Our own counterexample: the function that is 1 at one point and 0 elsewhere has integral 0. So on C\[a, b\] no identification of functions almost everywhere is needed, as it is for L¹.

**Paper or page:** [1-Seminorm on Continuous on Closed Interval Real-Valued Functions is Norm](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/1-Seminorm_on_Continuous_on_Closed_Interval_Real-Valued_Functions_is_Norm). It says: “Let ‖x‖₁ := ∫ₐᵇ \|x(t)\| dt be the 1-seminorm. Then ‖·‖₁ is a norm on C\[a, b\].”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, 1-Seminorm on Continuous on Closed Interval Real-Valued Functions is Norm](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/1-Seminorm_on_Continuous_on_Closed_Interval_Real-Valued_Functions_is_Norm)

### The graph norm reduces the closed graph theorem to inversion

**Remember:** Make the image part of the norm, then compare the two norms.

*True by definition.* MSC 46A30 (Open mapping and closed graph theorems; completeness (including \\(B\\)-, \\(B<sub>r</sub>\\)-completeness)), 47A05. arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a linear map T between normed spaces X and Y, the graph norm of x ∈ X is ‖x‖ₓ + ‖Tx‖ᵧ.

**Problem.** A linear map between Banach spaces is bounded if its graph, the set of pairs (x,Tx), is closed.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the graph norm turns a closed graph into a complete domain. The map x ↦ (x,Tx) preserves distances from this domain onto the closed graph in the complete product. The identity from the graph-norm domain to the original domain is a bounded bijection between Banach spaces. The bounded inverse theorem gives ‖x‖ + ‖Tx‖ ≤ C‖x‖, so T is bounded.

**Paper or page:** [Closed Graph Theorem/Banach Space](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Closed_Graph_Theorem/Banach_Space). It says: “is closed in the direct product X × Y equipped with the direct product norm”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The dual unit ball recovers the norm of every vector

**Remember:** Test with functionals that never stretch, and one test reaches the norm.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 46B10 (Duality and reflexivity in normed linear and Banach spaces). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The normed dual consists of the bounded linear scalar-valued maps, not all linear scalar-valued maps. Put f in its unit ball exactly when \|f(y)\| ≤ ‖y‖ for every vector y.

**Problem.** The norm of a vector in a normed space is the supremum of \|f(x)\| over the dual unit ball.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the dual unit ball gives the upper bound \|f(x)\| ≤ ‖x‖ for every test. For nonzero x, the functional f(tx) = t‖x‖ attains the bound on the line through x. The Hahn–Banach theorem extends it to the whole space with the same norm.

**Paper or page:** [Norm in terms of Normed Dual Space](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Norm_in_terms_of_Normed_Dual_Space). It says: “$\\ds \\norm x = \\sup\_{f \\in B<sub>X<sup>\\ast</sub>^-}</sup> \\cmod {\\map f x}$”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The quotient norm identifies its dual with the annihilator

**Remember:** Vanishing on the subspace means a functional sees only the coset.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 46B10 (Duality and reflexivity in normed linear and Banach spaces). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The dual of a normed space consists of its bounded linear maps to scalars, called functionals. The annihilator of a subspace M consists of those functionals that vanish on M. The quotient norm of a coset x + M is the infimum of the norms of its representatives.

**Problem.** For a closed subspace M of a normed space X, the dual of X/M and the annihilator of M are isometrically isomorphic. That is, they match by a linear bijection that preserves norms.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, taking the infimum over representatives preserves the bound on a functional that vanishes on M. Such a functional takes one value throughout each coset, so it defines a functional on the quotient. Conversely, composing a quotient functional with the quotient map preserves its bound because the map never increases norms. The two constructions undo each other, so the norms agree.

**Paper or page:** [Normed Dual Space of Normed Quotient Vector Space is Isometrically Isomorphic to Annihilator](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Normed_Dual_Space_of_Normed_Quotient_Vector_Space_is_Isometrically_Isomorphic_to_Annihilator). It says: “(X/Y)∗ is isometrically isomorphic to Y⊥”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The operator norm makes bounded maps a complete space

**Remember:** Take pointwise limits, then keep the same uniform error bound.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 46B28 (Spaces of operators; tensor products; approximation properties), 47A05. arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the operator norm of a bounded linear map T as the supremum of ‖Tx‖ over ‖x‖ ≤ 1. It measures error uniformly on the unit ball, unlike convergence tested on each vector separately.

**Problem.** Bounded linear maps from a normed space to a Banach space form a Banach space in the operator norm.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the operator norm gives one error bound for the whole unit ball. For a Cauchy sequence of maps, completeness of the target gives a limit at each vector. The resulting map is linear, and the uniform error bound still holds after taking the pointwise limit. Thus the limit is bounded and the maps converge to it in operator norm.

**nLab:** [Banach space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Banach+space). It says: “This will be a Banach space if (and, except for degenerate cases of V, only if) W is a Banach space.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Closed subspaces make distance a quotient norm

**Remember:** Only vectors in a closed subspace have zero distance from it.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 46B99 (Normed linear spaces and Banach spaces; Banach lattices). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A coset x + M consists of all vectors x + m with m in the subspace M. Its quotient seminorm is the distance from x to M.

**Problem.** For a closed subspace M of a normed space, distance to M defines a norm on the cosets.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, closedness ensures that distance zero puts x in M, so only the zero coset has length zero. Scaling and the triangle inequality give the other norm laws. Without closedness, take M to consist of the finitely supported sequences in the space of square-summable sequences. Truncating a sequence with infinitely many nonzero terms shows that its coset can have length zero even when the sequence lies outside M.

**Paper or page:** [Quotient Norm is Norm](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Quotient_Norm_is_Norm). It says: “Then $\\norm {\\, \\cdot \\,}<sub>X/N</sub>$ is indeed a norm.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Completeness lets pointwise bounds control operator norms

**Remember:** One bound per vector gives one bound for all operators on a Banach domain.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 46B99 (Normed linear spaces and Banach spaces; Banach lattices). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Banach space is a normed space in which all Cauchy sequences converge. A family is pointwise bounded if the values at each fixed vector are bounded across the family.

**Problem.** A pointwise bounded family of bounded linear operators from a Banach space into a normed space has uniformly bounded operator norms.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, completeness lets the Baire category theorem give a common bound throughout some ball. Subtraction gives a bound near zero, and scaling gives a bound on the unit ball. For a counterexample, take finitely supported sequences with the supremum norm and use the functionals x ↦ nxₙ. Their values stay bounded at each fixed sequence, yet their norms grow as n.

**Paper or page:** [From Uniform Boundedness to the Boundary Between Convergence and Divergence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13871). It says: “Let X be a Banach space and let Y be a normed space. Consider a family F of bounded linear operators T : X → Y. If F is pointwise bounded, then it is uniformly bounded.”

**Sources:**

- [Stefan Banach and Hugo Steinhaus, Sur le principe de la condensation de singularités, Fundamenta Mathematicae 9 (1927), 50–61.](https://doi.org/10.4064/fm-9-1-50-61)

### Quotient norms make the quotient map open

**Remember:** Below the radius means some representative is inside the ball.

*True by definition.* MSC 46B99 (Normed linear spaces and Banach spaces; Banach lattices). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The coset x + M consists of the vectors differing from x by an element of the closed subspace M. Its quotient norm is the infimum of the norms of those vectors. The quotient map sends x to x + M.

**Problem.** The map sending vectors to cosets of a closed subspace is open in the quotient norm. That is, it sends open sets to open sets.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the infimum puts a coset inside an open ball exactly when some representative lies in the original ball. Our own argument translates this fact from balls around zero to balls around any point. Open sets are unions of such balls, so no completeness or open mapping theorem is needed.

**Paper or page:** [Quotient Mapping Maps Unit Open Ball in Normed Vector Space to Unit Open Ball in Normed Quotient Vector Space](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Quotient_Mapping_Maps_Unit_Open_Ball_in_Normed_Vector_Space_to_Unit_Open_Ball_in_Normed_Quotient_Vector_Space). It says: “\\map \\pi {B<sub>X</sub>} = B<sub>X/N</sub>”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The quotient norm lets close cosets lift to close vectors

**Remember:** Choose short representatives of the differences between successive cosets.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 46B99 (Normed linear spaces and Banach spaces; Banach lattices). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In a quotient by a closed subspace M, the coset x + M groups vectors that differ by an element of M. Define its norm as the infimum of the norms of all its representatives.

**Problem.** The quotient of a Banach space by a closed subspace is again a Banach space.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the infimum lets us lift small differences between cosets to short vectors. From a Cauchy sequence of cosets, choose a subsequence whose successive differences have norms below 2⁻ⁿ at step n. Choose representatives of those differences with the same bounds and add them to a representative of the first coset. Completeness gives a limit whose coset is the subsequence limit and hence the limit of the Cauchy sequence.

**Wikipedia:** [Quotient space (linear algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_space_%28linear_algebra%29). It says: “If X is a Banach space and M is a closed subspace of X, then the quotient X/M is again a Banach space.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dense orthonormal spans turn Bessel’s bound into equality

**Remember:** A dense span leaves no part of the squared norm uncounted.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 46C05 (Hilbert and pre-Hilbert spaces: geometry and topology (including spaces with semidefinite inner product)). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** An orthonormal basis is a set of mutually perpendicular unit vectors whose finite linear combinations are dense. An orthonormal set without this density need not see every part of a vector.

**Problem.** For a countable orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space, the sum of squared magnitudes of the inner products with a vector equals its squared norm.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, dense span makes the error of projection onto the first n basis vectors tend to zero. Each projection gives the closest point in its span, so its error is at most that of any approximation there. Pythagoras expresses the squared norm as the partial coordinate sum plus the squared error. Taking the limit gives equality.

**Wikipedia:** [Orthonormal basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthonormal_basis). It says: “An orthonormal basis is an orthonormal system with the additional property that the linear span of S is dense in H.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dense span lets every orthonormal set extend to a basis

**Remember:** A Hilbert basis needs dense span, not finite formulas for every vector.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 46C05 (Hilbert and pre-Hilbert spaces: geometry and topology (including spaces with semidefinite inner product)). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** An orthonormal set consists of mutually perpendicular unit vectors. It is an orthonormal basis if finite linear combinations of its vectors approximate every vector arbitrarily closely.

**Problem.** Every orthonormal set in a Hilbert space extends to an orthonormal basis.

**How the definition helps.** Dense span makes a maximal orthonormal set a basis. Zorn’s lemma extends the given set to a maximal one. In our own argument, if its closed span misses a vector, subtract that vector’s orthogonal projection onto the span. Normalizing the nonzero perpendicular remainder would enlarge the set.

**nLab:** [orthogonal basis](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/orthogonal+basis). It says: “any maximal orthogonal set (which must exist by an application of Zorn's lemma) is necessarily a basis in the topological sense.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Inner product tests give bounded sequences weakly convergent subsequences

**Remember:** Weak convergence means convergence of inner products against every fixed vector.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 46C05 (Hilbert and pre-Hilbert spaces: geometry and topology (including spaces with semidefinite inner product)). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A sequence converges weakly to x if its inner products with each fixed test vector converge to the corresponding inner product with x. Norm convergence instead asks that the norm of the difference from x tend to zero.

**Problem.** Every bounded sequence in a Hilbert space has a weakly convergent subsequence.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, inner product tests on a countable dense subset of the sequence’s closed span suffice because the sequence is bounded. A diagonal subsequence gives convergence on those tests, and the uniform bound extends convergence to the whole span. Riesz representation gives the limiting vector there. Projecting any other test vector onto that span leaves all its inner products with the sequence unchanged.

**Wikipedia:** [Weak convergence (Hilbert space)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weak_convergence_%28Hilbert_space%29). It says: “every bounded sequence xₙ in a Hilbert space H contains a weakly convergent subsequence.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Orthogonal projection gives Bessel’s inequality

**Remember:** Project into the subspace so the remainder is perpendicular to it.

*True by definition.* MSC 46C05 (Hilbert and pre-Hilbert spaces: geometry and topology (including spaces with semidefinite inner product)). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The orthogonal projection of x onto a finite-dimensional subspace is the unique point p in it for which x − p is perpendicular to it. Equivalently, p is the closest point to x in the subspace.

**Problem.** For a countable orthonormal set in an inner product space, the sum of squared coordinate magnitudes never exceeds the squared norm of the vector.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the perpendicular remainder makes the inequality an application of Pythagoras to each finite projection. The coordinates of the projection are the inner products with the chosen perpendicular unit vectors. Thus every partial sum is bounded by the squared norm of x, giving the same bound for the series. Pythagoras also proves that the perpendicular projection is the closest point.

**Paper or page:** [Bessel's Inequality](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Bessel's_Inequality). It says: “∑ₙ₌₁∞ \|⟨h,eₙ⟩\|² ≤ ‖h‖²”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Vanishing at infinity means continuous at the added point

**Remember:** Small outside a compact set means near zero near the point at infinity.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 46E05 (Lattices of continuous, differentiable or analytic functions), 54D35. arXiv math.GN, math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let f be continuous and scalar-valued on a locally compact Hausdorff space X. It vanishes at infinity if {x : \|f(x)\| ≥ ε} is compact for every ε &gt; 0. In the one-point extension, complements of compact subsets of X form a neighbourhood base at the added point.

**Problem.** Let X be locally compact and Hausdorff. A continuous function that vanishes at infinity extends continuously to X ∪ {p}, with value 0 at p. These functions form a Banach space under the supremum norm.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, each ε gives a neighbourhood of the added point on which the extended function has magnitude below ε. This proves continuity there. Extension preserves the supremum norm and identifies the space with the continuous functions vanishing at the added point. These form a closed subspace of the Banach space of continuous functions on the compact extension.

**Paper or page:** [Extension of Continuous Complex-Valued Function Vanishing at Infinity to Alexandroff Extension is Continuous](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Extension_of_Continuous_Complex-Valued_Function_Vanishing_at_Infinity_to_Alexandroff_Extension_is_Continuous), [Space of Continuous Functions on Locally Compact Hausdorff Space Vanishing at Infinity is Banach Space](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Space_of_Continuous_Functions_on_Locally_Compact_Hausdorff_Space_Vanishing_at_Infinity_is_Banach_Space). It says: “Let f : X → ℂ be a continuous complex-valued function vanishing at infinity. Define f\* : X\* → ℂ by taking”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, Extension of Continuous Complex-Valued Function Vanishing at Infinity to Alexandroff Extension is Continuous](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Extension_of_Continuous_Complex-Valued_Function_Vanishing_at_Infinity_to_Alexandroff_Extension_is_Continuous)
- [ProofWiki, Space of Continuous Functions on Locally Compact Hausdorff Space Vanishing at Infinity is Banach Space](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Space_of_Continuous_Functions_on_Locally_Compact_Hausdorff_Space_Vanishing_at_Infinity_is_Banach_Space)

### Measuring derivatives as well makes the space of differentiable functions complete

**Remember:** Keep the derivatives close, so the limit still has a derivative.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 46E15 (Banach spaces of continuous, differentiable or analytic functions). arXiv math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a continuously differentiable real function f on \[0,1\], its C¹ norm is sup\|f\| + sup\|f′\|. This norm measures uniform errors in both the function and its derivative.

**Problem.** Continuously differentiable functions on \[0,1\] form a Banach space in the norm sup\|f\| + sup\|f′\|.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, a Cauchy sequence in this norm has uniform limits for both the functions and their derivatives. The fundamental theorem of calculus identifies the second limit as the derivative of the first. With only the supremum norm, the smooth functions √((x − ½)² + 1/n) converge uniformly to \|x − ½\|, which has a corner.

**Paper or page:** [Space of Continuously Differentiable on Closed Interval Real-Valued Functions with C<sup>1</sup> Norm is Banach Space](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Space_of_Continuously_Differentiable_on_Closed_Interval_Real-Valued_Functions_with_C^1_Norm_is_Banach_Space). It says: “is a Banach space.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Separating points is all that Stone–Weierstrass needs

**Remember:** To approximate everything, the algebra must tell every two points apart.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 46E25 (Rings and algebras of continuous, differentiable or analytic functions), 41A65. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A set A of functions on X separates points when its functions can tell any two points apart. That is, for any two different points x and y of X, some function p in A has p(x) ≠ p(y).

**Problem.** Let X be a compact Hausdorff space, and let C(X, ℝ) be the algebra of continuous real functions on X. A subalgebra of C(X, ℝ) that contains a non-zero constant function is dense in the uniform norm exactly when it separates points.

**How the definition helps.** Point separation gives the density criterion in the real Stone–Weierstrass theorem. For necessity, our own argument observes that uniform limits preserve equality at any pair the algebra fails to separate. Continuous real functions on a compact Hausdorff space separate every such pair.

**Wikipedia:** [Stone–Weierstrass theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone%E2%80%93Weierstrass_theorem). It says: “It turns out that the crucial property that a subalgebra must satisfy is that it separates points”

**Sources:**

- [M. H. Stone, Applications of the theory of Boolean rings to general topology, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 41 (1937), 375–481, doi:10.1090/S0002-9947-1937-1501905-7](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1937-1501905-7)

### Defining Lᵖ by completion gives completeness for finite p

**Remember:** Complete the simple functions, then identify the resulting limits.

*True by definition.* MSC 46E30 (Spaces of measurable functions (\\(L<sup>p\\</sup>)-spaces, Orlicz spaces, Köthe function spaces, Lorentz spaces, rearrangement invariant spaces, ideal spaces, etc.)), 28A25. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For 1 ≤ p &lt; ∞, define Lᵖ as the norm completion of simple functions that vanish outside a set of finite measure. To get the norm, integrate the pth power of \|f\| and take the pth root. Identify functions that agree outside a null set before taking the completion.

**Problem.** For 1 ≤ p &lt; ∞, Lᵖ is complete under its norm. Every sequence that is Cauchy in that norm has a limit in the space.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the norm completion supplies limits for all Cauchy sequences by construction (our own). The work is identifying this completion with measurable functions of finite norm, up to equality almost everywhere (our own). Choose a subsequence with summable norms of consecutive differences (our own). The triangle inequality and monotone convergence bound the sum of absolute differences and its tails, giving convergence almost everywhere and in norm (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lp space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lp_space). It says: “By construction of the integral, the vector space of integrable simple functions is dense in Lᵖ(S, Σ, μ).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Grading Lebesgue spaces by 1/p makes Hölder's inequality a graded multiplication

**Remember:** Use 1/p as the degree, and degrees add when you multiply.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 46E30 (Spaces of measurable functions (\\(L<sup>p\\</sup>)-spaces, Orlicz spaces, Köthe function spaces, Lorentz spaces, rearrangement invariant spaces, ideal spaces, etc.)), 26D15. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** On a fixed measure space, assign degree a to the space M(a) = L¹⁄ᵃ for every real a &gt; 0. Assign degree zero to M(0) = L∞.

**Problem.** If f lies in M(a) and g lies in M(b), then fg lies in M(a + b). In the usual indexing this is Hölder's rule 1/p + 1/q = 1/r.

**How the definition helps.** The reciprocal exponents in Hölder’s inequality are exactly the degrees, so multiplication adds degrees. Our own endpoint check uses the essential supremum bound when either degree is zero.

**nLab:** [Lebesgue space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lebesgue+space). It says: “If we take M<sup>p=L^</sup>(1/p), the spaces M<sup>p</sup> form a C-graded algebra, where C denotes complex numbers. This is a conceptual explanation for the appearance of formulas like 1/p+1/q=1/r in Hölder's inequality.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Lᵖ treats functions that agree almost everywhere as equal

**Remember:** In Lᵖ, what happens on a set of measure zero does not count.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 46E30 (Spaces of measurable functions (\\(L<sup>p\\</sup>)-spaces, Orlicz spaces, Köthe function spaces, Lorentz spaces, rearrangement invariant spaces, ideal spaces, etc.)). arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.
