**Remember:** Use one unit for both currencies, then convert the answer back.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91G20 (Derivative securities (option pricing, hedging, etc.)). arXiv q-fin.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f be the dollar price of one euro. In an intermediate currency, one euro costs √f and one dollar costs 1/√f. A payoff has degree one if multiplying both inputs by a positive factor multiplies the payoff by that factor.

**Problem.** In the paper’s euro–dollar model, consider options payable only at expiry with degree-one payoffs. The same pricing probability values options written on euros and options written on dollars.

**How the definition helps.** Measuring both currencies in the same unit gives both contracts the same pricing probability (our own). Degree-one scaling converts the amount paid at expiry into that unit (our own). The paper constructs the intermediate interest rate and proves that the corresponding pricing probability exists.

**Paper or page:** [Pricing FX Options under Intermediate Currency](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01387v2), [Pricing FX Options under Intermediate Currency](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01387v2). It says: “Then the arbitrage price of a European option on EUR with a payoff g(x; K) being homogeneous function of order 1 and maturity time T is given by”

**Sources:**

- [S. Maurer, T. E. Sharp, M. V. Tretyakov. Pricing FX Options under Intermediate Currency (2021).](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01387v2)

### Directional closure makes capital limits attainable

**Remember:** Including limits along the priced direction makes the boundary budget work.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 91G70 (Statistical methods; risk measures). arXiv q-fin.RM. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let A be an upward-closed acceptance set and π a linear price on eligible trades including U ≥ 0 with π(U) = 1. Put B = A + ker π, adding all zero-price trades. Directional closure requires x ∈ B whenever x + εU ∈ B for every ε &gt; 0.

**Problem.** Required capital is the infimum price of trades making a position safe. Fix any real budget m. Directional closure holds exactly when every position requiring at most m admits a trade costing m that makes it safe.

**How the definition helps.** A trade costing m works at x exactly when x + mU belongs to B (our own). Capital at most m gives membership at every budget m + ε, so closure gives membership at m (our own). Conversely, apply budget attainment to x − mU whenever x + εU belongs to B for every ε &gt; 0 (our own). With only strictly positive balances acceptable, every positive deposit works at zero, but zero fails (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A new view on risk measures associated with acceptance sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12320v2). It says: “holds if and only if A + ker π is (−U)-directionally closed.”

**Sources:**

- [A new view on risk measures associated with acceptance sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12320v2)

### Logarithms turn risk products into sums

**Remember:** Taking logs turns multiplication of risk bounds into addition.

*True by definition.* MSC 91G70 (Statistical methods; risk measures). arXiv q-fin.RM. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a positive loss factor X, let η(X) be the infimum price of an eligible payoff H that makes X/H acceptable. Use positive payoffs and prices. In logarithmic units, an eligible payoff becomes log H and its cost becomes the logarithm of its price.

**Problem.** Assume products stay in the loss domain and the risks are positive and finite. Then η(XY) ≤ η(X)η(Y) exactly when the corresponding risk on log losses is subadditive, meaning the risk of a sum never exceeds the summed risks.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation takes logarithms of both sides, turning a product bound into a sum bound. The essential identity says that the transformed capital requirement at log X equals log η(X). It follows by translating every acceptable trade and taking its infimum cost.

**Paper or page:** [Multi-asset return risk measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08763v2). It says: “is subadditive if and only if ηℜ is submultiplicative, i.e., ∀ X,Y ∈ C: ηℜ(XY) ≤ ηℜ(X)ηℜ(Y).”

**Sources:**

- [Multi-asset return risk measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08763v2)

### Moment bounds control worst-case risk

**Remember:** Match means and covariances with Gaussians, then measure their transport distance.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91G70 (Statistical methods; risk measures). arXiv q-fin.RM. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Quadratic transport distance minimizes root mean square separation over all joint realizations of two finite-second-moment laws. A transport ball bounds this distance from a reference law by a radius. A Gelbrich set imposes that bound on the Gaussian laws matching the respective means and covariances.

**Problem.** For the same reference law and radius, the supremum of risk over the Gelbrich set bounds the supremum over the transport ball from above.

**How the definition helps.** Using only means and covariances enlarges the set over which one takes the worst risk (our own). The Gelbrich inequality proves that replacing both laws by their matching Gaussians cannot increase their transport distance (our own). Set inclusion then gives the risk bound for each fixed loss function.

**Paper or page:** [Mean-Covariance Robust Risk Measurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09959v3), [Mean-Covariance Robust Risk Measurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09959v3). It says: “then we have 𝒲ᵨ(ℙ̂) ⊆ 𝒢ᵨ(μ̂, Σ̂).”

**Sources:**

- [Viet Anh Nguyen, Soroosh Shafiee, Damir Filipović, Daniel Kuhn. Mean-Covariance Robust Risk Measurement (2025).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09959v3)

## 92 Biology and other natural sciences

### Clock trees give ultrametric distances

**Remember:** Equal tip heights force the two largest distances in every triple to tie.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Use a rooted tree with the same total length from its root to every tip. This models a strict evolutionary clock for tips sampled at the same time. Allowing unequal root-to-tip lengths gives an ordinary weighted tree instead.

**Problem.** For any three tips of a clock tree with positive edge lengths, the largest two pair distances are equal. Its tip distances are therefore an ultrametric.

**How the definition helps.** Equal tip heights make each pair distance twice the height difference from its most recent common ancestor (our own). Among three tips, at least two pairs have the same oldest common ancestor, so their distances tie for largest (our own). This tie gives the ultrametric inequality, which bounds each distance by the larger of the other two (our own). A three-tip star with edge lengths 1, 2 and 3 instead gives distances 3, 4 and 5 (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Hit and Run Sampling from Tropically Convex Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15045v1). It says: “Then, u is an ultrametric if and only if T is an equidistant tree.”

**Sources:**

- [Peter Buneman, A note on the metric properties of trees (1974).](https://doi.org/10.1016/0095-8956(74)90047-1)

### Fitch sets count minimum changes

**Remember:** Intersect sets when you can and charge one change when you must unite them.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE, q-bio.QM. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Consider a rooted binary ancestry tree with known states at its leaves. Charge one whenever the states at the ends of an edge differ. For each vertex, keep every state it can take in an assignment minimizing the total charge within its subtree.

**Problem.** Starting at the leaves, use the intersection of the two child sets whenever it contains a state. Otherwise use their union and count one change. The total count is the smallest possible number of changes on the tree.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping every minimizing state tells the parent exactly when it can join both subtrees without paying for another change (our own). A parent state in a child’s set allows that subtree’s minimum cost (our own). Any other state costs exactly one extra because the joining edge can carry the change (our own). These two possibilities prove the recursion and explain why choosing one minimizing state early can overcount (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ancestral reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestral_reconstruction). It says: “if the intersection is the empty set, then it is the set union.”

**Sources:**

- [W. M. Fitch, Toward Defining the Course of Evolution: Minimum Change for a Specific Tree Topology (1971)](https://doi.org/10.2307/2412116)

### Split counts give a tree metric

**Remember:** Each split on which two trees disagree must change in at least one comparison.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For two unrooted evolutionary trees on the same labeled tips, list the partitions of tips obtained by cutting individual edges. Their Robinson–Foulds distance is the number of partitions present in exactly one list.

**Problem.** This distance is a metric on unweighted trees with the same labeled tips and no degree-two internal nodes. Identify trees when an isomorphism preserves their tip labels.

**How the definition helps.** Counting differing partitions turns tree distance into the number of unequal entries in two binary lists (our own). Each disagreement between the first and last trees must appear in at least one comparison through an intermediate tree (our own). This gives the triangle inequality (our own). Proving that distance zero identifies the trees requires the theorem that the partitions determine the tree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Robinson–Foulds metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson%E2%80%93Foulds_metric). It says: “the number of splits that differ between a pair of trees”

**Sources:**

- [D. F. Robinson and L. R. Foulds, Comparison of phylogenetic trees (1981).](https://doi.org/10.1016/0025-5564(81)90043-2)

### Tree splits explain four-point ties

**Remember:** For four tips, only their internal split can make the three sums differ.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the distance between two tips of an evolutionary tree by adding the lengths along their connecting path. Equivalently, sum the lengths of all edges whose removal separates those tips.

**Problem.** For four distinct tips, sum the two distances in each of the three possible pairings. The largest sum occurs at least twice in any tree with nonnegative edge lengths.

**How the definition helps.** Count each edge’s contribution to the three sums (our own). Edges separating one tip from three contribute equally, and edges separating none contribute zero (our own). All two-against-two edges induce the same split because tree edge splits are compatible (our own). Each adds twice its nonnegative length to both crossing pairings, so those sums tie for largest (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Tropical Grassmannian and Tropical Linear Varieties from phylogenetic trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0752v2). It says: “the maximum of three number is achieved at least twice D({i,j}) + D({k,l}), D({i,k}) + D({j,l}) and D({i,l}) + D({j,k}).”

**Sources:**

- [Peter Buneman, A note on the metric properties of trees (1974).](https://doi.org/10.1016/0095-8956(74)90047-1)

### Single-neuron updates prevent Hopfield cycles

**Remember:** Update one neuron at a time so each actual flip lowers the energy.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 92B20 (Neural networks for/in biological studies, artificial life and related topics). arXiv q-bio.NC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A finite Hopfield network has states ±1, symmetric connection weights and no self-connections. Update one neuron at a time to the sign of its weighted input, keeping its state at zero input. Visit every neuron infinitely often.

**Problem.** Every such update run eventually reaches a fixed state.

**How the definition helps.** Take energy to be minus the sum over undirected edges of weight times the product of endpoint states (our own). Its change equals minus the updated neuron's input times its state change, so every flip strictly decreases energy (our own). Finiteness allows only finitely many flips, and repeated visits then imply stability (our own). Under simultaneous updates, two positively coupled neurons starting in opposite states swap forever (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hopfield network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopfield_network). It says: “The constraint that weights are symmetric guarantees that the energy function decreases monotonically while following the activation rules.”

**Sources:**

- [J. J. Hopfield, Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities (1982)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.79.8.2554)
- [J. Bruck, On the convergence properties of the Hopfield model (1990)](https://doi.org/10.1109/5.58341)

### Crossover distances add across intervals

**Remember:** Count crossovers rather than just the pairs they switch.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D10 (Genetics and epigenetics). arXiv q-bio.GN, q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A crossover exchanges chromosome segments during the formation of a reproductive cell. Measure genetic distance in morgans by the expected number of crossovers on the transmitted chromosome between two markers. The recombination fraction instead counts the probability that the two markers come from different parental chromosomes.

**Problem.** Genetic distances add across adjacent intervals. If the crossover count has a Poisson distribution with mean d, the recombination fraction equals (1 − exp(−2d))/2.

**How the definition helps.** Adjacent crossover counts add on each transmitted chromosome, so their expectations add without any independence assumption (our own). Only an odd count switches the marker pairing (our own). For a Poisson count N of mean d, E\[(−1)ᴺ\] = exp(−2d) equals one minus twice the odd-count probability (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Centimorgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centimorgan). It says: “the distance in centimorgans does not correspond exactly to the probability of genetic recombination.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Linkage excess decays geometrically

**Remember:** Subtract independent pairing first, then recombination scales only the excess.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D10 (Genetics and epigenetics). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Choose one genetic variant at each of two positions on a chromosome. Subtract the product of their separate frequencies from the frequency of chromosomes carrying both. This difference D measures linkage disequilibrium.

**Problem.** In a deterministic random-mating model, D becomes (1 − c)D each generation. Here c is the fixed fraction of reproductive cells in which recombination separates the two positions. Assume no selection, mutation or migration.

**How the definition helps.** Recombination mixes the current joint frequency J with the independent pairing frequency pq (our own). Random mating gives J′ = (1 − c)J + cpq, while the separate frequencies p and q stay fixed (our own). Subtracting pq gives D′ = (1 − c)D (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Linkage disequilibrium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linkage_disequilibrium). It says: “recombination is expected to decrease the value of D in each generation by a factor (1 - c)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Relative fitness isolates selection

**Remember:** Divide each ancestor’s descendant count by the mean descendant count.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D15 (Problems related to evolution). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Assign each descendant to one ancestor and assume at least one descendant exists. Define each ancestor’s relative fitness as its descendant count divided by the mean count per ancestor.

**Problem.** The change in mean trait equals the covariance of relative fitness with ancestral trait, plus a transmission term. The transmission term averages, over ancestors, relative fitness times the change from the ancestor's trait to its descendants' mean trait. Both averages weight ancestors equally, and childless ancestors add zero.

**How the definition helps.** Using relative fitness gives weights with mean one, so reweighting ancestral traits adds exactly a covariance (our own). Add and subtract this reweighted ancestral mean when comparing the two generations (our own). The remaining difference measures change within families (our own). Predicting either term still requires a model of reproduction and transmission (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Price equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price_equation). It says: “The equation uses a covariance between a characteristic and fitness, to give a mathematical description of evolution and natural selection.”

**Sources:**

- [George R. Price, Selection and Covariance (1970).](https://doi.org/10.1038/227520a0)

### Log populations preserve volume

**Remember:** Use log sizes so each growth equation ignores its own coordinate.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D25 (Population dynamics (general)). arXiv math.DS, q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Use the logarithm of each population size as its coordinate. Assume each species’ per capita growth rate is a constant plus a sum of multiples of the other population sizes.

**Problem.** The flow preserves ordinary volume in log coordinates wherever the solutions exist and stay positive.

**How the definition helps.** Logarithms turn each per capita growth rate into a velocity independent of its own coordinate (our own). The diagonal derivatives therefore vanish, so the velocity has zero divergence (our own). The flow volume theorem then gives preservation of ordinary volume in log coordinates (our own). In population coordinates, the same volume weights each region by the reciprocal product of its population sizes (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On a quadratic Poisson algebra and integrable Lotka-Volterra systems with solutions in terms of Lambert's W function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.14720v2). It says: “with aᵢᵢ = 0 are measure preserving with density M = (∏ᵢ₌₁ⁿ xᵢ)⁻¹.”

**Sources:**

- [Peter H. van der Kamp, D. I. McLaren and G. R. W. Quispel, On a quadratic Poisson algebra and integrable Lotka-Volterra systems with solutions in terms of Lambert's W function (2024).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.14720v2)

### Reproductive value gives exact growth

**Remember:** Weight ages by what they contribute to future growth.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D25 (Population dynamics (general)). arXiv q-bio.PE, math.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Use a fixed age projection matrix to move the age counts forward one step. Weight each age by the corresponding entry of a positive left eigenvector for the dominant eigenvalue. This weighted count uses reproductive values instead of counting every age equally.

**Problem.** For a primitive age projection matrix, the weighted total grows by its dominant eigenvalue every step, from any starting age distribution. Primitive means that some power of the matrix has strictly positive entries.

**How the definition helps.** The eigenvector weights turn the age update into multiplication of one total by one factor (our own). For a row of weights w and projection matrix A, the left eigenvector equation gives wA = λw (our own). The Perron–Frobenius theorem supplies positive weights, and the age model relates them to discounted future offspring (our own). For a nonzero initial population, the ordinary head count’s growth factor generally approaches λ only in the limit (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Reproductive value (population genetics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproductive_value_%28population_genetics%29). It says: “he proposed that future offspring be discounted at the rate of growth of the population”

**Sources:**

- [Ronald A. Fisher, The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection (1930).](https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.27468)
- [P. H. Leslie, On the use of matrices in certain population mathematics (1945).](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/33.3.183)

### Effective reproduction locates infection peaks

**Remember:** Divide transmission per infected individual by recovery per infected individual.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D30 (Epidemiology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In the closed SIR model, susceptible and infected fractions satisfy S′ = −βSI and I′ = βSI − γI for constants β,γ &gt; 0. The effective reproduction number R = βS/γ compares the current per-infected transmission rate with the recovery rate.

**Problem.** If I starts positive and R starts above one, I has a unique peak when R reaches one.

**How the definition helps.** Using R turns the infection equation into the sign test I′ = γI(R − 1) (our own). While R ≥ 1, I stays above its positive starting value and S decreases at rate βSI (our own). Hence S crosses γ/β in finite time and continues decreasing, so growth changes to decline exactly once (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The SIR model of an epidemic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12029). It says: “The peak infection takes place when the effective reproduction number r₀ S = 1.”

**Sources:**

- [The SIR model of an epidemic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12029)

### Effective diversity scales with replication

**Remember:** Exponentiating entropy makes doubling equal, disjoint samples double their diversity.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D40 (Ecology). arXiv q-bio.QM. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For each species with positive frequency p, form −p ln p and sum over species to obtain Shannon entropy H. Define order-one Hill diversity as exp(H), the number of equally common species that would give the same entropy.

**Problem.** Pool equally weighted communities with disjoint species and the same species frequency pattern. The pooled order-one Hill diversity equals the diversity of one community times the number of communities.

**How the definition helps.** Exponentiation turns the additive entropy increase into a multiplicative change in diversity (our own). Pooling m equal communities replaces each frequency p with m copies of p/m because the species sets are disjoint (our own). Substitution in the entropy sum adds ln m, so the effective number of species grows by a factor of m (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Diversity index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversity_index). It says: “Hill numbers of order q or effective number of species”

**Sources:**

- [Lou Jost, Entropy and diversity (2006).](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2006.0030-1299.14714.x)

### Weighted contrasts give independent comparisons

**Remember:** Take the child difference and pass up the weighted mean.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology), 92B15. arXiv q-bio.QM. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At the tips, use the observed traits with variances given by their branches. For child estimates x,y with variances a,b, record (x − y)/√(a+b) and pass their inverse-variance weighted mean upward. For the next comparison, add the intervening branch variance to ab/(a+b).

**Problem.** Suppose changes on separate branches are independent centered Gaussian variables with variance proportional to positive branch length. The standardized differences are independent centered Gaussian variables with variance one.

**How the definition helps.** Inverse-variance weights make the estimate passed upward uncorrelated with the difference just recorded (our own). An ordinary unweighted mean lacks that property when branch variances differ (our own). The difference cancels the common ancestral value, and joint Gaussian variables with zero covariance are independent (our own). Updating the variance then lets the same argument apply at each parent (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Phylogenetic comparative methods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylogenetic_comparative_methods). It says: “transform the original tip data (mean values for a set of species) into values that are statistically independent and identically distributed.”

**Sources:**

- [J. Felsenstein, Phylogenies and the Comparative Method (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1086/284325)

### Spike edit costs vary continuously

**Remember:** Minimize unpaired spikes plus movement price times total paired displacement.

*True by definition.* MSC 92C20 (Neural biology). arXiv q-bio.NC, q-bio.QM. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For two finite spike trains, pair any subsets of their spikes one-to-one in chronological order. The Victor–Purpura distance at q ≥ 0 minimizes the number of unpaired spikes plus q times total absolute timing displacement over all such pairings.

**Problem.** For trains with at most one spike at each integer time from 0 to T, the distance is Lipschitz in q ≥ 0. Its change is at most T(T + 1) ÷ 2 times the absolute change in q.

**How the definition helps.** Each pairing gives an affine cost with slope equal to total displacement (our own). With k pairs, each ordered time differs from its partner by at most T+1−k, since both occupy the same rank (our own). Total displacement is at most k(T+1−k) ≤ T(T+1)/2 for integer T ≥ 1, and vanishes for T = 0 (our own). A minimum of functions with this common Lipschitz bound retains it (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Persistent Homology Pipeline for the Analysis of Neural Spike Train Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08637). It says: “Let 𝖲 and 𝖲′ be two spike trains over the time domain X = {0, 1, 2, …, T}. For any q,q′ ≥ 0, we have \|VP<sub>q</sub>(𝖲, 𝖲′) − VP<sub>q</sub>′(𝖲, 𝖲′)\| ≤ T(T+1)/2 \|q−q′\|”

**Sources:**

- [A Persistent Homology Pipeline for the Analysis of Neural Spike Train Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08637)

### Harmonic normalization removes sample-size bias

**Remember:** Divide the variable-site count by the harmonic sum for the sample.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D10 (Genetics and epigenetics), 92B15. arXiv q-bio.PE, q-bio.GN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Sample n ≥ 2 gene copies from a single randomly mating population of constant size. Count the sites where at least two copies differ. Watterson’s estimator divides that count by H = 1 + 1/2 + ⋯ + 1/(n − 1).

**Problem.** Use the standard neutral coalescent, a random ancestry tree where each pair of ancestral lines merges at the same rate. Assume no recombination and random mutations at a constant rate, each at a previously unchanged site. The estimator has expectation θ, the population-scaled mutation rate for the sequence.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by H removes the sample-size factor in the expected raw count (our own). With k ancestral lines, the mean waiting time is 2/\[k(k − 1)\] in units where each pair merges at rate one (our own). Multiplying by k and summing gives expected tree length 2H (our own). Each mutation adds one variable site, at rate θ/2 per unit of branch length (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Watterson estimator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watterson_estimator). It says: “When its assumptions are met, the estimator is unbiased”

**Sources:**

- [G. A. Watterson, On the number of segregating sites in genetical models without recombination (1975)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0040-5809(75)90020-9)

### Evolutionary stability rejects neutral ties

**Remember:** When payoffs against residents tie, compare both strategies against the mutant.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 92D15 (Problems related to evolution). arXiv q-bio.PE, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a symmetric game, both players use the same payoff rule. A resident strategy is evolutionarily stable if it beats each alternative in a population containing a sufficiently small positive share of that alternative. This requires at least a tie against residents and, in case of a tie, a strict advantage against the alternative.

**Problem.** In a finite symmetric two-player game, every evolutionarily stable strategy is locally asymptotically stable under replicator dynamics. Each strategy’s share grows at a per capita rate equal to its payoff minus the population mean. Populations starting sufficiently close stay close and converge to the resident.

**How the definition helps.** Evolutionary stability gives the resident a payoff advantage over every distinct sufficiently close population mix (our own). Under replicator dynamics, the derivative of relative entropy from resident to population equals minus that advantage (our own). This strict local Lyapunov function proves attraction and stability (our own). If only mutual B earns one, all-A is Nash but a rare B grows (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Evolutionarily stable strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionarily_stable_strategy). It says: “the population of players who continue to play strategy S has an advantage when playing against T.”

**Sources:**

- [John Maynard Smith and George R. Price, The Logic of Animal Conflict (1973).](https://doi.org/10.1038/246015a0)
- [Peter D. Taylor and Leo B. Jonker, Evolutionary stable strategies and game dynamics (1978).](https://doi.org/10.1016/0025-5564(78)90077-9)

### Weak reversibility excludes one-way sinks

**Remember:** Every reaction needs a return path, not necessarily a reverse edge.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 92E20 (Classical flows, reactions, etc. in chemistry), 92C42. arXiv q-bio.MN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Draw each reaction as an arrow between its reactant and product complexes. A network is weakly reversible if every arrow lies on a directed cycle. Its deficiency equals the number of complexes minus the number of undirected components minus the dimension spanned by reaction change vectors.

**Problem.** Suppose each reaction rate equals a positive constant times the product of reactant concentrations raised to their reaction coefficients. Every weakly reversible network of deficiency zero then has a positive equilibrium where incoming and outgoing rates balance at each complex.

**How the definition helps.** A return path excludes complexes that can only lose material in a one-way reaction (our own). For example, A → B has deficiency zero but no equilibrium with A positive (our own). The deficiency-zero theorem proves existence for every choice of positive rate constants (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Advancing Mathematical Epidemiology and Chemical Reaction Network Theory via Synergies Between Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00488). It says: “𝒩 admits a “complex-balanced” equilibrium, and all its equilibria are complex-balanced.”

**Sources:**

- [Advancing Mathematical Epidemiology and Chemical Reaction Network Theory via Synergies Between Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00488)

### Any orchard cherry reduction works

**Remember:** In an orchard network, any available cherry reduction keeps the process on track.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a rooted binary network, delete a cherry leaf sharing its parent with another leaf, or reduce a reticulated cherry. The latter cuts the edge from one leaf’s branching parent to the other’s two-parent vertex. After suppressing unary vertices, including a unary root, a network is orchard if some such sequence reduces it to one leaf.

**Problem.** Every maximal sequence of cherry reductions in an orchard network ends at one leaf.

**How the definition helps.** The definition lets us compare one successful sequence with every sequence that runs out of moves (our own). The hard step proves that any legal first reduction leaves another orchard network (our own). Each move shrinks the network, and every nontrivial orchard network has another move (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Defining phylogenetic networks using ancestral profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00109). It says: “Let 𝒩 be an orchard network, and let 𝒩 = 𝒩₀, 𝒩₁, …, 𝒩ₗ be a maximal cherry-reduction sequence. Then this sequence is complete.”

**Sources:**

- [Defining phylogenetic networks using ancestral profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00109)

### Child labels identify tree-child networks

**Remember:** A child with one parent appears in exactly one child set.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a network admitting the paper’s encoding, assign distinct labels to vertices and record one child-label set per parent. The network is tree-child if every parent has a child with exactly one parent.

**Problem.** For networks admitting this encoding, the network is tree-child exactly when every set contains a label occurring only once in the cover.

**How the definition helps.** Every occurrence of a label in a child set counts one parent (our own). Checking a child’s parent count becomes counting label occurrences (our own). The work lies in the earlier bijection between these covers and networks that admit the labeling (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Phylogenetic network classes through the lens of expanding covers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06519v2). It says: “Tree-child networks are in bijection with expanding covers for which each set contains an integer that appears exactly once in the cover.”

**Sources:**

- [Andrew Francis, Daniele Marchei and Mike Steel, Phylogenetic network classes through the lens of expanding covers (2024).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06519v2)

### Leaf correlations contract forest space

**Remember:** Shrink every off-diagonal correlation to zero and the leaves become isolated.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE, q-bio.QM. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Use forests with distinct labels on distinct vertices and labels on every vertex of degree at most two. Give edges positive lengths, and set the matrix entry for connected labels to exp(−d), where d is their path distance. Wald space consists of these matrices, with zero entries for disconnected labels.

**Problem.** Wald space can shrink continuously to the matrix for isolated labels.

**How the definition helps.** For 0 &lt; t &lt; 1, move every label onto a new pendant edge of length −ln(t)/2 (our own). Prune unlabeled dead ends and suppress unlabeled degree-two vertices, preserving distances between labels (our own). Every connected pair of distinct labels gains distance −ln(t), multiplying its correlation by t (our own). These matrices interpolate continuously between the original at t = 1 and isolated labels at t = 0 (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Foundations of the Wald Space for Phylogenetic Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.05332). It says: “Conveyed by the homeomorphism φ, 𝒲 is star shaped as a subset ℝᴺˣᴺ with respect to F∞ and hence contractible.”

**Sources:**

- [Foundations of the Wald Space for Phylogenetic Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.05332)

### Stack-free networks have unique profiles

**Remember:** Without stacks, ancestral path counts pin down the network.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology), 92D15. arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An ancestral profile records, for each leaf label, the path counts from all internal vertices in a common vertex order. An orchard network is one that repeated cherry reductions can shrink to a single leaf. A network is stack-free if no edge connects two vertices that both have multiple parents.

**Problem.** Among rooted phylogenetic networks on the same leaf labels, the ancestral profile determines a stack-free orchard network up to relabeling internal vertices.

**How the definition helps.** The stack-free condition rules out known orchard networks that share the same path counts despite having different shapes. The reconstruction proof must show how to identify a legal reduction from the profile and reverse that reduction uniquely (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Defining phylogenetic networks using ancestral profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00109). It says: “Then, up to isomorphism, 𝒩 is the unique phylogenetic network on X realising Σ𝒩.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Bai, P. L. Erdős, C. Semple and M. Steel, Defining phylogenetic networks using ancestral profiles (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mbs.2021.108537)

### Finite phase shifts test synchrony

**Remember:** Compose the two pulse responses before testing whether the phase gap shrinks.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 92B25 (Biological rhythms and synchronization), 92C20. arXiv q-bio.NC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Two identical oscillators advance uniformly in phase and pulse each other when they reach one and reset to zero. At fixed pulse strength the response F maps pre-pulse phase x to post-pulse phase x + g(x). Assume F increases, fixes both endpoints, and has derivatives on \[0,1\], using one-sided derivatives at the endpoints.

**Problem.** For two such oscillators that advance uniformly between pulses, simultaneous firing attracts nearby phases if \|F′(0)F′(1)\| &lt; 1. It repels nearby phases if this product has absolute value above one.

**How the definition helps.** The exact pulse map turns a full firing cycle into two evaluations of one function (our own). At each firing the next gap is 1 − F(x), with x the other oscillator’s phase just before the pulse (our own). Applying this rule twice and differentiating at zero gives F′(0)F′(1) (our own). A first-order approximation in pulse strength can give the wrong stability prediction.

**Paper or page:** [Infinitesimal phase response functions can be misleading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08392). It says: “Synchrony is g-attracting if \|(1 + ∂g/∂φ(0, ε))(1 + ∂g/∂φ(1, ε))\| &lt; 1,”

**Sources:**

- [Infinitesimal phase response functions can be misleading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08392)

### Subsamples inherit the same genealogy

**Remember:** Trace the same pedigree and then drop the labels you did not sample.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D10 (Genetics and epigenetics), 60J10. arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Represent ancestry at each past generation by a partition of the sampled labels. Each block records samples with the same ancestor, with that ancestor's type attached. Build the partition by tracing each label through the same realized population pedigree, not by simulating a second pedigree.

**Problem.** Suppose each type has fixed population size and relabeling parents within types leaves the joint offspring law unchanged. Keeping the first m of n sampled labels gives the same ancestry law as sampling those m labels directly.

**How the definition helps.** A shared family tree turns comparison of two random histories into deletion of labels (our own). Two retained labels have the same ancestor regardless of which other labels we trace (our own). The probabilistic work shows that this restricted history has the separately sampled history’s law under the relabeling assumption (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On the genealogy of multi-type Cannings models and their limiting exchangeable coalescents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10744). It says: “has the same distribution as the multi-type ancestral process”

**Sources:**

- [On the genealogy of multi-type Cannings models and their limiting exchangeable coalescents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10744)

## 93 Systems theory; control

### Transposition swaps controllability and observability

**Remember:** Transpose the dynamics and swap the input and output.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B05 (Controllability), 93B07. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Consider a continuous-time linear system with constant real matrices A, B and C for dynamics, input and output. Its dual uses Aᵀ for dynamics, Cᵀ for input and Bᵀ for output.

**Problem.** A finite-dimensional continuous-time linear system can reach every state from rest exactly when its dual can distinguish all initial states from their outputs.

**How the definition helps.** The matrix testing observability in the dual is the transpose of the matrix testing reachability in the original system. Transposition preserves rank. The work lies in proving that these ranks characterize which states inputs can reach and which states outputs can distinguish (our own).

**nLab:** [controllability and observability](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/controllability+and+observability). It says: “Now controllability of the original system corresponds to observability of the dual, and vice versa.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Gramians detect unobservable states

**Remember:** Zero output energy means the state left no trace.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B07 (Observability), 93C05. arXiv math.OC, eess.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let O send an initial state to its continuous output on a fixed interval of positive length, with zero input. The observability Gramian is W = O\*O, where O\* is the adjoint for the integrated output inner product. Thus xᵀWx is the integral of the squared output norm.

**Problem.** For a real finite-dimensional linear system, the observed output determines the initial state exactly when W is nonsingular.

**How the definition helps.** The squared output norm gives the Gramian and the observation map the same kernel (our own). Continuity makes zero integrated energy equivalent to zero output throughout the interval (our own). This replaces comparing entire output curves with checking a matrix (our own). Computing the observation map still requires solving the state equations (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Controllability and observability of tempered fractional differential systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05349v1). It says: “if, and only if, the observability Gramian matrix”

**Sources:**

- [Controllability and observability of tempered fractional differential systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05349v1)

### Error coordinates separate stability tests

**Remember:** Track the error and the two designs separate.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B52 (Feedback control), 93B53. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For state x and observer estimate x̂, the error coordinates are (x,e), where e = x − x̂.

**Problem.** Consider x′ = Ax + Bu with output Cx. Use feedback u = −Kx̂ and an observer that corrects its model prediction by L(Cx − Cx̂). The combined eigenvalues are those of A − BK and A − LC, counted with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** In error coordinates, subtraction gives e′ = (A − LC)e, independent of x (our own). Substitution gives x′ = (A − BK)x + BKe (our own). The resulting block triangular matrix has the eigenvalues of its two diagonal blocks.

**nLab:** [controllability and observability](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/controllability+and+observability). It says: “the design of a feedback controller and of a state observer are mutually independent.”

**Wikipedia:** [Separation principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_principle). It says: “the eigenvalues are just those of A − BK together with those of A − LC.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Strict properness prevents algebraic loops

**Remember:** One missing direct term breaks the instantaneous loop.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93B52 (Feedback control), 93C05. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A scalar rational transfer function is strictly proper if it vanishes identically or its numerator has smaller degree than its denominator.

**Problem.** Connect two proper finite-dimensional scalar linear time-invariant systems in feedback. If either transfer function is strictly proper, the current states and external inputs uniquely determine both current inputs.

**How the definition helps.** The strictly proper system supplies its output from its state, which lets us evaluate the other system next (our own). With direct dependence on both sides, the equations can fail (our own). Negative feedback around a static gain of −1 gives y = −(r − y), impossible for a nonzero reference r (our own). The direct gain equals the high-frequency limit of the transfer function (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Proper transfer function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proper_transfer_function). It says: “A strictly proper transfer function will approach zero as the frequency approaches infinity”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The bilinear transform preserves stability

**Remember:** The left half-plane goes inside the unit circle.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93C57 (Sampled-data control/observation systems), 93C80. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For step size h &gt; 0 and rate s ≠ 2/h, the bilinear transform gives the discrete multiplier z = (1 + hs/2)/(1 − hs/2).

**Problem.** If every eigenvalue of a state matrix has negative real part, every transformed eigenvalue has magnitude below one for every positive step size.

**How the definition helps.** A negative real part makes \|1 + hs/2\| smaller than \|1 − hs/2\|, so their ratio has magnitude below one (our own). The matrix result uses the fact that a rational function maps each eigenvalue to its value there (our own). Forward Euler instead sends the stable rate −3 to the unstable multiplier −2 at step size 1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Bilinear transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilinear_transform). It says: “The bilinear transform maps the left half of the complex s-plane to the interior of the unit circle in the z-plane.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Minimum-phase systems compose reversibly

**Remember:** Both the system and its inverse must be causal and stable.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93C80 (Frequency-response methods in control theory), 93D25. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A discrete-time linear time-invariant system is minimum-phase if both it and its inverse are causal and stable. Causal systems use only current and past inputs. Stability here means every bounded input gives a bounded output.

**Problem.** A series connection of discrete-time minimum-phase systems is minimum-phase. Its inverse is the series of their inverses in reverse order.

**How the definition helps.** Each inverse already preserves causality and boundedness, so applying them in reverse order gives a causal, stable inverse (our own). The stable transfer function (z − 2)/(z − ½) has a zero at 2 (our own). Its causal inverse has a pole outside the unit circle, so bounded inputs can produce unbounded outputs (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Minimum phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_phase). It says: “a linear, time-invariant system is said to be minimum-phase if the system and its inverse are causal and stable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Independent readings add information

**Remember:** Multiply Gaussian likelihoods by adding their information.

*True by definition.* MSC 93E11 (Filtering in stochastic control theory), 93E10. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a Gaussian state with nonsingular covariance, the precision matrix is the inverse covariance. The information vector is the precision matrix times the mean.

**Problem.** Start with a Gaussian prior and take linear measurements with centered Gaussian errors independent of each other and the state. Assume the prior and error covariances are nonsingular. Each measurement adds its own contribution to the precision matrix and information vector.

**How the definition helps.** The information form stores coefficients of the log density, so multiplying independent likelihoods adds their coefficients (our own). For a measurement y = Hx plus noise with covariance R, the contributions are HᵀR⁻¹H and HᵀR⁻¹y (our own). The work goes into converting the result back to a mean and covariance and propagating it through time (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kalman filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalman_filter). It says: “measurements can be filtered at each time step simply by summing their information matrices and vectors.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Chain-reachable sets are closed

**Remember:** Leave room for a last small jump, and limits stay reachable.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B03 (Attainable sets, reachability), 93B24. arXiv math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a metric state space, y is chain reachable from x if every ε,T &gt; 0 admit a finite chain from x to y. Each link follows an admissible trajectory for at least T, then jumps a distance less than ε.

**Problem.** The set of chain-reachable states from any fixed state is closed.

**How the definition helps.** A nearby chain endpoint can use its last jump to reach the limit point (our own). Choose an endpoint within ε/2 and reach it with jumps smaller than ε/2 and durations at least T (our own). The triangle inequality keeps the modified last jump below ε (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Chain controllability of linear control systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.14595v1). It says: “The chain controllable sets Cᶜ(x) and the chain reachable sets Rᶜ(x) are closed.”

**Sources:**

- [Chain controllability of linear control systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.14595v1)

### Detectability permits a convergent observer

**Remember:** An invisible error is harmless only if it dies out.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93B07 (Observability), 93B53. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Consider a finite-dimensional continuous-time linear system with constant coefficients. It is detectable if every zero-input motion with identically zero output tends to zero.

**Problem.** A linear observer estimates the state from the known input and measured output. An observer whose estimation error decays exponentially for every initial error exists exactly when the system is detectable.

**How the definition helps.** An invisible error receives no correction, so it must decay on its own (our own). For example, x′ = x with zero output hides a growing error (our own). In the observability decomposition, detectability makes the unobservable block stable (our own). Observer pole placement stabilizes the observable block, giving exponential decay in the full triangular system (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Observability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observability). It says: “A system is detectable if all the unobservable states are stable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Flat outputs generate trajectories

**Remember:** Choose a flat output path and differentiate to recover the motion.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B18 (Linearizations), 93C10. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A flat output is a signal computed locally from the state, input, and finitely many input derivatives. One may choose the signal freely within its domain. The signal and finitely many of its derivatives then determine the state and input.

**Problem.** Every sufficiently smooth choice of flat output gives a system trajectory, provided its derivatives stay in the domain of the reconstruction formulas.

**How the definition helps.** The reconstruction formulas produce a solution for every sufficiently smooth local choice of flat output (our own). Ordinary measured outputs need not determine the motion this way (our own). Finding the formulas and their domain replaces integrating the equations for each new trajectory (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Optimal Control for Kinematic Bicycle Model with Continuous-time Safety Guarantees: A Sequential Second-order Cone Programming Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08980v1). It says: “obtained by passing the parameterized flat outputs”

**Sources:**

- [M. Fliess, J. Lévine, P. Martin and P. Rouchon, Flatness and defect of non-linear systems: introductory theory and examples (1995)](https://doi.org/10.1080/00207179508921959)

### Hankel rank gives minimal dimension

**Remember:** Count the independent futures that past inputs can produce.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 93B20 (Minimal systems representations), 93B15. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Start a discrete-time linear system at zero and apply a finite input history. The Hankel map sends that history to all subsequent outputs when every subsequent input is zero. Its rank counts the independent future output sequences the past can produce.

**Problem.** For a finite-dimensional time-invariant linear system, the Hankel rank equals the smallest state dimension that reproduces its input-output behavior.

**How the definition helps.** Every past input affects future outputs through the current state, so the Hankel rank bounds every realization’s dimension from below (our own). The Ho–Kalman realization theorem attains that bound with a state space of independent future responses (our own).

**nLab:** [controllability and observability](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/controllability+and+observability). It says: “a system may be seen as giving rise to a map from an initial algebra to a terminal coalgebra which factors through it”

**Sources:**

- [B. L. Ho and R. E. Kalman, Effective construction of linear state-variable models from input/output functions (1966)](https://doi.org/10.1524/auto.1966.14.112.545)

### Minimality rules out hidden poles

**Remember:** In a minimal model, no internal mode can hide from the transfer function.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93B20 (Minimal systems representations), 93D25. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A realization writes a transfer function, which describes input-to-output behavior, as equations for an internal state. It is minimal if its input can reach every state and its output can distinguish all starting states.

**Problem.** Consider a minimal finite-dimensional continuous-time linear realization with constant coefficients. Bounded inputs give bounded outputs from rest exactly when every zero-input state tends exponentially to zero.

**How the definition helps.** Minimality makes every internal eigenvalue appear as a transfer-function pole, a point where the function is singular (our own). The realization theorem proves this correspondence (our own). Bounded inputs give bounded outputs exactly when every pole has negative real part. Without minimality, ẋ = x and output equal to input give a bounded response from rest while hiding a growing state (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Minimal realization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_realization), [BIBO stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BIBO_stability). It says: “model that is both controllable and observable and has the same input-output behaviour as the transfer function”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Tangent cones reject false tangency

**Remember:** Test the set’s directions, not just its equation.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93B27 (Geometric methods), 93C10. arXiv math.OC, eess.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At a point x of a closed set, take sequences of points y in the set tending to x. Divide each displacement y − x by a positive time step tending to zero. The tangent cone contains exactly the limits of these quotients.

**Problem.** Let a continuous vector field on ℝⁿ have unique global solutions. A closed set is forward invariant exactly when the field lies in its tangent cone at every boundary point.

**How the definition helps.** The cone measures feasible first-order directions even when the equation for the boundary is flat (our own). For the set x³ ≤ 0, the derivative test at zero accepts x′ = 1, but the tangent cone rejects it (our own). The work goes into the tangency theorem, which turns local feasible directions and uniqueness into entire trajectories that stay inside (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Safe Control Synthesis via Input Constrained Control Barrier Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01704v1). It says: “a closed set S ⊆ X is forward invariant for the system, if and only if”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Rich input windows span trajectories

**Remember:** Enough independent windows turn one experiment into many trajectories.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 93B30 (System identification), 93C55. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An input record is persistently exciting of order q if its overlapping windows of q consecutive inputs span all input sequences of length q. Distinct input values alone do not guarantee this property.

**Problem.** Consider a discrete-time linear time-invariant system with n states that can be steered between any two states. Record its states and inputs without noise, using an input persistently exciting of order L + n. The paired state and input windows span exactly the trajectories of length L.

**How the definition helps.** The definition turns a rich experiment into a rank condition on input windows (our own). Linear combinations of matching input and state windows are trajectories by linearity (our own). The work is the fundamental lemma, which uses the extra n steps and controllability to show that no trajectory directions are missing (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Fast and memory-efficient optimization for large-scale data-driven predictive control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.13090v1). It says: “is persistently exciting of order L + n.”

**Sources:**

- [J. C. Willems, P. Rapisarda, I. Markovsky and B. L. M. De Moor, A note on persistency of excitation (2005)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sysconle.2004.09.003)

### Invariant endpoints preserve plan feasibility

**Remember:** Shift the old plan and append one legal move.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B45 (Model predictive control), 93C55. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An invariant terminal set is a set of allowed endpoints with a feasible feedback move that keeps each endpoint in the set. A predictive controller requires its finite plan to end there. A plan with no such endpoint condition may end at a state with no legal next move.

**Problem.** Suppose a deterministic discrete-time model is exact and constraints stay fixed. After applying the first move of a feasible plan, another plan of the same length exists if the terminal set is invariant.

**How the definition helps.** The endpoint condition supplies one legal move to append after shifting the plan (our own). Exact prediction lets the remaining moves start from the actual next state (our own). Finding endpoints that always admit another legal move is the design work (our own). The cited paper proves feasibility for its controller with equilibrium endpoints.

**Wikipedia:** [Model predictive control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_predictive_control). It says: “Only the first step of the control strategy is implemented”

**Paper or page:** [On Model Predictive Funnel Control with Equilibrium Endpoint Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20090v1). It says: “implies its solvability at the next time step”

**Sources:**

- [On Model Predictive Funnel Control with Equilibrium Endpoint Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20090v1)

### Invariant error tubes protect constraints

**Remember:** Check every point in the error band.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B45 (Model predictive control), 93D09. arXiv math.OC, eess.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A tracking policy chooses inputs to keep the actual state near a planned state. An error set is invariant if this policy keeps the next tracking error inside whenever the current error belongs, for every allowed disturbance. Adding all errors in the set to each planned state gives a tube.

**Problem.** If the initial error belongs to the invariant set, every actual state lies in its corresponding tube section. If every section lies inside the allowed state region, every actual state meets the constraints.

**How the definition helps.** Invariance supplies exactly the induction step from one tube section to the next (our own). Checking the planned states alone would miss errors caused by disturbances (our own). The work lies in constructing the tracking policy and its invariant error set (our own).

**Paper or page:** [State-Dependent Dynamic Tube MPC: A Novel Tube MPC Method with a Fuzzy Model of Disturbances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19997v1). It says: “we need to constrain both the nominal state and the potential errors”

**Sources:**

- [State-Dependent Dynamic Tube MPC: A Novel Tube MPC Method with a Fuzzy Model of Disturbances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19997v1)

### Stabilizing Riccati solutions are unique

**Remember:** The right Riccati solution must stabilize the system.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93B52 (Feedback control), 93C05. arXiv math.OC, eess.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Q and R be symmetric, with R positive definite, and set G = BR⁻¹Bᵀ. Consider the symmetric solutions P of AᵀP + PA − PGP + Q = 0. A solution stabilizes the system if every eigenvalue of A − GP has negative real part.

**Problem.** At most one symmetric solution of this equation is stabilizing.

**How the definition helps.** Stability forces the difference D = P − S of two stabilizing solutions to vanish (our own). Write U = A − GP and W = A − GS (our own). Subtracting gives UᵀD + DW = 0, so exp(tUᵀ)D exp(tW) stays constant at D but tends to zero (our own). With A = 0 and B = Q = R = 1, only 1 among the solutions ±1 stabilizes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Algebraic Riccati equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_Riccati_equation). It says: “Though generally this system can have many solutions, it is usually specified that we want to obtain the unique stabilizing solution, if such a solution exists.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Weak equations give closed trajectory sets

**Remember:** Put the derivatives on the test functions before taking the limit.

*True by definition.* MSC 93C05 (Linear systems in control theory). arXiv math.OC, eess.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Consider homogeneous linear differential equations with constant coefficients on a time interval. Define a weak solution by multiplying by smooth test functions supported inside the interval and moving derivatives onto them by integration by parts. A square-integrable signal qualifies if all resulting integrals vanish.

**Problem.** The admissible signals for a linear constant-coefficient differential system form a closed subspace in the square-integrable norm.

**How the definition helps.** Moving the derivatives onto test functions makes each constraint continuous in the square-integrable signal norm (our own). Each constraint defines a closed linear subspace, and their intersection is closed (our own). For smooth signals, integration by parts and testing against every such function recover the original equations (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A continuous-time fundamental lemma and its application in data-driven optimal control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12179v1). It says: “is closed in L²”

**Sources:**

- [A continuous-time fundamental lemma and its application in data-driven optimal control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12179v1)

### Finite-step decrease permits temporary increases

**Remember:** Judge progress at the end of each block.

*True by definition.* MSC 93D15 (Stabilization of systems by feedback), 93B45. arXiv math.OC, eess.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix positive a,b,c, a positive integer m and 0 &lt; q &lt; 1. Require a‖x‖² ≤ V(x) ≤ b‖x‖² at every allowed x. Each such x admits a feasible m-step block with endpoint value at most qV(x) and all intermediate norms at most c‖x‖.

**Problem.** Under these bounds, every allowed initial state has a trajectory that obeys the constraints and converges to zero.

**How the definition helps.** A fixed block replaces the usual one-step decrease, so intermediate increases are allowed (our own). After k blocks the function is at most qᵏ times its initial value (our own). The lower quadratic bound forces the endpoint states toward zero, and the intermediate bound controls all other states (our own). Finding feasible blocks with these bounds remains the design work (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Flexible-step Model Predictive Control based on Generalized Lyapunov Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02780v2). It says: “there exists a feasible control sequence such that limₖ→∞ xᵏ = 0.”

**Sources:**

- [Flexible-step Model Predictive Control based on Generalized Lyapunov Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02780v2)

### Common Lyapunov functions handle switching

**Remember:** Switch the dynamics without switching what measures the state.

*True by definition.* MSC 93D23 (Exponential stability), 93C30. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A mode is one of the linear equations that a switched system can follow. A common quadratic Lyapunov function is a single positive definite quadratic form whose derivative is negative away from zero in every mode. Separate tests may use different forms.

**Problem.** Consider finitely many continuous-time linear modes with continuous state and finitely many switches on each bounded interval. A common quadratic Lyapunov function guarantees constants C, a &gt; 0 with ‖x(t)‖ ≤ C exp(−at)‖x(0)‖ for every switching sequence.

**How the definition helps.** One form decreases throughout every interval and keeps the same value across each switch (our own). Finitely many strict quadratic bounds give one common exponential decay rate (our own). Finding a common form is the hard part (our own). The cited theorem supplies one when all mode matrices are individually stable and simultaneously upper triangular in some complex coordinates.

**Paper or page:** [Feedback rectifiable pairs and stabilization of switched linear systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10591v2). It says: “the origin of the switched system is asymptotically stable for arbitrary switching”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Joint spectral radius detects switching instability

**Remember:** Take the limiting per-step growth of the largest product norm.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93D23 (Exponential stability), 93C30. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take a finite, nonempty set of square matrices of the same size. For each k, find the largest operator norm among all products of k factors from the set. The joint spectral radius is the limit of the kth roots of these maxima.

**Problem.** Uniform exponential decay means every k-step product has norm at most Cqᵏ, with common constants C &gt; 0 and 0 &lt; q &lt; 1. This holds exactly when the joint spectral radius is below one.

**How the definition helps.** The limit captures the worst growth across all products (our own). For a limit below one, choose q strictly between the limit and one, then increase C to cover the finitely many short products (our own). Conversely, taking kth roots in Cqᵏ bounds the limit by q (our own). Two matrices with sole entries 2 in opposite off-diagonal positions square to zero, yet their product has eigenvalue 4 (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Stability Analysis of Switched Linear Systems with Neural Lyapunov Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08190v1), [Stability Analysis of Switched Linear Systems with Neural Lyapunov Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08190v1). It says: “The corresponding switched linear system is stable if and only if ρ(Σ) &lt; 1.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Input-to-state stability makes cascades of stable systems stable

**Remember:** Bounded inputs give bounded states, so stable pieces chain together.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93D25 (Input-output approaches in control theory), 93D20, 93A13. arXiv math.OC, eess.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For every initial state, essentially bounded input and t ≥ 0, require \|x(t)\| ≤ β(\|x₀\|,t) + γ(‖u‖∞). Choose continuous β and γ once, with γ and each β(·,t) strictly increasing from zero. For every r, β(r,t) decreases to zero as t tends to infinity.

**Problem.** A cascade of input-to-state stable systems, where each one drives the next, is input-to-state stable. A cascade of systems that are only globally asymptotically stable with zero input need not be stable.

**How the definition helps.** The input-to-state stability cascade theorem composes the two estimates, preserving decay of the initial-state term (our own). Zero-input stability alone allows x′ = −x + yx², y′ = −y. Both components decay alone, yet some positive starts give finite-time blowup.

**Wikipedia:** [Input-to-state stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Input-to-state_stability). It says: “In contrast to cascades of ISS systems, the cascade interconnection of 0-GAS systems is in general not 0-GAS.”

**Sources:**

- [E. D. Sontag, Smooth stabilization implies coprime factorization, IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control 34 (1989) 435–443](https://doi.org/10.1109/9.28018)

### Scattering passivity survives feedback

**Remember:** An internal output costs one side exactly what it supplies the other.

*True by definition.* MSC 93D25 (Input-output approaches in control theory), 93B52. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A discrete-time system is scattering passive if it has a nonnegative stored energy with the following bound. At each step its increase is at most the squared input norm minus the squared output norm.

**Problem.** Connect two such systems by taking each internal output as the other system’s internal input. Assume the connection defines a system for the allowed external inputs. The resulting system is scattering passive.

**How the definition helps.** Using squared input and output norms gives each internal signal opposite signs in the two energy bounds (our own). Adding those bounds cancels the internal terms and gives the required bound for the sum of the stored energies (our own). Finding the component energies and solving the feedback equations are separate tasks (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A geometric framework for discrete time port-Hamiltonian systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01351v2). It says: “is scattering passive.”

**Sources:**

- [A geometric framework for discrete time port-Hamiltonian systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01351v2)

### Strictly small loop gain ensures stability

**Remember:** Each trip around the loop must shrink the signal.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93D25 (Input-output approaches in control theory), 93B52. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** From rest, the gain bounds the output norm by a constant times the input norm on every finite time interval. Use the least such constant, with compatible signal norms at connected inputs and outputs.

**Problem.** Suppose two systems use only present and past inputs, and their feedback equations have a unique causal solution for every external input. If their gains multiply to less than one, the feedback system has finite gain.

**How the definition helps.** The strict bound leaves a positive coefficient when one substitutes the two signal bounds into each other (our own). Dividing by that coefficient bounds the response in terms of the external input (our own). At equality, positive feedback through a unit delay and an identity system accumulates a constant input without bound in the maximum norm (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Small-gain theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small-gain_theorem). It says: “the closed loop system is input-output stable if ‖S₁‖ · ‖S₂‖ &lt; 1 and both S₁ and S₂ are stable by themselves.”

**Sources:**

- [G. Zames, On the input-output stability of time-varying nonlinear feedback systems, Part one (1966)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TAC.1966.1098316)

### Maximum extraction gives minimum storage

**Remember:** Every storage account must cover the largest possible withdrawal.

*True by definition.* MSC 93D30 (Lyapunov and storage functions), 93D25. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A storage function assigns nonnegative energy to each time and state. Its increase along any trajectory cannot exceed the net energy supplied. Available storage is the supremum of net energy extractable from that time and state, including zero for an immediate stop.

**Problem.** For the passive linear systems with time-dependent coefficients in the paper, available storage is the smallest storage function at every time and state.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the supremum turns every storage bound on a single withdrawal into a bound on available storage (our own). To prove the storage inequality itself, append a nearly optimal withdrawal to any initial trajectory segment (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Dissipative energy functionals of passive linear time-varying systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16347v1). It says: “and is minimal among all storage functions”

**Sources:**

- [Dissipative energy functionals of passive linear time-varying systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16347v1)

### Innovations isolate measurement corrections

**Remember:** Correct the prediction with only the unexpected part of each reading.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 93E11 (Filtering in stochastic control theory). arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Suppose Y starts at zero and its observation drift is H(t)X(t) + h(t). Let X̂(t) denote the conditional mean given observations through t. The innovation is V(t) = Y(t) − ∫₀ᵗ(H(s)X̂(s) + h(s)) ds.

**Problem.** Consider a continuous linear system with known initial state, deterministic coefficients, and additive Brownian noise with nonsingular observation noise covariance. The state estimate given the observations evolves by the predicted dynamics plus a gain times the innovation increment.

**How the definition helps.** Subtracting the predicted drift puts all measurement corrections into one term (our own). The filtering theorem determines the gain and proves that the update gives the conditional mean (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Optimal Control with Partial Observation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13632v1). It says: “V(t) ≜ Y(t) − ∫₀ᵗ \[H(s)X̂(s) + h(s)\] ds”

**Sources:**

- [Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Optimal Control with Partial Observation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13632v1)

### Occupation measures satisfy flow balance

**Remember:** Every visit either starts the run or comes from a previous visit.

*True by definition.* MSC 93E20 (Optimal stochastic control). arXiv math.OC, cs.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Markov decision process chooses its next state at random using the current state and action. Stop when it reaches a target. Its occupation measure counts expected visits to sets of state and action pairs before stopping.

**Problem.** Suppose every rule has finite expected stopping time from the initial distribution. For any set of nonterminal states, expected visits equal the probability of starting there plus expected later arrivals.

**How the definition helps.** Counting visits instead of recording their order splits the count into the initial visit and all later arrivals (our own). Weight each transition probability into the set by the occupation measure to count later arrivals (our own). Proving that a proposed measure comes from a rule requires further conditions (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Absorbing Markov Decision Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07059v2). It says: “satisfies the characteristic equations.”

**Sources:**

- [Absorbing Markov Decision Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07059v2)

### Transient Gramians stay finite

**Remember:** Remove the steady part before measuring the transient.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93B11 (System structure simplification), 93C05. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For x′ = Ax + Bu, suppose exp(tA) tends exponentially to J. The modified controllability Gramian is P = ∫₀∞ F(t)F(t)ᵀ dt, where F(t) = (exp(tA) − J)B.

**Problem.** The modified Gramian P is finite. It is the unique symmetric solution of AP + PAᵀ + (B − JB)(B − JB)ᵀ = 0 with JPJᵀ = 0.

**How the definition helps.** Subtracting JB gives exponential decay, while the ordinary integrand for x′ = u stays constant (our own). Integrating the derivative of FFᵀ gives the equation, since F′ = AF and F tends to zero (our own). JF = 0 gives JPJᵀ = 0 (our own). For two solutions with difference D, exp(tA)D exp(tAᵀ) stays constant at D and tends to JDJᵀ = 0 (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Gramian-Based Model Reduction of Directed Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.01285v2). It says: “are the unique symmetric solutions of the following sets of linear matrix equations”

**Sources:**

- [Gramian-Based Model Reduction of Directed Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.01285v2)

### Strong chain control sets are preserved by topological conjugacy

**Remember:** Let the allowed jump size depend on where the jump occurs.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 93B24 (Topological methods), 93C10. arXiv math.OC, math.DS. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Inside a strong chain control set, every point lies on a full controlled trajectory contained in the set. Every ordered pair admits a finite chain for every minimum duration T &gt; 0 and every positive continuous tolerance ε. Each segment lasts at least T and ends at z within distance less than ε(z) of the next point. Take a maximal set with these properties.

**Problem.** Suppose a homeomorphism H carries controlled trajectories of one system onto those of another while preserving time. Then E is a strong chain control set exactly when H(E) is one.

**How the definition helps.** A continuous jump allowance can absorb the varying distortion of a homeomorphism (our own). For each positive continuous target tolerance ε, the continuous minorant lemma gives a positive continuous source tolerance δ (our own). A jump from x shorter than δ(x) then maps to one shorter than ε(H(x)) (our own). Applying this in both directions preserves chain connectivity, full trajectories and maximality (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Strong chain control sets and affine control systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.18765v1), [Strong chain control sets and affine control systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.18765v1). It says: “Then E⋆ is a strong chain control set in M if and only if H(E⋆) is a strong chain control set in N.”
